name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Where exactly is Canaan, Conn.? There are at least two answers
description: North Canaan and Canaan, towns stacked just below the Massachusetts border, are used to being mixed up. But the names create real problems.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

A man walks into Canaan’s town hall to meet with his probation officer — but the probation officer isn’t there.
He didn’t get the time or date wrong, he got the actual town wrong. The man was supposed to meet his probation officer in North Canaan’s town hall, which is, fittingly, just a few miles north.
Johanna Mann, Canaan’s town clerk, wasn’t surprised by the mix-up. Official records meant for North Canaan come across her desk all the time.
“I think at this point, a [name change] would solve the confusion,” Mann said. “But I understand the history.” 

Town of Canaan Selectman Judy Jacobs laughs as she answers a question at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

North Canaan and Canaan, two Connecticut towns stacked just below the Massachusetts border, are used to being mixed up. That’s because Canaan is locally known as “Falls Village,” and North Canaan, in classic nickname style, prefers a simple “Canaan.” These unofficially official names are used everywhere short of some maps — even some state road signage refers to the towns by their nicknames.
While it may seem trivial, these town names create real problems. Land records, birth records, death records — even the amount of revenue sent to towns from the state tax on nips, the small bottles of alcohol — are confused. And snail-mail is a whole other issue.
“They have Canaan on their post office, and here we’ve got Falls Village on the post office,” Judy Jacobs, a selectman for Canaan and president of the historical society for the two towns, said. “But the government still recognizes us as town of Canaan and them as town of North Canaan. So it’s really, really confusing.”

Town of Canaan Selectman Judy Jacobs Looks at a map of the town of Canaan from 1853 at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The source of the confusion
For more than 100 years, the two towns were one united Canaan. But in 1858, they broke up.
“Basically, it stemmed from the convenience of getting to church,” Jacobs said. “People had to travel quite a distance to go to church in both directions, so they ended up dividing.”
The original town of Canaan was settled in 1738. But talks of division, at least informally, began shortly after. There was a religious division — involving two Ecclesiastical Societies — in 1769. Initial proposals to break the sprawling 52.7-square-mile town into two were recorded in 1810.
It took the local government decades to finalize the divide, but when it finally did, one town received the name North Canaan and the other Canaan.
These names stuck for a while, Jacobs said. The church was moved south, to Canaan, and North Canaan residents built their own churches. And nobody had to take a five-mile trek to get to their church.
But the Housatonic Railroad created a stop in Canaan called Falls Village, after the Great Falls located in the town. And from then on, the two towns would be forever confused.
“So, it became Falls Village and North Canaan, and then North Canaan just shortened themselves to Canaan,” Jacobs said. “It got really confusing.”
In 1968, historian Nellie Rodgers attempted to document the history of the split, which has early roots in the history of the state. But even 58 years ago, Rodgers flagged the name debacle in her work.
“Except for the confusion with the names, things seem to be satisfactory,” Rodgers wrote in a July 1968 work titled “A History of The Division of The Town of Canaan.”
“The names, North Canaan and Canaan, confusing even to the State of Connecticut, may some day be resolved. What action will ensue, I cannot predict,” Rodgers continued. “But if change does occur, to eliminate the confusion now taking place, then another chapter will have to be added to the present town division history.”
But Rodgers never added another chapter. 

A sign saying “Entering Falls Village” at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Data collection, death certificates and signs
On the same day of the probation officer mix-up, Mann, attending to her official town clerk duties in Canaan — er, Falls Village — opened a land record. But it was for land located in North Canaan.
These very common mix-ups actually result in increased postage fees for Canaan, Mann said. Birth certificates, death certificates, marriage certificates and firearms paperwork for North Canaan come across her desk all the time.
Every time she receives a record meant for their neighboring town, Mann either sends these records back to the original sender, sends them to the correct town or requests help in correcting digital data.
“If you’re part of anything in the town government, you realize,” Jacobs said. “If you’re a business owner, you realize. If you get your mail messed up, you figure it out. And any newcomer using GPS … they get very confused.”
In order to get ahead of at least some of this confusion, Mann has changed her name tag three times. The first one just listed her town as Canaan, CT. The other two include some variation of the name Falls Village.

Johanna Mann is the Canaan town clerk. She remade her name tag three times, all with different variations of the town’s names.  Credit: Sasha Allen / CT Mirror

People who did not grow up in one of the two towns tend to have the most trouble, Jacobs said. 
“When you go to school here, it’s kind of pounded into your brain that you’re the town of Canaan, Falls Village,” Jacobs said. “When you’ve grown up here, you quickly figure it out. But it’s hard for newcomers. They’re just like, ‘What? Where am I?'”
It’s not just the town names — within North Canaan is a small village called Canaan. Among the two towns, there are numerous unofficial (and sometimes mostly forgotten) villages: Canaan Valley, East Canaan, South Canaan, Canaan and Falls Village are among the most confusing. And then there’s the village of Sodom, in North Canaan.
To make matters worse, the Canaan and North Canaan share some road names. “Main Street” and “Railroad Street” are fitting for both, but the two towns also have a “Prospect Street.”
Some of the state road signage, which seemingly welcomes folks into multiple towns at once, doesn’t help.
So, it’s no wonder newcomers, and their GPS systems, are easily confused.
Real-world implications
This confusion isn’t limited to just Connecticut newcomers. These nicknames trick state officials, too.
A recent mix-up resulted in some of North Canaan’s money being sent to Canaan from the nip tax. This tax, which charged an extra 5 cents on every nip sold in a liquor store, was supposed to be returned to the municipality where the product was purchased.
Canaan, which is home to just one liquor store, was selling an average of 136,612 nips per year and getting nearly $10,000 in annual revenue, according to state data.
But the town’s lone liquor store — Falls Village Package Store — was definitely not selling more than 136,000 nips each year. 
Instead, two other liquor stores, Stateline Wine and Spirits and Canaan Liquors, were incorrectly listed as Canaan establishments by the Wine and Spirits Wholesalers of Connecticut. These two stores are actually in the town of North Canaan but in the village of Canaan. Since they’re in Canaan village, the address of the two stores shows up on Google maps as Canaan, CT.
The state corrected its error and now is distributing the revenue correctly. But this is just one of many possible issues caused by the names.
“I understand that it causes problems,” Michelle Hansen, the Canaan town treasurer said. “Believe me, it does. Our fire department gets dispatched to calls that are actually in North Canaan, not on Main Street.”
Hansen is also the emergency management director for Canaan. She said that, especially when a dispatcher is unfamiliar with the two towns, emergency services can be sent to the wrong location.
But her department has found ways to combat the issue. 
“I have a list that I have at home at work to look it up and see if the address is really ours,” Hanson said. “We’ve found a way to combat it pretty quickly and pretty easily so it doesn’t cause a delay in services.”
Even Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program data is likely incorrect. In 2022, the state recorded that 211 Canaan residents, or 19.5% of the population, were enrolled in the program. But 37 North Canaan residents, or 1.18% of its population, were recorded as enrolled in the program.
North Canaan has nearly three times Canaan’s population and has a lower median household income than its southern neighbor — making it unlikely that Canaan has nearly six times more SNAP recipients.
A 2024 Canaan housing profile from the Partnership for Strong Communities recorded that there were 583 federally assisted housing units in Canaan. But Hansen said the town only has three apartment buildings. And with just over 1,000 residents living in the town, some Canaan residents believe the number is likely inflated.
Vaccination numbers during COVID were also inflated — with more than 1,300 Canaan residents recorded as vaccinated as of February 2023 in a town of just over 1,000 residents.
Even with these issues, the proposal to change the name of one or both of the towns is still up for debate.

Town of Canaan Selectman Judy Jacobs looks over items from World War I on display at the Falls Village-Canaan Historical Society on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

To change or not to change
Hansen believes renaming Canaan as Falls Village could be even worse.
“I actually think changing it at this point would cause just as much of a nightmare as what it is,” Hanson said. “People know us as the town of Canaan, Falls Village, and if we were just to go to Falls Village, people are still going to call us the town of Canaan.”
Hansen also said the change would be a huge administrative lift. The town would have to change the names on letterheads, checks and stamps.
As for the emergency response side of things, changing the name could create an even bigger headache. 
“As emergency management director, all of my emergency plans and everything are for the town of Canaan,” Hansen said. “I can’t imagine changing all that to Falls Village.”
Jacobs said getting the name changed is difficult. Canaan would have to go through the state legislature to approve a name change, and all divisions of state and local government would have to make the administrative changes.
North Canaan has also discussed a name change. When the town of North Canaan put up signs that read “Welcome to Canaan,” Jacobs said they were encouraged to seek an official name change. Officially, though, the town is still named North Canaan.
As for the official town of Canaan — unofficial town of Falls Village — Hansen’s view is popular.
“A lot of people say, ‘Well, this is how we are historically. We are the town of Canaan,'” Jacobs said. 
But Jacobs herself takes a slightly different stance. 
“And I am a diehard historian for the town,” Jacobs said, “but I think we should be called Falls Village. If we could find someone to take this on, this challenge … I think most of the residents would agree with that.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The AI data center push has roiled Kansas politics. It may also define the race for governor.
description: Cindy Holscher has something she would like you to know. She changed her mind on data centers because she listens. “The subject was coming up over and over again,” she said of the 80 or so town halls she held in the last 12 months across Kansas. “It seemed to me at the time that […]
text:
Cindy Holscher, the Deomcratic nominee for Kansas governor, listens to teachers during a campaign stop on Sept. 27 in Emporia. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Cindy Holscher has something she would like you to know.
She changed her mind on data centers because she listens.
“The subject was coming up over and over again,” she said of the 80 or so town halls she held in the last 12 months across Kansas. “It seemed to me at the time that a lot of candidates were really wary of this subject and hadn’t figured out this was something people cared about.”
When Holscher, a state senator from Overland Park, won the primary to become the Democratic nominee for governor two months ago, it was partly fueled by her call for a state moratorium on new data center construction. Since then, public concern over data centers and alarm about artificial intelligence have accelerated, turning a wild card in the primary into what may be a defining issue for the governor’s race in Kansas and midterms across the country.
The data center divide is just one disagreement among many between Holscher and her opponent, Senate President Ty Masterson, an Andover Republican. But in a political climate where party lines have been scrambled because of populist resistance to big tech, it may prove a bigger factor than anyone would have guessed just a few months ago.
Masterson’s campaign acknowledged, but did not otherwise respond, to an emailed request from me for an in-person interview about data centers.
“You know, there’s a lot of great possibilities with A.I.,” Holscher told me during a Sept. 27 campaign stop at Emporia, “but when I talk to people like the teachers who were just here, it’s about the anxiety in terms of what it might mean for the future, what it might be in terms of job loss. And that’s something that’s not talked about much, because the focus has been on energy and water usage.”
Holscher had just spoken to a group of local educators about their concerns. She did more listening than talking, sometimes jotting notes, at other times offering a few words to acknowledge what the teachers were saying. Listening is not an easy skill, but Holscher looked at ease doing it.
She defeated Democratic rival Ethan Corson by 10 points in the August primary. Corson, a Johnson County attorney and political moderate, attempted to frame the contest in a PBS Kansas gubernatorial primary debate as a choice between someone who could hold the governorship for the Democrats in a deep red state and somebody who could not.
Corson was endorsed by outgoing governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat at the end of her second term. Kelly was propelled to office by voter distaste for the legacy of the failed economic tax-cutting “experiment” of former governor Sam Brownback, but she was often stymied during her tenure from expanding Medicaid and other issues by the Republican supermajorities in the Kansas Legislature. Kelly, a promoter of bipartisanship and big-ticket economic development, embraced some big-ticket initiatives, including coaxing the Kansas City Chiefs across the state line with a tax incentive package that included a billion dollars in public funding.
Holscher opposed the final deal to bring the Chiefs to Kansas.
It wasn’t the only time she and Kelly were at odds.
Holscher revealed some internecine fighting when she vented on social media that she and two other Democrats were told by the Kelly administration to stand aside for another candidate, a claim the governor’s chief of staff told the Kansas Reflector was a mischaracterization. Holscher said that such insider manipulation has frustrated many voters about Kansas Democrats.
After her primary win, the New York Times described Holscher as an “outspoken populist” who took on data centers and the political status quo. Some of the criticism leveled at Holscher by fellow Democrats during the primary campaign, that she was perhaps too far left, has been taken up and amplified by Masterson.
During the gubernatorial debate last month at the Kansas State Fair at Hutchinson, Masterson called her a socialist and the “most radical liberal progressive that’s ever been on a ticket.” Holscher responded by reminding Masterson to his support of the Brownback experiment, which defunded Kansas schools “to the crisis point.”
Masterson also challenged Holscher’s change of mind on data centers.
“My position has never changed,” Masterson said about data centers during the televised debate. “It’s about guardrails first.”
Masterson said guardrails were already in place thanks to S.B. 98, enacted in 2025. It shields consumers from electricity rate increases, he said, and protects the water and the land from pollution. He also urged decisions on data centers to be made at the local level.
“Let the locals decide,” he said. “There are places where they don’t make sense and places where they do make sense.” Why wouldn’t a city want significant property tax relief through data centers, he asked.
Holscher was an example of a “perfect politician” who flip-flips on an issue, he said, because she originally voted in favor of the measure encouraging data centers and now opposes them.
Masterson bowed out of two additional televised debates with Holscher, saying the public had already seen them together in multiple platforms. Both parties claimed victory in the state fair debate. So far, Masterson’s campaign has been largely conventional for a Kansas Republican, driven chiefly by a promise to stop “runaway” property taxes.
Masterson, who has the endorsement of Donald Trump, might have a difficult time changing his mind on data centers even if he wanted to. Allowing any daylight between himself and Trump, who has doubled down on data centers, could be taken by the president as a sign of disloyalty. And Trump’s enthusiastic messaging on data centers and artificial intelligence offers little room for nuance.
Communities that reject data centers, Trump said recently, will end up “backwards and poor.” But a Gallup poll from earlier this year indicates that about 70% of Americans don’t want AI data centers in their areas. More recent polling says 58% of voters believe new data center construction will have a negative effect on the country.
Trump has relied on tech oligarchs for money, influence, and the 2025 chainsaw attack on the federal government. A cheerleader for AI (which he would like to rebrand as “super intelligence”), Trump recently announced an “accord” in which tech giants agreed to police themselves on AI safety and development. But self-policing hasn’t worked for the Catholic Church, Wall Street, or the police. It didn’t work with nuclear weapons. We shouldn’t expect it to work for the players in the new AI smarts race, especially when humanity already seems to be lurching toward a silicon-spawned human extinction event.
That catastrophe seemed closer to hand Oct. 1 when the Trump Pentagon named Elon Musk, the wealthiest person in the world, the wielder of the DOGE chainsaw and the owner of xAI, to co-lead a 120-day project on the future of technology in warfare. This move is especially alarming, considering the U.S. and Russia recently colluded to block progress on a United Nations draft of an AI weapons pact, according to the Washington Post. Language that would have required human approval before AI pulled the trigger on enemies it had targeted were removed.
Presumably Masterson does not want to unleash autonomous killer bots on humanity, but he’s not urging caution, either. Aligning oneself with the Trump administration’s stance on AI leaves little room for a thoughtful consideration of the ethical and humanitarian concerns. As for Masterson’s call for allowing locals to decide whether to allow data centers in their communities? That sounds reasonable until you consider that some local governments in Kansas are vigorously pursuing data center projects, public opinion be damned.
In my town of Emporia, city officials have so far advanced a proposed data center at every step since it was announced June 2, despite fierce organized resistance. There were sign-waving protests, testimony at public hearings that ran about 8-1 against the project, and a flurry of petition drives. Two of those petitions were successful and resulted in Nov. 3 ballot measures that would, if they survive legal challenges, ban high-impact data centers and battery energy storage systems for 10 years. Other petitions seek a grand jury investigation and changing the city’s form of government.
Questions about data centers are also on the ballot in other Kansas communities, including Ottawa and El Dorado. Citizen-led groups elsewhere, including De Soto and Edgerton, are also seeking to place the issue before voters.
Resistance to data centers is a new phenomenon, and a year ago it wasn’t on the radar of pollsters and politicians in Kansas. A Democratic lawmaker from central Kansas told me in an informal conversation recently that when he voted for S.B. 98, he didn’t hear a peep of opposition from anybody.
Most state legislators voted for the measure, enacted in 2025, which provides a 20-year state and local tax exemption for data centers that meet certain criteria, including an investment of $250 million, a 10-year electrical utility partnership, and a promise to create 20 full-time jobs within two years of commencing operations.
During the final vote in the Kansas Senate on April 11, 2025, only one senator – Tory Marie Blew, a Barton County Republican – voted against it. In the Kansas House, the month before, 15 Democrats and two Republicans voted “nay.”
In the Fall 2025 “Kansas Speaks” statewide opinion survey, released a year ago this month, questions about artificial intelligence were limited to how people used the technology in their daily life and in their work. There were no questions about how state residents regarded the technology or whether they would support construction of a data center nearby.
In fact, the term “data center” does not appear in the survey.
Thirty-seven percent of respondents in the 2025 survey said they did not use AI at all. Another 18% were unsure if they did, and the remainder — about half of all respondents — said they used generative or non-generative AI in their daily lives.
The “Kansas Speaks” survey for Fall 2026 has not yet been released.
Holscher told me the gubernatorial race was a choice between a candidate who represented the people and one propped up by money from big tech companies. AI super PACs had spent more than $800,000 in support of  Masterson’s campaign, she said. When she mentioned the money she seemed a bit less at ease, perhaps because she’s being badly outspent.
She’s also trailing in the polls, according to the New York Times.
But the difference is single digits.
As Bob Beatty, a political science professor puts it, Holscher is an underdog who must do what no Democrat in 144 years of state history has done: replace a fellow Democrat as governor who is leaving office. Holscher, he said, is Rocky Balboa to Masterson’s Apollo Creed. As Beatty reminds us, Rocky didn’t win in the first movie.
Since 2016, I haven’t put much faith in polls, as we’ve been badly misled too many times. We’re also still a month out from the election, which is almost forever in political time.
Holscher told me the affordability crisis is still foremost among the issues for her campaign, but that the more she learns about artificial intelligence and data centers, the more concerned she becomes. She wasn’t optimistic about meaningful national regulation on AI, she said, considering the current administration.
She would reconsider her vote on S.B. 98 if she could.
“At the time, it was presented as a picture of all the potential economic development it would bring, what it would do for our communities,” she said. “But things look different, 15 or 16 months later, with new information and hearing from people across the state.”
Those who are pushing back against data centers and demanding more transparency from local governments are going the right thing, Holscher said, because the system is meant to turn on citizen engagement. She said she didn’t set a time limit for her moratorium, because she did not yet know how long would be enough to get some clarity. It might take six months, she said.
It might take longer.
The important thing, she said, was for the state to take the lead in establishing better safeguards for new data center construction so that communities could follow.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Your next car will be a luxury
description: The average price of a new car is now $50,089. That puts in it CT's 7.75% luxury tax category.
text:
It’s been a busy week on the transportation beat. Not much of it good:
Cheaper cars? The U.S. Dept of Transportation is rolling back Biden-era plans to require automakers to increase their fleet’s mileage performance. Rather than the goal of 50.4 mpg, the new rules will settle for 34.9 mpg by 2031. The White House claims this may save you $1,300 on the cost of a new car.



But savings on the sticker price won’t be free. Because the new cars won’t get the targeted mileage improvements, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates you’ll spend $1,624 more for gas over the life of your vehicle.
By the way, according to the industry ‘bible,’ Kelley Blue Book, the average new vehicle in the U.S. now costs $50,089, up almost 2% in one year.
That will puts new vehicle buyers in Connecticut into a higher tax bracket: 7.75% sales tax for “luxury cars” vs the usual 6.35%, meaning the average new set of wheels in Connecticut will now, legally, be a luxury.
Another CT highway worker death: For the second time in two years a Connecticut Department of Transportation highway worker has been killed doing his job. Sixty-year-old Elvin Hernandez was doing road maintenance on I-95 when he was hit by a car that was driving on the grass on the right shoulder near exit 20.

Elvin Hernandez, the CDOT highway worker killed by an out-of-control motorist. Credit: CTDOT

The driver of that car, Edward Myers, also age 60, was arrested and admitted to officers he’d just used heroin. Myers was convicted of driving under the influence this past April and has been on probation. He’s now being held on $2 million bond, charged with manslaughter.
Working alongside our highways with cars zooming by at high speed is a challenging and dangerous job. Recent efforts at placing speed cameras in work zones have seen some success. A pilot test for eight months in 2023 saw 24,900 warning notices issued to drivers, but only 750 violations. During testing this spring cameras clocked 8.4 million cars passing the work zones, 1.36 million of them exceeding the speed limit. More than 150 drivers were clocked in excess of 100 mph.
Tariffs and new rail cars: Metro-North parent MTA (the Metropolitan Transportation Authority) plans to spend $23 billion on new rail cars, subway cars and buses. But the price tag is being inflated by $1 billion due to new tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on imported components. That’s enough money to buy 150 Long Island Railroad train cars, almost 1,000 buses or more than 250 subway cars.
The White House tariffs on imported railroad gear “will not result in a [domestic U.S.] railcar manufacturing boom; it will only raise costs for transit agencies at a time when other construction costs are skyrocketing” the MTA board was told this week.
That’s code for eventually “higher fares.”
Brightline: As I predicted weeks ago, this modern, stylish, for-profit passenger railroad in Florida has filed for bankruptcy.
Ridership and fares are not growing as fast as hoped… revenue is less than half of what was predicted… so the railroad has had to restructure $2.5 billion in debt.
So much for the free market saving passenger rail, fueled by junk bonds.
Meanwhile, the railroad’s trains between Miami and Orlando will keep running. However, Brightline’s plan for a high-speed line from Southern California to Las Vegas is already behind schedule and still hunting for money.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC legislative leaders call for special session on high gas, diesel prices
description: North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Caldwell) and Senate Leader Phil Berger (R-Guilford) announced Saturday they’ve agreed to call the legislature into a special session to provide relief from high gas and diesel prices.  The leaders did not announce a date for the special session or details on what measures they plan to consider. With […]
text:
Gas prices in late September were $4.19 a gallon for regular unleaded and over $6 a gallon for diesel fuel in Raleigh, North Carolina. A sticker affixed to the gas pump blames President Donald Trump for the high prices.  (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Caldwell) and Senate Leader Phil Berger (R-Guilford) announced Saturday they’ve agreed to call the legislature into a special session to provide relief from high gas and diesel prices. 
The leaders did not announce a date for the special session or details on what measures they plan to consider. With only a month left until Nov. 3, it’s unclear whether they can or will call Republican lawmakers off the campaign trail before what’s expected to be a tough election for the GOP.
“Rising fuel costs are squeezing North Carolina families’ pocketbooks and creating challenges for farmers across the state,” Hall said in a social media post announcing the special session. “North Carolinians can’t afford to wait.”
Berger shared a similar message on social media, calling for “real relief” for families. 
The announcement comes three days after Gov. Josh Stein directed the state Department of Revenue to suspend penalties through the end of 2026 to allow farmers to use red-dyed diesel fuel on highways. 
Red-dyed diesel is exempt from state and federal fuel taxes and is intended for off-road agricultural equipment. Using it in vehicles that drive on public roads is generally illegal. 
Stein said North Carolina farmers have been strained by crop losses, drought and higher diesel costs. 
“I urge the federal government to join me in providing the same relief to North Carolina farmers and families,” he said. 
North Carolina’s gas tax is currently 41 cents per gallon. Lawmakers could consider suspending part or all of the tax during the special session, though leaders have not yet said what relief they propose. Other states have enacted similar measures. 
The move comes as poll numbers in N.C. show declining approval numbers for President Donald Trump and the generic Republican ballot. Friday, the Senate Leadership Fund decided to pull ad buys for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley. 
Republican super PAC pauses spending in North Carolina’s key US Senate race

House Democratic Leader Robert Reives (D-Chatham) criticized the announcement. He said Republicans are attempting to distract voters from their record on affordability ahead of the midterm election. 
“After sixteen years with nearly complete control of the state, Legislative Republicans have done nothing to make life more affordable for North Carolinians,” he said. “ In fact, they have made life harder and much more expensive for almost everyone.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Crimson Tide makes short work of previously unbeaten Bulldogs and a hobbled Kamario Taylor
description: Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell (12) runs for a touchdown against Mississippi State during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Starkville, Miss., Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
STARKVILLE — Kamario Taylor has had far better days this season and even last year as a freshman. He will have many much better days in the future. As has been written in this column several times, the gifted quarterback will win many, many big games at Mississippi State.
Rick Cleveland
But this sunny, humid Saturday at Scott Field was a reminder of two important facts:

One, for all his remarkable ability and his accomplishments to date, Taylor is 19 years young and will not turn 20 until February. Saturday was only his sixth college start. As good as he is, he’s far from as good as he will become. He made mistakes that cost State dearly.
Two, Alabama is still Alabama, which is elite. And we could add a third important factor: Crimson Tide quarterback Keelon Russell, like Taylor only a sophomore, seems a lock to be the next in line of so many splendid Crimson Tide quarterbacks (think Starr, Namath, McCarron, Hurts, Tagovailoa, Young and so many more). 

Russell, strong-armed and so uncommonly quick, passed for three touchdowns and ran for another as No. 7 Alabama raced past No. 16 Mississippi State 56-23 to remain undefeated and unceremoniously knock the Bulldogs from the ranks of unbeaten. 
Mississippi State head coach Jeff Lebby looks at the sidelines during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Starkville, Miss., Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/James Pugh
If you saw Russell play in in Alabama’s first two games and then saw him again against State, you can be excused for thinking you were watching two different quarterbacks. In a month’s time, the Duncanville, Texas, native has become much more efficient, much more confident and sure of himself, much quicker with his decisions. Saturday, he completed 16 of 22 throws for 275 yards and used his quickness and speed to escape State defenders, buy himself some time, and make accurate throws down the field. 
Some of Russell’s throws, particularly a couple of perfect back-shoulder tosses, almost didn’t seem fair. State defensive backs seemed in perfect position, running step for step with the receiver, and then the receiver stopped, turned around and snagged a perfectly timed pass. 
State defensive back Isaac Smith, one of the Bulldogs’ veteran leaders, offered no excuses. “Russell is a really good player, but we shot ourselves in the foot,” Smith said. “That’s on us, the players. It’s not on the coaches, not on the crowd. I apologize to our fans. I’ll take the blame. I’m the leader on the back end, and we just didn’t do our job.”
There were excuses that could have been made. Taylor came into the game hobbled with a lower leg injury, didn’t play the fourth quarter and limped off the field with his foot in a protective boot. Said State coach Jeff Lebby, “Kamario wasn’t able to do anything with his legs.” As anyone who has watched Taylor play knows, his long legs – and his foot speed – are so much of what make him who he is. 
Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor (1) looks downfield against Alabama during the second half of an NCAA college football game in Starkville, Miss., Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/James Pugh
Taylor did manage to throw for 258 yards and three touchdowns, but he suffered two interceptions, one a pick-6, and he lost a fumble. All three mistakes led to Alabama touchdowns.
The fumble actually led to Alabama’s first score when Taylor seemed to pump fake a pass, but the ball tumbled out of his hands. Bama recovered. Officials reviewed the play and the call on the field, a fumble, stood. Alabama quickly scored. 
Some day, perhaps, someone will explain that rule to me in a way I can understand it. Taylor’s arm was moving forward, the ball went forward and I’ve seen that ruled an incomplete pass as often as not. Maybe you have to be a mind reader to officiate that call. If so, clearly some refs read minds differently than others.
On State’s next possession, Taylor simply threw a bad pass, nowhere near the intended receiver, which Alabama cornerback Dijon Lee snatched out of the air and returned 30 yards for a second touchdown.
That was two touchdowns in 71 seconds, no way to start a game against anybody, much less against Alabama.
Lebby praised Taylor for his courage and grit, but at the same time also stated the obvious, that Taylor has to be more careful with the ball. 
State’s other valid excuse was that the Dogs’ best back by far, Fluff Bothwell, was banged up coming into the game and carried only one time for 1 yard before retiring to the sidelines. His absence was glaring.
But then, when Alabama loses a great back, the Tide just plugs in another, and they all run behind mammoth, yet mobile, offensive linemen who look as if they just walked off an NFL bus. Bama won the line of scrimmage on both sides as it usually does in this lopsided series which the Bulldogs have won only 17 of 109 meetings. 
At times, this writer felt as if I was watching a rerun of a bad movie I’ve seen maybe 25 or 30 times before. Indeed, Alabama has now won 17 straight games over State by an average of 26 points per game. 
Maybe a healthy Kamario Taylor is the quarterback who can finally snap that streak. State will have to improve greatly across both lines and play much more efficiently, Taylor included, to do so. Until then, the Tide will keep on rolling.

text:
After the failed execution of Christa Pike, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will resign, Gov. Bill Lee announced. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will step down, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday — three days after a botched execution attempt left Christa Pike on a ventilator in critical condition.
Strada offered his resignation, and the governor accepted, the news release said. Strada will step down from his role this month, it said. 
Pike, sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, had exhausted all appeals before her scheduled execution Wednesday. 
Tennessee governor orders third-party review, pauses all executions for the rest of the year

But the execution was halted after two failed rounds of a lethal injection protocol over a two-hour period. Media witnesses were then asked to leave the building. They reported Pike was making audible noises as they exited. Pike remains in critical condition at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. 
Pike’s was the second botched execution in Tennessee under his leadership. In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was halted after officials said they were unable to find a vein after trying for an hour and a half. As chief of the correction department, Strada oversees state executions.
In announcing his resignation, Lee said Strada had served “with integrity.” 
“I appreciate his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment,” read the statement from Lee.
Before Lee hired him in 2023, Strada served as a deputy commissioner in Arizona, where he oversaw three executions marked by problems.
Lee has ordered a third-party review of Pike’s attempted execution and a pause on all executions in Tennessee through the end of the year.
An interim commissioner will be announced at a later date, the governor’s news release said.

title: Delaware human trafficking summit seeks to turn awareness into coordinated action
description: Two-day Dewey Beach gathering brought community leaders together Thursday before more than six hours of training Friday focused on recognizing victims and improving Delaware’s response. By George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News. DEWEY BEACH, Del. — Delaware leaders spent two days this week examining how the state identifies and responds to human trafficking, begi[...]
text:
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors held its inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Thursday, Oct. 1, and Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach, 1301 Coastal Highway.
Two-day Dewey Beach gathering brought community leaders together Thursday before more than six hours of training Friday focused on recognizing victims and improving Delaware’s response.
By George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News.
DEWEY BEACH, Del. — Delaware leaders spent two days this week examining how the state identifies and responds to human trafficking, beginning with a closed-door executive roundtable Thursday and continuing Friday with an all-day summit for health care workers, social workers, law enforcement, advocates and other professionals.
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors held its inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Thursday, Oct. 1, and Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach, 1301 Coastal Highway.
Thursday’s program was an invitation-only executive roundtable that brought leaders and decision-makers together to discuss Delaware’s response to trafficking. Friday’s public and professional summit ran from Noon to 4 p.m.. It included keynote presentations, professional education, survivor perspectives and discussions involving medical providers, mental health professionals, law enforcement and direct-service workers.
Marcia Ferranto, president of the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, said the organization wanted the event to do more than raise awareness.
“Human trafficking affects Delaware communities, but too often it remains unseen or misunderstood,” Ferranto said. “We need residents, business leaders, educators, health care professionals, faith communities and policymakers to understand the warning signs and recognize that each of them can play a role in prevention.”
The two-day format reflected that goal.
Thursday concentrated on the people in positions to influence policies, organizations and systems. Friday focused more directly on the professionals and community members who may encounter trafficking victims but not immediately recognize what they are seeing.
The invitation-only roundtable brought together senior leaders from health care, law enforcement, government, social services, victim advocacy, education, behavioral health and community organizations. It also included political and public-sector leaders representing multiple levels of government, including federal homeland security officials, representatives of the governor’s office and county leaders.
Organizers said it was the first time Delaware had convened such a broad group of high-level decision-makers specifically to focus on human trafficking as a shared statewide challenge. The potential benefit is significant: stronger relationships among agencies, clearer referral pathways, more consistent training, better coordination when victims are identified and a greater chance that warning signs seen by one institution are connected with information held by another.
The coalition billed the gathering as Delaware’s inaugural statewide Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit. National experts and Delaware professionals participated as speakers, moderators and presenters.
A full day of training
Friday’s program began at 7:45 a.m. and continued until 4 p.m.
Nemours Children’s Health offered six continuing education hours for nurses and six continuing education credits for social workers participating in the program. The stated audience included nurses, social workers and others interested in human trafficking education.
Presenters included retired special victims detective Kevin McNeil; survivor, author and speaker Marti MacGibbon; Jennifer Cooper, BSN, RN, SANE-P; Andrea Repine, MSN, APRN, CPNP; attorney Shea Rhodes; Jose Alfaro; Jeanne Allert; Dana Kaplan, MD; and Heather LaRocca, LCSW.
The educational program was designed to help participants recognize behavioral, physical and situational indicators of trafficking, understand gaps in identifying victims and develop cross-disciplinary teams to support survivors.
Training included discussion of warning signs such as a victim lacking control of personal possessions or identification, inconsistencies in a person’s account, signs of branding or other physical indicators and behaviors that could suggest someone is being controlled.
The program also addressed the underrepresentation of male and LGBTQ+ trafficking victims in national data and how those gaps can affect the ability of professionals to identify victims.
Victims may already be in the system
A central message emerging from the summit was that trafficking victims frequently encounter institutions that could help them without ever announcing that they are being trafficked.

A nurse may treat an injury.
A teacher may notice chronic absences.
Police may encounter someone during a domestic dispute.
A social worker may see unstable housing.
A nonprofit organization may encounter someone unable to meet basic needs.
Those individual encounters may appear unrelated unless the people involved understand the larger patterns associated with exploitation.

Ferranto said that makes education across professions particularly important.
“Trafficking does not happen only somewhere else; it is affecting people here in Delaware,” Ferranto said. “When the public understands what exploitation looks like and knows how to respond, we become better able to protect vulnerable people, support survivors and make Delaware a much more difficult place for traffickers to operate.”
The summit’s professional education program specifically emphasized multidisciplinary, trauma-informed and survivor-centered responses rather than expecting a single agency or profession to identify and solve the problem alone.
Trafficking does not always begin with kidnapping
Presenters also challenged one of the most common public perceptions of trafficking — that victims are usually abducted by strangers and physically imprisoned.
That can happen, but speakers said trafficking frequently develops differently.
Victims can be manipulated through relationships, housing, employment, financial dependency, drugs, threats or promises of security.
The process may occur gradually through grooming rather than through a single dramatic event.
Someone who appears free to leave physically may believe leaving would result in violence, homelessness, withdrawal, financial ruin or harm to someone else.
That psychological control can make trafficking difficult for family members, employers, medical professionals and even victims themselves to recognize.
Why health care workers matter
Medical professionals were an important part of Friday’s program because health care may provide one of the few opportunities for someone outside a trafficking situation to interact privately with a victim.
The summit included training aimed at nurses and other medical providers on recognizing trafficking indicators and responding in ways that do not further traumatize patients.
Jennifer Cooper served as course director for the continuing education program, with Andrea Repine and Suzanne Rouleau among the planners.
The program emphasized that professionals need to know not only what to notice, but also what to do next.
Its learning objectives included establishing cross-disciplinary teams capable of supporting trafficking survivors.
That means a nurse identifying a possible victim needs to know who to call. Police need to understand available survivor services. Social workers need relationships with medical and behavioral health providers. Community organizations need to know where safe housing and other assistance can be found.
From executive discussion to front-line training
Holding the executive roundtable Thursday and the professional summit Friday created two levels of discussion.
One focused on leadership and institutional response. The other focused on people likely to encounter potential victims in their daily work.
For Ferranto and the coalition, connecting those levels is a major part of the effort. Delaware already has law enforcement agencies investigating trafficking, hospitals caring for vulnerable patients and nonprofit groups assisting survivors.
The challenge is ensuring those organizations understand what others are doing and know how to connect victims with the appropriate help.
The summit’s emphasis on building cross-disciplinary teams suggests organizers see coordination as an essential next step rather than treating trafficking solely as a criminal justice, medical or social-services issue.
The test comes after the summit
The event ended Friday afternoon, but the larger question is what happens next.
Participants returned to hospitals, police departments, schools, nonprofits, government agencies, and community organizations with a common set of questions:

Are staff members trained to recognize trafficking?
Do they know what to do when they suspect it?
Is there a clear referral process?
Do organizations know what services other groups provide?
Are victims being identified early enough?

And when someone is ready to leave an exploitative situation, does Delaware have the housing, treatment, and support necessary to help?
Those are questions the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors hopes the two-day gathering will continue to push beyond a conference room in Dewey Beach.
The coalition, formerly known as Meet Me at the Well Delaware, works in education, advocacy, survivor support and outreach and connects trafficking survivors with services including housing, employment and treatment.
Friday’s summit represented its most visible statewide effort yet to bring the different parts of Delaware’s response together.
The next measure of success will be whether those relationships produce lasting changes in how Delaware recognizes trafficking and helps the people caught in it.

title: Human trafficking is not what many Delawareans think it is
description: Two-day Dewey Beach summit brought together government leaders, law enforcement, health professionals, survivors and advocates while challenging common assumptions about how trafficking begins and who can become a victim. By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE news. DEWEY BEACH, Del. — A two-day human trafficking summit in Dewey Beach brought together government[...]
text:
The Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit, organized by the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, began Thursday with an invitation-only executive roundtable and continued Friday with an all-day public and professional program at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach for over 150 people.
Two-day Dewey Beach summit brought together government leaders, law enforcement, health professionals, survivors and advocates while challenging common assumptions about how trafficking begins and who can become a victim.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE news.
DEWEY BEACH, Del. — A two-day human trafficking summit in Dewey Beach brought together government leaders, law enforcement, health care professionals, survivors, advocates and community organizations this week to examine how Delaware identifies and responds to trafficking — and to challenge some of the public’s most common assumptions about what the crime actually looks like.
The Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit, organized by the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, began Thursday with an invitation-only executive roundtable and continued Friday with an all-day public and professional program at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach for over 150 people.
One of the clearest messages to emerge from the summit was that trafficking often does not begin with kidnapping, physical restraint or a stranger forcing someone into a car.
Jennifer Cooper, a Forensic Nurse Coordinator from Nemours Children’s Health and one of the summit organizers with the coalition, and fellow nurse Andrea Repine, Pediatric Nurse Practioner from Nemours led a “Human Trafficking 101” session focused on separating myths from reality.
“Most people think, when they think trafficking, that there’s a pimp involved,” Cooper said. “Human Trafficking involves a third party trading sex for value and can involve a boyfriend/girlfriend, family member, or employer and others”  She also pointed out “When it comes to minors, you don’t need that third party.”
Trafficking also does not necessarily involve an exchange of cash.
“It doesn’t have to be an exchange of money,” Cooper said. “It could be that they want food.”
That can mean a vulnerable young person exchanging sex for a place to sleep, food, transportation or something else of value.
Not always kidnapping either!
Cooper and Repine told participants that trafficking often develops gradually through grooming, manipulation, dependency, fraud or coercion.
A victim may never be kidnapped.
There may be no locked room.
And the person doing the exploiting may be a boyfriend, girlfriend, employer, acquaintance or someone who initially appeared to be helping.
Cooper described the session as an effort to explain “what trafficking is” by “breaking down the myths versus the reality.”
The distinction becomes particularly important when children are involved.
That means exploitation of a minor does not require a traditional pimp or third-party trafficker.
A person can be trapped without being locked up
Opening keynote speaker Kevin McNeil, a nationally recognized victim advocate, brought both law enforcement experience and personal experience to the discussion.
McNeil is a retired police officer and a survivor of trafficking and sexual abuse. His presentation, “Stuck in Traffic,” focused on how someone can feel trapped in a trafficking situation even when no physical barrier prevents that person from leaving.
The analogy began with something familiar: the frustration of sitting in traffic with nowhere to go.
For a trafficking victim, however, the barriers can involve fear, financial dependency, threats, homelessness, addiction or emotional attachment to the person doing the exploiting.
That type of psychological control can make trafficking considerably harder to recognize than the popular image of someone being physically held by a stranger.
Substance abuse can deepen the problem
Marty McGibbon brought another survivor’s perspective to the conference.
A therapist, author, comedian and trafficking survivor, McGibbon addressed the intersection between substance abuse and trafficking. She returned later in the program to discuss mental well-being, self-care and trauma-informed approaches for people working with survivors. Pasted text(20260818-140439)
Her presentations reinforced another theme of the summit: Trafficking often overlaps with other problems rather than occurring by itself.
A victim may also be dealing with addiction, homelessness, previous abuse, financial instability or an unhealthy relationship.
Those vulnerabilities can become tools for someone seeking control.
Cooper previously described the intersection between substance abuse and trafficking as “a huge problem, particularly here in Delaware and the surrounding area.”
Vulnerability matters
Presenters stressed that traffickers often exploit vulnerability rather than targeting one particular type of person.
A teenager without a stable place to live may be vulnerable to someone offering housing.
Someone struggling with addiction may become dependent on the person supplying drugs.
A worker may rely on an employer for transportation, housing or access to personal documents.
A person seeking affection or security may become emotionally dependent on someone who later begins exploiting the relationship.
Those situations do not automatically mean trafficking is occurring.
But understanding how dependency can turn into control can help families, teachers, medical professionals and others recognize when something may be wrong.
Why Delawareans should care
The summit’s message was not that every troubled teenager, unhealthy relationship or difficult workplace situation involves trafficking.
For people whose image of human trafficking still involves strangers, kidnapping and locked rooms, summit speakers offered a more practical starting point:

It was that trafficking can look remarkably ordinary from the outside.
It can look like a teenager suddenly depending on an older boyfriend or girlfriend for a place to stay.
It can look like someone working for an employer who controls transportation, identification or money.
It can look like a young person exchanging sex for food, shelter or something else of value.
And it can involve someone who technically can walk out the door but believes there is nowhere safe to go.

For parents, teachers, neighbors and other Delawareans, the goal is not to become investigators. It is to better understand what exploitation can look like so they recognize when something does not seem right.
Almost 700 victims connected to 330 human trafficking cases in Delaware since 2007, with 29 cases of trafficking in 2025. Advocates caution that these figures represent only reported and identified cases. The actual number of victims is believed to be significantly higher because many victims never come to the attention of authorities or service providers.delaware
Look for vulnerability, dependency and whether someone is using those vulnerabilities to control another person.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Whatever the motivation, Republican’s endorsement of Democrat deserves points for facts and reason
description: Since South Dakota’s Republican lame-duck Secretary of State Monae Johnson oddly endorsed the Democrat campaigning to replace her, voters reasonably might wonder: Is she for real? Even though she has been viewed at times during her tenure as just politically eccentric and confounding, this partisan betrayal was a core taboo, akin to political treason. Instea[...]
text:
Monae Johnson waits to welcome potential voters at an October 2022 meet-and-great in a Rapid City coffee shop, during her campaign to become South Dakota's secretary of state. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Since South Dakota’s Republican lame-duck Secretary of State Monae Johnson oddly endorsed the Democrat campaigning to replace her, voters reasonably might wonder: Is she for real?
Even though she has been viewed at times during her tenure as just politically eccentric and confounding, this partisan betrayal was a core taboo, akin to political treason.
Instead of taking this act of apparent partisan infidelity at face value, the current toxic divisiveness in American politics leads us to wonder whether Johnson’s decision was a genuine, evidence-based reversal of her previous MAGA-centric stances, an act of political revenge, or a calculated tactic to undergird an unstated future political ambition.
South Dakota’s top election official, a Republican, endorses a Democrat to succeed her

After all, like proverbial rats fleeing a sinking ship, more and more Republican candidates in the midterm elections this fall — and non-candidates like Johnson — seem to be running full speed away from the hard-core MAGA base and its election-denying messiah, President Donald Trump, to whom they’ve heretofore slavishly stuck like glue.
Even our own junior Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota — a sometime MAGA critic, to be fair — who is up for reelection to a six-year term in November, purposely decided to forgo the unusual 2026 Republican Midterm Convention on Sept. 9 in Dallas to instead confer with voters at coffees and meet-and-greets in 14 different South Dakota counties, according to The Hill, an influential Washington, D.C.,-based political news organ. 
The Hill article noted that Rounds, “who may face a tougher-than-expected challenge in a Republican-leaning state, said his time is better spent meeting with constituents in South Dakota” than gracing the vanity convention.
Still, questions abound about Johnson’s apparent stark betrayal of her political party.
Whereas she campaigned for secretary of state in 2022 refusing to clearly admit Joe Biden won the presidential election in 2020, making the conspiracy-theory concept “election integrity” a centerpiece of her platform, and releasing information that “revealed whether those on the state’s voter rolls were seeking government assistance such as food aid” (she apologized for that “accident”), she now says she’s changed her tune.
After the state Republican convention in June, where MAGA-aligned, hand-ballot-counting proponent Heather Baxter defeated her for the secretary of state nomination, Johnson announced in September she was endorsing the Democrats’ candidate, Terrence Davis, over Baxter. She stressed, “I cannot remain silent when I believe the integrity, stability, and professionalism of this office is at stake.”
Johnson wrote in a Sept. 19 letter published by South Dakota War College, a Republican blog, that she now believes:
“South Dakota deserves a Secretary of State who will strengthen confidence through performance rather than provocation; who will support election officials rather than burden them for political effect; who will protect voter access and election security without pretending those goals are enemies; and who will treat the office’s employees, voters, candidates, and business owners with dignity.”
In other words, much the opposite of what she originally ran on.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Whatever her real motivations, she gets points even at this awkward late stage for seeming to apply facts and reason to the 2026 election equation. Indeed, rather than parroting partisan political gospel, whether or not it actually makes any sense, the sacred motivator of every candidate and elected official should be identifying truth and presenting it fairly to voters. Which is to say public officials should always apply thoughtful, objective skepticism with good faith to societal problems, instead of knee-jerk, visceral bias.
“How tightly should you hold your beliefs?” Massimo Pigliucci, the K D Irani Professor of Philosophy at City College of New York, recently asked in Aeon, a digital magazine of ideas, philosophy and culture. “You face the question several times a week without noticing. Hold them too loosely and you don’t stand for anything, hold them too tightly and you become the sort of person no argument can reach.” 
“Most of us swing between the two and have no vocabulary for the ground in between,” he added in his fascinating essay. “A Roman lawyer [Marcus Tullius Cicero, 106-43 BCE] worked one out … and it is still the best answer available.”
Pigliucci noted that uber-skeptic Cicero believed, “a genuine sceptic, confronted with compelling new evidence, updates (beliefs) — whereas the contrarian does not: they shift goalposts, raise new objections, or ignore what they cannot explain.”
Monae Johnson’s intent in her political about-face might be noble. But who can really be sure in American politics these days?

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Proposed Trump administration changes would gut vital Head Start regulations
description: Head Start works comprehensively. The harm of the proposed rule does not come from any one of the above changes alone, it comes from the compounding impact of removing services and protections for the most vulnerable children and families.
text:
IN THE SPRING of 1965, President Lyndon Johnson announced the launch of a new initiative: Head Start, a program designed to support poor children’s readiness for kindergarten by not only offering them time in classrooms but by addressing their health and well-being and partnering with their families to improve their circumstances. Our nation responded to that vision. Just a few months later, communities across our Commonwealth and across the country welcomed children into Head Start centers.
Sixty-one years later, 28 Head Start agencies across Massachusetts continue to uphold that vision – that vulnerable children deserve the highest quality early education and wraparound supports to grow and thrive. The Head Start statute and regulations codified the early vision for the program and expanded it over time to serve children from birth until kindergarten. Now, that national commitment is at risk because of a recent proposal that would dismantle Head Start’s federal standards. 
In August, the Trump administration released a proposal to gut Head Start regulations and threaten the quality, scope, and services of Head Start. The proposed rule eliminates quality early learning standards; removes standards for critical wraparound services for children and families, including health and mental health services; reduces access and eligibility for children from families experiencing homelessness, children with disabilities, and foster children; and threatens learning outcomes for dual language learners.  
A child cannot learn if she is hungry. A family cannot focus on school readiness if they are facing eviction. A teacher cannot meet a traumatized child’s needs if her classroom is too large, her training is inadequate, and she has no classroom supports. These facts have been the basis of Head Start’s design for 61 years, and now that design is at risk. 
The federal proposal is framed as reducing federal burden and giving local programs greater flexibility. Massachusetts Head Start programs welcome meaningful flexibility. We already design services around the needs of our communities. But rather than addressing the real challenges facing Head Start — including rising operating costs, workforce shortages, and years of inadequate funding — the proposal punishes programs, families, and young children. It hands programs fewer resources and fewer protections at the same time, and it removes many of the evidence-based standards that best serve children and families.  
I see the difference those standards make across Massachusetts’s 28 Head Start agencies. Together, our programs serve more than 10,000 young children and families in ways that best meet the needs of their local communities, including full-day classrooms, home visiting models, and partnerships with early learning programs and public schools. 
Head Start programs enroll the most vulnerable children in their communities, who often need more than the basics that a licensed child care program provides. Head Start programs offer early education alongside health and dental care, developmental screenings, mental health support, nutrition, disability services, and family supports.  
Parents are partners and leaders in their children’s education and in the governance of their programs. And because the services are so customized to those who need them, the harms of the proposal will be felt most deeply by some of the most vulnerable families in our Commonwealth. 
In Massachusetts, 16 percent of Head Start children experienced homelessness during the 2024–25 program year—an 82 percent increase from just two years earlier. Yet the proposed rule would make it harder for families experiencing homelessness to access Head Start by requiring families to provide documentation proving their homelessness status, documentation that many families cannot produce. For a family already living in crisis, it can mean losing access to the very program designed to help them stabilize. 
The same is true for children who speak a language other than English at home. Sixty-four percent of Massachusetts Head Start children come from homes where English is not the primary language, the highest proportion of dual language learners in Head Start of any US state. 
Decades of research tell us that young children learn best when taught by bilingual educators who speak their home language. The proposed rule abandons that research, requiring all education and family services to be conducted in English while eliminating standards supporting bilingual personnel and culturally responsive services. 
Again, the impact is cumulative. These changes would mean less effective communication with families, weaker family engagement, and fewer opportunities for children to learn in ways that reflect how they actually experience the world. 
The proposed changes also threaten the people who make Head Start possible: its workforce. Massachusetts Head Start programs employ more than 4,000 people. These educators, family service workers, health professionals, bus drivers, and other staff build relationships that children depend on. But the proposal would increase class sizes, remove the ability for programs to invest in their workforce’s education and professional development, eliminate staff wellness and break requirements, and reduce key supports, including behavioral health and bus monitors.  
The federal analysis estimates that nearly 40,000 Head Start jobs could be lost nationally. Our standards should encourage recruitment and retention in our programs, not threaten it. 
Head Start works comprehensively. The harm of the proposed rule does not come from any one of the above changes alone, it comes from the compounding impact of removing services and protections for the most vulnerable children and families. The answer to Head Start’s challenges is not to expect less of it. It is to invest in the people and resources that allow it to deliver on its promise. 
I am grateful that in Massachusetts, our elected leaders know the value of Head Start and we have the full support of the Healey-Driscoll administration, the state House and Senate, and the Massachusetts congressional delegation in opposing the proposal. Public comment in the Federal Register on these devastating proposed changes is open until October 6. 
My organization has submitted comments – and urges others to do so as well – imploring the Trump administration to withdraw the proposed rule and protect the promise of Head Start for the next 61 years. 
Michelle Haimowitz is executive director of the Massachusetts Head Start Association, which serves as the voice of Head Start programs in Massachusetts.
