name: Washington State Standard
title: Judge permanently blocks WA sheriff standards law
description: A judge on Friday threw out tough new job standards for county sheriffs approved by Washington lawmakers this year that critics argued would force some out of office. The decision from Thurston County Superior Court Judge Christine Schaller permanently blocks the most controversial pieces of the Democrat-sponsored policy, pending an appeal by the state. A […[...]
text:
Mark Lamb, the attorney for Washington sheriffs, speaks in Thurston County Superior Court against a new law setting heightened eligibility standards for sheriffs as several county sheriffs observe on April 29, 2026. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)A judge on Friday threw out tough new job standards for county sheriffs approved by Washington lawmakers this year that critics argued would force some out of office.
The decision from Thurston County Superior Court Judge Christine Schaller permanently blocks the most controversial pieces of the Democrat-sponsored policy, pending an appeal by the state. A formal court order outlining the ruling is expected later this month.
The law’s supporters see it as vital to building trust in law enforcement by requiring sheriffs to meet the same standards as their deputies. But its opponents — including a dozen sheriffs who challenged the law – say it amounts to state overreach that could override the will of voters by ousting elected sheriffs.
“The First Amendment and democracy, for all of us to be participants in that, it requires that we have the belief that people may elect someone that we don’t like, people may vote for someone that we don’t like, and elected officials, as they frequently do, may say things that we don’t like,” plaintiffs’ attorney Mark Lamb said.
“And the remedy for that is not to have a commission that is able to remove them from office when they do something that they deem to be offensive or impermissible,” Lamb continued.
Mike Faulk, a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office, said the state plans to appeal the ruling to “defend this important state law.”
Senate Bill 5974 requires county sheriffs, who are usually elected, to meet the same minimum eligibility standards as police chiefs, who are appointed. Failure to do so or getting state certification revoked are grounds for removal from office under the law. The seldom-used recall process is currently how voters can remove sheriffs before their term ends. 
Schaller temporarily blocked much of the law on April 29 the day before it was set to take effect so elections for sheriffs this year moved forward without the new eligibility requirements. The state appealed Schaller’s earlier decision to the state Supreme Court, but a court commissioner chose to maintain the status quo and declined to lift the judge’s block. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The attorney general’s office defended the law in court.
“Voters place immense trust in sheriffs to faithfully execute the duties of office, and accountability, trust, and proper training are paramount,” Assistant Attorney General Kristen Valore said in court Friday. “The Legislature passed Senate Bill 5974 to further these interests and ensure that county sheriffs meet the same basic qualifications as other law enforcement leaders in the state.”
Democrats in the Legislature passed the law and Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it despite ardent opposition from Republican lawmakers. 
Schaller’s action sets aside the law’s imposition of new criteria that, in order to be a sheriff, one must have at least five years of law enforcement experience, no felony or gross misdemeanor convictions, be at least 25 years old and no history of actions that would get state certification as a peace officer revoked. They have to undergo background checks to confirm they meet the requirements. Under the law, if a sheriff is removed from office, county officials would appoint a replacement. 
The law sought to force sheriffs not already certified to get state certification from the Criminal Justice Training Commission within nine months of taking office. Under current law, they have a year. 
Five-member hearing panels from the Criminal Justice Training Commission make final decisions on decertification. The panels include two police officials. These decisions can be appealed. 
Examples of misconduct that has gotten officers decertified in recent years include crimes like domestic violence, harassment and sexual abuse, as well as interfering with an internal investigation and endorsing on social media police use of force against protesters.
The decision comes in response to lawsuits brought by sheriffs across the state. 
The sheriffs who brought the original litigation include: John Nowels of Spokane County, Glenn Blakeslee of Pend Oreille County, Brad Manke of Stevens County and Ray Maycumber of Ferry County. The Washington State Sheriffs’ Association filed a similar lawsuit of its own.  
Walla Walla County Sheriff Mark Crider said he and other sheriffs are “fairly satisfied” with the ruling, noting that the “majority of it that we thought was unconstitutional, she agreed with us.”
“I think it would’ve disenfranchised the voters,” said Crider, who is retiring this year. “That’s our big thing. The right of the people is being impaired because they don’t get to select who’s representing them.”
Anne Levinson, a retired judge who helped draft the law, countered in an email after Friday’s hearing that “there is great harm to the public and in particular to vulnerable individuals if top law enforcement officials are allowed to continue in office after having committed serious misconduct.”
Schaller’s ruling doesn’t appear to block other provisions in the law related to police chief standards and the use of law enforcement volunteers.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Christa Pike on a ventilator and unconscious after failed execution in Tennessee, attorneys say
authors: By Kim Chandler and Jamie Stengle, Associated Press
description: Photographs of Colleen Slemmer, who was murdered in 1995, are displayed outside Riverbend Maximum Security Institution before the planned execution of Christa Pike, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Christa Pike was placed on a ventilator and remained unconscious in a hospital in the hours after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.
This photo provided by the Tennessee Department of Correction shows Christa Pike on Jan. 12, 2023.  Credit: TDOC via AP
Hospital staff, her lawyers said, were working to save Pike’s life and as of late Thursday were trying to clear the two doses of the drug that the state uses to execute prisoners.
The stunning failure in Tennessee’s execution chamber on Wednesday has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an independent review.
The court filing offered the first detailed account of Pike’s condition after an ambulance carried her away from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said a day earlier that she was in critical condition.
Christa Pike’s attorneys point to problems with the IV
Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” they wrote in the court filing.
Instead of “remedying this failure,” they prepared and administered a second dose of pentobarbital, her lawyers said.
State officials have not offered any explanations about what went wrong.
Tennessee leaders want a review of execution methods
Lee demanded a review of the execution procedures and indefinitely postponed Pike’s execution and another that had been scheduled for this year. Republican Tennessee lawmakers said the state should review whether to stop single-drug lethal injections and consider other options to carry out death sentences.
The execution team worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs, said Pike’s defense lawyer Randy Spivey, who counted at least seven needles in her left arm.
Neither the initial nor the backup dose of pentobarbital worked. Pike was still snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.
Pike’s attorneys asked a state court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence from the failed execution.
“Preserving this evidence is essential to understanding what happened, ensuring accountability and protecting Christa’s legal rights,” two of her attorneys said in a statement.
She was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate in a jealous rage. She later became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.
Following the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, her attorneys said.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in an earlier clemency petition.
The mother of the 19-year-old woman Pike killed expressed frustration over the failed execution. “I didn’t get justice for my daughter,” Maya Martinez said Thursday.
Problems found with executions four years ago
Four years ago, Tennessee’s governor ordered another independent review into capital punishment after abruptly stopping the April 2022 execution of Oscar Smith. Lee then paused all executions after acknowledging the state had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were properly tested.
Months later, a report found the state hadn’t complied with its own lethal injection process since its revision in 2018, resulting in executions being conducted without proper testing of the drugs.
At the time, the state used a three-drug execution protocol of midazolam, vecuronium bromide and potassium chloride. The state later switched to using just pentobarbital.
Pentobarbital has been used to carry out death sentences in multiple states and by the federal government.
The review, led by former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton, also found that the state’s unidentified executioner had no formal healthcare training and learned the role mainly through on-the-job experience.
After the release of the report, the Tennessee Department of Correction fired its longtime top attorney and another employee.
___
Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Father and son arrested in Ole Miss kratom-suspected deaths
description: University of Mississippi students on campus, Thursday, March 26, 2026, in Oxford.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A father and son have been arrested for selling packages of kratom tied to the overdose deaths of two University of Mississippi students, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District announced Friday. 
Store clerk Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, each face federal charges of possession of controlled substances with intent to distribute. 
On Sept. 21, an Ole Miss student was found dead in his dorm room. An hour later in a separate location, another student was found dead. At both scenes, law enforcement found packages of suspected kratom derivatives, and some tablets were missing. 
A package of suspected kratom derivative substances is included in the criminal complaint charging Yahya Mohamed Mosleh and Islam Yahya Mosleh by the U.S. attorney’s office. Credit: U.S. Attorney's Office North District of Mississippi
Investigators used bank records to trace purchase of some of the kratom derivatives to an Oxford vape, tobacco and beer store, according to court records. An informant spoke to the elder Mosleh, the store clerk, who sold them kratom pills and warned them to be careful with them, according to the criminal complaint. 
Law enforcement executed several search warrants, resulting in the seizure of kratom substances from the store and the arrest of Mosleh and his son, according to a news release from the U.S. attorney’s office. 
The victims were identified in court records as Aidan Hamilton, 18, a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert Strang, 20, a junior from Atlanta. 
Hamilton enjoyed the outdoors, hiking and climbing and skiing and will be remembered as someone who was caring, loving and upbeat, according to his obituary. Hamilton is survived by his parents, a brother and a sister. 
Strang was a member of the Phi Delta Theta fraternity at Ole Miss who will be remembered for the joy he brought others and a strong sense of fairness, according to his obituary. He is survived by parents, a twin sister, a younger brother, other family members and his two dogs. 
A day after the students’ deaths, local law enforcement confirmed it was investigating their deaths and advised people to avoid kratom. 
Kratom is plant-based and, in its natural form, is considered a stimulant in low doses and an opiate-like sedative in higher doses, according to the U.S. attorney’s office. Derivatives of kratom are Schedule I controlled substances because they are more potent and associated with a high risk of addiction, overdose and even death. 
The Food and Drug Administration has not approved the extract. 
However, kratom is sold in many gas stations across the country, including Mississippi, to those over the age of 21. Lafayette County is one of 30 counties and cities in the state that have restricted or banned the sale of kratom. It can also be purchased over the internet. 
The Lafayette County Sheriff’s Department and the Oxford and University of Mississippi police departments are investigating the case with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC residents flagged by a federal database will be asked to confirm citizenship before voting
description: The North Carolina State Board of Elections is planning to ask the 1,599 registered voters flagged by a federal database as potential noncitizens to either confirm their citizenship or ask to be removed from the state voter list.  The letters will go out to those registered voters early next week, state elections board spokesman Jason […]
text:
Absentee ballot being handled by an employee of the Wake County Board of Elections. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)The North Carolina State Board of Elections is planning to ask the 1,599 registered voters flagged by a federal database as potential noncitizens to either confirm their citizenship or ask to be removed from the state voter list. 
The letters will go out to those registered voters early next week, state elections board spokesman Jason Tyson said Friday. 
The board announced in July that the federal SAVE database had flagged nearly 1,600 potential noncitizens registered to vote in the state. The board hadn’t acted on the information until the U.S. Supreme Court last week authorized the use of the SAVE database to find noncitizens on voter rolls. The North Carolina elections board decided last year to feed its voter list into the database. 
SAVE is run by Homeland Security and was built to check people’s immigration status to see if they are eligible for public benefits. But it has been prone to error when used as a voter screening tool.
NC has a list of nearly 1600 people flagged as noncitizens on its voter rolls. How will it be used?

Texas was one of the first states to use the SAVE database to look for noncitizens registered to vote. Recently, the Texas Secretary of State said in a press release that of the 2,724 people the database flagged as potential noncitizens, 578 were actually citizens.
A final copy of the North Carolina elections board letter was not ready, Tyson said, but it will ask residents to provide citizenship confirmation by email, fax, mail, or in person. The letter will also have instructions for residents who are registered by mistake and want to be removed from the rolls, Tyson said. 
“If you try to vote as a noncitizen, that’s a crime,” he said. 
Federal law bans voter roll purges in the 90 days before an election, a time called the “quiet period.” 
Tyson said the plan is a volunteer, individual process, so it is not a systematic removal of registrants that would be prohibited during the quiet period. 
Whether sending the letters violates the quiet period ban depends on what they say, said Jeff Loperfido, chief counsel for voting rights at the Southern Coalition for Social Justice. 
It will be fine if the letter advises people who are not citizens to terminate their registrations and tells people who are citizens that they can ignore the letter, he said. 
“If the letter says you must provide something to be able to vote, that’s more problematic,” Loperfido said. “The devil’s in the details.”
North Carolina has a voter ID law, but drivers licenses are not proof of citizenship. 
Tyson said people who receive a letter and show up to vote without having provided citizenship proof will still be able to cast a ballot. 
“Typically, they would not be turned away,” he said. “The process would happen on the backend.”
Loperfido said he hopes the letters don’t deter eligible voters from casting ballots. 
“I’d hate for the message to be intimidating to people,” he said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Possible measles exposure reported on Amtrak, at Minot train station
description: People on board an Amtrak train and at the Minot train station on Sept. 23 may have been exposed to the measles.  The North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services reported Friday that a westbound train passenger with the measles traveled through North Dakota, using the restroom at the Minot station about 9:30 a.m.  […]
text:
Photo of a single dose of the MMR vaccine. (Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)People on board an Amtrak train and at the Minot train station on Sept. 23 may have been exposed to the measles. 
The North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services reported Friday that a westbound train passenger with the measles traveled through North Dakota, using the restroom at the Minot station about 9:30 a.m. 
The passenger got on the Empire Builder in Chicago, but the agency did not know their destination, though it was not in North Dakota.
Misinformation, hesitancy could blunt impact of new cancer vaccines

People who think they may have been exposed and who have not received a dose of the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine should avoid contact with others and monitor for measles symptoms for 21 days after exposure, the agency said in a news release.
People who develop measles symptoms should notify their healthcare provider or a healthcare facility before seeking in-person treatment. This will allow the facility to make arrangements to prevent exposure to other patients and medical staff.
“This serves as a reminder to North Dakotans that measles continues to circulate with 2026 seeing the highest number of measles cases in the United States since 1986,” Mary Woinarowicz, North Dakota Health and Human Services immunization director, said in the news release.
North Dakota has had 38 confirmed cases of measles so far in 2026 but has not had a reported case since May.
As of Thursday, there had been 3,887 confirmed measles cases in the United States this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
Woinarowicz said the MMR vaccine is 93% effective after one dose and 97% effective after two doses and encouraged people to get vaccinated.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Flathead Valley Community College faculty irked by presidential appointment
description: The board of trustees at Flathead Valley Community College has chosen its first new president in more than a quarter century, but faculty allege the selection process lacked transparency and disenfranchised the campus. The board of trustees advanced this week the presidential appointment of Deborah Kish Stephan, who leads the Brandon Campus of Hillsborough C[...]
text:
Flathead Valley Community College in Kalispell. (Courtesy photo)The board of trustees at Flathead Valley Community College has chosen its first new president in more than a quarter century, but faculty allege the selection process lacked transparency and disenfranchised the campus.
The board of trustees advanced this week the presidential appointment of Deborah Kish Stephan, who leads the Brandon Campus of Hillsborough College in Florida. Final appointment is pending contract review.
A college and board of trustees spokesperson said the board collected information from many groups, including community, staff, students and faculty “who chose to participate.”
“Hiring a president is one of the board’s most important responsibilities, and trustees considered a wide range of input in making this decision,” said college and trustees spokesperson Julie Brempelis in an email.
Flathead Valley Community College is part of the Montana University System but governed by a locally elected board of trustees. It had 2,117 students enrolled last fall.
In February, President Jane Karas announced she would retire at the end of 2026 after 25 years in the role.
Board chairperson Callie Langohr said in an email the search for a new president followed the process set by trustees and ACCT Searches, the executive search firm hired for the national recruitment. The search led to four finalists.
But Conrad Rauscher, faculty union vice president, said the appointment didn’t reflect rankings from a faculty survey, and even worse, the process didn’t elicit feedback from different groups on campus.
Instead, he said, they all were offered the same QR code to give feedback.
“A lot of groups on campus felt pretty disenfranchised by that structure,” Rauscher said.
The survey rated Stephan as the faculty’s third choice, and it rated Andrew Fields, CEO of the University of Idaho Coeur d’Alene, as their top choice.
“A lot of people felt like he was a bit more of a fit academically, culturally and also with the trades,” Rauscher said.
Stephan did not respond to an email or request for comment.
But Rauscher said the fact the trustees didn’t align with the faculty wasn’t the most significant source of frustration.
“The biggest issue was that we just didn’t feel like they were open to a lot of feedback,” Rauscher said.
On the other hand, he said, the process gave the current president outsized influence in the decision — outside the public eye and after the board chair said the president wasn’t involved.
He said Karas had one-on-one meetings with finalists, and trustees closed part of their meeting to deliberate, but they allowed Karas to talk to the board privately — a process Langohr said is a standard part of the board’s reference and background review.
“President Karas did not design or lead the search process, and the selection of Dr. Stephan was the board’s decision alone,” Langohr said.
Rauscher said an email update from Langohr also misrepresented the appointment decision from the board as unanimous when the board took two votes Monday related to the hire and only one was unanimous.
Rauscher said, and Brempelis confirmed to the Daily Montanan, the board took one 4-3 vote to postpone approval of the contract for legal review. The board also took a unanimous vote to appoint Stephan pending the contract review.
The pending contract offers a salary of $250,000, an annual $60,000 housing bonus, and a $12,000 annual vehicle bonus. The contract is drafted for 3.5 years with rolling extensions of one year.
Housing costs in the Flathead Valley are notoriously expensive. The median household income in Flathead County is $73,925, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
Brempelis did not comment on the salary and bonuses the college is offering or the specific purpose of the legal review.
“The board will consider the terms, including compensation, at an upcoming public meeting, and the approved contract will be public once finalized,” Brempelis said.
She said “a single survey was used to collect all feedback from community, staff, faculty and students.”
In an email, Langohr praised Stephan’s “substantial” community college experience, including developing workforce programs, improving learning environments, securing resources and reducing barriers for students.
“The board was impressed by her breadth of leadership experience and her emphasis on listening, collaboration, transparency, shared governance and student success,” Langohr said.
Editor’s note: Staff reporter Micah Drew is an adjunct faculty member at Flathead Valley Community College. He was not involved in the production or editing of this story.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico open government group sues state Livestock Board official
description: The New Mexico Foundation for Open Government, a public records watchdog, sued a New Mexico Livestock Board official on Friday alleging that the board violated state public records law by illegally redacting investigative reports about former board employees.
text:
The New Mexico Foundation for Open Government, a nonprofit public records watchdog, sued the state Livestock Board on Oct. 2, 2026, in the First Judicial District after the agency responded to an Inspection of Public Record Act request with fully redacted documents. (File photo/Source NM)A public records watchdog sued a New Mexico Livestock Board official on Friday alleging that the board violated state public records law by illegally redacting investigative reports about former board employees. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Foundation for Open Government on Aug. 3 requested records under the state Inspection of Public Records Act regarding a private investigation that was conducted on former Livestock Board employees April Riggs, Ray Baca and Priscilla Peña over alleged misconduct. 
The lawsuit does not specify what misconduct the trio are alleged to have committed or what the investigation found. 
Livestock Board record custodian Julie Gauman, according to the complaint filed in the First Judicial District Court, then provided fully redacted documents of the investigation’s findings on Aug. 18.
Gauman, according to the lawsuit, said redacting the document is legal due to IPRA’s “catchall” exemption, which allows records to be redacted if their release violates other state laws, and a provision in IPRA that prohibits release of records in personnel files expressing a “matter of opinion.” 
However, NMFOG contends the Livestock Board’s justification is wrong and outdated. First, they argue that the “catchall” provision does not apply because no other state laws regarding employee confidentiality apply. 
The organization also cites a recent New Mexico Supreme Court ruling in a case between the Albuquerque Journal newspaper and the Albuquerque school board. The court ruled in late May, after a 12-year legal battle, that an investigation into former Superintendent Winston Brooks could not be withheld in its entirety even though portions of it expressed “matters of opinion.” 
“Instead of following the New Mexico Supreme Court’s mandate, the Livestock Board is doubling down on their efforts to keep the investigations secret, in violation of the public’s right to know,” NMFOG said in a news release.
Livestock Board officials told Source NM on Friday that they do not comment on pending litigation. Gauman also declined comment.
NMFOG asked the court to issue an order directing Gauman to satisfy IPRA requests and award damages and attorney fee costs to Henry, the prior litigant. 
Levin added that NMFOG doesn’t necessarily have an interest in the records themselves, but that their legal complaint is over upholding IPRA.
“A landmark decision comes out saying you have to produce these records,” Amanda Lavin, NMFOG legal director, told Source NM. “So we have a public agency flagrantly disregarding that. We want to make sure that public bodies are following the law.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Attorneys stress there’s help for Utahns seeking domestic violence protective orders
description: Utah law enforcers and attorneys are reminding survivors of domestic violence that help to obtain protective orders is available.
text:
Utah law enforcers and attorneys are reminding survivors of domestic violence that help to obtain protective orders is available. 
 Domestic violence resources
Help for people in abusive relationships is available in Utah:

Utah Domestic Violence Coalition: A confidential statewide, 24-hour domestic violence hotline can be reached at 1-800-897-LINK (5465)
YWCA Women in Jeopardy program: 801-537-8600
Utah child abuse and neglect hotline: 1-855-323-DCFS (3237)
National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233



Utah law enforcers and attorneys are reminding survivors of domestic violence that help to obtain protective orders is available, regardless of whether they want to pursue criminal charges against a perpetrator. 
Police, prosecutors and advocates gathered at the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office on Thursday to reinforce the message during a national month of awareness for domestic violence. 
The protective order process can be intimidating and requires filing paperwork in the state court system. But for those seeking help from the nonprofit Legal Aid Society of Salt Lake, it can start from the comfort of home with a call with a skilled paralegal, said Stewart Ralphs, the group’s executive director. 
“Most of our clients are working individuals, and having that option of doing it remotely is very beneficial for them,” Ralphs said. 
The nonprofit represented more than 2,500 people in its domestic violence program last year, and 200 more in a separate domestic relations program, he added.  
To obtain a protective order, Utahns don’t need to have been married or living with the other person. A civil stalking injunction is another option, and it’s based on an aggressor’s specific behavior rather than the type of relationship. Violating one of the orders is a criminal offense, with police required to make an arrest on the spot. 
Most of Utah’s various civil protective orders last three years, but provisions regarding custody and parent time run out much faster, after just 150 days, Ralphs noted. He said his organization can help people with custody or divorce cases, too. 
The Legal Aid Society helps low-income people within the bounds of Salt Lake County, but will refer those who don’t meet its restrictions on income or geography to other agencies, he said. 
On the criminal side, prosecutors can pursue other sorts of protective orders for victims when a case gets to their desks, said Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill. 
“We may have as many as six different kinds of protective orders in place throughout that process, working with our advocates, working with our counselors, and trying to meet the needs of our victim and survivor,” Gill said. “That is something I don’t think most people realize.”
For more information on particular protective orders and stalking injunctions, visit the state courts website: utcourts.gov.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Federal judge dismisses NAACP lawsuit over voter assistance limits in SC absentee ballot law
description: A federal judge tossed out a lawsuit this week from SC civil rights groups over state absentee voting assistance rules.
text:
Matthew J. Perry Jr. U.S. Courthouse in Columbia pictured March 14, 2025. U.S. District Judge Mary Geiger Lewis ruled this week the South Carolina NAACP and disabled residents didn’t have grounds to challenge a state law limiting assistance for absentee voting. (File photo by Abraham Kenmore/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A federal judge tossed out a lawsuit from South Carolina civil rights organizations over state absentee voting rules. In the lawsuit, the groups argued a law meant to prevent election fraud makes it harder for people with disabilities to vote.
The state NAACP and a trio of disabled nursing home residents filed suit last year challenging limits on assistance with mail-in ballots, arguing the limits violate the federal Voting Rights Act.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The 2022 law that created no-excuse-needed early voting set new parameters for voting by mail. People who can’t vote in person during the early voting window or on Election Day, including people with physical disabilities, can request a paper absentee ballot. But to prevent the possibility of fraud, legislators added a cap of five ballots that any one person could request or submit for someone else.
In nursing homes and group care settings, where residents often rely on a single staff member to help them vote, that makes casting a ballot difficult, attorneys for the state American Civil Liberties Union argued in a lawsuit filed in federal court in December 2025.
U.S. District Judge Mary Geiger Lewis ruled this week the state NAACP and disabled residents didn’t have grounds to challenge the law. Her order said the three nursing home residents never alleged they’d been denied assistance, only that they could be.
“Concern is understandable, but concern is not concreteness. A fear founded on future choices is too fragile for federal jurisdiction,” Geiger Lewis wrote in dismissing the case.
South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson celebrated the ruling Thursday, calling it “a win for election integrity in South Carolina.
“Citizens must have confidence that ballots are cast without interference in free and fair elections,” he added in a statement.
The ACLU’s legal director, Allen Chaney, said he’s disappointed.
The order “ignores the serious burdens that the challenged laws impose on disabled voters who rely on assistance to participate in our democratic system,” he said.
The ACLU is representing the NAACP in the case. Whether the groups will appeal is not yet decided, Chaney said.
Background on the case
The three voters named in the lawsuit include Robert Caldwell, a resident of a nursing home in Chester. According to the lawsuit, he’s relied on a single social worker, Barvette Gaither, to help him vote in years past.
Before the law, Gaither submitted between 10 and 25 ballots for residents each election. She’s since had to choose five residents to help and handed the rest off to other staff or the residents’ family, according to the lawsuit.
And Deborah Allen, an employee at Union Post Acute nursing home, helped most of its 25 residents submit ballots — including Jonathan Bell and Sherry Jenkins — because she knew the process and deadlines, the lawsuit said.
After the changes, Allen had to choose who to help. Bell had immediate family members nearby and therefore wasn’t among the five residents Allen opted to aid. Still, Bell worries he can’t rely on his family to help him fill out the ballot correctly and submit it on time, according to the lawsuit.
Federal lawsuit claims SC absentee ballot law makes voting harder for people with disabilities

In her ruling, Geiger Lewis said residents needed to show they were not only denied aid from the helper of their choosing because of the five-ballot limit, but that they had “no other permissible means of requesting or returning the ballot.”
“This is an encouraging reminder that the judicial system addresses real injuries, not speculation,” Wilson said in a statement.
The June 2022 primaries were the first election under the new law, which had the support of lawmakers and leaders of both parties.
State law already banned volunteers or employees for a candidate from collecting groups of ballots, a practice known as ballot harvesting.
The limit included in the change was a compromise, meant to also prevent people not associated with campaigns from collecting a massive number of ballots. The worry was people could potentially tamper with or discard the ballots, impacting a large number of votes, Rep. Brandon Newton, a Lancaster Republican who shepherded the bill through the House, previously told the SC Daily Gazette.

name: VTDigger
title: Disabled workers deserve an equal shot at jobs
description:
As technology erases jobs that disabled people once held, employers must make work accessible.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Disabled workers deserve an equal shot at jobs.
text:
This commentary is by Natalie Sinkew, who lives in St. Albans.
As a disabled citizen, I would like to address the struggles we face finding a place in the workforce. We are not asking for a job just because we have a disability. We are asking for the same opportunity as everyone else to apply for a job and show what we can do.
The world is changing quickly. Technology, automation and artificial intelligence are becoming a bigger part of everyday life and the workplace. These changes can make life easier in many ways, but they can also take away some of the jobs that were once available to people with disabilities.           
For example, office work used to include jobs such as filing papers, organizing documents, making copies and shredding paperwork. These jobs gave some people with disabilities an opportunity to work and contribute. Today, much of that work is done digitally or by machines. As technology changes the workplace, some jobs that people depended on are disappearing.
I understand we cannot stop the world from changing. I am asking that, as the world moves forward, we remember the people who may be left behind.
Many people with disabilities are able and willing to work. We may simply need accommodations to help us do our jobs. Some people may understand instructions better when they are shown with pictures or visual examples. Someone who uses a wheelchair or walker may need enough space to move safely. Someone who cannot stand for long periods may need to sit for part or all of their shift.
These accommodations may seem small, but they can make the difference between someone being able to work and not being able to work.
Unfortunately, accommodations are not always offered. Sometimes people with disabilities are denied job opportunities because an employer does not take the time to understand what they need or how a simple change could help them succeed. We are not asking employers to make our jobs easier.
We are asking employers to make our jobs accessible. There is a big difference.
As someone living with a disability, I feel there should be more opportunities for work-from-home jobs. For someone receiving support services to get to work, transportation can be affected if their staff is out for the day, sick or on vacation. For others, the opportunity to get to and from work can be affected if they can’t use public transportation as a backup. Working from home would help eliminate these issues.
We can work just as hard as anyone else. We may simply need different tools, different ways of doing things or reasonable accommodations. Having a disability does not mean that someone is lazy, unintelligent, unmotivated or unable to be a valuable employee.
There is also an emotional side to being repeatedly rejected for jobs. Imagine applying for job after job, hoping someone will finally give you a chance, only to keep hearing, “We found someone more qualified.” Imagine knowing you’re willing to work but feeling like employers focus more on what you can’t do, rather than on what you can.
After enough rejection, a person can lose confidence and begin to question whether they have a place in the workforce at all. 
We need employers who are willing to look beyond a disability and see the person. We need workplaces that are willing to provide reasonable accommodations. We need opportunities that allow people with disabilities to use their skills and talents instead of assuming that a disability means someone cannot be a productive employee. Most importantly, we need to be part of the conversation about the future of work.
We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for equal opportunity.
Give us the tools we need. Give us reasonable accommodations. Give us the chance to learn, contribute and prove ourselves. Please do not decide what we are capable of before giving us the opportunity to show you.
All we are asking is that, as the world changes, there is still a place for us in it.
Progress should not be measured only by how much technology can do. It should also be measured by whether everyone still has a place in the future that technology is creating.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: El Niño strengthens, could bring wetter winter weather to Kansas, expert says
description: TOPEKA — Kansas weather lived up to its tempestuous reputation Wednesday as the dregs of Hurricane Polo launched more than a dozen tornadoes throughout the state. “Kansas dished out tornadoes like Santa handing out candy canes,” wrote one storm chaser who posts online as Kansas Twisters. “No idea how many there were, but I was […]
text:
September storms dumped rain and lit up the sky near Topeka. Temperatures throughout the month were higher than normal, and some storms brought significant rainfall. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas weather lived up to its tempestuous reputation Wednesday as the dregs of Hurricane Polo launched more than a dozen tornadoes throughout the state.
“Kansas dished out tornadoes like Santa handing out candy canes,” wrote one storm chaser who posts online as Kansas Twisters. “No idea how many there were, but I was blessed to see 10-15 today.”
Accuweather reported that about 12 tornadoes touched down, but the severe weather created dozens of additional funnels. On Thursday, heavy rains resulted in flood watches. 
Recent weather has been unusual, with an “incredible run” of above normal temperatures for 37 days, as of Tuesday, said Matthew Sittel, assistant state climatologist. 
In a weekly climate report, Sittel said while high temperatures during the day were about normal, night temps weren’t falling into the lows expected for September. 
“The lack of chilly starts to the day at this point in the year is quite unusual and is, in some cases, unprecedented,” Sittel said. 
Goodland is an example, he said. The coldest temperature through Sept. 29 was 50 degrees, whereas the normal low is 45. 
“In over 130 years of climate data, there has never been a September at Goodland in which it didn’t fall into the 40s at least once,” Sittel said in the climate update. “It’s a similar story at Wichita, where 60 degrees is the coldest September temperature. This too is unprecedented.”
Sittel said that in 140 years of recordkeeping, 55 degrees is the warmest monthly minimum for September in Wichita.
 


What are El Niño and La Niña?
“During normal conditions in the Pacific ocean, trade winds blow west along the equator, taking warm water from South America towards Asia. To replace that warm water, cold water rises from the depths — a process called upwelling. El Niño and La Niña are two opposing climate patterns that break these normal conditions. Scientists call these phenomena the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle. El Niño and La Niña can both have global impacts on weather, wildfires, ecosystems, and economies. Episodes of El Niño and La Niña typically last nine to 12 months, but can sometimes last for years. El Niño and La Niña events occur every two to seven years, on average, but they don’t occur on a regular schedule. Generally, El Niño occurs more frequently than La Niña.” — National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
 



Winter weather projections may be affected by El Nino, a weather event that occurs when ocean temperatures rise, shifting wind patterns. Warnings of a “super El Niño” hit over the summer, with accompanying projections about what that means for the winter climate. 
Sittel said in an email to Kansas Reflector that the June, July and August average sea surface temperature was the “most above normal” for that time frame since 1950. 
“This is based on a new formulation called RONI, the Relative Oceanic Niño Index,” he said. “It’s an index that considers the temperatures with respect to a normal sea surface temperature that has changed over the years. Saying that it’s the warmest ever, if true, suggests this is all due to El Niño.”
Sittel hesitates to use the term “super El Niño,” which he said was coined by the news media and has no official definition. 
During an El Niño, the sea temperatures are warmer than average and, yes, it looks as if those temperatures are higher than in previous years. What does that mean for the upcoming months?
NPR reported that El Nino effects are ramping up the number of hurricanes in the Pacific and also responsible for the lack of hurricanes in the Atlantic. With no ocean in sight, what is Kansas likely to see? 
“That’s not a bad thing for Kansas,” Sittel said. “El Niño years on average have produced slightly above normal precipitation totals across Kansas during the winter months. The key here is this is an average; it’s not a guarantee that it will happen, just a tendency when all historical events are averaged.”
It is difficult to determine what will happen because there isn’t good historical data about strong El Niños, he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s brain drain problem starts with the first job, CEO says
description: Motorists traveling I-20 eastbound out of Louisiana into Vicksburg are greeted by a large "Welcome to Mississippi" sign, Friday, Aug. 22, 2025.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

Mississippi has spent years debating how to keep talented young people from leaving or to stop the brain drain.
Artificial intelligence adds a new dimension to that challenge. The risk is not simply that technology changes jobs. It is that employers use AI to remove the beginner work that once gave young people a reason to stay, learn and build a career.
A revised Stanford Digital Economy Lab analysis released this month found that employment among workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations was about 19% below where it would have been if it had kept pace with similarly aged workers in less-exposed occupations. The comparable gap in the July 2025 data vintage was 15%, and reduced hiring of young workers appears to be a major channel of adjustment.
That finding gives Mississippi employers a practical warning. If AI drafts the first memo, summarizes the first spreadsheet, prepares the first customer response and researches the first market question, the organization may gain efficiency while quietly deleting the experiences that teach a beginner how the business actually works.
Mississippi Today Ideas was launched in part to surface constructive solutions to the state’s long-running brain-drain challenge. One solution belongs inside the workplace: make the first job more developmental, not less.
Gleb Tsipursky Credit: Courtesy photo
Employers should create a first-project guarantee for entry-level knowledge workers. Every new hire in an AI-exposed role should own at least one meaningful project within the first 90 days, with AI handling some routine preparation while an experienced employee coaches the judgment around it.
The project does not need to be glamorous.
A new employee at a bank might use AI to organize customer information, then be responsible for identifying inconsistencies, documenting what requires human review and explaining a recommendation. A healthcare administrator might use AI to summarize scheduling or billing patterns, then investigate exceptions and speak with the people affected. A junior marketer might receive an AI-generated first draft, then test claims, interview a customer and defend the final message to a manager.
The common element is ownership. Beginners learn when they are responsible for getting from an imperfect starting point to a defensible result.
That requires managers to resist an understandable temptation. When AI saves five hours, the easiest move is to fill those five hours with more output.
The smarter move is to invest some of that time in supervised judgment. Pair newer employees with experienced reviewers. Give them difficult exceptions. Ask them to explain why an AI output is wrong, incomplete or inappropriate. Make them communicate the final answer to a real colleague or customer.
Then measure the outcome that matters: time to independent competence. How long does it take a new employee to handle a recurring decision without close supervision? How many coached reviews were required? Which exceptions still trip people up? Which AI-assisted tasks actually accelerate learning?
These questions turn workforce development from a training-calendar exercise into a management system.
They also fit Mississippi’s economic needs. A state worried about losing young talent cannot afford to offer graduates only two choices: leave for experience elsewhere or stay home for a job stripped of the experiences that build a career. Employers need to create roles in which young people can see a path from beginner to trusted professional.
AI can help. It can remove tedious preparation, surface examples quickly and give employees more chances to practice. But that benefit appears only when leaders deliberately preserve the human learning loop around the technology.
Mississippi does not need to protect every old task. It needs to protect the pathway from novice to capable worker. The employers that do that will not merely keep pace with AI. They will give more young Mississippians a reason to build their future at home.

Named the “Office Whisperer” by The New York Times, Gleb Tsipursky helps tech-forward leaders stop overpaying for AI while boosting engagement and innovation as the CEO of Disaster Avoidance Experts. His eighth book, due out with Georgetown University Press this fall, is “The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results.” Tsipursky earned his doctorate in the history of behavioral science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 2011, his master’s at Harvard University and his undergraduate degree at New York University. A proud Ukrainian American, he lives in Columbus, Ohio. In his free time, he said he spends abundant quality time with his wife to avoid his personal life turning into a disaster. See his full bio.

title: Highest monthly total of new voters since 2024 register to vote in Kentucky elections
description: More than 12,000 Kentuckians registered to vote in September — weeks ahead of midterm elections.  Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams’ office released the latest voter registration numbers Friday afternoon. The 12,380 new voters is the highest monthly total since 2024, which was a presidential election year.  The office said independent and third-par[...]
text:
Voting is one of the duties and privileges of living in a democracy. You'll also get one of these stickers. The deadline to register to vote in Kentucky is Monday, Oct. 5.  (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony) More than 12,000 Kentuckians registered to vote in September — weeks ahead of midterm elections. 
Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams’ office released the latest voter registration numbers Friday afternoon. The 12,380 new voters is the highest monthly total since 2024, which was a presidential election year. 
The office said independent and third-party voters again out-paced Republicans and Democrats’ registrations. 
“Polls across the country show tightening races. In Kentucky, too, voters who do not affiliate with Democrats or Republicans will decide whether Democrats or Republicans win our elections,” Adams said.
Kentucky has closed primaries, meaning independent and third-party voters do not vote in primaries, but they can vote in general elections. Adams has previously told the Kentucky Lantern he supports the idea to open the state’s primaries. 
Last month, net registration rose by 7,323 with 5,057 voters removed for various reasons. Of those removed, 3,626 were deceased, 876 had felony conviction, 420 moved out of state, 39 were adjudged mentally incompetent, 61 were duplicate registrations and 35 voluntarily de-registered.
Overall, Republicans make up 48% of registered voters in Kentucky, or about 1.6 million voters. Democrats are 41% of voters, or 1.3 million. Other political affiliations, like independent, make up 11% of voters. 
Monday, Oct. 5, is the last day to register to vote ahead of the general election on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Polls circulate showing tight secretary of state race, plus Bo Duke actor weighs in
description: Political polls are backing up what extensive campaign advertising indicates — that the Indiana secretary of state race is tight as early voting starts next week.
text:
Secretary of state candidates, from left: Independent Greg Ballard, Democrat Beau Bayh, Republican Max Engling and Libertarian Lauri Shillings. (Photos provided by campaigns)Political polls are backing up what extensive campaign advertising indicates — that the Indiana secretary of state race is tight as early voting starts next week.
Polling figures that spread online Friday show Republican nominee Max Engling and Democrat Beau Bayh within a few percentage points of each other and far ahead of Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings.
A poll from Hoosier Leadership for America, a political group associated with U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, found Engling with 38% support to Bayh’s 37%. Shillings had 6% support and Ballard 5% with 14% undecided in the poll of likely voters taken Sept. 27-30.
Engling was a top staffer to Banks before the Republican senator endorsed him in May over current Secretary of State Diego Morales for the GOP nomination.
Bayh’s campaign, meanwhile, put out figures from an early September poll showing Bayh ahead of Engling 42%-36%, with Ballard and Shillings both at 5% and 12% undecided.
That poll of likely voters was taken Sept. 1-3, about three weeks after Bayh had started statewide television advertising and before Engling’s broadcast ads began in mid-September.
The campaign of Ballard, a former Republican Indianapolis mayor who is running under the Lincoln Party banner, was rankled by the low figures from those polls. The campaign knocked the Hoosier Leadership for America poll as coming from a dark-money group that gave an improper $60,000 contribution to Engling’s campaign.
“If they think these numbers for Mayor Ballard are accurate, why are they spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to attack him on TV?” Ballard’s campaign said in a statement.
Shillings was encouraged by the poll, saying “Just 10% in this race changes Indiana politics forever. It sends a clear message that we’ve had enough and we aren’t going to be manipulated anymore. This poll has us at a strong 6% in a Republican sponsored poll. With 14% still undecided, we can make it past the 10% mark and send a clear, undeniable message to those who stopped listening to us long ago.”
Monday is the voter registration deadline for the Nov. 3 election. Early in-person voting starts Tuesday.
Bo Duke actor knocks Beau Bayh in video
Engling’s campaign also circulated on social media an video endorsement from 1980s TV series “Dukes of Hazzard” star John Schneider, who described himself as “the original Bo.”
Schneider, an outspoken President Donald Trump supporter from Louisiana, says in the one-minute video that Engling is “a real conservative, a real Republican with real experience” and disparages Bayh.
“I want you to listen to this Bo, OK?” Schneider said. “Not the other Beau. I mean, come on, he’s a cute kid, but he’s a cute kid who’s a Democrat running on Republican values and a Republican platform.”
