title: Amid bleak financial forecast, Brown Health announces buyouts, executive layoffs
description: The state’s largest hospital operator is offering buyouts to 200 non-clinical supervisors and laying off 10 executives amid financial pressures. Brown University Health announced a series of cost-cutting measures on Thursday, the first day of its new fiscal year. Like healthcare providers nationwide, the hospital conglomerate is struggling against rising cos[...]
text:
Rhode Island Hospital, the largest hospital in the state, is also a founding and principal teaching hospital of Brown University Health and The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The state’s largest hospital operator is offering buyouts to 200 non-clinical supervisors and laying off 10 executives amid financial pressures.
Brown University Health announced a series of cost-cutting measures on Thursday, the first day of its new fiscal year. Like healthcare providers nationwide, the hospital conglomerate is struggling against rising costs, a function of market pressures and federal budget cuts under H.R. 1.
“Healthcare organizations across the country continue to face significant financial pressures, and Brown Health is no exception,” John Fernandez, president and CEO of Brown University Health, said in a statement. “Rising pharmaceutical, labor and supply costs, combined with increasing levels of uncompensated care, insurer denials and bad debt, are creating unprecedented challenges. The actions we’re taking will help strengthen our financial foundation while protecting access to care and supporting future growth.” 
Brown Health has been sounding the alarm on its lopsided ledger for more than a year, suggesting in July 2025 that it might close the Newport Hospital birthing center, among other program and service cuts. It later committed to keeping the 10-unit labor and delivery center open amid pressure from local and state officials and advocates, and a $1.6 million earmark in the state’s fiscal 2027 budget.
But an increase in uncompensated care, the result of new federal policies restricting Medicaid eligibility and ending discounts for people who purchase their own insurance through state health exchanges, have started to take hold. 
Brown Health reported $90.5 million in costs associated with charity care, debt and insurance denials in the three-month period ending June 30, equal to more than 8% of the company’s net revenue. The company remained in the black, with a $23.4 million operating profit for that quarter — the most recent financial data available
But projections for fiscal 2027 look bleak. Brown Health said it expects to spend $346 million on charity care, insurance denials and debt in the new fiscal year — $71 million more than it spent in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 — due to federal policy changes.
The healthcare operator projects a $64 million deficit for this fiscal year.
That’s after a series of “efficiency measures,” including an executive restructuring completed in September that included consolidating or eliminating 10 jobs, as first reported by WPRI-TV 12. 
Voluntary buyouts were offered for up to 200 supervisors, managers and directors, who were eligible if they are 60 or older and have been with the company for five years as of Sept. 30. And, starting Jan. 1, Brown Health’s employee health plan won’t cover GLP-1 drugs prescribed solely for weight loss, though insurance coverage will continue for employees who use the medication to treat diabetes.
Information on how many employees use GLP-1s for weight loss was not immediately available.
The Newport Hospital birthing center was not named as a program at risk of closing, nor were any other services at The Miriam, Rhode Island Hospital, and Bradley. 
Jessica Wharton, a Brown Health spokesperson, confirmed in an email Friday that the birthing center will remain open, with fundraising efforts underway to close the $4.6 million gap needed to sustain the labor and delivery program. There are no plans to close or reduce other clinical programs right now, Wharton said.
Capital projects at The Miriam and Rhode Island hospitals, already underway, are expected to continue in fiscal 2027, with $210 million budgeted for facility upgrades, Brown Health said. There will also be a merit increase for employees in January, and ongoing investments in technology and equipment upgrades.
“Building a financially sustainable organization is essential to our ability to serve patients, support our workforce and invest in the future,” Fernandez said. “These decisions position Brown Health to continue delivering high-quality care and meet the evolving needs of the communities we serve.” 
While Brown Health’s bottom line has dipped into the red on and off since the pandemic, its Rhode Island hospitals remain profitable, with a $97.4 million combined revenue in the first nine months of fiscal 2026. By contrast, its Massachusetts hospitals, purchased from bankrupt former owner Steward Health Care in 2024, have underperformed. Staffing shortages and low patient volume led to operating losses at St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River, Morton Hospital in Taunton, and associated ambulatory centers. 
Results of the full fiscal 2026 financial performance, including breakdowns by hospitals are expected to be published by the end of the month. 
Doctors picket outside Rhode Island Hospital
On Friday, unionized resident physicians staged a picket and rally outside Rhode Island Hospital . The 700-member labor group, the first unionized doctors in Rhode Island, have been locked in contract negotiations with Brown Health for almost a year.
Melissa Uribe, a spokesperson for the Committee of Interns and Service Employees International Union, said salary and benefits are the major points of contention. However, doctors also want Brown Health to establish policies limiting access for federal immigration agents at the Providence hospital, and ensuring employees who need to miss work for mandatory immigration visa appointments don’t lose their jobs.
Dr. Samantha Palacios, a senior resident physician in the hospital emergency room, acknowledged the financial challenges her employer is facing, but insisted residents and interns should not sacrifice their demands for wage increases.
“It doesn’t change what our bottom line is,” Palacios, 30, said in a phone interview after the picket. “We are aware there are issues across all of the United States when it comes to funding things. We shouldn’t be what gets cut.”
A Nevada native with more than $400,000 in student loan debt, Palacios said she has not had a raise, even for cost-of-living, in her two years working for Brown Health.
“Our ability to live a life where we can survive can’t be what’s on the chopping block at the end of the day,’ she said.
Kelly Brennan, a Brown Health spokesperson, did not comment on the picket, but said there has been “substantial progress” in the negotiations with union doctors, including 90 tentative agreements.
“We remain focused on reaching a fair, sustainable agreement that recognizes the contributions of our interns and residents while ensuring we can uphold our commitments to high-quality patient care, our workforce, and the communities we serve,” Brennan said in a statement.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico group seeks to ban all corporate, ‘dark’ money spending on politics
description: A new coalition concerned about money’s growing influence on New Mexico politics is urging state lawmakers to consider legislation this January that would ban corporations from political spending.
text:
A new group, Money Out of Politics New Mexico, formed Oct. 1, 2026, to push the New Mexico Legislature to take up a measure that would prohibit corporations from spending money on political campaigns. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A new coalition concerned about money’s growing influence on New Mexico politics is urging state lawmakers to consider legislation this January that would ban corporations from political spending. 
The newly formed group, Money Out of Politics New Mexico, announced Thursday that it was launching a campaign modeled after similar efforts in Montana and Hawaii. Chair Natalie Wright Curley told Source NM that eliminating corporate and “dark” money from politics is a key step in returning democracy to the hands of regular people instead of the wealthy. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The “Corporate Money Out of Politics Act” would revoke corporations’ power to donate to political campaigns or ballot measures. 
Wright, a patent attorney, argues that states have constitutional authority under the 10th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution — which grants all powers to states that are not explicitly granted to the federal government — gives the Legislature authority to regulate state-issued corporate charters. That includes revoking corporate ability to spend money directly on campaigns or political action committees. 
The legislation aims to bypass the 2010 Citizens United ruling from the U.S. Supreme Court, which held that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend unlimited funds on campaigns. 
In May, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green signed Act 11, which established new restrictions on political spending activities by corporations and other “artificial persons” and limited the powers granted to those entities.
Groups including the Hawaii Chamber of Commerce have already challenged the law in court on First Amendment grounds, citing the Citizens United ruling.
Montana voters this November will also have a chance to pass a similar law through a ballot initiative known as the Montana Plan. 
According to Wright’s group, corporations and businesses have spent at least $3.7 million on various political campaigns so far in 2026. The group, citing news reports and Secretary of State’s Office filings, has totaled at least $2.6 million in “dark or otherwise opaque” spending this year, as well.
So-called “dark” money refers to donations from corporations or others funneled through Super PACs, a practice that leaves the public unable to determine donors’ identities. 
New ‘dark money’ group backs array of New Mexico House Democratic candidates

Wright said her group has already received tentative interest from lawmakers interested in carrying the bill, though the coalition is still securing a sponsor for the 60-day session beginning Jan. 19. 
The bill is necessary to begin to undo the damage of unfettered corporate spending in politics over the last 16 years, she said. 
“After Citizens United came out in 2010, I think it totally changed how our democracy operated,” she said. “It just really concerns me, how that’s continued to grow and be a problem, and how it affects the voices of everyday Americans.”
The group’s proposal follows a suite of legislative ethics reform proposals unveiled earlier this week by the think tank Think New Mexico, including several aimed at closing loopholes around “dark” money in state politics.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi households could pay more for energy because of federal policy changes
description: FILE - A natural gas meter operates Jan. 22, 2025, in Portland, Ore. (AP Photo/Jenny Kane, File)
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Households in the contiguous United States will pay thousands of dollars more for energy through 2040 because of federal policy changes since President Donald Trump returned to office such as canceling new clean energy projects, according to modeling released Friday by a nonpartisan think tank.
The Energy Innovation analysis found that households will pay an average of $6,500 more for energy, cumulatively through 2040. In five states, households will pay roughly $9,000 more: Oregon, Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia and Wyoming.
The California-based think tank said there will be more demand for natural gas for electricity because the administration is canceling new wind, solar and hydrogen projects and there will be more gasoline demand for transportation because Trump and Congress are revoking policies that incentivized efficient and lower-emissions vehicles. Higher demand increases prices.
Energy prices are elevated in many countries. The International Energy Agency said after Russia invaded Ukraine, record prices were observed between 2022 and 2024 in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan and Korea. In many countries, the rise has outpaced income growth and inflation since 2019, including the European Union and the United States.
In some areas of the U.S., demand from data centers is being blamed. The Iran war has sent oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, too. The Energy Information Administration expects residential U.S. customers to pay about 18.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2027, compared to 17.3 cents in 2025 and 18.2 cents in 2026.
FILE – Cars drive through an intersection along the Las Vegas Strip, May 1, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/John Locher, File)
The independent research firm Rhodium Group has also examined the issue, saying in April the U.S. has entered a new period of rising electricity prices. It cited increasing price volatility in natural gas, which is increasingly used to generate power; needed grid improvements; inflation; storm recovery and wildfire mitigation; and shifting policies.
Absent significant policy action, electricity prices likely will continue their significant rise over the next five years, the firm said.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Wednesday that lowering electricity prices remains a top priority and Trump is unleashing reliable energy like coal and natural gas to reverse the damage Democrats did to the grid by increasing clean energy. A 2025 Department of Energy report, mandated by Trump, warned of increasing blackouts if the U.S. continued closing coal and natural gas plants.
“Joe Biden created a grid crisis; President Trump is fixing it,” Rogers wrote in an email. “If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.”
The Republican president prioritizes fossil fuels to produce electricity, unlike Biden, who saw clean energy as a climate solution. The conservative Institute for Energy Research said in December that blue states have high rates because they have embraced aggressive renewable mandates, 100% carbon-free targets, premature coal and nuclear retirements and restrictions on natural gas infrastructure. It said high electricity prices are not an inevitability; they are a choice.
Analysis examined impact on states solely from federal policy changes
It focused on the sweeping package of tax breaks that slashed funding for clean energy tax credits, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump signed; environmental rollbacks, including clean air and power plant rules and the revocation of a scientific finding that underpinned the U.S. fight against climate change; the loosening of fuel economy standards and blocking of California’s novel rule banning the sale of new gas-powered cars by 2035; and federal actions to stop wind, solar and hydrogen projects.
FILE – Cars drive through an intersection along the Las Vegas Strip, May 1, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/John Locher, File)
These changes will result in annual household energy costs rising in every state in the contiguous U.S., plus job losses in 47 of 48 states and losses to the gross domestic product in 46 states, Energy Innovation said. It’s projecting 37,000 additional premature deaths from air pollution, $72 billion in additional healthcare costs and more than 9 billion tons of additional carbon pollution because of the environmental rollbacks. The analysis did not include Alaska or Hawaii because key federal data is not available for those two states, said Robbie Orvis, senior director for modeling and analysis.
“Across pretty much every state, things are worse. The outlook now is worse for states and the affordability crisis will be worse because of the combined set of policies,” Orvis said.
Climate Justice Alliance legislative director Mar Zepeda said her Washington, D.C., electric bill increased $200 in the past month. Zepeda blames electricity demands from data centers, and said federal “affordability” policies only exacerbate this.
“They may call it affordability, but affordable for whom and at what cost? Not for regular people,” Zepeda said in an email.
White House says the think tank is partisan
Rogers said it is “irresponsible” to classify Energy Innovation as nonpartisan because its employees have donated to Democrats and worked with Democrats on climate policy.
Spokesman Silvio Marcacci said Energy Innovation works with policymakers who want to cut emissions and lower bills, regardless of party. He said multiple Republican-led states have used their tool designed to model policies affecting energy use and emissions. Much of their data comes from government sources, including the EIA.
Rogers also said states led by Democrats that have embraced aggressive renewable mandates see higher energy costs, notably California and New York. She said this proves Republican policies are working.
However, in the Energy Innovation analysis, three of the five states facing the highest costs have Republican governors. Its research has found that states with high levels of wind and solar generation, including Republican-led Iowa and Oklahoma, have experienced the lowest rate increases.
The average price residential customers pay for electricity increased during Biden’s term and has continued to rise under Trump, according to EIA data.
Oregon households’ annual energy spending slated to increase the most
The modeling projects federal policy changes will increase annual energy spending in Oregon by $840 per household in 2035 and $1,200 per household in 2040, with a cumulative $9,300 increase from 2026 to 2040 — the highest of any state.
The Oregon Citizens’ Utility Board advocates for residential utility customers. Executive Director Bob Jenks called those numbers “frightening” because Oregon already has an energy affordability problem. He cited steep rate increases as utilities make upgrades and data centers use more power.
As costs rise, Jenks expects utilities to disconnect more customers who can’t afford their bills.
Jenks said wind and solar are essential for affordable electricity, and he wants the federal government to partner with states to develop the energy they need.
“We’re trying to optimize among the resource options we have, and they’re trying to take things away and raise the costs,” he said.

title: Pillen declares emergency for southeast Nebraska after heavy rain, severe flooding
description: LINCOLN — Southeast Nebraska is under a state of emergency following heavy rain and severe flooding as state officials assess damage to potentially apply for federal support. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen declared the emergency Thursday afternoon while surveying affected areas in northern Lancaster County, as first reported by 10/11 News, which was reporting on s[...]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, front, is briefed on heavy rain and severe flooding in northern Lancaster County that occurred the night before on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)LINCOLN — Southeast Nebraska is under a state of emergency following heavy rain and severe flooding as state officials assess damage to potentially apply for federal support.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen declared the emergency Thursday afternoon while surveying affected areas in northern Lancaster County, as first reported by 10/11 News, which was reporting on scene before the governor arrived. The record-setting rainfall Wednesday resulted in flooded roadways and multiple rescues of stranded motorists.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signs a disaster declaration following heavy rain and severe flooding in northern Lancaster County that occurred the night before on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)
Lancaster County Engineer Pam Dingman told KETV Newswatch 7 that the storm could have lasting effects on county infrastructure, such as bridges and the county pipe culvert system.
“Please continue to exercise extreme caution around flooded areas and damaged infrastructure, and join me in expressing gratitude for the first responders and road crews who have worked around the clock responding to this flooding and keeping Nebraskans safe,” Pillen said in a Thursday social media post.
A spokesperson for the governor said Friday that damage assessments are still occurring, so the state will identify specifically affected counties later.
The declaration frees up state resources for recovery and requires state and federal agencies to support the state’s adjutant general, who leads the Nebraska Emergency Management Agency.
NEMA and the Nebraska National Guard, plus representatives for Lancaster County and the Lower Platte South Natural Resource District, joined Pillen in surveying the damage.
NEMA is working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Small Business Administration and Natural Resources Conservation Service, Pillen’s office said Friday, to sling resources as damage assessments are completed. The governor’s office said that work will help determine if and what level of assistance will be available for recovery.
A disaster declaration for southeast Nebraska following heavy rain and severe flooding Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC State’s decision to ax 9 degrees follows report on unpopular programs statewide
description: While South Carolina State University is the least compliant with the state's "program productivity" standards, it’s far from the only public university offering degrees with little-to-no participation.
text:
A South Carolina State University student walks outside the school's new engineering building Tuesday, Feb. 25, 2025. Only 36% of degrees at the historically Black university meet state enrollment and graduation benchmarks for productivity — the lowest rate of compliance in the state. (File photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Just over a third of South Carolina State University’s degree programs meet state policies for enrollment and graduation — the lowest rate of compliance among the Palmetto State’s public, four-year schools.
Leaders of the historically Black college are taking steps to change that.
Meanwhile, Statehouse leaders have signaled they’ll continue pushing schools to control their costs and phase out less popular academic programs that lose money or won’t land graduates a good-paying job.
At the heart of the matter is setting students up for success rather than trapping them under student loans they can’t afford to repay, as well as ensuring the state’s taxpayer-supported colleges are financially sound, especially as declining birthrates have universities competing over a smaller pool of college-age students nationwide.
It’s against that backdrop that the governing board of SC State voted last week to eliminate nine degree programs from its catalog — four of which have not enrolled a single student in the past decade.


“We understand that decisions involving academic programs can create anxiety and uncertainty for students, faculty, staff, alumni and others who care deeply about SC State,” reads a joint letter last Friday from university President Alexander Conyers and Interim Provost Louis Whitesides.
“At the same time, we must look ahead,” the letter continued.
“The needs of South Carolina’s workforce are changing, and SC State must continue to evolve with them.”
Out of compliance
While SC State is the least compliant with “program productivity” standards, with just 36% of programs meeting the state’s definition, it’s far from the only public university offering degrees with little-to-no participation.
On average, 20% of degrees at South Carolina’s 13 public, four-year colleges don’t meet either enrollment or completion benchmarks, according to the latest data from the SC Commission on Higher Education, released in June.
Those benchmarks are pretty low.
A bachelor’s degree program meets compliance with just 13 students enrolled and at least eight students graduating yearly, using an average over five years. The benchmarks for master’s and doctorate degree programs are even lower.
Noncompliant programs can be under probation for at least six years before the higher education agency even puts it on the termination list.
Colleges are supposed to use the productivity report to measure whether they’re offering degrees students actually want for careers and employers actually need. The commission’s review is also supposed to reduce duplication among South Carolina’s colleges. But the agency has been several years behind on producing the report.
SC colleges pushed to trim expenses, degree programs in preparation for ‘enrollment cliff’

Besides, the agency has no authority to force colleges to end programs. It can only make recommendations. The decision lies with each college governing board.
This leads to inconsistency across colleges, said Oran Smith, who sits on both the higher education commission and the governing board for Coastal Carolina University.
“Many boards only meet four or five times a year. Usually, there’s a packed agenda. There isn’t much discussion of these types of matters,” he said.
That’s changing due to the debate by Statehouse budget writers who control how much taxpayer money the colleges receive.
“The Legislature’s action, asking for programs to be reviewed, has caused more discussion of this issue,” Smith said. “I think that’s very healthy because someone needs to be paying attention.”
GOP leaders in the House tried to force cuts this year.
A rule in the initial version of this year’s state budget, as passed by the House, would have required colleges to suspend at least half of their programs that lose money for four consecutive years. The chamber also sought to route money to degrees in science, technology, engineering and math fields, which tend to have more job openings.
But senators removed that proposal after college officials cited unintended consequences of tying cuts to a degree program’s profitability. Looking at the ledger alone could inadvertently include in-demand careers, such as nursing, that have high operating costs, they said.
Reconsidering standards
House Ways and Means Chairman Bruce Bannister said legislators’ push for change will continue next year.
“The purse strings are where we get our influence,” the chamber’s chief budget writer told the SC Daily Gazette. “We will keep trying to make the dollars follow the colleges whose programs deliver the most return to students.”
SC’s largest colleges celebrate record applicants for fall 2025. Most aren’t from SC.

The “program productivity” report will be part of the discussion when college officials come before budget writers with their requests, said the Greenville Republican.
But the Commission on Higher Education also questions whether its benchmarks for enrollment and graduation rates adequately measure a program’s success.
This summer, the commission began a revamp of its monitoring process, which should be completed by the end of this fiscal year. Changes could include measuring whether cuts actually save money.
At Coastal, for example, Smith said, officials have determined that programs with low enrollment don’t lose money when the classes involved are part of students’ general education requirements for other degrees. The professors are still needed.
In its June report, the higher education agency recommended termination for 137 of the roughly 1,000 programs reviewed at South Carolina’s public universities. For 135 of those, it’s the graduation benchmark where they consistently fall short. An additional 51 programs don’t meet the benchmarks and are flagged for review over the next six years.
Statewide, colleges have committed to ending 43 programs on the list.
‘Best interests of our students’
Programs recommended for the chopping block largely fall into four categories:

Education degrees tied to a specific subject area, such as those to become a K-12 science teacher, a math teacher or a special education teacher
Language, religion and cultural studies
General science and math degrees, such as chemistry, biology, physics or economics
Arts degrees, such as theater, music, English, philosophy or history

SC State’s flagged courses are no exception.
But before now, the governing board of the Orangeburg college has been more reluctant than its counterparts at other schools to eliminate and replace programs.
Over the past five years, for example, the University of South Carolina has terminated 26 programs, including all of its foreign language degrees, and replaced them with 28 higher-demand programs.
And in March, Clemson officials told legislators they shut down about 10 programs a year on average.
Elimination of underperforming programs is something Conyers has advocated since taking the helm at SC State in April 2022. The debate in the Legislature may have aided his case to the board.
“Ultimately, we believe these actions are in the best interests of our students, the university, and the taxpayers of South Carolina,” reads the joint letter from Conyers and Whitesides. “They also will position SC State to invest its resources strategically and develop new academic programs aligned with emerging workforce needs and career opportunities.”
While the Commission on Higher Education can’t force colleges to end programs, it does have authority in approving new programs.
And having so many underperforming degrees on its books makes it difficult for SC State to get that approval for degrees in greater demand, said SC State spokesman Sam Watson.
In addition to ending the nine degrees, the board approved cancelling more than 200 classes that had fewer than 10 students enrolled this fall. Many of those courses were consolidated, changing some students’ class times but increasing the number of students in the classes.
The changes impact 111 students, 3% of the Orangeburg college’s student body, across five programs. While no new students can enroll, those already in the programs can finish their degrees.
The axed program with the largest enrollment — 82 students — will shift from an engineering technology degree, centered around the hands-on construction of systems, to a straight engineering degree more focused on system design.

 Eliminated degrees
No students enrolled:

Business education
Technology education
Dramatic arts education
Professional land surveying

Combined enrollment of 29 students:

Art education
Social studies education
Middle-level education
Mathematics

82 students enrolled:

Mechanical engineering technology

Source: South Carolina State University


Some of the course closures involved specialized, degree-specific classes that are no longer needed, Watson said.
While the school is deleting programs, that does not mean all the courses associated with those programs will go away. Those that are essential to other degree programs remain.
For example, while SC State students can no longer get a bachelor’s degree in mathematics, math courses essential to science, engineering and other degrees continue.
Conyers estimates the closures could save the school more than $5 million but did not say how staffing levels might change.
State Rep. Jerry Govan, D-Orangeburg, agrees it makes little sense to offer courses where students aren’t taking the classes. The SC State graduate said that’s where the board of trustees comes in.
“That’s why we appoint them,” he said. “They are the boots on the ground and are supposed to be making these decisions.”
Bannister, the House budget chief, also commended Conyers for taking action. 
A turnaround success
The president wants to ensure his alma mater doesn’t get back into a fiscal hole.
A decade ago, it was in danger of shutting its doors.
Amid the Great Recession, the school faced shrinking enrollment and declining revenues but did not make the cuts necessary to match, leading to budget deficits. To fill the holes, it transferred millions of dollars meant for agriculture research, contributing to its cash flow crisis, according to a 2014 report from the state inspector general.
Accreditors with the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges put the school on probation, putting the school at risk of losing its accreditation. Students cannot receive federal financial aid at unaccredited colleges.
Legislators and then-Gov. Nikki Haley responded in 2015 by wiping out the entire S.C. State board of trustees.
They also bailed the college out with more than $18 million in loans and a one-time payment of $4.6 million to pay off other debt. They then struck a deal to forgive much of the debt.
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-Columbia, one of S.C. State’s most prominent and powerful alum, supported the overhaul, which then saw the college taken off probation as legislators elected new leadership.
New research status for SC State highlights its enrollment, fiscal turnaround

The new board installed one of its own, James Clark, as president in 2016. The school saw financial and enrollment improvements over Clark’s tenure, but alumni and faculty criticized him for those numbers not growing fast enough.
The board fired Clark in 2021 and Conyers took over a year later.
Since then, SC State has boosted its research profile, last year reaching the second-highest level of research under the Carnegie Commission on Higher Education’s ranking system.
It also has seen a rebound in enrollment but has yet to return to the high of 4,650 students it boasted in 2007. Leadership has cited a lack of student housing as holding it back from further growth.
Bannister, the House budget chief, commended Conyers for putting SC State and its students on a path for success. 
Govan also said legislators should not discount the impact historical racial discrimination has had on the state’s only public, four-year historically Black university.
“I don’t think we can talk about one without the other,” he said.
In 2023, the U.S. secretaries for education and agriculture sent a letter to Gov. Henry McMaster saying SC State was historically underfunded by nearly $500 million over 30 years compared to Clemson, the state’s predominately white land-grant university.
More recent data show that’s no longer the case. In 2020, SC State received $13,768 in state funding per student versus $8,691 at Clemson.
Bannister said the Legislature has sought to direct more dollars to SC State in the last few budget cycles, in particular to refurbish old facilities and build more housing.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Internal poll shows Democrat Dembo leads GOP’s Alvarado in central Kentucky House race
description: An internal poll from Democrat Zach Dembo’s campaign shows the candidate with a five-point lead over Republican Ralph Alvarado in Kentucky’s central congressional district.  Pollster GQR, which tends to favor Democratic candidates, found in a survey of 401 likely voters, 42% backed Dembo, 37% backed Alvarado and 11% supported third-party or independent candi[...]
text:
Zach Dembo speaks to constituents at a campaign fundraiser on Sept. 11, 2026, in Paint Lick, Kentucky. (Photo by Arden Barnes for KY Lantern)An internal poll from Democrat Zach Dembo’s campaign shows the candidate with a five-point lead over Republican Ralph Alvarado in Kentucky’s central congressional district. 
Pollster GQR, which tends to favor Democratic candidates, found in a survey of 401 likely voters, 42% backed Dembo, 37% backed Alvarado and 11% supported third-party or independent candidates. The survey says 9% of the voters were undecided. The poll, which had a margin of error of 4.9%, surveyed voters between Sept. 25 and 30.
In a statement to the Kentucky Lantern, Dembo said the poll shows that “Central Kentucky families are fed up with a system they know is rigged against them.
“We’ve got more work to do with a month left until the election — and it’s all gas, no breaks.”
The poll comes on the heels of an independent election predictor, Sabato’s Crystal Ball out of the University of Virginia, moving the outcome of the race in the 6th Congressional district toward Dembo, calling it a “leans Republican” district. The predictor had previously rated the race as safe for the GOP. 
“This one is real, as noted by race raters who moved this race in Dembo’s direction,” GQR’s conclusion said. “A combination of a toxic environment for the ruling party, a flawed Republican nominee and an appealing, centrist Democratic candidate has pushed Dembo into a lead.” 
The poll is one data point, but it follows a national trend of a midterm election that favors some Democrats in red states. Stephen Voss, a political science professor at the University of Kentucky, said “there are a variety of reasons why internal polls tend to look better for the campaign that paid for them other than because of bias in the data.” 
Voss said respondents may pick up on which candidate’s poll they are answering and respondents may also face “desirability effects” where they pick the answer that is more desirable to the interviewer.  
The GQR poll findings said that while 70% of voters know of Alvarado, his favorability is low, with 22% having a favorable opinion. On the other hand, 34% had an unfavorable opinion. 
Plus, the favorability of President Donald Trump, who endorsed Alvarado in the primary, has lowered in the district. During the last presidential election in 2024, Trump carried the 6th Congressional District by 15 points. Of those surveyed in the poll, 57% had an unfavorable opinion and 39% a favorable opinion. Trump is slated to campaign in other states ahead of the November midterm elections as his approval ratings fall nationwide. 
Dembo was recognized by 63% of those surveyed with a 30% favorable opinion and an 18% unfavorable opinion.. The state’s top Democrat, Gov. Andy Beshear, who has campaigned with Dembo, has a 62% favorable rating against 29% unfavorable. In the 2023 gubernatorial race, Beshear won the district by 19 points. 
As for the overall numbers, the findings said that independent Jay Bowman and the Kentucky Party’s Pete Lynch “account for 11 percent of the vote share and provide a destination for the growing number of disgruntled Republicans.” With the third-party and independent vote and undecided voters allocated, Dembo leads 46% to 43%. 
Ralph Alvarado is the Republican nominee in the 6th Congressional District. (Photo provided by Ralph Alvarado’s campaign)
Public independent polling has been scarce in the race. An August poll from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which is backing Dembo, had the race tied at 47% between Dembo and Alvarado. 
Another race watcher, the Cook Political Report, moved the race from solid Republican to likely Republican in July. 
Voss, the political science professor, also said campaigns in general get more internal polling than what is publicly available and are “cherry-picking what to show.” Journalists may get one poll while fundraising emails reference another. 
“It’s not a bias in the data. It’s a bias in the release of the data,” Voss said. 
Tres Watson, a former spokesperson for the Republican Party of Kentucky, said that campaigns mainly release polls for fundraising as “people want to donate to the winner.” Hearing the top-line results of the poll, he didn’t feel like it matched what he sees on the ground in Central Kentucky and added the seat has been in Republican hands since 2012.
Kentucky is also one of the hardest states to poll in, Watson said. People don’t answer the phone or may lie to pollsters.
“There’s distrust of the polling apparatus, distrust of pollsters, distrust of national politicians — regardless of party,” he said.
Polls can be useful to campaigns for checking trends among voters and not necessarily forecasting the outcome of an election.
Hearing that the latest poll had 11% backing an independent or third-party candidate, Watson said that was a “ridiculous number,” adding that “there is a 0% chance that independent and third party candidates will get 11%.”
The central Kentucky House seat is open this fall as Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr is running for U.S. Senate. 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. 
This is a developing story.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Risch campaign says rumors of using 1917 Idaho law to avoid Senate election are ‘completely false’
description: As the Nov. 3 general election nears, rumors have cropped up that a never-used, 1917 Idaho state law could be used to circumvent the race for U.S. Senate.  The campaign for incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch strongly denied these rumors. The more-than-a-century-old law states that if a U.S. senator from Idaho resigns or dies […]
text:
Bonneville County residents cast their votes during the May 21, 2024, primary election at The Waterfront Event Center in Idaho Falls, Idaho. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)As the Nov. 3 general election nears, rumors have cropped up that a never-used, 1917 Idaho state law could be used to circumvent the race for U.S. Senate. 
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, delivers remarks during the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine USS Idaho’s commissioning ceremony at Naval Submarine Base New London in Groton, Connecticut, on April 25, 2026. (Photo by Chief Mass Communication Specialist Darren M. Moore/U.S. Navy)
The campaign for incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch strongly denied these rumors.
The more-than-a-century-old law states that if a U.S. senator from Idaho resigns or dies within 30 days of the general election, then the governor could appoint a replacement and “no election for United States senator to fill said vacancy shall be held at such general election.” 
Risch is running against Todd Achilles, who has taken heat from from Risch’s campaign for running as an independent after serving in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat.
“This rumor is completely false,” Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email. “Jim Risch is leading in the polls. He is running an aggressive campaign. He will be victorious on November 3. This conspiracy theory is being perpetrated by our desperate opponent to take attention away from his liberal record. The only people who gamed the system this election were our opponent’s supporters who coerced Democrat David Roth to drop out and clear the field for Todd Achilles.”
A spokesperson for the Achilles campaign denied the rumors started with the independent candidate’s campaign. 
“What’s concerning is that Jim Risch is pointing fingers instead of assuring voters that he won’t use the law in a way that would bypass the will of the voters,” Achilles’ Communication Director Crispin Gravatt wrote in an email. “He should clearly state that he will remain in the race through Election Day and, if elected, intends to serve the full 6-year term until he is 89 years old.” 
U.S. Senate candidate Democrat David Roth won his primary election in May, but withdrew from the race and removed his name from the ballot in September, citing a lack of support from his party. 
The Idaho Capital Sun reached out to the governor’s office for comment, but did not receive one.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How are the other Idaho U.S. Senate candidates responding? 

At a candidate forum held Wednesday evening in Caldwell, Risch’s opponents addressed the possibility of the law being put to use. Risch wasn’t in attendance at Wednesday’s forum. 
“This has bubbled up recently. I don’t know if you guys have seen this,” moderator McKay Cunningham, a director of the master of applied public policy at College of Idaho, told candidates Wednesday. “Is this conspiracy theory? … What is the likelihood of this sort of thing happening? Maybe you haven’t even heard of it, but I’d like to get the candidates’ impressions on this question,” Cunningham said. 
In this file photo, Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Independents Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, each said they thought the law’s use wouldn’t be well-met with Idaho voters. Most expressed doubt that it would be. 
“I think if it were tried, it would be challenged in courts, and it would be a whole big mess,” Loesby said. 
He said a more likely situation would be for Risch, who is 83, to retire after winning the election at some point into the six-year term. 
Fleming said the idea was “frightening,” but that she is “not predicting that would happen.” 
“If they were to try that, it would cause, I think, great outrage within the state of Idaho,” Fleming said. 
Achilles said he thought the move would be unconstitutional. 
“It creates, I think, a very dangerous situation where you’re getting into a never-ending loop of never electing another senator in the state of Idaho,” Achilles said. “… I don’t think Idahoans would stand for that.” 
 What are the legal considerations of the law? 

Cunningham in a Thursday interview with the Idaho Capital Sun noted that constitutionality of the law has never been put to the test because it’s never been used. Courts have not had the chance to weigh in on the law. 
McKay Cunningham
“I think the arguments (against the law) would stem from provisions in the Idaho Constitution as well as in the U.S. Constitution that provide qualified citizens the right to vote,” he said. “There are a lot of Supreme Court cases that talk about this constitutional right.” 
He said he could imagine candidates bringing another claim against the law over potential violations to their due process rights for their candidacy if no election took place. 
“It would create such a mess,” Cunningham said. “I think at the heart of it, and this is not a legal argument necessarily, but the heart of it is representational democracy and the right to vote is preservative of all other rights.” 
In 2025, Idaho state legislators proposed House Bill 324, which would have amended this law to allow the governor to select a day for a special election in the case of a U.S. Senate vacancy within 30 days of the general election, rather than appoint the replacement. 
The bill was introduced by then-Rep. Kevin Andrus, R-Lava Hot Springs, and Rep. Josh Tanner, R-Eagle. The legislation never received a hearing and did not advance.

text:
Luther College and a Minnesota public school district have partnered to offer students preferred admission and scholarship funding. (Photo courtesy of Luther College)Luther College is partnering with a Minnesota school district to provide its students with preferred admission guidelines and scholarship funds.
The Decorah private college announced in a news release it has launched a Preferred Admission Partnership with Rushford-Peterson Schools, a public school district in Rushford, Minn. According to the release, this partnership is similar to one the college entered into with Decorah Community School District just over a year ago.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Strengthening connections with schools in our region is a priority for Luther College, and we are excited to add Rushford-Peterson Schools as our first partner from Minnesota,” said Luther College President Brad Chamberlain in the release. “Luther and Rushford-Peterson have long-standing connections, and we are excited for how this will deepen our relationship.”
Through the new partnership, students who maintain an unweighted grade-point average of 3.25, complete Algebra II by the end of their junior year and decide to opt in will receive preferred admission and become eligible for a $500 scholarship and others offered by the institution, the release stated.
Matthew Beatty, vice president for enrollment manager at Luther College, said in the release that the institution and school district “have a long-standing relationship,” and Rushford-Peterson students have seen success at Luther. The “clear and supportive pathway” from Rushford-Peterson to a Luther degree helps to build on that relationship.
“The Preferred Admission Partnership opens doors for Rushford-Peterson students to pursue an excellent academic opportunity close to home, recognizing their hard work and supporting their next steps,” said Rushford-Peterson Schools Superintendent Ben Bernard in the release.

title: Federal funds for local police enforcement accelerated Trump immigration crackdown
text: WASHINGTON — This summer, arrests of immigrants in the United States soared to the highest levels since President Donald Trump returned to office.An unprecedented increase in cooperation between local and state law enforcement and federal immigration officers through collaborations known as 287(g) agreements helped drive numbers up. The agreements allow state and local law enforcement agencies to enforce parts of federal immigration law and have become an arm of Trump’s mass deportation campaign. Republicans in Congress have provided billions in federal funding for local departments that accept the agreements, creating a deluge of new partners.Theresa Cardinal Brown, a senior Department of Homeland Security official during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, said the billions in new funding has helped the program grow. “Mostly, 287(g) agreements were voluntary, and the costs were borne by the state and local government to train their own people,” she said. “Now, the federal government has money to pay them, and so that's encouraging more states and localities to do it because it's a budget plus-up.”In June, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded roughly 43,000 immigration arrests, followed by 49,000 in July and nearly 51,000 in August. ICE does not distinguish between arrests initially made by local law enforcement or federal officials.Those three months also saw the most new 287(g) agreements signed since Trump took office, according to a States Newsroom analysis of government data.“ICE has increased efforts with state and local law enforcement to assist federal immigration officers in our efforts to make America safe again,” a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement to States Newsroom.But those efforts have generated protests in some of the communities where they’ve appeared.Democrats in Maryland and Maine passed laws restricting cooperation between local police and ICE. The Maryland measure’s supporters said it would reduce distrust of police.Skyrocketing growthThe president's signature 2025 domestic policy bill, the “One, Big Beautiful” Act, set aside about $4 billion for state and local governments to conduct immigration enforcement, including 287(g) programs. The Secure America Act passed in June allocated more than $31 billion to implement those agreements as well. Both packages were passed by Republicans through a legislative maneuver known as reconciliation that did not need Democratic votes. The funds incentivized massive growth. Before Trump took office in January 2025, the federal government had agreements with 135 state and local police departments. As of Oct. 1, those agreements skyrocketed to 2,608, according to DHS data. Local departments or state agencies in 38 states have 287(g) agreements, with the highest numbers in Texas and Florida, where there are state laws requiring local law enforcement to partake in the program. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday the Florida Highway Patrol was eligible for $26 million in reimbursements from the federal government for arrests from April through June.“My educated guess would be that a large number of the arrests and detentions that we've seen increasing in recent months in the summer were because there was an increase in 287(g) agreements in Texas and Florida, but other parts of the country as well,” said Ariel G. Ruiz Soto, a senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a think tank that studies global migration.ICE does not always specify when an immigration arrest is made through the partnership program, but the Deportation Data Project, a project of the University of California schools in Berkeley and Los Angeles that analyzes government immigration enforcement data, has attributed at least 6,150 arrests in July, about 12.5% of all arrests for that month.Only 12 states have no such agreements. They are California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington state.Three modelsThe partnership program was created in a 1996 law, but not actively used until the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It first received federal appropriations in 2006.Three types of partnerships operate within the program.The loosest type of agreement is the jail enforcement model, where deputized officers can inquire about the immigration status of people arrested on state or local charges, as well as hold a noncitizen for ICE to pick up for up to 48 hours. In another model, the warrants service officer model, ICE trains, certifies and allows state and local law enforcement to issue administrative warrants, which are not signed by a judge, but by an ICE official requesting the arrest of a noncitizen. Local law enforcement officers under this model do not inquire about immigration status. The task force model, which involves the greatest immigration enforcement by local officers, allows for immigration officials to deputize local officers to partake in immigration duties such as asking about immigration status or even detaining people and transferring them to ICE.As part of its immigration crackdown, the second Trump administration revived the task force model after the Obama administration discontinued it in 2012 over concerns of racial profiling. It has seen the largest increase under Trump, Ruiz Soto said.More than 71% of 287(g) agreements now use the task force model, according to Titus Consulting, a firm that tracks the agreements. About 7% use the jail enforcement model and more than 21% use the warrant model. The task force model is “hands down,” the most effective method in arresting noncitizens, said Todd Bensmen, a senior research fellow for the Border Security and Immigration Center at The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank. “If they're not deputized under that, they just come into contact with people that are fully … deportable, and then just leave them be,” he said of local law enforcement. “They can just arrest them on the spot and call ICE, and that way you have a really dramatic force multiplier and ICE doesn't have to do anything but come and pick them up.” Program changesIn 2006, the Bush administration took an interest in exploring 287(g) programs, specifically the jail enforcement model because it was easy for ICE to identify people who are subject to an immigration arrest, said Brown.“If your job is to find people, wow, that's the easiest thing to do,” she said of the jail model. Brown said that spurred the idea for the Secure Communities program. Under the program, the FBI automatically sent fingerprints of a person booked in custody to DHS to check against its immigration database. If the person was a noncitizen who was unauthorized in the U.S., then ICE was notified.The program was voluntary, but there was pushback from immigration advocates during the Obama administration, Brown said. “There was a concern that this was mixing criminal enforcement and immigration enforcement in ways they weren't meant to, (and) it was creating fear among immigration communities of reporting crimes for fear that they would be arrested,” she said. The Obama administration pulled back and redirected the Secure Communities program to a federal government model.  “They turned it from like a community-by-community rollout to just a federal-to-federal information sharing agreement that remains in place today,” she said. Brown said the difference now is that some communities have decided when ICE is notified, if at all, and whether or not to honor detainers, which are requests from ICE to hold an immigrant until federal immigration officers arrive. Local governments that have not wanted to participate in federal immigration enforcement have been dubbed sanctuary cities. The Trump administration has threatened to pull federal funding from those cities that don’t want to aid in immigration enforcement and has offered an influx of cash to states and local governments that have agreed to participate. The Republican Congress has funded the program for the next three years, Ruiz Soto noted.“It would then come to … what a future administration or a future Congress would do to continue expanding this or not fulfill them anymore,” he said. “But clearly right now ICE has significant funding to last for 287(g) and much more other enforcement in the near future.”

RULEVILLE – A nonprofit that supports organizations that advance social justice is enabling the expansion of the Fannie Lou Hamer Digital Driving Tour as the country commemorates the 109th anniversary of the civil rights icon’s birth.
The Jonathan Logan Family Foundation awarded $25,000 to the “Fannie Lou Hamer’s America” project to support research and the production of 12 new tour stops and multimedia resources, highlighting historic locations connected to Hamer’s grassroots organizing, voting rights work, civic participation, food justice and community empowerment.
Each location will include short documentary-style videos, archival audio, historical photographs, news articles and immersive digital resources that make Hamer’s story more accessible.
The Jonathan Logan Family Foundation earlier invested in the award-winning documentary film “Fannie Lou Hamer’s America” that aired on PBS and WORLD Channel in 2022 and supported community engagement.
“Monica Land’s acclaimed documentary film ‘Fannie Lou Hamer’s America’ helped bring her aunt Fannie Lou’s story to national audiences through rare archival footage and speeches,” Foundation President and CEO Jonathan Logan said in a news release. “The driving tour is the perfect complement to the film, allowing even more people to learn about the people and places that shaped Hamer’s life and work.”
The original 10-location driving tour was part of the film’s “Find Your Voice” K-12 curriculum. Land and videographer and editor Tommy Kirkpatrick of CommonHouse Productions produced a relaunched tour in August with 12 short videos featuring archival footage, photographs and historical materials with sites in Mississippi and Atlantic City. 
The driving tour is available on the film’s website and features additional resources, and their YouTube Channel. 
Born on a plantation in rural Mississippi on Oct. 6, 1917, Fannie Lou Hamer was a voting rights advocate, humanitarian and community organizer who became one of the most powerful voices of the Civil Rights Movement. 
The Logan Foundation supports organizations that advance social justice through investigative journalism, documentary film and arts and culture. 
The Jonathan Logan Family Foundation is a Mississippi Today donor.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Will Mississippi better prepare for the next winter storm? Officials are dubious.
description: Winter storm snow and ice cover the landscape near Boyle on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
As autumn begins to take hold in north Mississippi, leaves are falling onto roads still littered with tree limbs and other debris from last winter’s torment, state officials said. 
Over eight months since Winter Storm Fern, the Mississippi Department of Transportation said its “massive” debris cleanup effort will likely last until Halloween. Officials in three counties – Lafayette, Union and Tishomingo – estimated they amassed roughly 2.5 million cubic yards – one cubic yard is about the size of a dishwasher – of debris in those places alone. 
CLICK HERE: Mississippi Today’s disaster guide
Federal dollars are slowly arriving to assist Mississippi’s local and state recovery efforts. As of late September, the Federal Emergency Management Agency awarded nearly $200 million in public assistance grants to Mississippi, roughly half of the $416 million the state reported in damages, data from the agency shows. 


In a state much more accustomed to flooding, tornadoes and hurricanes, the January storm was one of Mississippi’s deadliest natural disasters of the 21st century. The last comparable event, most in the state say, was the Great Ice Storm of 1994. Thirty people died, largely from a mix of house fires and hypothermia. Many more suffered with limited access to food and water, stranded in dark homes along roads too dangerous to drive on. 
In the following months, residents and public officials underscored the state’s lack of preparedness for winter disasters, Mississippi Today reported. They pointed to days-long waits for water, food and generators, as well as the many critical facilities – such as hospitals, drinking water systems and prisons – that lacked sufficient back-up power.
State officials have since pointed to tangible solutions, such as storing resources in north Mississippi, improving disaster aid and maintaining trees near power lines. But they also argued there isn’t much more Mississippi can do to mitigate a once-every-30-year event. 
Now in October, discussion of Fern has largely melted away. 
In June, the Mississippi Public Service Commission held a two-day summit in Tupelo focused on lessons learned from the storm. The idea, Northern District Public Service Commissioner Chris Brown said, was to leave better prepared for the next bout of brutal cold weather. 
“Preparation is wisdom, we owe that to the people we serve,” Brown said after quoting Proverbs 27:12: “ A prudent man foreseeth the evil and hideth himself, but the simple passeth on and are punished.” 
While the summit elicited some specific suggestions – largely calls for more generators – it was unclear how those ideas would be executed. Brown’s office did not respond to multiple calls about possible next steps. 
At the event, held in a Tupelo High School auditorium, meteorologist Matt Laubhan underscored that the next large winter storm could hit any year. 
“There’s no guarantee it’s 30 years from now when we have the next one of these,” Laubhan told the couple dozen people in attendance. “It easily could be this next year.  There’s no magic thing that keeps it being that spread out.
“Knowing your weaknesses today, it’s necessary to fixing tomorrow.”
Frozen limbs droop near Boyle on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026. Credit: Gunner Sizemore
‘You can’t prevent the weather’
Overall, interviews with north Mississippi lawmakers revealed a sense that little could be, or even needed to be, changed to better handle future winter storms.
“As far as legislation, I mean, you can’t prevent the weather,” Rep. Clay Deweese, a Republican from Oxford, said. “An ice storm, the event we had up north is just… Do you need to be prepared? Sure, you do. But that’s just not really very predictable.”
Rep. Sam Creekmore, a Republican from New Albany, echoed the sentiment. 
“I’m not sure legislatively what we need to do to help better prepare Mississippi than what we’ve already done,” he said. “I mean, it’s not going to prevent the storm.”
Lawmakers reiterated the infrequency of such an event, arguing it’s hard to fund mitigation against a once-every-30-year event.
“ I think there’ll be lessons learned, and there will be takeaways, and there’ll be improvements,” said Sen. Daniel Sparks, a Republican from Belmont. “But it’s hard to turn around then and legislate based on the outlier.”
Sen. Daniel H. Sparks discusses a bill during the Senate Finance Committee meeting at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson, Miss., on Monday, March 17, 2025.  Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
‘You can’t do nothing’
While Mississippi officials underlined the infrequency of winter storms of Fern’s magnitude, climate experts agreed there’s no telling when another event will hit the state.
“I wouldn’t say put your money on that you’re going to see more of these events next year or the year after, but you will eventually,” said B.J. Baule, a climatologist at the Southern Regional Climate Center at Texas A&M University. “So being prepared, having that capacity, knowing where the vulnerabilities are is important.”
David Holt, a geography professor at the University of Southern Mississippi who specializes in climate and resilience, called it “foolish” to rely on the once-every-30-year frequency in predicting future winter storms. 
“To fall back on saying we’ve got another 30 years before we have another Fern come along, it’s naive at best,” Holt said. 
Scientists are still studying whether any link between climate change and winter storm intensity or frequency exists, such as with flooding or extreme heat. But climate variability, researchers say, has increased. There’s less certainty today over how often an event like Fern might occur than there was in 1994, Holt and Baule agreed. 
George and Mary Robinson sit on the porch of their home as they talk about how they have been surviving after the winter storm Thursday, Jan. 29, 2026, in Tchula. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“ The reality is we can’t predict if we’re going to have a colder winter or a hotter winter,” Holt said. “We can estimate or give you statistical probabilities, but we can’t guarantee it. But what we can guarantee is that we expect there to be greater variability.”
It’s more likely a similar event happens sooner than 30 years from now because of increasing temperatures that lead to more moisture and more precipitation, including ice, Holt said.
“My professional gut opinion is that it feels like it’s more likely to happen again sooner than later because we just see this variability,” he said. 
While temperatures have risen in Mississippi over the last century – although not as much as in other parts of the country – residents and officials have noticed a string of harsh winter events in recent years, such as in 2021 and in 2023. 
 ”North Mississippi has been impacted by a winter weather event consistently  over the last five years,” said Beau Moore, a public information officer for Lafayette County. “ As our weather patterns are changing, we need to also have (more) resources available in north Mississippi.” 
Baule explained that, more recently, the Arctic is warming faster than the equator, leading to more north-to-south jet streams. That phenomenon brings cold fronts farther south, such as what Mississippi saw with Fern. Baule said data is insufficient to make a definite connection, but the trend “could be attributable to climate change.”
Mississippi Emergency Management headquarters located in Pearl, Friday, July 18, 2025. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
New warehouse in north Mississippi?
One potential fix officials are discussing, aimed at reducing delivery times for resource requests, is to build a new warehouse in north Mississippi to store items like food, water, tarps and cots. 
“I would like to have MEMA have a warehouse in north Mississippi with some materials on hand for a rapid response,” Sen. Chad McMahan, a Republican from Guntown, said.
Moore told Mississippi Today that Lafayette County officials are looking to do just that. He said the county is talking with the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency about securing funds for the project – estimated to cost around $2 million. 
“They’ve been good talks, good conversations, it’s just sometimes these items take time to get done,” he said.
MEMA confirmed it was in discussions with Lafayette County.
“We prepositioned personnel and supplies before Winter Storm Fern and would certainly not hesitate to move materials to the Lafayette County location if it is deemed necessary for a particular event,” Scott Simmons, the agency’s director of external affairs, told Mississippi Today.


A permanent disaster loan program?
Another solution to improve preparedness is to make a recently created emergency loan program permanent, some lawmakers said. 
In April, the Legislature created a temporary revolving loan program to help cities and counties hurt by Winter Storm Fern while they awaited federal assistance funding. While technically a loan, the 3% interest rate only kicks in if an applicant doesn’t receive the same amount through FEMA’s Public Assistance grants. 
As of Oct. 1, the state had awarded $79 million in loans to over 20 cities and counties.
Creekmore said he would support a permanent version of the program that can quickly kick in once a disaster strikes. The temporary program is set to expire in July 2027. 
“It’d be nice to have that kick in and give these people peace of mind,” Creekmore said, calling the program a “saving grace” for areas hit by the winter storm. “We’re fortunate we were in session to do that (right after Fern).” 
Deweese, who introduced the House’s version of the program, said a permanent loan program is “something we may need to look at.”
Rep. Sam Creekmore speaks during a press conference on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Fortifying the electric grid
Winter Storm Fern took out power for roughly 300,000 residents, or more than one in 10 Mississippians, state officials estimated in the disaster’s aftermath. 
Keith Hayward, the general manager of the Northeast Mississippi Electric Power Association, said the utility’s biggest obstacle to restoring power was the amount of fallen trees and limbs that stood in the way. 
“I equate it to a F2 or F3 tornado that basically went across our whole system,” Hayward said, adding it took three weeks before every customer’s lights were back on.
After the last comparable winter storm in 1994, the utility more aggressively trimmed the hanging limbs and vegetation in its rights-of-way, or the areas around power lines and poles. Legally, the utility can tackle vegetation up to 30 feet away from power lines, Hayward said. 
Another utility manager, Sean McGrath of the Alcorn County Electric Power Association, said increasing power companies’ easements would help prevent outages. Most power outages are caused by fallen trees or vegetation originating on private property, McGrath said.
“ I think we need to look at possibly changing easement law and giving us the opportunity to cut a hazardous tree when the homeowner doesn’t necessarily want that tree cut,” he said. “ If you really want to look at hardening your infrastructure, it starts with your easement laws.”
Hayward agreed some private property owners are making outages worse.
A lineman with H. Richardson & Sons reconnects power to homes on Pecan Street in Rolling Fork, Monday, Feb. 2, 2026, days after an ice storm struck the area. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“ When you have a community that loves their trees and has a tree board and their tree that they’ve been trimming on for 30 years, is four foot thick and falls across a three-phase line and breaks 10 poles, what are you going to do?” he asked.  
Sparks, the senator from Belmont, said while he would entertain the idea it would be hard to pass legislation limiting private property owners’ rights. 
“That’s going to be super tough,” Sparks said. 
Another question officials raised after Fern is whether it makes sense to put power lines underground so they’re not susceptible to disasters like winter storms or tornadoes. While underground lines are more resilient to storms, they’re also significantly more costly to build. 
In his area, Hayward said subdivisions built since the 1990s are required to build their lines underground. But in rural areas, where one line may stretch over 20 miles to reach just a few homes, the price tag usually isn’t worth it, he added, especially because the utility has to pass those costs on to its ratepayers. 
In Oxford, Mayor Robyn Tannehill said new lines there have been built underground for the last 20 years. Tannehill said the city’s goal is to bury other, older lines, but after Fern she isn’t sure how soon Oxford can afford to do so.
Shifting responsibility to locals
During the last legislative session, north Mississippi lawmakers criticized state agencies for not doing enough to prepare for Winter Storm Fern. But one Coast senator argued that it’s local officials who need to be ready to take on more responsibilities, especially as the federal government tries to overhaul FEMA. 
Earlier in the year, a council appointed by President Donald Trump – including former Gov. Phil Bryant – released a list of recommended changes to FEMA, which followed Trump’s statements that he wished to get rid of the agency altogether. While the recommendations didn’t go that far, they did call for shifting responsibilities away from FEMA to state and local governments. 
Loleeta Cobbins sits in her car to keep warm at Hartwood Apartments after January’s winter storm Thursday, Jan. 29, 2026, in Durant. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Sen. Scott DeLano, a Republican from Biloxi involved in much of the state’s disaster legislation, said he expects the new version of FEMA to send grants to counties so local officials can handle more storm responses without outside assistance. When that transition happens is just a matter of time, the senator said. 
“ What we do know is they’re going to push more responsibilities down to the locals,” DeLano told Mississippi Today. “ The time of the mayors calling MEMA and saying, ’Where’s my water truck, where are my generators, where are my tarps?’ That’s gone.”
But that process will require more resources and training at the local level, he added. Winter Storm Fern was a perfect example. 
“ When you look at what happened in the winter storm event, the reality is there were a lot of communities that had not faced that type of widespread disruption, and a widespread demand for response in many, many, many years,” DeLano said.
He said there should be better protocols to ensure critical facilities like water systems, hospitals and prisons have backup power, calling that the “lowest hanging fruit.” 
“There were things that may have fallen through the cracks over the years that we should certainly use as lessons learned,” DeLano said.

title: Hiring slows in September with job growth of 29K
description: Jobs across the United States rose by 29,000 in September, a disappointing result as recent growth was also revised down in Friday’s monthly jobs report, the last one before midterm elections.  September growth was a large dip from a strong August number that was revised down from 162,000 to 133,000 in the new report. July […]
text:
Providers give emergency care to patients via telehealth at Dartmouth Health, based in Vermont and New Hampshire, which announced last month it would lay off 124 employees and cancel 303 positions. Nationwide, health care jobs continued to grow in September but at a lower pace as hospitals continued to seek financial stability. (Photo courtesy of Dartmouth Health)Jobs across the United States rose by 29,000 in September, a disappointing result as recent growth was also revised down in Friday’s monthly jobs report, the last one before midterm elections. 
September growth was a large dip from a strong August number that was revised down from 162,000 to 133,000 in the new report. July jobs were also revised from an increase of 21,000 to a decrease of 10,000, according to the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly report. 
“This is a textbook weak jobs report,” economist Kathryn Anne Edwards said on a live chat on Substack after the release.
The fact that earnings, up 3%, are not keeping up with 3.4% inflation, means “We can say pretty categorically that things got worse for workers this month,” Edwards said.
US employers shed 23K jobs in July

Average hourly earnings increased slightly to $37.81, up 3% from a year ago. The unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% from 4.1% in August, but still a decrease from 4.4% in September 2025. 
Speaking on Fox News, Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, tried to frame the joblessness increase as a result of a labor market that more potential workers have returned to since August. 
“People are seeing the strong labor market and they’re saying, ‘Oh I need to get back in the labor force because I’m going to make so much money.’ That’s one reason why the unemployment rate just ticked in a different direction,” Hassett said. 
The labor force increased by 485,000 people in September, according to the report, but that’s still a decrease of a million from September 2025.  . 
Black unemployment jumped 1 point to 7% for the month, though it also is down from 7.6% in September 2025. 
Health care jobs led September job growth at 16,700. That’s still a slowdown from an average of 33,000 per month over the past year as hospitals continue to seek financial stability. Some health systems had layoffs last month in Vermont and New Hampshire. Government jobs dropped by 17,000, mostly in local governments. 
The freight economy has been reeling from the impact of high diesel prices, and job losses have been announced in that industry. Nonetheless the federal statistics show a monthly job increase of 2,600 in September for truck transportation jobs, but a drop of 4,100 in warehousing and storage jobs. 
An alternative jobs report from payroll processor ADP found a 90,000-job gain in September, with more than half of those coming gains in the Mid-Atlantic region of New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania.  
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.
