name: Rhode Island Current
title: Healey wants Trump administration’s help on bringing more gas into Massachusetts
description: This article first appeared on CommonWealth Beacon and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. Here’s something you probably didn’t have on your bingo card: The Democratic governor of Massachusetts asking President Trump’s administration to move faster in approving a gas expansion project. That’s exac[...]
text:
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey rolls out details of her fiscal year 2027 state budget proposal on Jan. 28, 2026. (Photo by Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)This article first appeared on CommonWealth Beacon and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
Here’s something you probably didn’t have on your bingo card: The Democratic governor of Massachusetts asking President Trump’s administration to move faster in approving a gas expansion project.
That’s exactly what Gov. Maura Healey did on Thursday, imploring Energy Secretary Chris Wright in a letter to move with a “sense of urgency” in issuing required permits for the project to quickly move forward.
Healey, citing her “all of the above” approach to energy issues, previously expressed support for the proposal, a relatively small expansion of 73,500 dekatherms per day of an existing gas pipeline owned by Canadian energy company Enbridge. State regulators approved contracts earlier this year for Eversource to purchase the additional gas from the expansion project, known as the Reliable Affordable Resilient Enhancement, or RARE.
But now, as Healey hunts for ways to bring down soaring gas and electric costs and campaigns for reelection in a race defined by the affordability crisis gripping the state, the governor sees an opportunity to appeal to the fossil fuel-friendly Trump administration to bring more natural gas into the state to both power and heat homes and businesses.
What’s more, Healey said that she and Wright have “on several occasions” discussed their “mutual desire” to bring more gas into New England.
“I ask that you work across the Administration to ensure that the federal reviews and permits needed for RARE move without delay; that agencies establish clear schedules and coordinate their work wherever legally permissible; and that sufficient staff and resources are dedicated to completing the required reviews in time to preserve the project’s planned 2028 in-service date,” Healey wrote to Wright.
The overture from Healey is noteworthy, too, because of how critical she has been of the Trump administration for raising energy costs by canceling new offshore wind projects and launching hostilities in the Middle East that have sent oil prices surging.
In this case, Healey is backing the RARE project citing expectations that it would deliver real savings to customers, though the expansion isn’t planned to be ready until 2028. The Department of Public Utilities found that RARE would save about 600,000 Eversource customers roughly $40 million per year over the course of a decade by displacing reliance on more expensive, foreign liquefied natural gas delivered through the Everett Marine Terminal.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission began its review this past February.
“While we anticipate significant cost and reliability benefits for our natural gas customers from this precedent agreement, by no means will it solve our region’s energy affordability challenge alone,” William Hinkle, an Eversource spokesperson, said in a statement. “As we continue working to advance the Commonwealth’s decarbonization and electrification goals, it’s our responsibility to evaluate any and all solutions that will improve reliability and affordability for our customers, including additional natural gas supply.”
High energy costs have emerged as the top household concern in Massachusetts, with electricity prices reaching double the national average, though Bay State voters by and large hold Trump — not Healey — as primarily responsible for that dynamic, according to a recent CommonWealth Beacon poll.
Natural gas remains the backbone of New England’s electric grid, accounting for roughly half of all electric generation in the region, as power demand is projected to rise.
Healey’s championing of RARE, though, is likely to ignite the ire of environmental advocates concerned that locking in more natural gas runs counter to the state’s commitment to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Just two years ago, dozens of green groups demanded that Northeast governors oppose a different major pipeline expansion proposal that ultimately fizzled.
Environmental nonprofit Acadia Center found that despite a sharp increase in the use of natural gas for power and heating in New England since the start of the century, energy prices have only gone up, too. Gas capacity in the region rose by about a third between 2010 and 2024, but prices nevertheless increased, according to the analysis.
Caitlin Peale Sloan, vice president for climate and energy at Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement that “this letter unwittingly adopts the false narrative that expansion of gas infrastructure will lower heating costs.” And Amy Boyd Rabin, vice president of policy and regulatory affairs at Environmental League of Massachusetts, said that “more natural gas supply is not the answer to Massachusetts’s rising energy costs.”
Healey’s letter didn’t stop at advocating for RARE. She cracked open the door to a much larger and potentially more controversial pipeline expansion that Enbridge is actively considering known as Project Beacon.
That proposal, about four times larger than RARE, would increase gas supply by as much as 10 percent on the Algonquin pipeline system and potentially start operations in 2030. Enbridge executives said on an earnings call over the summer that interest from energy producers and suppliers in purchasing the additional gas “exceeded our initial expectations.”
Getting RARE quickly approved, Healey said, could be the start of a new paradigm — and a sign that “all of the above” really could mean much more additional gas.
“There may be,” she wrote to Wright, “more opportunities ahead.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT is getting a lot less money from the federal government
description: Connecticut is receiving an estimated $2 billion less in federal funding under the Trump administration, a new report shows.
text:
Connecticut is receiving an estimated $2 billion less in federal funding under the Trump administration, according to a new tracking tool released by two nonpartisan pro-democracy organizations.
The tool, Lost Funds, tracks federal funding by compiling publicly available data from USAspending and Court Listener. The tool found that across the nation, states are getting an estimated $174 billion less in federal funding under the Trump administration.
This funding in the state used to go to things like emergency preparedness, fighting pollution and health education.
The largest single cut was for Connecticut disaster relief funds that were originally granted to state and local agencies. Roughly $341 million in disaster funds were “disrupted” through funding slowdowns.
Funding to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program going to Connecticut residents was also heavily impacted, reflecting decreases in the program’s enrollment. 

Health-related grants, taken together, have lost the most money out of all funding categories in the state. For Connecticut, this includes money going towards infectious disease control as well as biomedical research and health education funding.
This is also true nationally — the tracker found that $58.9 billion has been disrupted related to health initiatives across the country.
Connecticut is one of 26 states suing the Trump administration on the administration’s distribution of federal funds. In July, Connecticut joined a lawsuit claiming “unlawful conditions” on conditions attached to federal funds used for disaster preparation and response.
“Once again, Donald Trump is playing politics with disaster relief. He cannot hold billions of dollars in funding hostage to force states to carry out his political agenda,” Attorney General William Tong wrote in a July press release. “This is not how our Constitution works and not how federal grants work. We stopped similar illegal threats in court twice before, and we’re going to do it again.”
Some states are seeing larger disruptions in prior federal funding. But in Connecticut, an estimated half of the $4 billion the state expected from the federal government has been lost.

title: Indiana AG Todd Rokita sues disciplinary officials, alleging retaliation over political speech
description: Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita sued current and former members of the state’s attorney disciplinary commission Thursday, alleging years of retaliation and asking a federal judge to block a demand that he answer an ethics grievance tied to his personal jet ski transaction. The 34-page complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern […]
text:
Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita sued current and former members of the state’s attorney disciplinary commission Thursday, alleging years of retaliation and asking a federal judge to block a demand that he answer an ethics grievance tied to his personal jet ski transaction.
The 34-page complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, alleges disciplinary officials have targeted Rokita over his public statements on abortion, immigration and other issues since 2022.
The latest trigger, however, is a grievance questioning whether Rokita used his office to pursue a personal dispute with a jet ski seller — an allegation that Rokita denies.
The lawsuit names nine current members of the Indiana Supreme Court Disciplinary Commission, five former members and Executive Director Adrienne Meiring.
Indiana judge rejects challenge in lawsuit over AG Todd Rokita’s jet ski purchase

The Republican attorney general is seeking an order to block what he alleges is a pattern of retaliation, along with compensatory and punitive damages over alleged disclosures of confidential disciplinary proceedings.
“General Rokita does not forfeit the freedom of speech by serving as Attorney General or by holding a law license,” his attorneys wrote. “The First Amendment forbids government officials from retaliating against a speaker for protected speech, and it does not permit a disciplinary bureaucracy to be turned into an instrument for punishing an elected official’s participation in public debate.”
In a Friday news release, Rokita accused the commission of political bias and singled out member Bernard Carter, the Lake County prosecutor, for supporting his election opponent while the commission was investigating him.
“The First Amendment does not disappear because someone holds a law license or is in an elected office,” Rokita said in the release.
This latest dispute centers on a grievance filed by Jess Sampson, a Rochester man Rokita’s office is separately suing over alleged consumer protection violations following a personal jet ski transaction by the attorney general.
Sampson questioned whether Rokita was using his office to pursue a personal grievance. Rokita denied misusing his authority and argues that reporting suspected wrongdoing to his office’s Consumer Protection Division was constitutionally protected.
Rokita wants the federal court to declare that he need not respond to Sampson’s grievance, according to court filings.
A July 29 letter attached to the lawsuit shows the commission demanded a written response and warned that failure to cooperate could lead to suspension of Rokita’s law license or other discipline. The letter said a preliminary investigation would determine whether to dismiss the grievance or pursue further investigation.
Rokita’s lawsuit frames that demand as the latest in a series of retaliatory investigations dating to 2022. His disciplinary history includes a 2023 public reprimand from the Indiana Supreme Court over his televised comments about Dr. Caitlin Bernard, who provided an abortion to a 10-year-old rape victim from Ohio.

title: 2 UVM Medical Center unions vote to authorize strike
description:
The support staff and technical staff unions, which represent 3,300 members, announced the vote result Friday.

text:
Vermont Federation of Nurses and Health Professionals President Nicole DiVita, right, and Jacob Berkowitz, president of UVMMC Support Staff United, pictured on Oct. 2. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger
BURLINGTON — Two UVM Medical Center unions said Friday they have voted to authorize a strike. 
The vote gives the union leadership the authority to call for a strike and begin the legal notification process before staff officially take to the picket line. Union representatives said that 82% of voting members cast ballots in favor of authorizing the strike. 
The support staff and technical staff unions, which represent 3,300 members and have been jointly bargaining over their two separate contracts, are asking the medical center for more say over staffing levels as the hospital network undergoes layoffs and restructuring to meet tight financial pressures. 
Last week, the hospital’s bargaining team gave the union its “last, best and final” offer, which in turn initiated the weeklong vote surrounding strike approval. The two groups have been in negotiations since April.
The hospital network did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Delaware
title: Meyer vetoes bipartisan effort to put checks on emergency powers
description: Governor rejects four bills passed by General Assembly, including measures that drew overwhelming bipartisan support DOVER, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer vetoed four bills approved by the Delaware General Assembly, including a bipartisan measure that would have given lawmakers new authority to check a governor’s power during an extended state of emergency. Meyer ve[...]
text:
Photo: Governor Matt Meyer courtesy of the Governor’s Office.
Governor rejects four bills passed by General Assembly, including measures that drew overwhelming bipartisan support
DOVER, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer vetoed four bills approved by the Delaware General Assembly, including a bipartisan measure that would have given lawmakers new authority to check a governor’s power during an extended state of emergency.
Meyer vetoed House Substitute 1 for House Bill 329, Senate Bill 231, Senate Bill 279 and House Bill 393 on Sept. 30.
The four vetoes put Meyer at odds with substantial majorities in the Democratic-controlled General Assembly. Two of the measures — the emergency-powers bill and a utility consumer-protection bill — passed both chambers without a single opposing vote.
A veto is part of the governor’s constitutional role in Delaware’s legislative process. The General Assembly can override a gubernatorial veto if it secures the votes required under the Delaware Constitution.
Lawmakers seek check on prolonged emergency power
HB 329 was specifically written to establish additional checks and balances between the executive and legislative branches during a prolonged state of emergency.
Under the final version, a governor could declare and maintain an emergency for the first 180 days without legislative approval.
After that point, the governor could continue renewing the emergency, but the General Assembly would gain explicit authority to amend or terminate the order. The administration also would have been required to report to lawmakers every 30 days during a continuing emergency.
The legislation was sponsored by Rep. Rich Collins, R-Millsboro, and Sen. Kyra Hoffner, D-Dover-area, and attracted sponsors from both parties.
It passed the House 39-0 and the Senate 20-0, with absences in both chambers.
Lawmakers also amended the legislation so its restrictions would not apply to Meyer during his current term. The new provisions would have taken effect only after the governor serving when the bill became law left office.
That meant the legislation was largely establishing rules for future governors rather than restricting Meyer’s own emergency authority.
The measure grew out of Delaware’s experience during the COVID-19 pandemic, when then-Gov. John Carney repeatedly renewed emergency orders while lawmakers had limited formal authority over whether those orders continued.
Supporters argued that a governor needs broad authority when a crisis begins but that an emergency lasting six months raises a separate question about the role of the legislative branch.  Meyer stated that the bill would have unnecessarily constrained the executive branch’s ability to respond to emergencies and could create uncertainty during future crises.
Ramone criticizes veto
Mike Ramone, the Republican nominee for state treasurer, criticized Meyer’s action during two campaign events Thursday night.
Ramone, who served in the General Assembly from 2008 to 2024, including as House minority leader, said the veto reinforced his argument for greater transparency and stronger checks on state government.
“This is yet another reason transparency is critical in state government at all levels,” Ramone said. “Too much power left in one person’s hands, and inside a state government managed by one party, is a problem.”
Ramone pointed to the unanimous legislative support for HB 329.
“Republican and Democratic legislators understood that,” he said. “And yet, a reasonable bill was vetoed, leaving one person to leverage his power to impact life in our state indefinitely.”
Ramone’s comments reflect the argument made by supporters of HB 329 that long-running emergencies should eventually involve both the executive and legislative branches.
The veto leaves Delaware’s existing emergency-power structure in place.
Consumer protection bill also vetoed
Meyer also vetoed HB 393, a bipartisan consumer-protection measure involving third-party electricity suppliers.
The legislation passed the House 40-0 and the Senate 21-0.
The bill would have imposed additional disclosure, reporting and customer-notification requirements on companies selling electricity as alternatives to standard utility service.
Among other provisions, suppliers would have been required to notify customers before contracts renewed and before certain rate changes. Regulators also would have received additional pricing information allowing them to compare third-party rates with standard-offer electricity rates.
Rep. Debra Heffernan, D-Bellefonte, the bill’s prime sponsor, criticized the veto and disputed concerns that the measure could reduce competition or strengthen the position of a dominant electricity provider.
Heffernan said the bill was developed with the Meyer administration, the Public Advocate and Public Service Commission and was intended to address constituent complaints about customers being attracted by introductory offers before later paying significantly higher prices.
The governor’s legislative advisory identifies the veto but does not provide a detailed written explanation of his objections.
Two school compensation measures rejected
Meyer also vetoed two bills affecting school employee compensation.
SB 231 would have provided an additional salary supplement to school social workers who passed the Association of Social Work Boards National Clinical Examination and held a licensed clinical social worker license.
The bill passed the Senate and House without an opposing vote.
A fiscal analysis estimated the state cost at approximately $343,000 in fiscal 2027, increasing in subsequent years.
Meyer had previously signed separate legislation expanding salary supplements for several categories of school professionals, including social workers. The governor’s published veto notice does not state whether that overlap, the additional cost or another concern was the basis for rejecting SB 231.
SB 279 addressed salary placement for school-based occupational therapists.
Supporters said employees with comparable professional education can be placed on different salary levels because occupational therapy degree programs award credits differently.
The legislation would have established a more uniform method of recognizing master’s and doctoral-level occupational therapy education within the state salary schedule.
The bill passed the Senate 20-0 and the House 40-1.
Fiscal analysts estimated the state and local cost at roughly $224,000 in fiscal 2027, increasing in later years.
The governor’s published legislative advisory does not provide a detailed explanation for the SB 279 veto.
Four vetoes, different policy disputes
The measures covered different issues, but all four had substantial support in the General Assembly.
HB 329 and HB 393 passed without an opposing vote. SB 231 also passed without opposition among lawmakers voting, while only one House member voted against SB 279.
The vetoes do not negate the General Assembly’s votes. Under Delaware’s constitutional system, legislation approved by lawmakers is presented to the governor, who may sign it or veto it. Lawmakers may then consider whether to attempt an override.
HB 329 is unusual because the legislation itself dealt directly with that division of governmental power.
It would have preserved broad gubernatorial authority during the first six months of an emergency while creating a formal legislative role once the emergency became prolonged.
Meyer’s veto means that change will not take effect unless lawmakers override him or adopt similar legislation in the future.
TO GO BOX

What happened: Gov. Matt Meyer vetoed four bills Sept. 30.
Emergency powers: HS 1 for HB 329 would have given the General Assembly authority to amend or terminate a state of emergency after 180 days and required continuing reports to lawmakers.
Vote: HB 329 passed the House 39-0 and Senate 20-0.
Utility consumers: HB 393 imposed additional requirements on third-party electric suppliers. It passed 40-0 in the House and 21-0 in the Senate.
School social workers: SB 231 would have provided additional compensation for qualifying licensed clinical social workers working in schools.
Occupational therapists: SB 279 would have changed salary placement rules for qualifying school-based occupational therapists.
Political reaction: Republican state treasurer nominee Mike Ramone said the HB 329 veto demonstrated the need for greater transparency and checks on executive authority.
What happens next: The General Assembly may consider whether to attempt veto overrides.
Learn more: Bill texts, votes, fiscal notes and legislative histories are available through the Delaware General Assembly at legis.delaware.gov.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont’s plan to send gift cards to former SNAP recipients stalls
description: About 25,000 former SNAP recipients were to receive $300 grocery gift cards, but the state has delivered less than 6% of the pledged relief.
text:
Nearly two months after 25,000 former SNAP recipients were to begin receiving state-sponsored $300 grocery gift cards, Gov. Ned Lamont’s administration has delivered less than 6% of the pledged relief.
Through Thursday, only 1,425 cards worth a collective $427,500 had been distributed, a state Department of Social Services spokeswoman confirmed. The state didn’t provide full contact information for all eligible recipients to the nonprofits assisting with distribution until the program’s second month, she said.Still, the administration pledged to intensify outreach immediately and get the remaining $7.1 million promised to 23,570 food-insecure residents as soon as possible.
“It does take time to stand up a new program and ensure that taxpayer dollars are not being wasted and abused,” Christine Stuart, the social services department spokeswoman, said about the delay in a written response to questions from the Connecticut Mirror.
“We expect to distribute as many [cards] as possible,” she said, adding “we will continue to evaluate options for improving the process.”
That includes sending postcards next week to remind eligible individuals who still haven’t received the $300 benefit. But social services officials also are asking anyone previously notified to reach out immediately to any of the nine nonprofit Community Action Agencies helping with distribution. 
Lesser: ‘Bureaucracy has gotten in the way of helping people’
Still, the delay is far from what the administration envisioned.
Andrea Barton Reeves, Lamont’s social services commissioner, called the gift cards “real, immediate help” when distribution began on Aug. 4 to ease the pain of SNAP cutbacks ordered in July 2025 by President Donald Trump and the Republican-led Congress.
The governor and his fellow Democrats in the General Assembly’s majority used $500 million in state reserves last November and another $50 million in May to create a state “response fund” to mitigate federal cutbacks, chiefly in healthcare and nutrition programs.
“Connecticut will not stand by as the Trump administration uses hunger as a weapon against working families, veterans and our most vulnerable populations,” Lamont said.
The Lamont administration drew $8.5 million from the fund last June, designating $7.5 million to buy $300 gift cards for 25,000 former SNAP recipients and another $1 million to cover administrative costs.
The social services department notified those recipients via text that they could obtain these cards from any of the community action agencies, Stuart said. There was no formal application process. 
But while the department initially provided agencies with some information about eligible recipients, a “more robust” list, including the contact information needed to easily confirm identities, wasn’t provided until “the beginning of September,” she said.
The department delayed that transfer to investigate whether sharing former SNAP recipients’ personal data would violate federal privacy rules, Stuart added.
But by failing to provide timely data, critics said, the department complicated what should have been a simple process.
“Unfortunately, bureaucracy has gotten in the way of helping people, and the need out there is real,” said Sen. Matthew Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chairman of the Human Services Committee. “We have the resources to take care of people in the state.”
Lamont could have delivered all pledged assistance by now had he followed Illinois’ Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s example, according to The Connecticut Project, a nonprofit social and economic advocacy group focused on making the state more affordable.
Starting in August, Pritzker sent $400 assistance payments to about 100,000 Illinois residents who had lost SNAP benefits. Officials added the funding to the electronic debit card the state uses to distribute nutrition and other cash benefits.
“The state’s ongoing failure to meaningfully respond to the SNAP crisis remains unacceptable,” said Meghan Holden, The Connecticut Project’s communications director. “The one-time grocery cards were always going to be a Band-Aid at best, and from the beginning, the state set them up to leave people behind … We’re talking to hungry people every day who are desperate for Connecticut to see them, listen to them, and help them. … For the lucky few who do get cards, they often last a week. Our state has to do better than this.”
Grocery gift cards weren’t enough for all in CT who lost SNAP
Others say Lamont’s assistance plan was too small from the start, aimed at just a subset of residents who’ve lost SNAP benefits since July 2025.
The governor stipulated that benefits would go to “able-bodied adults without dependents” who failed to meet more restrictive federal work requirements. The $300 cards were designed as a bridge to assist them until they could secure jobs.
Washington canceled work exemptions for the first time for certain categories of immigrants, people facing homelessness, older adults and children ages 14 and 15. It’s also squeezing states to scrutinize SNAP applicants and shrink program error rates.
Connecticut Voices for Children recently estimated that SNAP enrollment in Connecticut is down an unprecedented 62,770 people since July 2025, and the Washington, D.C.-based Center on Budget and Policy Priorities says the erosion during that period includes 18,900 kids.
The United Way of Connecticut, which runs the state’s 2-1-1 human services referral line, reported about 23,000 phone and web inquiries regarding food assistance in September, up 84% from the same month in 2025.
“That’s staggering,” said Lisa Tepper Bates, president and CEO of the Connecticut chapter, who added that hunger-related calls happen lately with “a higher level of urgency.”
Sen. Cathy Osten, D-Sprague, co-chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, said “We should have opened it up [gift cards] to people who lost SNAP, no matter what.”
“Every bit of help the state provides matters, however, the gift cards are woefully insufficient,” added Emily Byrne, executive director of Connecticut Voices. “No child should go to bed hungry, and families should not have to wait on pantry lines to feed their children.”
Connecticut still has $260 million in its federal response fund and could easily afford to help more than 25,000 people removed from SNAP assistance, anti-hunger advocates note. But Lamont anticipates Connecticut will need much of that funding next year to assist families losing federal tax credits that help pay for health insurance and to mitigate new federal cutbacks in Medicaid coverage.
A fiscal moderate running for a third term this fall, the governor also has balanced appeals to mitigate SNAP cuts with continuing to pay down the state’s hefty pension debt.
Connecticut still carries more than $30 billion in unfunded pension liabilities, one of the largest burdens, per capita, among all states. This problem, largely created prior to 2011, has been whittled down significantly, however, under Lamont’s tenure.
Using aggressive budget caps that force huge surpluses, the governor has used $11 billion since 2020 to shrink pension debt.
But Osten, Lesser and several anti-hunger groups want to explore creating an ongoing, state-funded nutrition benefit when the 2027 General Assembly session launches in January. It would help certain residents cut off from SNAP until they secure job training and employment or provide long-term assistance to those deemed unemployable.
Lamont has been wary to commit state funds to replace canceled federal aid on an ongoing basis.
But Osten said Connecticut faces a social and economic crisis if tens of thousands of residents are unable to eat regularly.
“Feeding people has been my No. 1 concern,” she said. “Hunger matters to people.”
Note: The Connecticut Project is a funder of The Connecticut Mirror.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Golf cart raises questions at Hinds DA’s office. Where did the money come from?
description: A golf cart belonging to former district attorney Jody Owens is parked near the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Sitting in a corner of a parking garage underneath the Hinds County Courthouse is an electric golf cart with chrome wheels, white stitching on black seats, and a gray seal on four sides bearing the name of the Hinds County District Attorney’s Office and its former leader, Jody Owens. 
The vehicle turned up next to a back door to the courthouse sometime after June 29, when Owens pleaded guilty to a federal corruption charge and resigned.
In the three months since, Owens’ appointed successor, Brad McCullouch, said his staff can’t find records showing when the lithium-battery-powered cart was purchased, how much it cost or where it came from. The golf cart could now play a role in a state audit looking into the finances of the district attorney’s office. 
A golf cart belonging to former district attorney Jody Owens is parked near the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
State funds were not used to purchase the golf cart, said Marcy Scoggins, spokesperson for the Mississippi Department of Finance and Administration. And the vehicle also does not appear on Hinds County’s inventory. 
Owens told Mississippi Today in August that he bought the golf cart for community engagement purposes, including parades and tailgating with staff at Jackson State University football games. 
“On the record, just to be clear, the golf cart has never been on a golf course,” Owens said. He couldn’t remember when, which funds he used or how much he paid. 
Dirt in the tread of the tires suggests the golf cart was used. But Mississippi Today could not find any pictures on the office’s social media accounts of the vehicle. 
If the golf cart was purchased for more than $5,000, it would have been subject to procurement laws in Mississippi, said Billy Morehead, a Mississippi Christian University accounting professor and past member of the Mississippi Public Procurement Review Board. 
Without knowing where the money came from, Morehead said, it is difficult to determine which government entity — the state, Hinds County or the DA’s office — would have been responsible for following those requirements. 
In Mississippi, DA’s offices are funded through a combination of state, county and self-generated revenue, subjecting their spending to a patchwork of accountability. 
The golf cart is made by a manufacturer called Vivid EV, according to a label on the dashboard. The company’s website appears to be defunct. 
Mississippi Today hasn’t been able to independently determine what the DA’s office paid for the cart and whether it exceeded the threshold for county bid requirements. Online golf cart reselling sites list various models made by Vivid EV starting at a little over $8,000. 
A golf cart belonging to former district attorney Jody Owens is parked near the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Soon after being appointed by Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, McCullouch said he was alarmed by the lack of financial documentation in the DA’s office. In a written response in September to a public records request from Mississippi Today, McCullouch said his office did not find any bids, invoices, requisitions or receipts documenting the golf cart’s purchase. 
McCullouch said he would not release any records, if any exist, about the golf cart, citing a state attorney general’s opinion that allows DAs to withhold records that are part of active criminal investigations. McCullouch declined to elaborate.
Regardless of how the golf cart came to be in the DA’s possession, Morehead said a record of it should exist in an inventory log. 
Neither the state auditor’s office nor the Department of Finance and Administration has such a log for the Hinds DA’s office. Mississippi Today obtained Hinds County’s asset inventory through a public records request, but it did not include a listing for the golf cart. 
“I’m not sure exactly the source of funds, but it didn’t come through our purchasing,” said Hinds County Administrator Lynn Seals, who added that golf carts do not have to be registered in Hinds County. 
If Owens used self-generated funds to buy the golf cart, state or county officials would not have had oversight. DAs can use self-generated funds for a range of law enforcement activities.
It’s common for law enforcement agencies in Mississippi to have golf carts. The Hinds County Sheriff’s Office, for example, uses golf carts to patrol the state fair. 
Nevertheless, Morehead questioned why a DA would need a golf cart. In Hinds County, prosecutors work on the fifth floor of the courthouse, taking an elevator to attend trials happening in courtrooms below. 
“Where is the DA trying to go?” he asked. 
Owens, a Democrat, was elected Hinds DA in late 2019. He frequently pushed for more funding for the office, including state appropriations to purchase electronic case management software and hire additional prosecutors. 
In 2023, Owens was among several Jackson officials who were ensnared in a wide-ranging FBI probe into corruption in Mississippi’s capital city. He is set to be sentenced in November.

name: Missouri Independent
title: FEC questions thousands of donations to Eric Schmitt tied to prolific online donors
description: In December 2023, a woman living in a small community near Austin, Texas, made a $78.08 contribution through WinRed. A few weeks later, she made another. Then came four more contributions in January 2024. Those were the first six entries under her name in Federal Election Commission records stretching back decades. Since then, her name […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt speaks to reporters after the Governor's Ham Breakfast at the Missouri State Fair in Sedalia in August 2024 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).In December 2023, a woman living in a small community near Austin, Texas, made a $78.08 contribution through WinRed. A few weeks later, she made another.
Then came four more contributions in January 2024.
Those were the first six entries under her name in Federal Election Commission records stretching back decades. Since then, her name has appeared 126,739 times — including 1,011 times in reports filed by U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri.
And she is one of 13 donors with numerous contributions flagged in three letters the FEC sent this year to Schmitt’s campaign committee asking about donations that appear to exceed federal limits and other issues with his reports.
None of the 13 donors flagged in the FEC letters live in Missouri, and none gave to Schmitt when he sought election to his first term in the Senate in 2022. He has raised $4.3 million since the start of 2025 for the 2028 election.
Those 13 donors are, collectively, listed in Schmitt’s FEC reports almost 5,700 times, donating $85,672 after accounting for negative amounts entered for each donor in subsequent and amended reports. The totals for each donor range from just over the donation limit of $3,500 to more than $10,500.
The Independent unsuccessfully attempted to contact the donors to understand why their names had been listed so many times.
How a Nebraska veteran unwittingly became a repeat donor to a Missouri county campaign

The records offer a window into the increasingly automated world of online political fundraising, where a small number of donors can generate thousands of transactions and campaigns must keep track of whether those contributions exceed federal limits.
Online fundraising platforms can process recurring contributions automatically, and a single donation can generate multiple entries in federal records as money moves through a platform, political committee and candidate campaign. That can leave regulators sorting out whether unusual patterns reflect legitimate giving, reporting errors or contributions a donor may not have intended to continue.
The issue is familiar in Missouri. Lawmakers this year tightened state campaign finance rules after The Independent reported that a 92-year-old Nebraska veteran had become an unwitting recurring donor to former state Sen. Bill Eigel’s campaign for St. Charles County executive. State and local candidates now must obtain clear consent for recurring contributions, send a receipt after every donation and stop them when asked or after the election. No such restrictions exist at the federal level.
Schmitt’s campaign did not respond to a request for comments on the FEC letters.
The first FEC letter raising concerns about Schmitt’s fundraising listed 10 contributors with at least 20 donations during 2025. The second, sent after Schmitt’s campaign filed its report for the first quarter of the year, included inquiries about seven donors, six of whom were also listed in the first letter. 
The third letter, sent after the report for the second quarter of the year, listed 10 donors, including eight listed in one or more of the previous letters.
The FEC letters do not establish that Schmitt’s campaign or any donor violated federal law. They are requests from commission staff seeking corrections or explanations for apparent problems in campaign finance reports.
“It does not mean there’s been a violation of the law,” Bradley Smith, a former chairman of the FEC, told The Independent. “It does not mean there’s going to be a fine on the campaign. It’s simply saying you’ve got reporting problems, and we’d like to either have this corrected or explained.”
The letters raise other issues as well, including incomplete information about some donors, donors who made single or a handful of donations that exceed the limits and information about the source of donations passed through a conduit to the campaign.
Federal candidate campaigns are allowed to accept donations of up to $3,500 from individuals for each election. A campaign can collect that amount for the primary election and again for the general election and can accept funds for the general election before the primary is held.
The letters said Schmitt’s campaign had the option of redesignating excessive amounts for the primary to the general, splitting the donations from joint banking accounts between the individuals on the account, refunding the money or, when the donor could not be reached, turning it over to the U.S. Treasury.
“Although the commission may take further legal action concerning the acceptance of excessive contributions, your prompt action to refund, redesignate, and/or reattribute the excessive amount will be taken into consideration,” the first letter stated.
In response to the first letter, Janna Rutland, Schmitt’s campaign treasurer, wrote that an amended report was filed addressing the issues.
“After filing the original report, the committee discovered that a software error caused donor information to be mismatched, which resulted in reporting errors,” Rutland wrote.
The amended report included “any necessary reattributions, redesignations, or refunds,” Rutland wrote.
Rutland has submitted similar letters responding to the FEC’s other letters. 
 Recurring contributions

Most of the 13 people the FEC inquired about had infrequent, if any, contributions to federal candidates prior to the advent of online donation portals. 
Democrats launched the first one, ActBlue, in 2004. The Republican alternative, WinRed, was founded in 2019. Both platforms have faced scrutiny over online fundraising practices, including recurring contributions and whether donors always understand how frequently they have agreed to give.
The Electronic Frontier Foundation, in a 2021 article, wrote that many times, the design of the donation page is intended to draw your eyes away from the notice that it will be a recurring donation. 
“A pre-checked box to donate more than you intended is just one example of a ‘dark pattern’ — a term coined by user experience (UX) designer Harry Brignull to define tricks used in websites and apps that make you do things that you didn’t mean to, such as buying a service,” the organization reported.
During the 2015-16 election cycle, the 13 Schmitt donors were listed 128 times in FEC reports, with seven not appearing at all. For the 2025-26 election cycle, those 13 donors are listed almost 600,000 times across federal campaign finance records.
The number includes multiple entries tied to the same donation, with initial recipients reporting, as well as the campaigns and PACs that receive a share. 
Smith was a Republican member of the FEC from 2000 to 2005 and was appointed chairman by President George W. Bush. After leaving the commission, Smith founded the Center for Competitive Politics, now the Institute for Free Speech, and his academic work was cited by the U.S. Supreme Court in the Citizens United decision allowing corporations to spend directly in political campaigns.
The practices of both parties’ online fundraising efforts need to be investigated, Smith said.
“My sort of vague sense,” Smith said, “is that the FEC has probably not done enough to either investigate these items or ask campaigns to install certain safeguards to make sure that you don’t end up with people sending multiple contributions.”
The case of the woman from Texas who had no donations before 2023 and more than 125,000 entries in the records in the past two years is particularly troubling, he said.
“This kind of thing, were I still sitting on the commission, it would raise my eyebrows,” Smith said.
There are many explanations for why a particular donor would have duplicate entries associated with the same contribution, Smith said.
That would explain some, but not all, of the entries associated with each name, he said.
“When you have a number as large as you have in this case, certainly this should raise questions,” he said.
U.S. Rep. Eric Burlison of Springfield, a Republican seeking reelection this year in the 7th District, said he opposes trying to ban or limit recurring donations.
“Whether you’re using your credit card online to make any kind of contribution or purchase anything, I’ve always fallen under the belief that people are intelligent agents,” Burlison said. “They know what they’re doing. It’s their money. They have every right to make those decisions. And as long as you’re being clear on the form and giving everybody the ability to choose, I don’t see what the problem is.”
 Not alone

Schmitt is not alone in receiving recurring campaign donations. And four other Republicans from Missouri — Burlison, U.S. Reps. Jason Smith of Salem and Ann Wagner of St. Louis County as well as U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley — have received numerous contributions from some of the same donors listed on the letters to Schmitt.
The WinRed site is a great help to campaigns, Burlison said.
“It’s a very effective tool, and it’s easier for people to be able to make contributions,” he said. “As candidates, we’re able to save money on our fees for credit card fees.”
But the volume of small donations it creates means campaigns must watch whether another $5 or $10 contribution will push a donor over the federal limit. 
Like Schmitt, Burlison has received letters from the FEC seeking information, and one included a list of his donations from the Texas woman with more than 125,000 donations nationally also highlighted in FEC letters to Schmitt.
The letter was troubling, Burlison said.
“We blocked her back in July because of the volume of the transactions. It just seemed when we got the letter, we agreed that, yeah, that’s a strange volume of contributions,” Burlison said. 
The 286 donations listed in his reports were coming daily, sometimes twice a day, he said. The smallest contribution was 25 cents. The largest was $30.
“In her case,” Burlison said, “we blocked her because it was so continuous and it was almost like being spammed with these small dollar donations.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Braun appoints new leader for troubled public access counselor’s office
description: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun selected a new chief for public access requests and grievances, after months of complaints about his previous pick's responsiveness.
text:
Brittney Long. (Photo courtesy of Indiana governor's office)Indiana Gov. Mike Braun selected a new chief for public access requests and grievances, after months of complaints about his previous pick’s responsiveness.
Brittney Long, who has been deputy general counsel for the Indiana Department of Natural Resources, will serve as the state’s next public access counselor, the governor’s office said Friday. Her first day is Monday.
“Brittney has the legal credentials and passion for public service that makes her an excellent fit for the job,” Braun said in the announcement. “As our next PAC, Brittney will bring added transparency and accountability to our state.”
Long was a magistrate judge for the Bartholomew County Circuit Court from 2022 until March. Previously, she spent nearly 11 years as a law clerk and attorney at the Indianapolis law firm Voyles Lukemeyer Baldwin Webb & Helmond.
Long will replace Public Access Counselor Jennifer Ruby, whom Braun appointed in March 2025. Her tenure has been plagued by complaints of no or slow responses, with some news media organizations threatening a lawsuit over delays.
The governor’s office didn’t immediately respond Friday to a request for comment about the circumstances of Ruby’s departure.

name: Nevada Current
title: Area Trump apologists lecture community on ‘character’
description: A pregnant woman shot dead in a parking lot. What a horrible tragedy. And if you’re the political professionals trying to reelect Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, what a fabulous campaign issue. Lombardo’s campaign and allied PACs and organizations have been hammering Lombardo’s Democratic opponent, Attorney General Aaron Ford, for sponsoring a pardon hearing a[...]
text:
President Donald Trump and character witness Joe Lombardo. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)A pregnant woman shot dead in a parking lot. What a horrible tragedy.
And if you’re the political professionals trying to reelect Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, what a fabulous campaign issue.
Lombardo’s campaign and allied PACs and organizations have been hammering Lombardo’s Democratic opponent, Attorney General Aaron Ford, for sponsoring a pardon hearing application for Norman Smith.
Smith had been initially charged with murder with a deadly weapon in the death of Tineshea Adams in 2015. According to the Review-Journal’s coverage of the case, the scene involved what the police report described as “multiple people,” and Smith’s attorney, assisted by surveillance video, argued during Smith’s trial that the gunshot that killed Adams was unintentional. Smith was ultimately convicted of voluntary manslaughter.
By the time he was convicted in 2018, Smith was already incarcerated for convictions connected to his participation with a half dozen other people in a spree of robberies and assaults earlier in 2015 (again according to the R-J). 
Now that Lombardo’s campaign and its organizational PACs and allies are focusing so much attention on the matter, Smith’s multiple sentences have helped create competing interpretations of which sentences were up for pardoning.  
KLAS took a good swing at trying to unpack the details: Ford’s office contends the pardon was about the robbery charges, not the manslaughter conviction. Smith’s attorney argued in the parole application that Smith had already served the minimum 8 years on the manslaughter sentence. The Department of Corrections disagrees.
There’s a lot going on, you see, and the matter isn’t as plain and simple as Lombardo’s campaign and its allies want voters to think.
That said, Ford’s explanations have been opaque, which is not a preferred behavior from a politician but an exceedingly common one.
Meanwhile, it would be nice — refreshing, even — to believe Lombardo and his campaign affiliates are sincerely upset by Ford signing an an application for a state board to hear an argument for a pardon.
Alas, the relish of their enthusiasm for the issue casts doubt on the genuineness of their disapprobation.
An ad by the Lombardo-supporting Better Nevada PAC, evidently an organization that is not shy about racist tropes, hammers Ford on the pardon issue by running pictures of Black men in scary poses and a voiceover of what sounds like a white suburban mom saying things like “gruesomely gunned down” and “gang member” and “siding with criminals.” 
Familiarity with ads nationwide would be required to guess which Republican race-baiting campaign ad will win the 2026 election cycle’s Willie Horton sweepstakes, but the entry by the pro-Lombardo PAC must be a strong contender.
And running ads like that is a lot easier than defending Trump’s economy.
But might we all take a moment to note that what we have here is Joe Lombardo, a defender of and apologist for Donald Trump, asking the Nevada voting public to be outraged over the prospect of a convicted criminal getting a pardon?
The star of Lombard’s 2022 campaign for governor was the one he wore on his sheriff’s uniform in illegal campaign ads. Brave, strong, straight-shootin’ lawman of the West is Lombardo’s assiduously cultivated political brand.
Trump indiscriminately pardoned 1,600 people who stormed the Capitol, including those who had been convicted of violent crimes against Lombardo’s fellow law enforcement professionals (more than 140 of whom were injured in the insurrection and five of whom would end up dead). Asked at the time about Trump’s pardons of the January 6 rioters, Lombardo failed to respond.
Web searching reveals no evidence that the former sheriff has muttered a public peep about those reckless and disgusting pardons ever since. Nor is there a readily available trace of Lombardo commenting on any of Trump’s multiple pardons of violent drug traffickers, both foreign and domestic, let alone Trump’s many, many pardons of grifters, cronies, conmen, and general purpose skanks, often in a pay-to-play fashion.
When Lombardo, like good little obedient Republicans from coast to coast, endorsed Trump for president in 2024, Trump had already been found liable of sexual abuse by one jury, and found guilty of 34 felonies by another for covering up hush money payments to a porn star. And four years earlier, in the course of attempting to overthrow the U.S. Constitution and steal an election, Trump had tried to nullify the majority of ballots cast by Nevada voters.
Lombardo’s regard for law and order can be situational. 
So voters can be forgiven for assuming Lombardo’s concern about Ford sponsoring someone’s application for a pardon hearing is not driven by Lombardo’s devotion to law and order, but pure politics.
Hoping to attract more attention to what it obviously feels is a much more important issue than affordability, Lombardo’s campaign in a press release Wednesday declared Ford’s purported sins with respect to a pardon application reflect Ford’s “character.”
You know what else reflects a politician’s character? Bowing before and sucking up to the most venal, corrupt, and immoral president in U.S. history.
If Lombardo agrees with his own campaign’s assertion that an elected official’s character is a matter of such crucial concern, he should take a good look at the president he folds for on command. And for that matter, a mirror.
And if voters decide Ford signing an application for a pardon hearing is a deal breaker, that’s their business. But they should keep in mind that the Lombardo campaign and its PACs and allies can be deliberately unreliable sources.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Who should bear the cost of University of Minnesota’s budget problems?
description: In the University of Minnesota’s announcement of $225 million in budget cuts over two years beginning in July 2027, President Rebecca Cunningham described the decision as an “institutional inflection point.” The financial pressures facing the university are real, but who bears the greatest costs remains a choice. Will Cunningham and the Board of Regents cont[...]
text:
University of Minnesota students leave Pioneer Hall in November 2022. (Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)In the University of Minnesota’s announcement of $225 million in budget cuts over two years beginning in July 2027, President Rebecca Cunningham described the decision as an “institutional inflection point.”
The financial pressures facing the university are real, but who bears the greatest costs remains a choice. Will Cunningham and the Board of Regents continue placing that burden on students, staff and faculty, or pursue solutions advancing the land-grant mission by empowering Minnesota’s working families?
While the scale of these cuts is staggering, faculty, staff and students are accustomed to austerity budgets expecting them to do more with less. 
In July, the University announced higher employee health costs beginning in January 2027, the same day the regents extended Cunningham’s contract and added up to $1.48 million in retirement contributions through 2031. These decisions followed two years of budget cuts and tuition hikes that demanded sacrifice from students and workers while the University created a new vice presidency. It also committed $15 million over five years to a marketing contract that produced the discarded “Leave a Future” slogan.
The U’s budget tables for 2025 show $138.2 million in consulting and professional services spending from nonsponsored funds — meaning the operating budget, nothing tied to external funding like federal research grants. 
A Star Tribune analysis found “academic administrative” headcount grew 32% from 2017 to 2025, compared with 6% for faculty, while its payroll share rose from 11% to 13% as faculty’s fell from 29% to 27%. Because that category includes research, student services and technology, the numbers are not proof of waste. But they raise the question: Why is sacrifice concentrated elsewhere?
We have little reason to expect the coming budget cycles to be different under Cunningham and the Board of Regents’ leadership. 
The Morris campus, my alma mater, has already endured years of cuts to academic programs and staffing. More cuts would undermine efforts to increase enrollment while reducing the value Morris offers. Although Morris reports the lowest average student debt in the university system, that means less if cuts eliminate the programs students came to study, push professors to seek better pay elsewhere and leave faculty stretched too thin to offer the learning experience students deserve.
But this does not have to be how Cunningham and the Board of Regents “leave a future” for Minnesota’s working families.
In the announcement, Cunningham promised to restructure the university’s budgeting process to allow broader input in financial decisions. (Transparency would help, too: The budget is far too opaque for average people to examine.) 
University leadership has a responsibility to establish a genuinely democratic process, giving Minnesotans a voice through sharing real deliberation, rather than lip service. As a former student body president, I am familiar with the administration’s tendency to invite consultation without meaningfully sharing power. This moment calls for the University to forgo that pattern and treat people’s voices as more than a box to check.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The moment also calls upon university leadership to consider how it shares in our sacrifices by reining in their worst excesses. While it may not be enough to offset the costs of the forthcoming cuts, it would be meaningful if Cunningham paused spending on exorbitant consultant contracts, froze hiring of new senior leadership positions, or asked the university’s highest-paid executives — herself included — to accept temporary pay cuts before asking others to sacrifice even more. 
Public university presidents have set a precedent of accepting pay cuts in similar moments of financial crisis. Even a modest reduction would demonstrate that university leadership is committed to working families and bearing some of the burden being asked of us.
I came to the University of Minnesota from the Rosebud Indian Reservation in 2019. Growing up in a community devastated by poverty, pursuing a college education and using it to make positive change was my greatest dream. My Morris experience made that dream real and even inspired me to continue my education at the U’s Humphrey School of Public Affairs. I still believe in the opportunity of higher education, I still believe in the U, and I share Cunningham’s hope these cuts will create a sense of mission and collective purpose.
But collective purpose cannot be imposed from the top down, and sacrifice cannot always be demanded from the bottom up. 
University leadership has a choice: continue down the familiar path of austerity, or build a future worthy of the working families this university exists to serve.

title: Back after 1,076 days, Wahkeem Roman Returns to the Blue Hens’ Huddle
