name: Arkansas Advocate
title: AI companies could learn safety lessons from the history of nuclear weapons
description: An AI model built by US tech company OpenAI has hacked into the Australian government healthcare portal, Medicare. The news, which emerged on Sept. 23, follows a string of similar incidents reported over the summer by OpenAI and its main rival, Anthropic. These reports have underscored fears that AI labs may be losing control of […]
text:
A recreation of the gate that separated Los Alamos, New Mexico from the rest of the world during the Manhattan Project (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)
An AI model built by US tech company OpenAI has hacked into the Australian government healthcare portal, Medicare. The news, which emerged on Sept. 23, follows a string of similar incidents reported over the summer by OpenAI and its main rival, Anthropic.
These reports have underscored fears that AI labs may be losing control of their creations. They also helped feed the most recent spate of doomsday warnings about the risks posed to human civilisation by AI.
The CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, has called for the pace of AI development to be slowed, a proposal backed by OpenAI head Sam Altman and Elon Musk. There have also been calls for national regulation and greater international cooperation to counter the threat.
The current debate over how to control AI bears striking parallels with how the world tackled another existential threat to human civilisation: nuclear technology.
J. Robert Oppenheimer oversaw development of the first nuclear weapons through the US government’s Manhattan Project. But Oppenheimer also lobbied for international control of these weapons. The Acheson-Lilienthal Report, published in March 1946, aimed to prevent a destructive arms race between the US and Soviet Union. It was largely written by Oppenheimer.



Let us know what you think...


 


A revised version of the report was later presented to the UN as the Baruch plan.
The Soviet Union rejected it, reading it as an attempt to consolidate America’s technological advantage, much as China has done recently with calls for an AI slowdown.
International cooperation around nuclear non-proliferation became possible only many years after the Baruch plan, following a spate of security incidents and near-misses. The International Atomic Energy Agency was created in 1957, and the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons did not come into force until 1970.
Even if US president Donald Trump agreed with the idea of an AI slowdown – which he does not – calling for international cooperation to regulate AI development is a highly unlikely solution for today’s safety concerns.
A mushroom cloud forms after the initial atomic bomb test explosion off the coast of Bikini Atoll, Marshall Islands, in July 1946. (Photo by Keystone/Getty Images)


 The ‘demon core’

	
One major difference between AI and nuclear technology is that the latter was developed by states, not private industry, so regulation and control were more straightforward than they are today.Yet this still did not stop nuclear accidents, suggesting that neither regulation nor international cooperation would meaningfully address AI safety concerns.Take, for example, what has become known as the “Slotin incident”. Louis Slotin was a scientist involved in the Manhattan Project at the Los Alamos research facility in the US state of New Mexico. On the afternoon of May 21 1946, he was performing an experiment in front of seven colleagues.The experiment used the same type of plutonium-gallium core that sat at the heart of the first atomic bombs. It was supposed to demonstrate how close the core was to criticality – where a nuclear chain reaction becomes self-sustaining.
The core was encased by two hemispheres made of beryllium, which had to be kept apart as they reflected radiation back on the core, making it go critical. Closing them would produce a potentially lethal burst of radiation. Slotin used a screwdriver to keep the two hemispheres separate.
At 3.20pm, the screwdriver slipped and the hemispheres closed. Observers in the room reported seeing a blue flash as the core released an intense burst of neutron particles. Slotin quickly flipped the upper hemisphere away with his bare hand, which probably saved his colleagues – but he absorbed the largest dose of radiation.
Slotin was rushed to hospital but died nine days later. Other observers received significant radiation doses. One, Alvin Graves, had to wear gold caps over his teeth as protection from radiation emitted by his own fillings as a result of the accident.
About a year earlier, the same plutonium core killed another scientist, Harry Daghlian, who was also edging it towards criticality. After the Slotin incident, this plutonium sphere became known as the “demon core”, as if it had developed an evil, scientist-murdering personality.
It was melted down and recast, which seems remarkable given scientists’ supposedly rational orientation. Subsequently, more safeguards were introduced, with criticality experiments requiring a significant safety distance.
Anthropic Co-Founder & CEO Dario Amodei speaks onstage during TechCrunch Disrupt 2023 at Moscone Center on Sept. 20, 2023 in San Francisco. Anthropic is the first major AI company to reach a settlement in multiple lawsuits by authors alleging tech companies used copyrighted material to train their systems. (Photo by Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch)
 
Safety first

	
Elaborate safety systems and maintenance schedules became central to managing nuclear technology. But ironically, these safeguards themselves sometimes caused nuclear accidents.
In 1980, during routine maintenance in a Titan II nuclear missile silo in Damascus, Arkansas, a technician dropped a tool that punctured the missile’s fuel tank. The resulting explosion killed one person and hurled the missile’s nine-megaton warhead out of its silo, fortunately without detonating it.
Nuclear accidents have continued to occur, despite government control and international agreements. That is because accidents are organisational problems that require organisational solutions.
An elaborate system of safeguards is one such response. However, some experts suggest that a reliance on safeguards can also make organisations complacent. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic noticed their models had slipped out of their sandboxes.
Their belief in the effectiveness of their safeguards was misplaced, and the history of how nuclear technology was managed could have told them so. Amodei’s call for an AI slowdown is helpful in this regard, because reducing the speed of development would give organisations time to consider how to address accidents.
Rapid response

	
Rather than solely developing more elaborate safeguards which future, more capable models may find ways to circumvent, AI companies should also invest in monitoring for potential accidents – and invest more in rapidly responding to them. Recent hacking incidents suggest they may not have paid adequate attention to this.
Doomsday warnings about AI invite further comparisons with nuclear weapons. It’s tempting to see parallels with Oppenheimer having simultaneously led the development of “the bomb” and pushed for controls on it.
But this is not how we are used to corporations behaving. The tobacco industry only put warnings on cigarette packs once they were forced to, and they knew for years how lethal their products were.
If AI models went rogue and destroyed the world’s digital infrastructure, then frontier labs would be liable for billions or even trillions of dollars in damage.
By demanding political solutions for organisational problems, Amodei and other tech leaders could be evading their corporate responsibility to safely develop and manage their own products. As nuclear history shows, there is no substitute for vigilance and an ability to quickly identify and respond to accidents when they happen – which they will.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Don’t eat the candy!
description: Voters beware! At the end of your ballot, you’re asked to approve permanent changes to the North Carolina constitution that will harm families for generations. In particular, a proposed amendment to cap local property taxes looks appealing, but it’s really a gift to data centers, Duke Energy and Raleigh politicians. The ballot question reads, “For […]
text:
Wording of the proposed property tax amendment on the North Carolina's  2026 NC general election ballot. (Photo: Laura Leslie/NC Newsline) Voters beware! At the end of your ballot, you’re asked to approve permanent changes to the North Carolina constitution that will harm families for generations.
In particular, a proposed amendment to cap local property taxes looks appealing, but it’s really a gift to data centers, Duke Energy and Raleigh politicians.
The ballot question reads, “For or Against: Constitutional amendment requiring limits on property tax increases by local governments.”
But if it passes, the actual sentence added to the constitution reads, “The General Assembly shall enact general laws limiting the amount by which the levy of taxes on property may increase, which may include exceptions.”
That last phrase – “which may include exceptions” – opens the door for super-sized property owners to lobby state legislators for special tax breaks and extra protection the rest of us won’t get.
In other words, the amendment not only gives control of local property taxes to politicians in Raleigh; it also tells them they can hand out favors to whoever they want.
The big winners will be corporate owners with lobbyists and campaign money to attract the attention of political leaders.
In Wake County, as in many other counties, Duke Energy is the biggest property taxpayer, followed by tech giants, drug makers, banks, and major office park/apartment owners.  Wolfspeed Inc., the data center chipmaker, ranks first in Durham County, followed by Eli Lilly & Company.
Corporate owners lead city and county lists across the state, from Alamance to Wilson.  And they provide a crucial share of the tax revenue needed to finance public services, as they should.
The top 25 property taxpayers in Wake County pay more than 33,000 families in homes worth $400,000.  You can understand why corporations will lobby for special treatment if this amendment passes.
And they’ll find a way to win.  Ten years ago, IBM and its data center in the Research Triangle Park outranked Wolfspeed as the number one property taxpayer in Durham County.  Today, IBM has dropped off the top 25 list, due to its persistent litigation and lobbying.
Even if the legislature doesn’t pick favorites for “exceptions” and instead limits everyone’s tax payment, we will still lose.  The big taxpayers will benefit the most and leave a giant hole in local budgets.  We’ll have to fill the hole with higher fees and sales taxes that hit low- and middle-income families hardest – or we lose the funds needed for public safety, schools, water and sewer service, etc.
Voter Guide: 2026 NC voter guide

Like many civic groups, the nonpartisan League of Women Voters recommends that voters oppose the property tax amendment.  LWV says it “would shift greater authority over local funding decisions to the state while leaving the actual limits, formulas and possible exceptions to future legislation.”
Another constitutional amendment on our ballot would cap the state’s income tax rate at 3.5%.  The cap bans a system that taxes the super-rich and corporations at a higher rate than moderate-income residents – and will force increases in service fees and sales taxes.
Earlier this year, Missouri voters defeated a so-called tax reform referendum after a months-long campaign exposed it would primarily benefit billionaires and “stick each working family with a bill of about $500 more each year.”
We have very little time to spread the truth about the harmful impact of the tax amendments on our ballot.
The NC Budget and Tax Center points out that the property tax amendment doesn’t guarantee a lower tax rate for homeowners; it just gives state legislators authority to pick who gets relief and who pays more.
The center also estimates the income tax amendment could eventually require replacing lost revenue with higher sales taxes that cost the average working family over $900 a year.
Spread the word far and wide.  Go to https://ncvoteagainst.org to learn more.
Like Halloween candy offered by a suspicious stranger, voters have good reason to reject proposals that look good on the surface, but actually give more power to state politicians and wealthy corporations at our expense.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Candidates for WV’s 2nd congressional district seat support different legislation for data centers
description: Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., and Ace Parsi, his Democratic opponent for the U.S. House District 2 race in the upcoming November election, are proposing two different federal bills for data centers, which may be top of mind for some residents as the state aims to attract the developments over environmental concerns. Parsi — a former […]
text:
Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., has agreed to one debate with his Democratic opponent Ace Parsi. (Photos courtesy of Ace Parsi and Congressman Riley Moore)Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., and Ace Parsi, his Democratic opponent for the U.S. House District 2 race in the upcoming November election, are proposing two different federal bills for data centers, which may be top of mind for some residents as the state aims to attract the developments over environmental concerns.
Parsi — a former Morgantown community organizer and Irani who immigrated to the United States as a child, announced last week a data center bill is the first piece of legislation he would introduce if he’s elected. 
“I find when I go out on the (campaign) trail that there is one issue that Democrats, Republicans, and independents, which I would be seeking to represent all of them, agree on, that these things do not have a place in their in their homes, in their backyards,” Parsi told reporters during a Zoom call. 
Parsi narrowly won the Democratic nomination in May over runnerup Stephanie Tomana, a Fairmont teacher. 
His proposed “Neighbors, Not Servers Act” would pause the construction of new large data centers while a national study looked at the costs, his campaign said in a news release. It would also require a local vote before any project moves forward.
“Families here are paying higher power bills, and they’re being asked to live next to the noise, the diesel generators, and the drain on their water, while the deals get cut behind closed doors. If a community is going to carry the cost, it should get to decide. That’s what this bill does: neighbors, not servers,” Parsi said in a news release.
Several data centers have been proposed in different parts of the state, including the Monarch Compute Campus, under development in Mason County, a Google Data Center planned for Putnam County and a data center and power plant complex planned for Tucker County. 
Opponents have raised environmental concerns about data centers, which require electricity to function and cooling systems that require lots of water to prevent equipment from overheating. 
West Virginia lawmakers passed House Bill 2014, Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s priority bill meant to incentivize data center development in the state. The law allows data centers to curtail local zoning ordinances and other regulatory processes and creates a specialized tax structure for data centers and microgrids, which must be placed in designated districts. Local governments have little say or control over those districts, which are established at the state level. 
Opponents of the bill voiced concerns about potential for electric rate increases and discontent with measures that removed local control and enforcement of certain regulations for counties and municipalities where data centers could be built. Last month, Morrisey unveiled a plan for a data center development that includes local input and ratepayer protection. 
Parsi said his bill would bring transparency to data center construction by prohibiting the use of non-disclosure agreements between developers and public officials. 
“These (non-disclosure agreements) are really frustrating in an open democracy, (for) our constituents,” he said. “(The bill) would bring about transparency of who’s assigning these (non-disclosure agreements), and they would bring transparency to when these data centers are getting built, where and what the impact will be.” 
Moore is seeking his second term in Congress. Before being elected in 2024, he had been the West Virginia state treasurer since 2021. 
Moore is a co-sponsor of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require state utility commissions to consider adopting a federal standard directing large data centers to pay the full cost of the electricity upgrades needed to serve them. 
“West Virginians need a voice in this important debate. It is critical that America wins the AI race against countries like China, but we must do it responsibly,” Moore said in a statement to West Virginia Watch. “I’m for local control. Local communities need to have a say about whether to build data centers in their backyard, and we need to ensure that Americans are not being forced to foot the bill for increased energy demands and water usage. 
“That’s why I proudly cosponsored and voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act in the House to ensure that local communities have a voice in these important decisions and ensure that West Virginians are not being forced to foot the bill for data center development,” he said. 
His campaign didn’t respond to a followup question about how the Ratepayer Protection Act would allow communities to prohibit data centers from being built in their area. 
The Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House of Representatives with a vote of 417 to 3, but was blocked by Democrats during a Senate vote this week. 
Democrats called the legislation “toothless” and ineffective because it does not actually require states to adopt standards that require companies to pay for the additional costs and could lead to no action. 
They’ve called for legislation that actually mandates that tech companies cover the electrical costs associated with the projects, according to reporting by The Hill. 
In an email to West Virginia Watch, Morgan King, climate and energy program manager for West Virginia Citizen Action Group, said the group supports any bill that ensures “bring-your-own generation and infrastructure, particularly renewables, for new large load customers.”
 “We also recognize that there should be a federal requirement that all generation and infrastructure required for new large load customers cannot fall on ratepayers,” she said. “Federal legislation can and should urgently address the harm caused by lack of community control and benefit in HB2014.”
The general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Stockard on the Stump: Tennessee governor defends Correction commissioner in failed executions
description: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee continues to give his top correction official a get-out-of-jail free card for botched executions. Correction Commissioner Frank Strada got the job in January 2023 despite overseeing three problematic executions as a deputy commissioner in Arizona, then helped put together the protocol used in two botched executions in Tennessee, inclu[...]
text:
“So far as we know, the Department of Correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined and vetted and approved by the attorney general’s office," said Gov. Bill Lee at a Thursday press conference of Wednesday's failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee continues to give his top correction official a get-out-of-jail free card for botched executions.
Correction Commissioner Frank Strada got the job in January 2023 despite overseeing three problematic executions as a deputy commissioner in Arizona, then helped put together the protocol used in two botched executions in Tennessee, including this week’s failed lethal injection of Christa Pike.
Asked Thursday if he bears some responsibility for hiring and keeping Strada amid the series of troubled executions, Lee avoided a straight answer.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“So far as we know, the Department of Correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined and vetted and approved by the attorney general’s office. At this point, that is all we know, which is the very reason why we will have an investigation,” Lee told reporters following a ribbon cutting for a Goodwill campus in Nashville.
Lee declined early this week to grant a reprieve to Pike even though her attorneys argued that she suffered through sexual abuse and neglect as a child before being convicted of killing classmate Colleen Slemmer, a factor they said wasn’t considered adequately when she was sentenced in a 1996 trial.
To his credit, Lee ordered an immediate investigation of the botched execution Wednesday night after two rounds of injections failed to put Pike to death. The question is: How many independent investigations does it take to figure out the protocol is a failure?
Media witnesses at Riverbend Maximum Security Facility, said they could hear her breathing and “snoring” after two injections but couldn’t see what was happening before she was taken to a hospital for treatment. 
Federal public defenders filed an emergency motion to end the execution Thursday night and are seeking a commutation. 
Tennessee Commissioner of Correction Frank Strada oversaw three fouled-up executions in Arizona before Gov. Bill Lee picked him to lead Tennessee’s death row executions. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
It marks the second failed execution out of the last three performed in Tennessee. 
Lee called off the execution of Tony Von Carruthers and gave him a one-year reprieve in May after a physician tried — and failed — for more than an hour to insert backup and central intravenous lines required by protocol. 
Republican senators this summer called for a third-party review of the Carruthers case and independent investigation. But Lee refused.
Mismanaged
Democratic Sen. Raumesh Akbari said Thursday the state’s “mismanagement” of death row is “cruel and inhumane.”
“What happened Wednesday night was not an isolated failure. It is a pattern,” Akbari said. She cited the 2022 halting of the Oscar Smith execution after state officials admitted lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested as part of the state’s guidelines. 
Lee postponed all executions at that time until a full review was done. He did the same thing Wednesday night but didn’t know Thursday who would conduct the new investigation or how long it would take.
The Department of Correction said Thursday it followed “every step” of its lethal injection protocol, which has been consistently effective and doesn’t allow for “additional procedures. It didn’t answer questions about whether Strada was culpable.
But Akbari said, if the Department of Correction followed its protocol in the Pike case, then the protocol itself is the “problem.” She urged lawmakers to get involved, and they are likely to when the General Assembly convenes in January, even though some sort of “compassionate conservatism” coined by former President George W. Bush is likely to go nowhere.
“The governor’s third-party review is a start, but it is no substitute for oversight. It is time for the General Assembly to exercise its oversight function over the executive branch,” Akbari said as she called the death penalty a policy failure.
Good luck, though, with looking over the governor’s shoulder on this not-so-touchy-feely topic.
Tennessee’s frontrunner to be governor, Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, previously said she wants to reinstate the electric chair and reiterated her stance Thursday, saying she supports an independent review but wants to bring back a modern form of “Old Sparky.”



Quotation







The governor’s third-party review is a start, but it is no substitute for oversight. It is time for the General Assembly to exercise its oversight function over the executive branch.


– Sen. Raumesh Akbari, D-Memphis


Here’s a prediction: The state will jump through the bureaucratic hoops of a full review, which is likely to stretch well into 2027. Then Blackburn will kindly toss it into a trash can and push for resumption of the electric chair. 
In fact, death row inmates can request electrocution under a 2014 law if the state can’t obtain the proper drugs for lethal injection. Five inmates opted for electrocution in 2018 and 2019.
Lawmakers have talked about hangings and firing squads in the last few years. It wouldn’t be a stretch to see the electric chair return with a vengeance. After all, the death penalty is designed to get revenge, even if that’s not the kind of penalty Jesus envisioned as they nailed him to the cross.
Better late than never
Twelve years after the state identified problems with the cell-door locks at Tennessee’s Morgan County prison, Corrections Officer Dustin Pedigo was killed in February when inmate Reginald Steed jimmied his cell door and allegedly stabbed Pedigo to death.
Replacements aren’t coming at breakneck speed, either.
The Department of Correction knew the locks could be opened with a piece of paper in 2013 but prioritized all other prisons and put off replacing them because the Morgan County facility was the state’s newest, District Attorney Russell Johnson of East Tennessee told a Senate corrections subcommittee this week, reiterating what Strada previously told lawmakers.
The state won’t finish installing new locks until October 2029, Johnson said, referring to an August report from Strada.
The sense of urgency, or lack thereof, within the department is saddening.
Tennessee senators’ unannounced prison visit irritates correction commissioner

Steed, who had said in letters, phone calls and an interview with a U.S. marshal that he would kill a prison officer, according to Johnson, was found dead in his cell Sept. 22 at the Riverbend Maximum Security Facility in Nashville where he’d been transferred.
Davidson County District Attorney Glenn Funk asked the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation to investigate the death, which is being done in a “parallel process” with the Department of Correction, according to Johnson.
The TBI is also looking into the stabbing incident at Morgan County, and a Morgan County grand jury is gathering information on the incident, according to Johnson.
Strada didn’t attend this week’s corrections subcommittee hearing, but a Department of Correction official acknowledged that the door-lock project is nearing a start.
Subcommittee Chairman Tom Hatcher acknowledged that replacing cell-door locks is a major undertaking but was hardly satisfied with the project’s time line.
“If I’d had one of my employees murdered at the facility and it was because of the locks, that would have been my priority,” Hatcher told the Lookout. 
Blackburn challenges phone subpoena
The New Civil Liberties Alliance filed a complaint Wednesday on behalf of U.S. Sen. Blackburn, the Republican gubernatorial candidate in Tennessee, saying former special counsel Jack Smith violated her rights by subpoenaing her phone records in connection with his investigation into whether President Donald Trump tried to derail the 2020 presidential election.
The filing in the U.S. District Court in Nashville contends then-Attorney General Merrick Garland illegally named Smith as special counsel in November 2022 and gave him sweeping powers, without a nomination by President Joe Biden or congressional approval. 
The nonprofit group says Smith, the Department of Justice, FBI, special counsel’s office and Public Integrity Section obtained a non-disclosure order requiring Verizon to conceal the subpoena from Blackburn and 20 other Republican lawmakers, a move that stripped her of the constitutional right to challenge it. The subpoena enabled the special counsel to find out who Blackburn talked to on the cell phone, when and for how long.
Stockard on the Stump: Jan. 6 probe creeps into Tennessee gubernatorial race

The lawsuit asks the court to declare Smith’s appointment unconstitutional; the seizure of her toll records unlawful and a violation of the Free Speech or Debate Clause, the First Amendment right of association and the Fourth Amendment’s protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. The filing also seeks an order for the return of records and the award of $1 in damages. They must be working cheap.
“Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the president of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation’s history. This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation’s justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people,” Blackburn said in a statement.
The filing points out the investigation was called Arctic Frost in reference to an orange, mocking President Trump’s complexion.  
Smith testified before a Senate committee this week about his investigation and said he would seek to indict Trump on criminal charges for trying to obstruct the election and for keeping boxes of classified documents at his Florida compound.
The Blackburn filing, of course, fails to mention that Trump stood in a bunker and watched video of the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol that led to the death of multiple police officers, nor does it refer to those who participated in the riot as insurrectionists. It also skips the fact that Blackburn voted to certify the election of Biden, even as Trump claimed, and still does, that the election was stolen.
That could be one reason Trump declined to endorse Blackburn in this year’s Republican primary against U.S. Rep. John Rose.
The silver lining
Notably, Trump did attend the University of Tennessee football game in Knoxville last week in the Vols’ loss to No. 1-ranked Texas, causing security headaches and requiring students to enter the stadium early rather than tailgate until the last minute. 
No debate: After criticizing U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn for not participating in gubernatorial debates, Democratic nominee Jerri Green is getting picky about appearing in forums with independent candidates. (Photo:John Partipilo/Tennesee Lookout)
The university felt so bad about the situation that it sold beer at half-price during the game, which isn’t a terrible trade-off, all things considered
Green pulls a Black(burn)
Blackburn has been taking shots from critics for months for refusing to debate opponents in the gubernatorial race. After declining to go head-to-head with Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts in the primary, she doesn’t appear likely to join a debate sponsored by the Tennessee Press Association for the general election either. 
Democratic candidate Jerri Green seemed to be taking the high road in this philosophical standoff. But now she’s using technicalities to avoid debating independents David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston, saying they haven’t raised enough money or gotten enough polling points to justify her joining a debate.
So much for standing up in a public forum to argue for your political life. This leaves us wondering: Is Green pulling a Marsha?

title: Tennessee faces estimated $220M in extra SNAP costs under new federal rules
description: Tennessee may have to carve out an additional $220 million from its budget next year to continue funding the state’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program after President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill passed more of the program’s costs to states. The total new costs to Tennessee depend, in part, on the state’s SNAP payment error […]
text:
Tennessee could need to carve an additional $220 million out of its budget to meet new federal SNAP cost sharing requirements. (USDA Photo by Lance Cheung)Tennessee may have to carve out an additional $220 million from its budget next year to continue funding the state’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program after President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill passed more of the program’s costs to states.
The total new costs to Tennessee depend, in part, on the state’s SNAP payment error rate — a measure of the number of households that receive either less or more food assistance than they are entitled to. States whose error rate exceeds the 6% goal set by Congress will be financially penalized starting in October 2027.
Those changes went into effect Thursday. The federal spending bill also increased states’ share of administrative costs from 50% to 75%. The increase tacked on an extra $58 million to the Department of Human Services budget in fiscal year 2026, Tennessee’s budget shows.
Tennessee’s error rate was 9.44% for the 2025 fiscal year, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data, below the national average of 10.62%. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act allows states to choose to use error rates from either 2025 or 2026 to calculate how much they will need to contribute. While fiscal year 2026 ended Sept. 30, the error rate data is not expected to be released until June 2027, so Tennessee may not know how much it will be responsible for until then. 
The potential budget challenges for Tennessee’s next governor

If Tennessee did not improve its error rate in 2026, it could be on the hook for 10% of SNAP benefit costs, equaling an estimated $162 million to $171 million, according to nonpartisan policy research center The Sycamore Institute.
The SNAP program helped feed 682,128 beneficiaries in Tennessee as of June 2025, according to USDA data, with rural counties tending to have the highest participation rates.
The new rules under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act stipulate that states with error rates between 6% and 8% must cover 5% of the state’s SNAP benefit costs, which historically have been federally funded. States with error rates between 8% and 10% must pay 10% of SNAP program costs, and those with error rates between 10% and 13.34% must pay 15% of program costs.
A handful of states whose error rates exceed the 13.34% threshold will be given an extra year to improve before the cost-sharing requirement takes effect.
The USDA specifies that SNAP error rates do not indicate fraud. Rather, “payment accuracy errors in SNAP are largely unintentional” and due to administrative mistakes or eligibility errors, according to the USDA.
Previous changes to SNAP work requirements that eliminated waivers for families with children, seniors, veterans, unhoused individuals and children aging out of foster care compounded the program’s bureaucratic complexity, according to Tennessee Justice Center Director of Nutrition Advocacy Signe Anderson. 
Since those changes, more than 100,000 people in Tennessee have lost access to SNAP, Anderson said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Movie made inside Beckley Exhibition Coal Mine shows truth is scary as fiction
description: “Dark Hollow” is a West Virginia horror film shot inside of a coal mine. And while I’ve never watched a horror movie, I’m looking forward to this one. It is heavier on drama and the supernatural elements than gore I have been told. I’ll be able to handle it. The plot follows a monster lurking […]
text:
"Dark Hollow," a horror movie filmed in Beckley, West Virginia, will show at the Colonial Arts Center in Buckhannon, West Virginia, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Paula Kaufman for West Virginia Watch)“Dark Hollow” is a West Virginia horror film shot inside of a coal mine. And while I’ve never watched a horror movie, I’m looking forward to this one. It is heavier on drama and the supernatural elements than gore I have been told. I’ll be able to handle it.
The plot follows a monster lurking in an Appalachian coal mine and a mother who must defeat it to protect her family. 
The film is written and directed by internationally award-winning filmmaker Daniel Byers, who is known for incredible wildlife and culture documentaries. But he also has a bloodthirsty side. 
A West Virginia native, Byers has filmed in more than 60 countries, documenting subjects as varied as a harpy eagle — the world’s largest and most powerful eagle; a wolf he tracked by bicycle and on foot for hundreds of miles; and he filmed remote doctors on a Nepalese eye-care mission. 
But for “Dark Hollow,” Byers turned his camera toward smaller — albeit much older — mountains: Our own. West Virginia is king of goth, of spook, ghosts and cryptids. We have one of the largest underground cave networks in North America, alongside miles of abandoned coal mine tunnels.
The film portrays the real horrors of inequality: of poverty and the “resource curse” of coal. It’s a film that tries to call out the real villains and flip the script on its head. 
The screenplay to “Dark Hollow” — originally called “Paradise” — won the 2023 Austin Film Festival Screenplay Competition out of over 11,000 submissions. 
Why? Perhaps because it challenged the line between truth and fiction. Creating a horror story about coal mining is complex; the past is not yet past and the present is just as scary. 
The film is an indictment on power politics that put profit and greed above dignity and a miner’s health and humanity and above the environment, water and earth. Enough is enough. 
Unfortunately, that trauma is alive and feeding. It is uncomfortable fictionalizing a horror when the real horror is still unfolding.
Mountains are still being blasted for coal. Since the 1990s, more than 2,000 miles of headwater streams have been buried beneath mining debris. And folks in the southern coalfields still can’t drink their water. And black lung disease — referenced in the film — has reached a 50-year high.
Maybe it takes the movie’s fictional monster to neutralize, neuter and defang the real one. 
And, like in most films made in the state, the geography is a protagonist. Mountains are the plot, narrative, story. It’s the people who are the supporting actors. And in “Dark Hollow,” the monster is a nightmarish coal-man creature. 
So, why make a film in West Virginia? In an audio message, Byers pointed to the economic advantages. He noted that New York and Los Angeles are increasingly unaffordable places to make independent films compared to West Virginia. But he emphasized something beyond dollars and cents. He said filmmakers come to West Virginia for its “unique stories, beautiful landscape, culture, music and heritage that are fertile ground for storytelling and making art.” 
That sense of place extends into the film’s music. The epic score was performed by Daniel’s sister, professional vocalist and composer Barbara Byers. She contributed original Appalachian songs through her voice, mountain dulcimer, bowed (and plucked) psaltery, kacapi, jaw harp, spoons and flutes. Some of the music was inspired by a shape-note choir ballad from 1819. 
For the  95-minute film, Byers handled the majority of its roughly 330 visual effects. It is an ambitious and personal project. It shows this month in Buckhannon and Huntington. The Floralee Hark Cohen microtheatre in Charleston will be an extra spooky location because the theatre is so tiny you can nearly feel someone’s knees behind you.
And how neat to watch in Beckley, where the film was shot inside the Beckley Exhibition Coal Mine, or Franklin-near Spruce Knob, another filmed location where the cast camped out in all elements to shoot scenes. Franklin’s historic Warner Drive-in Theatre is going to be a terrific venue. Park your car, pull out a blanket, set out a chair and watch the horror unfold under one of the darkest night sky locations on the east coast. 
Because it’s all mixed in together. Mountain music, folklore and stories in West Virginia are inextricably intertwined. And the biggest monsters are those with enough power and money to end inequality, indifference and pain–and don’t. 
The mountains are sending an SOS. Are we listening?

Floralee Hark Cohen Cinema, Charleston, Oct. 7, 14, 21
Colonial Arts Center, Buckhannon, Oct. 13
Warner Drive-in, Franklin, Oct. 16
Marquee Cinemas, Beckley, Oct. 17
Foundry Theater, Huntington Oct. 18

name: Virginia Mercury
title: FOIA Friday: Virginia faces scrutiny over public records transparency
description: One of the less noticed features of the Virginia Way is the long-running tendency of the commonwealth’s leaders to conduct their decision-making behind closed doors. While the Virginia Freedom of Information Act presumes all government business is by default public and requires officials to justify why exceptions should be made, too many Virginia leaders in[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)One of the less noticed features of the Virginia Way is the long-running tendency of the commonwealth’s leaders to conduct their decision-making behind closed doors. While the Virginia Freedom of Information Act presumes all government business is by default public and requires officials to justify why exceptions should be made, too many Virginia leaders in practice take the opposite stance, acting as if records are by default private and the public must prove they should be handled otherwise.
In this feature, we aim to highlight the frequency with which officials around Virginia are resisting public access to records on issues large and small — and note instances when the release of information under FOIA gave the public insight into how government bodies are operating.
 Richmond faces scrutiny over Flock contract records

Richmond said it had no records. Then, after requests were reworded, it produced them — at least three times over nine months, according to The Richmonder, raising questions about the city’s effort to improve transparency. 
One request focused on the city’s contract with license plate reader company Flock, which has faced privacy criticism across the commonwealth. Some localities have publicly supported using the cameras to help solve crimes.
The Richmonder said Chesterfield and Henrico sent copies of their contracts. Richmond Police said it found “no relevant documents,” and the city’s procurement office said the same, each directing The Richmonder to the other’s office.
“Why did the city say two departments doing two searches for the contract had turned up nothing?” The Richmonder wrote.
In a third attempt, the outlet changed its request from “Flock Safety Inc.” to the contractor’s name, “Insight Public Sector,” to search for the contract for nearly 100 cameras in the city.
The city also rejected two other requests. One involved the Richmond Flying Squirrels, which operates under the legal business name Navigators Baseball LP. Another sought a water-funding spreadsheet, but the city rejected it because the request contained a typo.
Mayor Danny Avula vowed to improve the city’s responsiveness. After multiple records requests for the Flock contract, he told The Richmonder that he believes employees made an honest effort to find it and that the procurement office’s search process wasn’t comprehensive enough. 
“Our FOIA officers work really hard to identify responsive records the requester is asking for, and we definitely encourage FOIA officers to ask clarifying questions to help scope the request, but there are undoubtedly times where they just do a search for the words that were asked for,” Avula said.
The Richmonder said Avula’s administration didn’t directly answer who decided to say there was no Flock contract.
 Mold forces temporary closure of Obama Elementary

Mold that shut down Richmond’s Barack Obama Elementary School at the start of the school year has prompted recommendations to remove and replace building materials, according to a contractor’s report obtained by WTVR.
The contractor said the school’s HVAC and moist pipes caused the mold. The assessment identified a broader pattern of moisture intrusion, leaks, water-damaged materials and areas where moisture could remain hidden. 
WTVR’s records request included the contractor’s room-by-room assessment, prior work orders, information about leaks and the HVAC system, and remediation recommendations. Priority repair areas included areas affected by active plumbing leaks and roof leaks.
Students returned to school after nine days.
WTVR questioned Richmond Public Schools about the work-order descriptions and whether repairs had been completed. RPS said many of the underlying issues have since been addressed and that it is adding ongoing monitoring.
The city of Richmond is one of 47 localities seeking voter approval in November to collect a 1% sales tax for school construction and modernization to address aging facilities. Obama Elementary, formerly J.E.B. Stuart, opened in 1922.
 Court sides with parent in Spotsylvania FOIA delay case

A parent seeking records about her children’s education plans won a partial victory in the Virginia Court of Appeals, which sent part of her FOIA case against the Spotsylvania County School Board back to the trial court. 
Tamara Quick, the parent of two students, sought documents related to their individualized education programs, customized learning plans for students with disabilities. 
The Virginia Coalition for Open Government, a nonprofit alliance promoting open government, published a copy of the Aug. 4 opinion, drawing attention to questions about the school division’s compliance with Virginia’s FOIA response deadline. Quick alleged that the division had failed to respond within five business days, instead taking more than a month. 
Quick lost in the trial court after arguing that the school division had not responded properly or quickly enough under Virginia FOIA. She appealed.
The appeals court upheld the lower court’s finding that Quick’s April 18, May 6, and May 23 inquiries were not FOIA requests.
However, her Oct. 4 request was a valid FOIA request because it explicitly referenced FOIA and was sent to the school superintendent and FOIA officer.
The appeals court sent the issue back to the lower court after the school division produced records more than a month later, on Nov. 8.


The Mercury’s efforts to track FOIA and other transparency cases in Virginia are indebted to the work of the Virginia Coalition for Open Government, a nonprofit alliance dedicated to expanding access to government records, meetings and other state and local proceedings.

The trial court must examine whether the division produced the specific records requested Oct. 4 and whether it violated FOIA’s five-working-day requirements.
The appeals court rejected Quick’s two other FOIA requests on procedural grounds. Her Nov. 5 request was not in the record, so she could not establish what she sent or to whom. Her Jan. 13 request was sent to the school system’s private attorneys rather than the school system itself.
 Residents use FOIA to uncover data center projects

Residents in Franklin and Roanoke counties used public records requests to uncover details about proposed data centers as scrutiny of the projects grows, WVTF reported.
In Franklin County, resident Laura Carter told WVTF that her FOIA request about the county’s zoning ordinance and process uncovered references to “Project Flash.” The project was later identified as a proposed data center development at Summit View Business Park, just north of Rocky Mount. 
As details emerged, residents opposed the project, and the county announced in mid-August that it was not moving forward.
In a separate case, the Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance used records requests to piece together a potential agreement involving a data center at Wood Haven Technology Park in Roanoke County.
That project ultimately fell through.
“It’s a helpful illustration of how some of these deals can come together, but it is also a case where we got lucky this time,” Ben Verschoor, alliance organizer, told WVTF. “We should be taking measure to ensure it doesn’t happen.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: The simple affordability fix Virginia just can’t seem to make
description: Across the political spectrum, people who do the math come up with the same answer: the cheapest kilowatt-hour is the one you don’t need to use. A well-insulated building outfitted with LED lighting and energy-efficient appliances saves money for occupants over time even when upfront costs are higher. It’s astounding, then, that Virginia’s residential buildi[...]
text:
Townhomes under construction in Richmond, Va. on May 15, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Across the political spectrum, people who do the math come up with the same answer: the cheapest kilowatt-hour is the one you don’t need to use. A well-insulated building outfitted with LED lighting and energy-efficient appliances saves money for occupants over time even when upfront costs are higher.
It’s astounding, then, that Virginia’s residential building code treats these elements as optional luxuries rather than as basic standards that all home buyers and renters should expect, even – or perhaps especially – in an entry-level home. 
Key efficiency provisions of Virginia’s housing code have not been strengthened in a decade and a half, lagging far behind national model standards that many states regularly adopt each time the model standards are improved.  
Even more astounding, Virginia’s Board of Housing and Community Development (BHCD), which updates Virginia’s code every three years, is set to propose an “updated” building code with efficiency standards that lag even the 2012 edition of the national standards. 
The national model code is called the International Energy Conservation Code, or IECC. Its globalist name notwithstanding, it is overwhelmingly a U.S. standard and serves as the basis for the efficiency provisions of most state and local building codes. 
Every three years the International Code Council updates the IECC, almost always ratcheting up standards in line with improved technologies and capabilities.  
If you buy a new house in Maryland, which regularly adopts the latest IECC, you can be assured of a weather-tight home built to a solid efficiency baseline. Across the Potomac in Virginia, your new house is likely to be built to lower standards, even by the same builder. 
The builder may have saved a little money building the Virginia house, but whether you will save anything on the purchase price is questionable. As every buyer knows, supply and demand matter much more than a builder’s cost in determining how much you pay for your home.  
What is absolutely clear (and demonstrated by research in case the point isn’t sufficiently intuitive) is that you will spend more money over time to heat and cool and power a less efficient home. By the time you’ve paid off your mortgage, Virginia’s lax standards are likely to have cost you tens of thousands of dollars. 
Sure, once you’ve bought that Virginia home you can then spend more money to upgrade lighting and appliances and possibly do some extra weatherizing, assuming you are even aware that better performance is possible. But you’re pretty much stuck with whatever insulation the builder put into the walls. That’s why the time to maximize energy efficiency is when the home is being built, not later.  
What’s especially irritating is that Virginia’s failure to adopt higher standards comes in spite of the General Assembly’s efforts to raise the bar. Legislators are hesitant to wade into the minutia of building codes, but twice in the last ten years they have passed laws nudging the Board towards stronger energy conservation standards.  
Virginia law now calls for the Board to adopt a code that permits buildings to be “constructed, rehabilitated and maintained at the least possible cost consistent with recognized standards of health, safety, energy conservation and water conservation.” 
It instructs the Board to have “due regard” for the “generally accepted standards” recommended by the International Code Council and the National Fire Protection Association. (The fire standards have done very well as a result; the efficiency standards, not so much.) 
More pointedly, a 2021 act added a requirement that when the International Code Council issues an updated version of the IECC, the Board must consider adopting amendments to the Virginia building code that are “at least as stringent as” the provisions of the latest IECC. 
In doing so, the Board must assess “the public health, safety, and welfare benefits of adopting standards that are at least as stringent as those contained in the IECC, including potential energy savings and air quality benefits over time compared to the cost of initial construction.”
I’m sure the Board would say that it does consider these things, right before dismissing them. We should take that with a grain of salt; the BHCD has long been dominated by builder interests. 
And according to Bill Penniman, an activist and attorney who participates in the BHCD process, the board operates according to a rule it made up that says there must be “consensus” among the members of the various working groups that review the code before a more stringent provision makes the final cut. 
But, according to Penniman, the board defines “consensus,” to mean unanimity, and thus consensus is never reached in favor of strengthening energy conservation provisions because, again, builders and their allies dominate the process. (Interestingly, he notes, non-unanimous proposals to weaken the code don’t suffer a similar fate.)
And so, in spite of the law, Virginia’s wall insulation and air-leakage standards remain weaker than IECC standards from 2012, 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024. 
Now, according to Penniman, the BHCD plans to submit to the governor proposed code amendments that once again fall short of even the 2012 IECC. At a July 13 meeting, the board rejected even an amendment offered by Penniman and other efficiency advocates that would have brought wall insulation requirements up to the IECC standard in effect from 2012 to 2018. 
Penniman says there will be a final vote in December before BHCD publishes the proposed rule for “updates” that will take effect in 2028. 
Having written on this topic before, I’ve heard from home builders who say that increasing the efficiency of new homes makes them too expensive for entry-level buyers. The choice, they say, is not between building homes to lower standards or higher standards, but between building them to lower standards or not at all.
Houses can be built to use much less energy. Why aren’t they?

If you really want to add to the housing stock, they urge, you need to make homes as cheap to build as possible, including skimping on energy-saving measures. And since it wouldn’t be fair to have higher standards for well-off buyers than for poorer folks, everyone alike must suffer from below-standard housing.  
Well, okay, they don’t put it in quite the same words I use, but so far they have won the argument at the Board. 
What is interesting here, however, is that while most homebuilders focus on maximizing profit by building as cheaply as possible, companies like Habitat for Humanity and Viridiant, which regularly serve low-income communities, consistently choose EarthCraft or Energy Star standards –  which both exceed code. They know a home isn’t affordable if the occupants can’t afford to pay for heat and electricity.
Clearly it is time for the governor to weigh in. Her just-released Energy Plan has a lot of welcome language on energy efficiency as well as other technologies that save money while lowering carbon emissions. (I’ll unpack it in more detail in a future column.) 
The plan leans in on the importance of home efficiency and touts state programs that provide support for retrofits of existing homes. But while it also notes that adopting the latest model building codes could yield billions of dollars in energy cost savings over the life of new homes, it does not actually call for Virginia to take that path. 
Residential heating and cooling is a significant expense for most households. An energy affordability agenda that leaves out home efficiency is one with a gaping hole in it.

title: ‘Super Intelligence,’ featuring Speaker Mike Johnson, adds to worries over potential AI disaster
description: President Donald Trump’s attempt to rebrand artificial intelligence and place himself in lockstep with the industry’s leaders this week are the latest examples of how the administration has taken a hands-off regulatory approach to the rapidly evolving technology.
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., speaks at a campaign event for U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans in Virginia Beach, Virginia, on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)President Donald Trump’s attempt to rebrand artificial intelligence and place himself in lockstep with the industry’s leaders this week are the latest examples of how the administration has taken a hands-off regulatory approach to the rapidly evolving technology.
It does little to assuage growing concerns that autonomous AI poses a risk to public safety, national security and other vulnerable infrastructure. U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, has contributed to this apprehension, ignoring bipartisan calls from his colleagues in Congress to act on legislation that would place guardrails around AI development.
“They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow it down, they should,” Johnson said. AI companies should “self-regulate” and “self-police,” the speaker said last month shortly before sending House members home for a seven-week break to campaign for the midterm elections. 
Driving the demand for regulation are outright acknowledgements from the AI industry that it has struggled to contain the technology’s ability to teach itself. The most recent proof has been in the emergence of Claude Mythos, a product in development that its creator Anthropic recently deemed too dangerous to release because of its ability to hack through cybersecurity. 
In July, OpenAI confirmed two of its models escaped from its digital labs and infiltrated a competing AI startup’s infrastructure. The incident has been described as a hacking system that  took offensive steps to steal the answers to a test it was taking.
These ominous clouds hung over a White House meeting Trump hosted Tuesday with Johnson and AI industry executives, including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and leaders from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Nvidia. 
Anyone with hopes the tech titans would emerge contrite and careful after the meeting saw them dashed that same day when Trump issued an executive order to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence.” The edict applies to all official correspondence, public communications and policy documents within the executive branch.
No one expected Trump or Johnson to conceive a strict regimen to keep AI in check, but the executive order made it abundantly clear the president and speaker have no intention of reining in the industry. 
This was reinforced with the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, a document all six CEOs at the meeting signed, according to Trump. That the president, who blurs ethical lines to the point of obliteration, described the document as a “morally binding” accord is reason enough to doubt its value. Johnson went an octave higher on the oxymoronic scale when he said the agreement includes “voluntary” commitments.
Let there be no question that AI has the capacity to achieve huge advancements in fields that could better mankind. Medicine, agriculture and the environment come to mind as areas where “super intelligence” could help make historic strides. 
But our chief executive and highest-ranking lawmaker, standing on the edge of the digital frontier with the ability to steer America into a better future, have chosen to be neutral passengers rather than thoughtful navigators.
Super intelligence, indeed.     
It brings to mind the rise and fall of disaster movies and TV shows from the 1970s. The most notable from the genre were “Towering Inferno,” “The Poseidon Adventure” and multiple iterations of “Airport.” There were also far less memorable offerings with not-so-creative titles such as “Flood,” “Earthquake,” “Meteor” and let’s not forget “The Bees.”
And then there was “Supertrain,” a short-lived series from NBC in 1979 that welcomed small-screen viewers aboard a nuclear-powered, cross-country bullet train with an itinerary filled with mayhem. Most episodes featured a cavalcade of vintage Hollywood stars — imagine “Love Boat” but with Charro as a homicidal maniac.
How bad was “Supertrain?” Dick Van Dyke, quite possibly the most beloved figure in TV history, was cast in Episode 2 as an unhinged man who wants to pay back a stranger’s act of kindness by killing the man’s ex-wife.
In what had to be an act of desperation, the team behind “Supertrain” added a canned laughter track to its ninth and final episode. Its plot included a passenger who’s a murder suspect as well as a hostage situation. Chuckles galore, right?
The Trump-Johnson treatment of artificial intelligence feels like a disaster movie in the making, but without the formulaic script that assures us a square-jawed, steely-eyed hero will save the day in the end. 
It doesn’t bode well for a sequel.

name: National
title: After states sue, Trump administration walks away from disability rights enforcement
description: A court battle that began when conservative-led states sued to block protections for transgender people has ended in a rollback of protections for people with disabilities — a result disability advocates have feared for months. At the end of August, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services joined the handful of conservative-led states suing […]
text:
Disability rights advocates rally at the Missouri State Capitol to protest the state’s participation in a lawsuit that began as an effort to block protections for transgender people but ended in a rollback of protections for people with disabilities. Missouri eventually withdrew from the suit, but five Republican-led states did not. (Photo by Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)A court battle that began when conservative-led states sued to block protections for transgender people has ended in a rollback of protections for people with disabilities — a result disability advocates have feared for months.
At the end of August, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services joined the handful of conservative-led states suing it, and asked a court to strike language from a federal disability-rights regulation that directed states to prioritize serving disabled people in their communities rather than in nursing homes or institutions.
Last week the judge did so, ending the case, Texas v. Kennedy, by removing all mentions of community integration from the regulation that implements a piece of landmark federal disability law known as Section 504.
The Trump administration’s move — along with a June memo from the Justice Department that argued federal law doesn’t require states to provide community-based services for disabled people — marks a sharp about-face for the federal government, which has long been the chief enforcer of such protections.
The change to the Section 504 rule, disability rights advocates fear, will make it harder for disabled people to receive services they need to live in their communities — and to stay out of institutions.
“This affects children, this affects adults, it affects your elderly parents. It affects everyone,” said Charlotte Cravins, a Baton Rouge, Louisiana, attorney whose toddler son Landry was born with Down syndrome and has impaired vision.
Landry receives publicly funded therapies that have helped him learn to crawl, pull himself up to stand, and to use American Sign Language, all while being able to live at home with his family.
But Cravins worries the ruling threatens those gains. Her husband, who was Landry’s main caregiver, recently had to return to work, and so Cravins is now caring for their son while also working. They’re hoping to get Landry assessed for nursing services and other aids that can help with daily living.
“But those services are at risk now of being unavailable,” she said.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services told Stateline in an email that the department “remains firmly committed to protecting the civil rights of individuals with disabilities” and enforcing applicable disability rights law.
“Our commitment to ensuring that individuals with disabilities are treated with dignity, afforded equal opportunity, and are able to meaningfully access community services remains unchanged,” he said.
The U.S. Department of Justice, in an email to Stateline, said the court’s order “answered an ordinary-course request” about updated federal guidance and clarified the “proper scope” of Olmstead v. L.C., the landmark 1999 Supreme Court ruling that people with disabilities have a civil right to live and receive services in their communities rather than institutions.
Previous administrations have relied on Olmstead’s precedent to compel states to provide community-based services.
As federal protections fade, disabled Americans fear a return to institutions

States that were plaintiffs in the lawsuit have told the court they don’t want federal interference: They said that Biden-era updates to Section 504 unfairly restricted how they’re able to spend money, and prevented them from deciding how best to care for their own residents. They said their budgets, strained by rising costs and workforce shortages, can’t always accommodate expensive services required by the law, and that with smaller Medicaid budgets they’re having to make hard choices. Removing the federal “integration mandate” would give them more flexibility.
“Florida joined this lawsuit to serve as a check on federal power, not to deny care,” Jae Williams, press secretary in the office of Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, a Republican, told Stateline in a statement.
“Reclaiming state authority gives Florida the flexibility needed to address critical public safety and homelessness issues while ensuring proper care for individuals.”
The resolution of the case “achieves the right balance,” said Sam Curtis, information officer for the Alaska Department of Law, “by keeping historical Section 504 protections in place and vacating only the unlawful new provisions that threatened Alaska’s Medicaid program, home and community based services, and systems of care for Alaskans with complex needs.”



Quotation







It’s part of this bigger effort from the federal government to walk away from their longstanding commitment to the right to community living. 


– Alison Barkoff, director of the Hirsh Health Law and Policy Program at the Milken Institute School of Public Health at George Washington University


But the change to how the feds enforce Section 504 means states may no longer have a federal monitor ensuring they provide community services, disability advocates and experts told Stateline.
“It’s part of this bigger effort from the federal government to walk away from their longstanding commitment to the right to community living,” said Alison Barkoff, director of the Hirsh Health Law and Policy Program at the Milken Institute School of Public Health at George Washington University.
Disabled people still have a legal right to receive community-based services, she said, “but the right is only as good as the enforcement.”
Gender dysphoria to disability rights
The case began back in 2024, when 17 Republican-led states sued the Biden administration over its inclusion of gender dysphoria as a protected disability under Section 504.
But then the suit morphed into something different.
After Trump was reelected and his administration made clear it would not enforce the Biden rule, several states pulled out of the lawsuit. Their attorneys general scrambled to distance themselves from it, amid a swift backlash from the disability community that warned the suit imperiled federal protections for all people with disabilities.
But in a surprising move, a handful of states chose to stick with the lawsuit. In January, they amended their complaint to ask the court to strike down the Section 504 rule that directs states to provide disabled people services in their communities whenever possible, rather than in institutions such as nursing homes and state hospitals.
By September, more states had dropped out, leaving five — Alaska, Florida, Louisiana, Montana and Texas — when the Trump administration joined them in asking the court to strike the integration provisions.
In  an email to Stateline, a spokesperson for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, connected the lawsuit and its resolution to the original complaint about the inclusion of gender dysphoria, saying it defeated a “woke” rule that “would have endangered disability funding for the sake of promoting the radical trans agenda.” He did not address the removal of the integration mandate.
“This resolution ensures that Texans who rely on Section 504 and disability assistance are fully protected,” he said. “It supports family choice, ensures healthcare providers are able to provide the best possible care to Texans, and guarantees that all protections that existed prior to the 2024 Biden rule are upheld and permanently preserved.”
Barkoff emphasized that the ruling doesn’t change disability rights protections that are baked into other federal laws, such as the Americans with Disabilities Act, and precedent-setting cases such as Olmstead.
“These rights still exist, and people need to understand that,” Barkoff said.
M. Geron Gadd, a senior attorney at the National Health Law Program who focuses on disability rights cases, agreed that the ruling doesn’t eliminate states’ legal requirement to provide community-based services to disabled people.
However, she said, “it can make it much harder for people with disabilities and their families, who often are already struggling, to obtain needed services.”
States get a boost
One practical result of the judgment in this case — and the Department of Justice’s June memo that reinterpreted federal disability law and the Olmstead decision — is that disabled people may have to go to greater lengths, including suing states, to get services if they’re denied them.
How a legal challenge over gender dysphoria became a fight for disability rights

The department has already retreated from disability rights cases against states including Florida and Texas, which have long pushed back against Olmstead’s scope in the hopes of persuading the feds to narrow their interpretation of disability law.
In 2023, a U.S. district court found that Florida had kept children with complex medical needs unnecessarily institutionalized in nursing facilities, violating federal disability rights law and the Olmstead integration mandate. The Justice Department filed the lawsuit during the Biden administration. The department shifted its stance this year and asked the court to vacate its decision.
The Justice Department also dropped out of a long-running case centered on claims Texas has been illegally placing thousands of disabled people in nursing homes for decades.
Disability rights groups and advocates have called for protection of federal integration requirements. Late last month, a bipartisan group of congressional representatives cosponsored a resolution to reaffirm Olmstead and the right of disabled people to receive services in their communities. A group of 100 Democratic members of Congress also signed a letter in July calling on the Justice Department to rescind its memo.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore signs executive orders to remove hurdles to new housing approval, construction
description: Gov. Wes Moore continued a statewide push against administrative barriers to new housing development Thursday, signing executive orders to identify administrative bottlenecks that delay project permit approvals and to speed construction of those units.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore signed two executive orders Thursday aimed at removing administrative hurdles in permit approval for new housing developments and the construction of housing units. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore continued his push against administrative barriers to new housing development Thursday, signing executive orders to identify administrative bottlenecks that delay project permit approvals and to speed construction of those units.
The new “Housing Innovation” and “Permitting and Licensing Acceleration” executive order signings came on the same day as the start of two laws pushed by Moore to boost housing production — and just days after a new independent report showed that the state’s housing shortage has led to high housing costs are a significant contributor to the state’s poverty levels.
Moore’s announcement builds off previous executive orders and legislative priorities to get more new housing units built quickly to counter those rising rent and housing costs.
21% of poverty in Maryland driven by high housing costs, report says

“Here’s what today means: we’re building faster, we’re building smarter,” Moore said at the construction site of a modular home near Curtis Bay. “We’re building a Maryland where more people have a place to call home.”
The construction of modular housing options is a feature in the Housing Innovation executive order. It aims to encourage construction of modular housing for “faster and more cost-efficient way of building more homes in our neighborhood,” Moore said. The order also boosts workforce training opportunities in modular home construction for future and current construction workers.
That same order also creates the so-called “Maryland Housing Innovation Incubator,” which will function as a “space for entrepreneurs and housing experts to identify and scale best practices to bring innovative housing solutions to market,” Housing Secretary Jake Day said Thursday.
“We’ve underproduced housing at a rate of 8,000 units a year for 20 years … Maryland’s housing shortage wasn’t created overnight, and we know it won’t be solved overnight,” Day said.
“The governor’s housing acceleration executive order will help expedite more affordable units,” Day said, “by supporting innovation of new construction techniques, financing, and incubation of emerging technology startups, while complementing them with regulatory reform and a pathway to workforce development in new industries and new fields.”
The other executive order signed Thursday creates a new council to assess permitting and licensing processes to identify potential regulatory hurdles delaying housing projects in the state.
“When permits get stuck, projects don’t get built. It’s that easy,” Moore said. “If red tape is a thing that keeps shovels from getting in the ground, if permitting is a thing that keeps people from becoming homeowners, then we have a fundamental problem that we need to fix.”
Housing Secretary Jake Day says new executive orders will help find innovative ways to solve Maryland’s housing shortage. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Just this week, Pew Charitable Trusts released a report identifying Maryland as a state where above-average housing costs is a leading driver of poverty, with approximately 21% of the state’s poverty level attributable to housing costs and rent.
Experts with Pew suggested Maryland and states in similar situations boost housing supply enough to slow rising rents and housing costs, through reworking the permitting laws that govern approvals of new developments and by giving more flexibility for different housing options.
Those suggestions largely align with the Moore administration’s previous efforts during his term.
Thursday was the official start date of two new laws Moore pushed this past legislative session. The first is the Maryland Housing Certainty Act, which aims to boost housing production by granting developers “vesting rights,” ensuring that their projects are less likely to be delayed due to changing local housing or zoning policies. Another new law encourages housing development around transit-oriented locations, by restricting parking minimums and other local decisions in specific situations.
Moore issued a similar executive order last year to reduce permit approval timelines at the Department of Housing and Community Development along with other state agencies and better utilize state land that could be repurposed for housing development.
He insisted that efforts to speed up project approvals and construction will not compromise health, safety and environmental regulations.
“We can keep standards, we can move faster and we can protect our people. We don’t have to choose between those things,” he said.
