name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Arts Commission refuses grant funding to 2 LGBTQ+ organizations
description: South Carolina’s Arts Commission denied grant funding to a pair of LGBTQ+ arts groups in the Upstate.
text:
The Greenville Gay Men's Chorus, founded in 2011, consists of more than 35 tenors and basses "dedicated to artistic excellence, meaningful collaboration, and the power of choral music to build community and connection," according to the group's website. (Photo courtesy of Nakeshia Shannon)COLUMBIA — The governing board of the South Carolina Arts Commission denied grants to a pair of LGBTQ+ arts groups in the Upstate without giving a reason.
The commission’s board voted 5-3 Thursday to reject giving $13,000 to the Greenville Gay Men’s Chorus and almost $4,000 to Spartanburg’s Proud Mary Theatre Company.
The meeting comes more than a month after the agency’s governing board approved a combined $3.7 million for more than 170 other arts organizations. In August, the board asked these two groups to provide additional information, despite having received funding in past years and an independent review panel also recommending them for approval.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Representatives of the groups, along with the state’s American Civil Liberties Union chapter, decried the decision as discrimination.
“Only these two groups are denied funding. Only these two are singled out, are made to jump through additional hoops,” said Matt Butler with the ACLU.
“Somethings rotten in South Carolina,” he added. “It is not a good day in South Carolina for arts artistic expression or for the First Amendment.”
None of the board members talked about their vote during Thursday’s virtual-only meeting, and no public comments were taken.
However, emails provided to the ACLU through public records requests show that at least two board members, Russell “Rip” Park of Easley and Jessica Rourke of Columbia, singled out applications by the choir and theater company ahead of a meeting in June.
“While these organizations have every right to promote their agendas privately, it is not the role of a state funded agency to promote them. I cannot support these requests. In the future, I would appreciate your bringing controversial requests to the commissioners’ attention in advance for discussion,” Parks wrote to the commission’s director June 12.
“I could not defend these programs to concerned legislators who could pull funding for the entire Commission over support of these organizations,” he continued.
That same day, in a separate email, Rourke wrote she would vote no.
“My decision is based on a personal and governance principle that commission funding should not be directed toward organizations structured around specific sexual orientations, nor should public funds support drag performances,” she wrote.
Rourke did not specify what performances she was talking about. But in July, the theater group held its fourth annual fundraiser featuring a drag show and silent auction.
Some lawmakers call SC Arts Commission funding a ‘waste.’ Supporters say it’s essential.

The board ended up not making any grant decisions in June, postponing them until Aug. 20, when Parks made the motion to pull the two groups’ grant requests for further consideration.
“The General Assembly holds this commission accountable for maintaining community standards, and the commission has concerns about two programs that were presented,” he said. “What we question is the artistic merit of these two programs.”
But the commission did not ask additional questions related to artistic merit.
Instead, it asked each group to submit a line-item breakdown of their budgets and the names of all employees and vendors paid with state grant funding.
They also asked if the grant funding would cover the cost of any programming in K-12 schools; the chorus and theater both said no. All questioning occurred through emails ahead of Thursday’s meeting.
The state Arts Commission is a frequent target of the hardline House Freedom Caucus, which attempts unsuccessfully during budget debates to cut the agency’s funding.
At a candidate forum ahead of June primaries, GOP Rep. April Cromer, a caucus member from Anderson, highlighted Arts Commission grants to the Gay Men’s Chorus and Upstate SC LGBT+ Chamber of Commerce as “appalling” examples of why she can’t support the budget.
Rep. Thomas Beach, another member of the uber-conservative caucus, applauded the board’s decision Thursday.
“There is no reason tax dollars should be spent on inappropriate art that is politically charged,” the Piedmont Republican told the SC Daily Gazette in an email after the meeting. “Further, too many South Carolinians are now struggling to make ends meet, facing economic crisis. It is the obligation of the government to the taxpayer to exercise fiscal restraint at this time.”
He did not elaborate on what he thought made these two groups’ productions inappropriate.
According to its application, the Proud Mary Theatre Company requested less than $4,000 to cover expenses related to its upcoming productions of “The Book of Merman,” a spoof on the Broadway musical “The Book of Mormon;” and “Stage Frights,” a Halloween-themed Broadway revue featuring songs from “The Little Shop of Horrors,” “Phantom of the Opera” and “Beetlejuice.”
The Greenville Gay Men’s Chorus, which received a $4,750 grant last year, asked for about $13,000 for general operating expenditures, such as security for its shows, bookkeeping and storage.
Founded in 2011, the chorus represents LGBTQ+ individuals and strives to “build community, foster compassion, and inspire activism at home and around the world through our music and message,” according to its online mission statement.
Some of the group’s recent and upcoming shows include its annual Christmas concert, which in the past has featured songs from films such as “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” and a show called “Raise Your Voice” featuring songs from popular artists, such as Lady Gaga, Billy Joel, N’Sync and Josh Groban.
Mary Adam, executive director of the Gay Men’s Chorus, said the decision left her “disappointed and stunned.”
The agency’s independent judges of grant applications gave the group 91 points out of 100 on artistic merit. When it tried to offer the governing board more documentation of its artistry, she said, the commission refused the additional materials.
The chorus answered all questions and met all criteria, she said. She believes the only reason the chorus didn’t get a grant is because the singers are gay.
The loss of funding does not mean the group won’t perform. The request amounted to 13% of the chorus’ overall budget, Adam said, and private donations have covered the gap.
But Adam said it’s more about fairness in the process, who the commission cut out and why.
She said the decision smacked of homophobia and “blatant bigotry.”
Butler said the decision will have a “larger chilling effect.” The commission is saying to South Carolina artists that “if you’re LGBTQ, keep moving,” he said.
John Fagan, a prominent local director in the Upstate, said the Warehouse Theater, where his organization puts on plays, received funding despite putting on some of the same productions as the Proud Mary Theatre, including “Kinky Boots,” a musical about a struggling show factory in England that avoids bankruptcy by selling sturdy stilettos to drag queens.
Fagan, a longtime director of the Upstate Shakespeare Festival, said the Arts Commission appeared to “change the rules at the very end” after all groups had already submitted applications. He said it sends a dangerous message to LGBTQ+ people “that your voice is not important; that your voice does not need to be heard.”
It also sets a precedent for the future, Fagan told the SC Daily Gazette.
The other “no” votes came from board members Danielle Thompson, of Sumter; and Linda Stern and Bhavna Vasudeva, both of Columbia.

name: Maryland Matters
title: New law on youth charging welcomed, but it’s not the end of the fight, advocates say
description: It took more than a decade to get this far, but lawmakers and advocates who gathered Thursday at the Baltimore City Juvenile Justice Center to celebrate the new youth sentencing act were reminded that they are not finished yet.
text:
Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel) speaks at a press conference Thursday outside the Baltimore City Juvenile Justice Center. Bartlett was a House sponsor of the Youth Charging Reform Act, which took effect Thursday after years of fighting for it. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)It took more than a decade to get this far, but lawmakers and advocates who gathered Thursday at the Baltimore City Juvenile Justice Center to celebrate the new youth sentencing act were reminded that they are not finished yet.
“The law that takes effect today is a step in the right direction and is progress,” said former state Sen. Jill P. Carter, who advocated for the law for years. “But it doesn’t end auto charge, which is the goal and which we should all want. All of us should actually seek to end automatic charging children as adults.”
She was speaking at a news conference alongside members of the Maryland Public Defender’s Office, criminal justice advocates and other supporters.
The Youth Charging Reform Act that took effect Thursday makes it more difficult to charge juveniles as adult and try them in adult court. But serious charges, such as first-degree murder or rape, still go directly to adult court for some youth; and prosecutors can still request the court that a youth charged with a certain crime can still have the case heard in adult court.
“We’ve had the data and the evidence that the majority of children that are automatically charged as adults have their cases adjudicated ultimately in the juvenile system, or are ultimately dismissed in the adult system,” said Carter, who said she believes it took 15 years or more to get the current law passed.
Former state Sen. Jill P. Carter is credited in champion the Youth Charging Reform Act, which became law Thursday after years of trying. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The law raises the age from 14 to 16 when a youth can be tried as an adult for most crimes. It would still send 14- and 15-year-olds to adult court for first-degree murder or rape charges, but specifies that 16-year-olds charged with offenses such as first-degree assault and some firearms offenses would start in juvenile court.
The bill also prohibits youth charged as adults from being “detained or confined” in an adult prison, except when no “secure juvenile detention area” is immediately available, in which case a youth could be processed in an adult jail, but not be held for more than six hours.
Maryland’s system of automatically charging youth as adults in some cases was an outlier among states, with only Alabama sending more 14- to 17-year-olds to adult court.
The measure that passed this year, sponsored by Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), also requires annual reports, beginning Oct. 1, 2027, by the Governor’s Office of Crime Prevention and Policy to the General Assembly and the Commission on Juvenile Justice and Emerging and Best Practices. The reports will include the number of youths charges as adults, the charges they faced, and the number of federal violations that prohibit youth “from having sight and sound contact with adult offenders.”
Smith wasn’t in attendance Thursday, but he did release a statement.
“The savings we achieve by reducing the wasteful practice of automatic charging in cases that rarely result in conviction will be reinvested in treatment, prevention and community-based services,” said Smith, who chairs the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee. “Long-term community safety is achieved by giving young people the support they need, and reducing the likelihood they will reoffend.”
But advocates such as Jordan Ross, 18, said more work must be done by making sure all youth get the services needed and are not housed among adults.
“The Youth Charging Reform Act protects 55% of Maryland youth, but I say, protect us all,” said Ross, a freshman at Morgan State University in Baltimore. “We all deserve a chance at a future. A chance to make decisions, to learn from them. But do your job, adults.”
Jordan Ross, 18, spoke in support of the new Youth Charging Reform Act on Thursday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The adult state legislators will hear and see criminal justice advocacy as the 2027 legislation session approaches Jan. 13.
Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel), who sponsored the House version of the Youth Charging Reform Act, said one focus she will have in the next session is to ensure funding is provided for youth services.
Bartlett, on hand for Thursday’s news conference, said some of those services would include cognitive behavioral therapy, mentoring services and continued investment in the Thrive Academy. Thrive, which is managed by the state Department of Juvenile Services, is a gun-violence prevention program that offers wraparound services and uses mentors who are “credible messengers” to help youth steer away from gun violence.
A major challenge to maintain or fund new programs will be the state’s financial situation: The fiscal 2028 budget is projected to have a structural budget gap of about $3 billion, with wider gaps projected in the coming years.
“A budget is a reflection of your ideals and your morals,” Bartlett, chair of the House Judiciary Committee, said after the nearly 40-minute press conference. “So, our budget should reflect that.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Five Haitians from Springfield, Ohio have been deported after Trump ended protected status
description: Five Haitians from Springfield, Ohio have been deported back to Haiti after President Donald Trump revoked their legal status, said Theresa Hice-Fromille, a board member of the Haitian Community Help and Support Center.   More than 470 people have been deported from the United States to Haiti between Aug. 20- Sept. 17 — including some with […]
text:
Signs of support for Haitians in Springfield after temporary protected status for Haitians ended on July 27. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).  Five Haitians from Springfield, Ohio have been deported back to Haiti after President Donald Trump revoked their legal status, said Theresa Hice-Fromille, a board member of the Haitian Community Help and Support Center.  
More than 470 people have been deported from the United States to Haiti between Aug. 20- Sept. 17 — including some with pending asylum claims, according to Haiti’s National Office for Migration. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This is happening after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled at the end of June that the Trump Administration could end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled violence in their home country. Legal protected status officially ended for Haitians on July 27.
“The Trump administration is engaged in an all-out assault on our immigrant communities across the United States,” U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-MD, said during a U.S. Senate spotlight hearing this week.
“ICE has already forced hundreds of Haitian TPS holders back into danger in Haiti.” 
The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited healthcare,” according to the agency.
A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June. 
“The fear of going back to Haiti is so palpable and so strong,” Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church, said during the Senate hearing. 
Deportation flights to Haiti have increased from once a month to once a week. Flights are landing in Haiti’s second-largest city Cap-Haïtien because criminal groups have made the airport in Haiti’s capital Port-au-Prince unsafe, according to a recent report from Human Rights Watch. 
Upon arrival, migration officials give deportees a meal, a drink, and 10,000 Haitian gourdes (around $77). The Departmental Judicial Police Service takes the deportees to a central police station for more registration, and then they are left on their own, according to Human Rights Watch. 
Human Rights Watch interviewed officials from nine Haitian government institutions for their report. 
“All said Haitian authorities lack the capacity to provide shelter, continuing food assistance, safe onward transportation, sustained health or psychosocial care, or an established channel with US authorities to help deportees recover missing belongings,” HRC said in the report. 
At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 were injured in Haiti from April 1-June 30, according to the Human Rights Service of the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti. 
“Now we’re saying to these people, hundreds of them, go back into this situation, this dangerous situation. It doesn’t have to be this way,” U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-IL, said during the hearing. 
“Protect the people who are the most vulnerable, refugees who leave countries and situations not of their own creation, but are just trying to keep their children alive and keep themselves alive.” 
Durbin shared how he once visited Haiti with Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine when they served in the U.S. Senate together. 
“Mike did more than visit,” Durbin said. “He and Fran went there regularly and adopted churches and groups to try to help them along.” 
Mike and his wife Fran DeWine help support the Becky DeWine School in Haiti, named after their late daughter, but the school had to close due to gang activity in 2024. 
The U.S. House voted in April to extend TPS for Haitians through 2029. The bill is now in the U.S. Senate, but the White House said Trump would veto the bill.
Van Hollen introduced a Senate bill that would provide TPS recipients a pathway to citizenship in the United States.
U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-CA, talked about Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Wright State University student, who died in an apparent suicide on Aug. 31, which his family said happened after he was forced to wear an ankle monitor by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
Signs at a rally for Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Wright State University student, who died in an apparent suicide, that his family said happened he was forced to wear an ankle monitor by ICE. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal).
“Pierre’s story is a tragedy and an insult to our history as a nation of immigrants, and that’s what this administration is causing to so many across the country,” he said. 
“It’s a powerful reminder of the human consequences of irresponsible and short-sighted decisions being made by this administration.”
Pierre’s funeral is Saturday afternoon in Springfield, hours before Trump will be speaking about 25 miles away in Vandalia at a rally ahead of the midterm elections. 
“(Pierre’s) friends and family have told me that the relentless fear, shame, and pressure created by ankle monitoring weighed heavily on him,” Ruby said. 
“His death shook our Haitian community to its core.”
About 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal statuses. Springfield became a flashpoint in the 2024 Election when Donald Trump and JD Vance spread racist lies about Haitian immigrants there. 
“Springfield’s Haitian community are not a burden. They are a blessing,” Ruby said.
“(Ending TPS) has made Springfield more vulnerable economically, socially, and spiritually. Springfield cannot afford to lose them, and morally, we should not be willing to.”
About 50 Haitians used to regularly worship at Ruby’s church, but that number dropped to two when ICE arrived in Springfield over the summer.   
“Families who had prayed with us, sung with us, and served alongside us are now afraid to leave their homes,” Ruby said. 
Springfield’s faith community is delivering food to Haitians, helping pay rent for families who are no longer able to work, and driving students to and from school because their parents are afraid to leave their house, Ruby said. 
“I wish (Trump) could see firsthand how terrified people are of being sent back to Haiti, and to see what it’s like to see whole families hiding behind locked doors,” he said. 
Nearly 75 Haitians living in Ohio have been detained since July 27 at one of four Ohio detention facilities that contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to a report from the Ohio Immigrant Alliance. 
Haitians living in Springfield have been receiving letters requiring them to report to the ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville to accept ankle monitors after TPS ended. ICE has also recently started using the smartphone app SmartLINK to track Haitians in Springfield.

title: How is Ohio doing amid safety-net cuts? Trump hasn’t released the data
description: Women — especially women of color — continue to lag average Americans in measures of wealth and wellness. But when it comes to tracking how Ohio women are doing in the aftermath of last year’s deep cuts to the social safety net, people who study the issue say they’re flying blind. That’s because the Census […]
text:
Two children help their mother pick up food from a food bank in Wilmington, Ohio. Some experts cautioned that Tuesday’s census data on poverty doesn’t reflect the effects of new federal policy changes that will be hitting households hard this year. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Women — especially women of color — continue to lag average Americans in measures of wealth and wellness. But when it comes to tracking how Ohio women are doing in the aftermath of last year’s deep cuts to the social safety net, people who study the issue say they’re flying blind.
That’s because the Census Bureau under President Donald Trump has indefinitely delayed or stopped releasing important data. 
The American Community Survey collects detailed information on economics, housing and demographics. Until this year, the Census Bureau published it annually since its full inception in 2005. It’s delayed publication this year, saying it’s ending an obscure procedure meant to protect confidentiality.
And the Trump Agriculture Department in 2025 announced it was ending a key measure of food insecurity.
Last year, congressional Republicans passed — and President Trump signed — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. While it gave $1 trillion in tax cuts to the richest 1% of Americans over 10 years, it cut nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid and $187 billion from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program over the same period. 
Because of the cuts, 5 million Americans lost their food assistance by June 2026. That includes 100,000 Ohioans.
And after Congressional Republicans extended tax cuts weighted toward the rich, they allowed pandemic-era subsidies to help purchase health insurance under the Affordable Care Act to expire. 
By February 2026, 2.6 million Americans, or about 10% of those enrolled, dropped their coverage. Ohio saw the biggest losses of any state — 32.4%, or 161,000 people.

Given those deep cuts to the safety net, it would make sense for the government to track what happens to the most vulnerable Americans — and to track it right down to the state and community level. But that’s not what it’s doing, said Amy K. Matsui, vice president for child care and income security at the National Women’s Law Center. 
“We don’t (have state and local information) with regard to poverty data and that’s because the Trump administration is holding on to a specific dataset,” she said in an interview Monday. “That’s where we get our quality state-level and demographic data about poverty and income, but the Trump administration has put it on indefinite hold.”
Other census data show severe disparities between minority women and white men. 
For example, more than 20% of Black and Hispanic women lived in poverty in 2025 compared to 8.7% of white men. And nearly a third — 29.3% — of families headed by single women lived in poverty, according to the Women’s Law Center.
The American Community Survey provided state and community-level estimates about things like employment, poverty, housing and insurance by demographic group.
It’s “an ongoing survey that provides vital information on a yearly basis about our nation and its people,”the Census Bureau website says. “Information from the survey generates data that help inform how trillions of dollars in federal funds are distributed each year.” 
The bureau typically publishes the survey for the previous year in September. But publication is being delayed indefinitely this year.
Asked why, the bureau gave a technical explanation.
“The release date for the 2025 ACS 1-year estimates is being determined,” the bureau’s public information office said in an email. “The Census Bureau is assessing the impact of the new departmental administrative order (DAO), Department of Commerce Disclosure Avoidance for Statistical Products, and seeking DAO-compliant solutions to allow the release of the ACS 1-year tables later this year.”
The order prohibits the use of a technique called “noise infusion” to avoid disclosure of protected information.
The rule the Census Bureau referenced didn’t give a reason for the change other than to say it had to balance privacy with accuracy and, “Any use of noise infusion is inconsistent with the Department’s policies.”
In an Aug. 17 post, the Census Bureau said the change was due to “concerns that adding noise made the statistics less accurate and less trustworthy.”
But the academic journal Science in July reported concerns among scientists that it was an attempt by Trump to politicize the census and science itself. The administration banned “essentially all modern techniques for preserving privacy in large datasets,” the journal quoted a University of Texas computer scientist as saying.
“The change marks the first time political appointees have dictated the (Census Bureau’s) statistical methods, census watchers say,” the story said. “It will affect the 2030 census, which is used to apportion seats in the House of Representatives by state every decade and determine the distribution of trillions of dollars annually in federal funds.”
While that story focused on the change’s impact on the 2030 Census, Matsui of the Women’s Law Center said she believed it serves another purpose — to obscure the human consequences of slashing the safety net.
“We really think this is a mechanism to hide from view certain disfavored demographic groups, whether that’s women, people of color, LGBTQ… They’re really trying to hide from view what people are experiencing,” she said.
For its part, the Census Project, a group of former Census Bureau directors, business associations and others, on Sept. 4 wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees the bureau. Speaking on behalf of 800 organizations, the group said the government was abandoning a security technique “federal statistical agencies have used for years” and delaying vital information.
“Our members depend on reliable, high-quality census data to analyze changing U.S. economic and demographic trends,” the letter said. American Community Survey “data are especially critical to their planning, investment decisions, market strategies, and public services, for example, on behalf of businesses, state and local governments, consumers, veterans, and children.” 
Matsui said the Trump administration is also blocking other measures of its policies’ fallout.
Last year, less than three months after cutting $187 billion from federal nutrition assistance, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced that it was ending its annual Household Food Security Reports. The highly partisan press release seemed an attempt to justify the deep cuts.
“For 30 years, this study—initially created by the Clinton administration as a means to support the increase of SNAP eligibility and benefit allotments — failed to present anything more than subjective, liberal fodder,” it said. “Trends in the prevalence of food insecurity have remained virtually unchanged, regardless of an over 87% increase in SNAP spending between 2019 — 2023.”
The statement didn’t mention the global pandemic and consequent job loss that took place between 2019 and 2023. Matsui said the Trump administration ignored other facts as it squelched the report.
“Right at the time when there were really deep cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, food prices are skyrocketing, and food banks can’t keep up with demand, (the Trump administration is) trying to prevent this very consistent, reliable and trusted report on families’ food insecurity,” she said. “They’re just stopping it,”

title: Nebraska retirement board meeting leaves questions about new leadership
description: LINCOLN — A special meeting of the Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Board ended with several unanswered questions about the sudden resignation of the agency’s latest executive director, as well as who will replace him. The current executive director of the state Public Employees Retirement System, Thomas Pfeifle, submitted his resignation letter Sept. 21[...]
text:
Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Board members (from left to right): Jake Curtiss, Patrick Bourne, Gerald Clausen and Janis Elliott at a special board meeting Sept. 30, 2026. (Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A special meeting of the Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Board ended with several unanswered questions about the sudden resignation of the agency’s latest executive director, as well as who will replace him.
The current executive director of the state Public Employees Retirement System, Thomas Pfeifle, submitted his resignation letter Sept. 21, roughly three months after he was selected to lead the agency on June 15. His official last day with NPERS is Oct. 31.
The board accepted Pfeifle’s resignation at a special meeting Sept. 30. In his resignation letter, read by board Chair Janis Elliott, Pfeifle said he was leaving the agency to be closer to his children in Colorado. Elliott said Pfeifle shared the news of his resignation with her immediately after the board’s last regular meeting.
Tag Herbek, NPERS legal counsel, said in an email that the board did address Pfeifle’s previous residency in Colorado and his commitment to relocating to Nebraska during the interview process.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
During public comment at Wednesday’s meeting, NPERS accounting staff Teresa Zulauf said that since submitting his resignation Sept. 21, Pfeifle has not been present in the NPERS office. Zulauf asked if Pfeifle would continue to be compensated through Oct. 31.
The board did not answer Zulauf’s question at the meeting, which is customary for public comment periods. Herbek later said NPERS cannot comment on employee personnel details.
Herbek did not answer a question about whether Pfeifle would continue working from NPERS’ Lincoln office through Oct. 31 or whether the position can be handled remotely.
It took the board roughly 18 months to select Pfeifle as executive director after the previous director John Murante left in December 2024. During most of this stretch, former deputy director Tyler Cummings served as NPERS’ interim director. He was recommended to replace Murante, but Gov. Jim Pillen rejected his appointment.
Cummings left the agency this April, and a new deputy director has not been named, according to NPERS’ website. The board did not share details of who would serve as interim director at Wednesday’s meeting, but Elliott said the search for a new executive director had already begun.
Herbek said the board will address further leadership succession issues at its next regular meeting Oct. 19.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: ‘Still anyone’s ball game’ Bowling Green poll finds statistical tie in Ohio’s race for governor
description: Let’s take a quick look at where the race for Ohio Governor stands.  But first, a caveat.  This is not a prediction about who will win the November 3 election.  Polls are not predictions, and the BGSU Poll is no different from any others in that way.  Instead, surveys are a snapshot of where we think likely […]
text:
Vivek Ramaswamy, left, and Dr. Amy Acton, right. (Photo by Morgan Trau & WEWS.)
Let’s take a quick look at where the race for Ohio Governor stands.  But first, a caveat.  This is not a prediction about who will win the November 3 election.  Polls are not predictions, and the BGSU Poll is no different from any others in that way.  Instead, surveys are a snapshot of where we think likely voters stand at the time the survey is administered.
The Bowling Green State University Democracy and Public Policy Network has released the September 2026 BGSU Poll, a web-based survey of 1,000 likely Ohio voters conducted from September 1-10, 2026. The poll has a margin of error of just about four percentage points.
Currently Democrat Dr. Amy Acton leads Vivek Ramaswamy 48% to 45%, which places this race clearly within the margin of error.  More specifically, that means we are pretty confident that Dr. Acton’s actual level of support is somewhere between 44% and 52% and Mr. Ramaswamy’s is between 41% and 49%.  Because those ranges overlap, the race is said to be a statistical tie.
Currently Dr, Acton leads among Independents 45% to 34%.  Women, younger voters, Blacks, and Hispanics support her, while men and older and white voters prefer Mr. Ramaswamy.  Those with a four-year degree or more overwhelmingly support Dr. Acton, while those without a four-year degree more narrowly support Mr. Ramaswamy.   These are not surprising results, as these are not new relationships in the current American political landscape.
Perhaps the most interesting finding is with regard to political party. As expected, Democrats support Dr. Acton, while Republicans support Mr. Ramaswamy.  However, the difference in the strength of that partisan support may be meaningful.  Currently, 96% of Democrats support Dr. Acton, while 87% of Republicans support Mr. Ramaswamy.  Five precent of Republicans support Libertarian candidate Don Kissick, while three percent say they plan to vote for someone else.
One may conclude from this that Dr. Acton has already solidified her support with the Democratic base, while Mr. Ramaswamy has some work to do there.  One potential problem with doing that, though, is that campaign messages that may appeal to the Republican base may be off-putting to moderates and Independents.
Perhaps the safer route the Ramaswamy campaign and its supporters will take with the huge amount of money they have to spend is just to continue personally attacking Dr. Acton to try to increase her “unfavorables.”  Currently Dr. Acton holds a net favorable/unfavorable rating of -1, while Mr. Ramaswamy has a net favorability rating of -11.
Finally, political scientists often think of mid-term elections as either a referendum on the incumbent or as being driven by the increased enthusiasm of the party that most recently lost the presidency.  In other words, people vote on whether they think the party occupying the White House is doing a good job, or the voters who lost that election become extra energized to show up to the polls in the mid-term.
Currently both of these factors seem to be helping the Democrats.  President Donald Trump is -16 in net favorability, and Democratic-leaning voters are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about showing up to vote by a factor of nearly two to one.
Given that it’s football season, why not conclude with a potentially over-used sports metaphor? The Ohio Governor’s election is tied, but the Acton campaign has they ball and they are at the 50 yard line (or, if you’re in Canada, the 55 yard line).  There’s two minutes to go.  Still anyone’s ballgame.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Trump midterm rally draws thousands of supporters to Oklahoma town
description: President Donald Trump on Thursday told an adoring and boisterous crowd to vote like he was on the ballot. Trump launched what is expected to be a month-long campaign blitz in Oklahoma in hopes of energizing Republicans going into the midterms. “We do great when I’m on the ballot,” Trump told thousands packed into the […]
text:
Donald Trump waves during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)President Donald Trump on Thursday told an adoring and boisterous crowd to vote like he was on the ballot.
Trump launched what is expected to be a month-long campaign blitz in Oklahoma in hopes of energizing Republicans going into the midterms.
“We do great when I’m on the ballot,” Trump told thousands packed into the Choctaw Event Center, which is located about 2.5 hours southeast of Oklahoma City.
Many supporters waited hours in the rain to see Trump. Trump said more were still waiting outside the event center after it reached capacity.
“When I’m not on the ballot, people don’t go and vote so much,” Trump said. “Pretend I’m running please, because I’m on the ballot.”
Donald Trump gestures as he exits the stage during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Donald Trump dances during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)U.S. Sen. James Lankford waves during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)President Donald Trump kisses Margo Martin, one of his communication staffers, during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Mike Mazzei waves during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)An event attendee who was interviewed earlier in the day was brought on stage by Donald Trump during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Two event attendees who were interviewed earlier in the day are brought on stage by Donald Trump during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Blake Marnell, also known as Brick Suit, is recognized by Donald Trump during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Cindy Byrd is recognized by Donald Trump during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Former NBA players Dennis Rodman and Enes Kanter Freedom are recognized during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Event attendees cheer while Donald Trump speaks during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)An event attendee laughs during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Donald Trump walks onto the stage during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Markwayne Mullin walks onto the stage during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Mike Mazzei and Kevin Hern hug during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Harold Hamm speaks during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)T.W. Shannon speaks during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Brandon Beach, the treasurer of the United States, shows the new Trump coin during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Honor guard presents the flags during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)A man attends a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)Josh Brecheen speaks during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)
Trump is serving his final term, and said he hopes Republicans will maintain control of Congress to help his agenda. He acknowledged that maintaining control of the U.S. House and Senate hinges on the outcomes of about two dozen races. Oklahoma, he said, was not one of those battlegrounds. 
Trump’s favorability rating has declined significantly nationwide as the war with Iran has increased gasoline prices and inflation and tariffs have hit pocketbooks.
Trump, though, spoke about what he viewed as his administration’s economic successes, which he said have gone unreported by the media, and the benefits of the war in Iran.
Trump said it is important that Iran never has a nuclear weapon, adding that other presidents should have dealt with the country’s nuclear aspirations a long time ago.
Trump reminded voters he won all 77 Oklahoma counties the three times that he appeared on the ballot.
He touted his policies for reducing crime, lowering taxes and prescription drug prices and securing the border.
He took several swipes at Democrats, blaming them for high inflation, soaring energy prices and a huge trade deficit. Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress.
Trump also accused Democrats of supporting socialists and communists.
He said the country is experiencing a “golden age” and will go back to the dark age under Democrats.
“If the Republicans win the House and the Senate, I am going to give all adult citizens of the United States a check for $5,000,” Trump said.
The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget warned last month that Trump’s plan would cost about $1.2 trillion, and “explode” the nation’s deficit.
Trump mentioned his plan to build a massive aluminum smelter Inola, which has become an issue in the Oklahoma gubernatorial campaign. 
Local residents in the town of about 2,000 located about 25 miles east of Tulsa have pushed back against the project, which supporters say will create over 1,000 jobs. They’ve extended a moratorium blocking the project until local residents can vote on its fate in April. 
The smelter, which would produce about 600,000 tons of aluminum, is part of Trump’s $200 billion deal with the United Arab Emirates.
 Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Mazzei, who spoke at the rally and has been endorsed by Trump, supports it.
“You are going to build the largest aluminum factory, perhaps in the world, and you’re going to make a fortune with it,” Trump said.
Trump said tariffs that he has imposed have generated trillions in revenue and created jobs.
Several notable politicians were in the crowd, including Gov. Kevin Stitt, members of Congress and the Oklahoma Legislature. Several spoke, including U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former Republican U.S. senator from Oklahoma.
Donald Trump walks onto the stage during a midterm election rally at the Choctaw Event Center, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Durant, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jessica Tobias/For Oklahoma Voice)
They encouraged rally attendees to vote Republican on Nov. 3.
Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain, arrived hours before Trump’s speech, saying it is a big deal when the President comes to Oklahoma.
“I am a big President Trump fan and I wanted to come and see him,” Hamilton said.
Thousands were on hand to hear Trump, who began his speech about two hours late and spoke for a little over an hour.
Some wore T-shirts that read “Don’t tread on me,” and “God, Guns and Trump.”
One man wore a flag that said “Trump is my president.”
Some brought school-aged children while others pushed friends and family members in wheelchairs.
While waiting for Trump, they chanted “USA. USA. USA.”
Donald Knopes, a veteran from Durant, said he supports Trump despite the economy, saying no man is perfect.
“He is the less than all the evils that are out there,” said Knopes, who arrived at noon to hear Trump, who began speaking shortly before 8 p.m.
Beth Mills, of Shawnee, said she came to enjoy the patriotic feeling of seeing the president.
“I think he is doing what he can,” she said. “I think he has been crippled by the Congress not taking action and getting some of the agenda things done. I think that hurts him.”
Mills said she believes in Trump’s agenda.
Trump is expected to travel to Alabama on Friday, to Ohio over the weekend and Nebraska on Monday.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: US House candidates disagree on tariffs, but find common ground on opposition to Trump beef imports
description: SIOUX FALLS — During a Thursday night debate, the Republican candidate in the race for South Dakota’s lone seat in the U.S. House of Representatives joined a chorus of his party’s members in criticizing President Donald Trump’s approach on beef imports. Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley faces Democrat Nikki Gronli in the Nov. 3 general […]
text:
Democratic U.S. House of Representatives candidate Nikki Gronli, left, and Republican candidate Marty Jackley participate in a debate at the Sioux Falls studios of South Dakota Public Broadcasting on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — During a Thursday night debate, the Republican candidate in the race for South Dakota’s lone seat in the U.S. House of Representatives joined a chorus of his party’s members in criticizing President Donald Trump’s approach on beef imports.
Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley faces Democrat Nikki Gronli in the Nov. 3 general election. Gronli is a small-business owner, and was South Dakota’s director of rural development for the U.S. Department of Agriculture under President Joe Biden.
The two sparred in Sioux Falls during a debate co-hosted by South Dakota Public Broadcasting and South Dakota News Watch. 
Jackley said he largely agrees with Trump on tariffs, which are taxes paid by companies importing foreign goods. But Jackley said Trump’s push to import Argentinian beef to ease high consumer prices earlier this year was the wrong approach.
South Dakota’s US House candidates clash over Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions

“If you do away with tariffs, that doesn’t protect our beef anymore,” Jackley said. “That opens the flood market for foreign beef.”
Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden said during a debate with his Democratic opponent last month that he disagrees with Trump’s beef import plan. Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who ran unsuccessfully in June for the Republican nomination for governor, has also criticized it, as have South Dakota’s Republican U.S. senators, John Thune and Mike Rounds.
Tariffs on Chinese goods, Jackley said, are important tools for balancing what the Republican candidate described as that country’s unfair trade practices.
“We need to make sure, with respect to targeted tariffs, that we’re doing everything we can to promote American jobs and to get our products a fair deal and a fair trade,” said Jackley.
Gronli repeatedly lambasted Trump’s approach to tariffs. She said Trump’s tariffs and tariff threats have created a chaotic environment for the state’s farmers and have cost families dearly.
“All Americans are suffering under the tariffs,” Gronli said, pointing specifically to tariffs on Canada, South Dakota’s top trading partner.
“The next Congress needs to take this on,” Gronli said. “They need to be a check on the executive branch and take back their power.”
Gas prices, energy
Gronli also pointed to the war in Iran, which has disrupted global oil shipments, as a Trump administration policy that’s done damage to South Dakota’s farms, families and small businesses. Diesel prices have climbed higher than $6 a gallon.
Farmers “can’t plan right now,” Gronli said. “They had high input costs in the spring, and now they’re dealing with high, high diesel costs this fall. They’re wondering if they’re going to break even when they take their crops out.”

Jackley said he believes the war in Iran “needs to wind down” now that the U.S. has “addressed the nuclear capabilities” of that country.
But high prices at the pump and at the grocery store had more to do with the slowdown of fossil fuel development during President Biden’s time in office, Jackley said, calling the price spikes from the Iran war a “short-term” factor. 
“Under President Biden, he shut down refineries day one,” Jackley said. “He closed oil pipelines. He stopped leases and exploration on federal land. We have to have energy independence.”
Healthcare
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 put $50 billion toward rural healthcare in the coming years, while cutting federal funding for healthcare through work requirements for Medicaid recipients, among other changes.
Trump championed the bill, and all three members of South Dakota’s congressional delegation voted for it. 
South Dakota has been given $189 million so far for rural health transformation, and the state is in the process of deciding what to do with the money.
Democrat for US House unveils proposals to lower tariffs, stabilize Social Security

Debate moderator Jackie Hendry asked both candidates if they felt the rural health funding would do enough to address the needs of South Dakotans.
Jackley said sending money to the states to upgrade health infrastructure is the right approach. 
“What the Big Beautiful Bill did was put dollars in the hands of the state, who knows best where those dollars need to go,” he said.
Jackley said the solution to healthcare affordability is to incentivize competition in the private sector, rather than support what he described as government-funded “socialized medicine.” 
He also said tightening restrictions on benefits will make sure tax money is spent where it’s needed and not used for fraudulent purposes.
Gronli argued that the changes to programs like Medicaid, a state-federal health insurance program for the elderly, children and people with disabilities, will blunt the impact of the rural health grants.
“People aren’t going to have access to health insurance,” said Gronli. “It doesn’t really do much good to invest in technology and things in hospitals if people can’t actually access healthcare.”
Agreement, disagreement on tribal issues
Gronli and Jackley both decried the federal government’s failure to adequately fund services for members of the state’s nine tribal nations.
Jackley said the Department of Interior has failed to adequately fund law enforcement, and pointed to his office’s efforts to offer law enforcement training to tribal officers as proof that he understands the issue and is prepared to take steps to address it in Congress.
Gronli said a 16-year-old girl in Fort Thompson, a community on the Crow Creek Reservation, told her she waited two hours for a law enforcement response after calling 911 about “some scary people” outside her home.
“That’s unacceptable,” Gronli said. “We shouldn’t have this poor girl by herself and scared. So public safety is a critical need.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The candidates disagreed on restarting a Biden-era program to continue studying the long-term impact of Native American boarding schools. For decades, students were taken from their homes, forced to cut their hair, abandon their language and culture, and assimilate to non-Native society.
Gronli said that “wasn’t very long ago,” noting that she’s 53 and grew up alongside Native Americans who were among the first members of their family for several generations to have grown up outside the boarding school system.
In 2025, moderator Hendry noted, the National Congress of American Indians passed a resolution condemning the Trump administration for rescinding grants to continue research into the boarding school era. Gronli said the funding should be restored.
“Generational trauma is real, and our tribal members are still living it,” said Gronli.
Jackley, however, said federal money is better spent on addressing immediate issues in tribal areas through consultation with tribal leaders.
“We should have these conversations, and we should move forward instead of just spending dollars researching it and accomplishing nothing for our Native American tribes,” Jackley said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: We’re asking the right questions about CT education, but is it enough?
description: The question should not simply be whether Connecticut increases the ECS formula, but whether that reflects the actual cost of educating a child.
text:
​The members of Connecticut’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Education Funding deserve credit for their hard work. It’s an uphill battle.
​For months, the commission has been digging into the mechanics of how education funding actually reaches students. The recent discussion around the Education Cost Sharing (ECS) formula demonstrates a willingness to confront issues that many have avoided for years.
​As a Bridgeport Board of Education member representing the state’s largest and highest-need urban school district, the latest meeting of the commission left me encouraged, yet concerned that we may still be underestimating the magnitude of the challenges facing districts like Bridgeport.
​The commission’s sample scenarios explored increasing the ECS foundation, expanding poverty weights, and adding a special education weight. More importantly, commissioners repeatedly returned to an important question, is it enough?
​The question should not simply be whether Connecticut increases the ECS foundation from one number to another, but whether the foundation reflects the actual cost of educating a child in Connecticut today.
​Let’s run the sample numbers through using my beloved City of Bridgeport and its 20,000 students. New Haven, Hartford, New Britain, New London, Waterbury, Meriden, and others, take note; many of your districts will be similarly impacted.  Run your numbers.
​In the 2027/2028 school year, Bridgeport faces an estimated $25 million loss of one-time revenue alongside approximately $15 million in recurring cost increases. That creates a $40 million structural need before any discussion of new programs or expanded services. $40 million over last year is break-even; we won’t even be able to purchase an additional pencil.
​Under the commission’s model, Bridgeport would receive roughly $23 million in additional recurring ECS funding if all sample reforms were adopted. That helps substantially, but it still leaves a gap of nearly $17 million.
​Districts like Bridgeport are fighting for the survival of public education amid rising special education costs, increased transportation expenses, runaway healthcare inflation, and labor contracts for our underpaid workforce.
​Several commissioners questioned whether the foundation amount adequately reflects current costs, noting that distributing supplemental aid outside the ECS formula may simply codify existing structural funding issues rather than create meaningful new revenue. These are exactly the questions the commission should be asking.
​Implementation is another pressing concern. Assuming the commission recommends a higher foundation amount, increased poverty funding, and additional special education support, this best-case scenario still leaves districts significantly short today. That reality becomes even more troubling if increases are phased in over several years. Bridgeport’s $40 million challenge is not being phased in, nor are rising special education, transportation, or healthcare costs. The bills arrive every day.
​Legislative leaders responsible for balancing the state budget reminded commissioners that education spending competes with other priorities. That is where the commission needs to push back hardest. The commission’s task must be to first determine the overall fiscal needs of CT’s 500,000 students, not adhere to an artificial ceiling under today’s inequitable tax structure.
​If Connecticut determines the current foundation amount is inadequate, equity should not become a long-term goal; it must become an urgency. A district cannot pay this year’s bills with funding promised in 2032.
​Another issue deserves greater attention: how Connecticut measures a community’s ability to pay. The current ECS formula relies heavily on property wealth. Many municipalities today are property rich, but cash-poor. They have substantial grand lists on paper, yet struggle with high poverty, tax-exempt properties, aging infrastructure, and residents with limited income.
​Commissioners discussed whether Connecticut should revisit the 70% property wealth and 30% income wealth weighting that drives ECS allocations. The ratio should be closer to a 50/50 split, if not totally inverted. An equity-based funding system must recognize the actual capacity of residents to support public education through local taxation.
​Accountability is also critical. Taxpayers, families, educators, and policymakers deserve to know that education dollars are being spent wisely. Increased funding and accountability are not mutually exclusive responsibilities, but accountability cannot deflect the state’s responsibility to adequately fund our schools.
​The tale of two Connecticut education systems cannot continue to be our story. We cannot celebrate the success of some while ignoring that high-need districts spend thousands less per pupil than wealthy communities, nor allow cost concerns to distract from the state’s moral and constitutional obligation to provide all children with an adequate education.
​Ultimately, adequacy and equity must remain the guiding principles. Let the legislature figure out how to pay for it, either by dropping guardrails, reducing spending elsewhere, fixing the tax structure or any combination.
​The Blue Ribbon Commission demonstrates a growing consensus that small adjustments over time are not enough. Free from the constraints of a poorly designed survey they did not create, and an expert they did not choose, the commission is asking the right questions and must come up with firm numbers that close the gap for all districts.  Now the governor and legislature must accept the answers, even if they require us to invest more deeply in the students who need it most.
​For Bridgeport and districts like it, the issue is not whether we can afford educational equity. The question is whether we can afford to continue as a society without it.
Joseph Sokolovic lives in Bridgeport.

text:
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear speaks at the Democratic fundraising event, Ballots, Blue Jeans, & BBQ on Thursday, October 1, 2026 in North Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has a three-step guide to winning in a typically Republican state, he told Arkansas Democrats at a Thursday night fundraising dinner.
“Focus, talk normal, and lead with your ‘why,’” he told an audience of about 200 people at the state Democratic Party’s Ballots, Blue Jeans & BBQ event in North Little Rock.
Beshear, who is widely considered a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, reminded the Arkansas audience that he won reelection by 5 percentage points in 2023, a year before 65% of Kentucky voters supported President Donald Trump’s reelection.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“I am living, breathing proof that Democrats can win anywhere and we should be fighting everywhere, including right here in Arkansas,” Beshear said.
Republicans have held every statewide and federal office in Arkansas since 2014. Trump’s approval rating in Arkansas and nationwide has been declining, and state and national Democrats have said they expect to make inroads in next month’s midterm elections.
In a lively half-hour speech that ended with a standing ovation, Beshear said he’s often asked how he managed to win and retain office in the South. He said national Democrats have made southerners “forgotten and left out, even looked down on,” and state-level Democrats have a responsibility to change this perception of the party.
“We win by staying true to our values of compassion, of empathy, of doing right by our neighbors, and by focusing on people’s daily and most pressing needs,” he said.
He also said Democrats should “start talking like normal human beings again” in order to win over people who might not be inclined to hear them out.

Hallie Shoffner, Arkansas’ Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, takes the stage on Thursday, October 1, 2026 at the Ballots, Blue Jeans, & BBQ fundraiser in North Little Rock. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
 

“If we’re going to win both chambers [of Congress] and we’re going to turn that around, it’s not by saying kids are food insecure. It’s that they’re hungry,” Beshear said.
Former Democratic U.S. Sen. Mark Pryor noted while introducing Beshear that the Kentucky governor has “stood up for the things he believes in, sometimes when it’s hard to do and sometimes when it’s politically unpopular.”
Pryor served two terms in the Senate before losing reelection in 2014 to Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, who now faces a challenge from Democratic rival Hallie Shoffner.
Arkansas Democrats have expressed hope they can pull off an upset in November and have pointed to a poll indicating tight races for Senate and central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District. But they still face an uphill challenge in the state, with Republicans heavily outspending them in top races.

Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

 

Beshear has routinely vetoed bills passed by the majority-Republican Kentucky Legislature meant to target transgender children’s healthcare and participation in sports. He defended his vetoes in 2023 by saying, “My faith teaches me that all children are children of God.”
He said Thursday that the following day, “a guy in a trucker hat” told him he respected his decision and supported him even if he disagreed.
“That’s the day I learned that explaining our ‘why,’ having the respect for each and every voter, can create grace and space to not just be anti-this or pro-that and have a real conversation,” Beshear said.
Earlier on Thursday, Beshear promoted his recently published book, “Go and Do Likewise,” at the Central Arkansas Library System’s main branch in Little Rock. The book covers the intersection of Christianity and progressive politics. He also was in Bentonville for an announcement about maternal health grants Kentucky and Arkansas will receive.
Beshear has not confirmed rumors of a 2028 presidential run. He told Thursday’s audience that he expects the next president to be a Democrat, “whoever that may be.”
Beshear is among several potential 2028 Democratic hopefuls who have visited Arkansas in recent months. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have also made stops in the state.
Beshear touted his administration’s work to build affordable housing fueled by solar energy in an eastern Kentucky community devastated by flooding during his first term.
“Our job is to revive the American Dream and make sure it burns bright in the minds of the next generation,” Beshear said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Despite vow of bipartisanship, gubernatorial candidates spar in first televised debate
description: Maine’s three gubernatorial candidates exchanged sharp attacks over each other’s records during their first televised debate Thursday, even as all three pledged at the end of the night to work across party lines. The first of four planned debates was hosted by News Center Maine and the Maine Chamber of Commerce at the Cross Insurance […]
text:
Republican Bobby Charles, Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett on stage at the Cross Insurance Arena in Portland on Oct. 1. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Maine’s three gubernatorial candidates exchanged sharp attacks over each other’s records during their first televised debate Thursday, even as all three pledged at the end of the night to work across party lines.
The first of four planned debates was hosted by News Center Maine and the Maine Chamber of Commerce at the Cross Insurance Arena in Portland Thursday evening. 
Throughout the event, Democrat Hannah Pingree, independent Rick Bennett and Republican Bobby Charles often detoured from answering questions about housing prices, property taxes, energy costs and healthcare to take swipes at each other.
But after criticizing each other for an hour, all three responded to the final audience question about whether they would commit to bipartisanship by promising if elected to work with lawmakers across the aisle.
”I am not interested in being a partisan governor because I cannot get done what I think this state needs,” Bennett said. “We need to get back to a politics of collaboration and compromise.”
But most of the night was less harmonious.
Pingree and Charles sparred over a topic the Republican had brought up in a press conference a day before: a state grant made to Pingree’s husband’s film production company while she was in charge of Gov. Janet Mills’ Office of Policy Innovation and the Future.
“Bobby has been spewing … misinformation,” Pingree responded, denying his allegations that it had been improperly awarded.
Charles went after both Bennett and Pingree for being “Augusta insiders.”
“I find it ironic that two people who’ve served for 30 years and 25 years are saying that we need to fix the system,” he said.
Bennett predominantly focused his barbs on Charles, but said Pingree’s track record in state government was inadequate, particularly her time in the Mills’ administration.
“Hannah Pingree has been in charge of housing for seven years, and she’s been calling it a crisis,” he said.“But when you have a crisis, you act like there’s a crisis, and you get it done. If you don’t do that job, you don’t merit a promotion.”
Amid one heated moment between the two men over the Republican nominee’s time in Washington D.C., Pingree interjected with: “This is why we need women in charge,” eliciting the largest cheer of the night from the crowd of business owners.
Housing 
All three candidates highlighted their various plans to lower property taxes and the cost of housing, while also critiquing their opponents’ ideas. 
Pingree reiterated her commitment to spending $100 million on housing each year to accelerate housing production. She also said she would mandate a 90-day timeline for the Maine Department of Environmental Protection to respond to new housing proposals. Finally, she proposed making a change to the Maine Constitution in order for the state to be able to tax second homes owned by people who only live in Maine during the summer.
“I think housing is the fundamental issue that is holding back the state of Maine,” she said. “We need to build more housing to ensure that young people can afford to stay here, we need rentals that people across our workforce can afford, and we need to make it happen quickly.”
Charles said Pingree’s $100 million was not enough to address housing shortages.
“The only way you get the housing stock up is to methodically encourage building,” he said, which he said would require reducing red tape to ensure speedier housing construction.
Bennett also critiqued Pingree’s plan, saying, “A $100 million sounds like a lot of money, but when you go to per unit, it gets us nowhere near what we need to do.”
The independent candidate echoed the need to build more housing, but said he would do that by reviving manufactured housing, which he described as a heritage industry in western Maine where he lives, and by conducting an audit to figure out what causes regulatory delays in permitting.
His housing plan would also reduce down payments for first-time homebuyers by using state funds as a guarantee for banks.
Taxes and spending
When asked about the economy, Charles was the only candidate to commit to cutting taxes — a campaign promise he has emphasized for months.
He also said he wants to provide a $100,000 property tax exemption for all Mainers and cut income taxes, although he did not explain by how much. Maine’s current income taxes are between 5.8% and 7.15% for single filers, with a newly implemented millionaire’s tax.

The Republican nominee said the state can make up for the lost revenue by investigating agencies such as the Maine Department of Health and Human Services and shrinking state government. 
“We’re also going to cut the funding for non-residents,” he said. “We’re going to not provide free housing to non-citizens, and we’re not going to be providing free health care to them.”
Bennett said Charles “just doesn’t simply understand how the fiscal process works, which doesn’t surprise me because inspector generals and auditors at the federal government cited him dozens of times for mismanagement of federal spending,” referring to the Republican’s time at the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs under President George W. Bush.
Rather, Bennett said the state needs to increase oversight of its budget process. He said the fact that it does not allow for public hearing is “the reason that the state budget has grown 77% in 10 years, twice the rate of inflation.”
Bennett’s biggest priority in terms of cutting taxes is addressing high property tax rates, which he said are inequitable and volatile. He proposed addressing that by expanding the fairness tax credit, a state income tax relief program that gives money back to eligible homeowners and renters
Pingree partially agreed with Bennett on expanding the fairness credit, saying, “middle and low income Mainers are paying too much of their income right now in all forms of taxes.” But she also called him out for not supporting the recently passed millionaire’s tax, which she supports.
The new tax imposes a surcharge of 2% on wealthy Mainers, specifically on the portion of a resident’s taxable income beyond $1 million for single filers, $1.5 million for heads of households and $1.5 million for people filing jointly. The tax is expected to impact 2,631 tax returns and generate $150 million in the next biennium.
“I believe in taxing wealth, not work, and we’re going to have to work hard to do that in the next couple of years,” she said.
Pingree did not commit to cutting government spending, acknowledging that the next budget is going to be a challenge due to a $1 billion shortfall Mills’ successor will have to deal with.
“What we are spending money on is healthcare, which keeps our hospitals afloat, education — keeping it at 55 percent,” she said. “A lot of these things go out to communities.”
