title: In first debate, LePage and Dunlap clash over healthcare, affordability, immigration
description: Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage met for the first time on the debate stage Thursday night, where they continued their clash over healthcare and traded barbs over each other’s records in state government. The state auditor and former governor are vying to replace outgoing Rep. Jared Golden in the U.S. House of Representatives […]
text:
U.S. House candidates Democrat Matt Dunlap (left) and Republican Paul LePage (right) met for the first time on the debate stage on Oct. 1. (Photos by Jim Neuger and Andrew Clark/ Maine Morning Star)Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage met for the first time on the debate stage Thursday night, where they continued their clash over healthcare and traded barbs over each other’s records in state government.
The state auditor and former governor are vying to replace outgoing Rep. Jared Golden in the U.S. House of Representatives for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.The WMTW debate quickly settled on a familiar theme: the candidates’ opposing stances on healthcare and how to reduce rising costs.
Throughout the Democratic primary, Dunlap campaigned on his support for Medicare For All, placing him in stark opposition to LePage, who oversaw dramatic cuts to Maine’s healthcare programs as governor and vetoed several bills to expand MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program. 
And while Dunlap acknowledged that universal healthcare would take time to implement, a more immediate solution he said he would advocate for in Congress is reestablishing marketplace insurance subsidies that congressional Republicans allowed to expire at the beginning of 2026.
Of the 61,000 Maine people who enroll through CoverME.gov, the state’s online marketplace, 85% relied on those premium tax credits to reduce their monthly costs. The lapse of the subsidies are contributing to spiking insurance costs in Maine and across the country.
“If you restore the subsidies to the Affordable Care Act, they’d see it immediately in January, as soon as we could enact it, and the president would sign it into law,” Dunlap said. “So I think that would be an immediate relief.”
In contrast, LePage said he would not support expanding Medicaid — even if it lowered the number of uninsured Mainers — and underscored his opposition to a universal healthcare system.
“The reason I have a problem with Medicare For All is they’re not telling you the truth,” LePage said. “If you’ve not lived in Canada, you don’t understand socialized medicine. What happens is your insurance coverage that you have now at work goes away. Bureaucrats make decisions on your healthcare, not your doctor.”
When Dunlap pushed back, LePage repeatedly questioned if he had lived in Canada and experienced the system to understand how it works. Dunlap said he had lived in Maine his whole life.
“I do understand how it works, and people in Canada are not flocking to Maine to get less insurance,” Dunlap said.
“No, they’re flocking to Maine to get cancer treatments and heart treatments,” LePage responded. 
Fate of Medicare, Medicaid emerge as key issue in 2nd District race

Dunlap also criticized cuts to federal healthcare programs under President Donald Trump, and said they would only make things more expensive for Mainers. But LePage defended the president’s policies, specifically the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which was passed to partially offset the dramatic cuts to Medicaid, though experts say it remains to be seen how those funds will be distributed.
“[Dunlap] says we’re going to lose Medicaid after the election,” LePage said. “No, you’re not. There’s $50 billion that’s going to be spent across the nation in rural communities to help sustain and have healthcare provided to those in need.” 
“Which won’t replace the trillion dollars worth of cuts,” Dunlap interjected. 
LePage also repeated the claim that there is extensive fraud in Maine’s benefit programs, which are currently being investigated by the state Department of Health and Human Services. 
“I’m sorry to say that there’s fraud in Maine, fraud across the country in Social Security, and in our Medicaid and in our welfare programs and I experienced it,” LePage said. “I’ve been fighting this battle since 2015 and it’s only now coming to the surface.”
In the most recent federal review, Maine’s Medicaid payment error rate was 2.4%, lower than the national average of 3.2%. And only about 0.1% of total program spending was confirmed by federal reviewers to be definitively incorrect. 
Dunlap pushed back on the claim, arguing that Republicans’ focus on fraud is a cover for cutting program funding. 
“When J.D. Vance, however, talks about Medicaid fraud, I want to be clear: he’s not interested in rooting out Medicaid fraud,” Dunlap said. “They’re interested in rooting out Medicaid, and I think that’s something we should be very wary of in the Congress.”
Tackling affordability challenges
Healthcare wasn’t the only divisive issue on the debate stage. The candidates clashed over housing, affordability issues, foreign conflicts and even what has been said on the campaign trail.
“You said that just last week that if you’re elected, you’re not going to do anything for two years because you’re going to be impeaching the president,” LePage said to Dunlap. 
“I did not say that,” Dunlap answered. “What I said was that people should have the expectation that even if the Democrats take control of both chambers, President Trump probably won’t be signing very much that comes out. But however, we can still maintain our constitutional role of oversight of the executive branch, and that’s what we should be doing.”
Along with emphasizing his record as Maine governor, LePage pointed to his relationship with Trump and his access to the president. 
“I know him personally, and I will say right now, I will be able to get into the Oval Office,” LePage said. “My opponent will not.”
Dunlap countered that Congress is meant to hold the president accountable, not maintain close ties.
On the issue of affordability, LePage said one of his top priorities if elected is to ask the president to put restrictions on diesel exports, echoing a call from top congressional Republicans, and would advocate for the state and federal government to suspend taxes on fuel. 
Dunlap said he had heard from many people in the district that rising fuel and heating oil prices were already straining their budgets. 
“One thing that we could do to help lower the cost of energy very quickly is to pass a war powers resolution and stop this war in Iran, which my opponent won’t say whether or not he supports,” Dunlap said. “So if we stop the war in Iran, we’ll see the price of oil start to come down, and that’s something that will provide almost immediate relief.”
LePage said he did not believe in the War Powers Act and that the president has constitutional authority over the military. 
“I do not support the war in Iran,” LePage said. “I do support not allowing Iran to get the nuclear power, nuclear bomb, and so I’m urging the president to work as fast, as vigilant, as possible to get this done quickly. Let’s get out of it.”
The lack of access to affordable housing was also something the candidates were asked about.
Dunlap said he has spoken to people in construction and development, and said a key way Congress can help Maine’s housing crisis is by making more financing available. 
“When you talk to people who work in the field of affordable housing and construction of it, they have a hard time accessing capital and financing,” Dunlap said. “And this is something that Congress can do and has done in the past: make funding available on a rotating basis, a revolving loan fund, so that it’d be easier for some of these developers to do.”
LePage agreed that Congress should provide funding, but he said that it should be focused on housing for the elderly. He then quickly pivoted to immigration.
“Housing costs remain out of control, first and foremost, stopping the illegal aliens from coming into our state and taking what housing is available should be stopped,” LePage said.
LePage said that he believes President Joe Biden let “millions and millions” of people enter the country illegally. And while he said he doesn’t disagree that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has “run roughshod” over communities, he believes the agency can be improved with proper training.
“I think we need to have a robust law enforcement division of our country that deals with it,” LePage said. “However, we should be able to have transparency, and if there are robust investigations, and if there’s a problem, then we need to account and make them accountable.”
The federal government has so far declined to investigate or reveal any information about the fatal shooting of Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, the Biddeford man who was killed by federal agents in July, a pattern seen across the country in response to violence and wrongful detentions by ICE. 
Dunlap said that while ICE should exist in some capacity, it shouldn’t be in the way the agency is functioning today. 
“Gov. LePage has talked very strongly about being tough on illegal immigration, being tough on the border, until of course somebody he knew very well ran into some immigration trouble,” Dunlap said, referring to LePage’s recent comments that his daughter-in-law’s father had immigrated legally but was deported.
“Then he kind of changed his tune a little bit,” Dunlap continued. 
LePage said that was a personal situation, and has nothing to do with illegal immigration or ICE. 
On the issue of trade, LePage said he does not support the tariffs as they are currently structured, but that the country has gotten a “bad deal” for many years with many countries. 
“These issues are real, and they and they need to be addressed,” LePage said. “We need to de-escalate the rhetoric, and we need to get the president and the prime minister of Canada back to the negotiating table.”
The Canadian tariffs that went into effect Sept. 8, are expected to impact $170 million of Maine exports.
Dunlap said it’s Maine residents who are paying for the tariffs, and Congress should exercise more authority over the issue.
“Tariffs are a tool, they should not be used as a blanket policy,” Dunlap said. “And my opponent said that he was all for the tariffs when they first started being applied, and now apparently, now apparently he’s changing his tune a little bit.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Gov. Armstrong presents Rough Rider Awards to Bismarck wrestling legends
description: Gov. Kelly Armstrong presented Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Awards Thursday to two of North Dakota’s most acclaimed wrestlers and coaches. Terry and Troy Steiner, twin brothers born and raised in Bismarck, received the awards for their individual wrestling achievements and their work as coaches and ambassadors for the sport over the past 40 years, accordin[...]
text:
Troy Steiner speaks to event attendees after he and his twin brother, Terry Steiner, received the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award at the Capitol on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Gov. Kelly Armstrong presented Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Awards Thursday to two of North Dakota’s most acclaimed wrestlers and coaches.
Terry and Troy Steiner, twin brothers born and raised in Bismarck, received the awards for their individual wrestling achievements and their work as coaches and ambassadors for the sport over the past 40 years, according to the Governor’s Office.
“Troy and Terry have carved a place for themselves in the pantheon of wrestling greatness,” Armstrong said during a ceremony at the Capitol. “As coaches and ambassadors, their impact and influence on the sport of wrestling cannot be measured. They have inspired countless men and women to pursue the sport of wrestling.”
The brothers competed for Bismarck Century High School with Troy Steiner winning three individual state titles across three different weight classes from 1986 to 1988. Terry Steiner won back-to-back state titles in 1987 and 1988 in two weight classes.
Upon graduation, the brothers attended the University of Iowa, where Troy Steiner was honored as a four-year All-American while Terry Steiner was awarded the same honor for three years. Each brother won an individual NCAA wrestling championship, Troy Steiner in 1992 and Terry in 1993, according to Armstrong’s office.
Terry Steiner, right, and his twin brother, Troy Steiner, center-right, view their official portrait before receiving the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award at the Capitol on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Both went on to be part of the U.S. National Team with Troy Steiner placing third at the U.S. Olympic Trials in 1992 and 1996.
“North Dakota didn’t teach us how to work hard, North Dakotans did,” said Troy Steiner during his acceptance speech to more than 300 attendees in Memorial Hall.
He said it was farmers, ranchers, teachers, coaches, and moms and dads raising families who taught them to show up, care for their neighbors and how to respond when things get hard.
“Eventually, those examples become part of you,” Troy Steiner said.
Scheel recognized for joy, vision, success through North Dakota Rough Rider Award

After their days of competition concluded, both men went on to historic coaching careers, Armstrong’s office said.
Troy Steiner coached wrestling at multiple Division I schools: Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, Oregon State and Fresno State, and is the head coach of the Gopher Wrestling Club in Minneapolis. Terry Steiner became head coach of the women’s U.S. National Wrestling Team in 2002 and led the organization to become one of the fastest growing female sports in the country, the governor’s office said.
Troy Steiner said before his father died he told the brothers to “pay it forward.” During his acceptance speech, he announced the establishment of the Steiner Rough Rider Foundation.
“We want to help create those same kinds of opportunities for another generation of young North Dakotans,” Troy Steiner said. He added the mission will be to help under-resourced young people in the state “move forward through sport.”
Terry Steiner thanked his family and friends, but also the community that shaped himself and his brother.
“We are grateful for your confidence in us and for allowing us to join a group of North Dakotans whose accomplishments have brought pride and distinction to our great state,” Terry Steiner said. “No matter where our careers have taken us, North Dakota has always been home.”
First North Dakotan to fly in space awarded state’s top honor

Armstrong said he didn’t believe anyone in the United States had done more for the growth of women’s wrestling across the country than Terry Steiner.
The Steiner brothers were the 51st and 52nd recipients of the Theodore Roosevelt Rough Rider Award since it was established in 1961. The award recognizes present and former North Dakotans who achieve national recognition in their fields.
“I would go to the mat every day, and twice on Sundays, to defend this selection for the Rough Rider Award,” Armstrong said. “Because without question, Terry and Troy have brought distinction and recognition to their home state, their country and indeed the world.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland officials say changes to electric grid governance aren’t enough
description: Leaders throughout the region overseen by power grid operator PJM Interconection have long called for states to have a greater voice in grid decision-making, but governance reforms advanced this week by PJM left advocates feeling disappointed.
text:
Maryland Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) speaks during a July rally calling for changes to management of PJM, the multistate electric grid operator, outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. (Photo by Mayah Nachman/Maryland Matters)Democratic leaders in Maryland and around the region have long called for PJM Interconnection, which administers the regional electric grid, to give more weight to state voices in its decision-making.
But at the conclusion of PJM’s process to reevaluate its governance structure Wednesday, the lawmakers leading the charge were dissatisfied with the result. Critics said that while PJM members would give states some additional say, they kept most of the decision-making authority for themselves.
“The fact that companies that benefit from the current rules get to write and approve their own reform highlights the broken system Marylanders are footing the bill for,” Gov. Wes Moore (D) said a statement released by his office.
“FERC [the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission] gave clear direction to PJM and its members to give states a real voice, but PJM’s members responded with a term sheet that stifles the states by handing those same members a veto over any proposal the states bring forward,” Moore’s statement said. “Maryland strongly rejects this move, and the PJM Board and FERC should too.”
PJM was reevaluating its governance structure at the direction of the FERC, after Chair Laura Swett in July urged PJM to make “meaningful” reforms amid mounting pressure from states, including a leading state in Pennsylvania, and the White House.
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery) and Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) joined other lawmakers at a May rally in Baltimore.(Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“I want you all to hear this plainly: If the stakeholders cannot reach a set of credible, meaningful reforms or an agreement in principle by the end of September, then this commission is not going to hesitate to use the full extent of our legal authority to implement reforms necessary to restore confidence in PJM’s governance,” Swett said at the time.
The governance decision, announced Wednesday, was “PJM’s opportunity to show that it heard Chairwoman Swett’s warning,” said Pennsylvania State Rep. Danielle Friel Otten, part of the collaborative of Democratic legislators pushing for change at PJM.
Instead, PJM members, including transmission owners and generators, gave themselves “veto power over the very decisions at issue,” Friel Otten said in a statement Thursday.
The proposal advanced by PJM members, if approved by FERC, would let the state’s executive branches participate for the first time in the Organization of PJM States, or OPSI. It is currently made up of state utility regulators — in Maryland’s case, the Public Service Commission.
But PJM’s member committee would still get to make the final decision on the filing of key documentation before FERC, under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act. And two-thirds of members would need to support a proposal from OPSI for it to move forward.
PJM members also voted Wednesday to add one state seat to their nominating committee, which decides PJM’s board members. At least one competing proposal, from PJM staff, would have added two seats for states on the nominating board, plus the opportunity for an additional independent appointee.
Maryland Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) said the governance plan offered by PJM members made states “spectators” to the process.
“PJM’s decisions shape what families pay for electricity, whether our grid is reliable, and whether states can carry out the energy policies their residents elected them to pursue,” said Hester. “States cannot be treated as spectators in a system whose decisions have such enormous consequences for our constituents.”
Hester has been among the Maryland legislators and climate groups criticizing PJM for slowing the arrival of clean energy to the grid and inadequately managing a data center boom, which has placed immense strain on the regional grid.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) speaks at the PJM Interconnection annual meeting in Baltimore on May 11, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Jeff Shields, a spokesman for PJM wrote that Wednesday’s vote represents “an important step in the governance reform process and reflects substantial work by PJM members and stakeholders over the past several weeks.”
“At the same time, we recognize that differences remain, particularly regarding the appropriate role of states in PJM’s governance and stakeholder processes,” Shields wrote in a statement.
“PJM will continue working with its Board, FERC, and stakeholders towards meaningful governance reforms that improve decision-making, preserve PJM’s independence, and appropriately consider the perspectives of states, members, consumers, and other stakeholders,” Shields said.
For several Maryland legislators, Wednesday’s decisions from PJM were not enough.
“We have known for a long time that PJM is controlled by the for-profit energy and transmission companies that profit by slow-walking the clean energy transition and keeping consumer prices high,” said Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery). “Today’s vote by those same members made it clear that these members are willing to vote to protect their profits, even in the face of FERC directing them to reform the system.”
Climate group the Chesapeake Climate Action Network agreed.
“PJM proved once again that its governance is broken, and FERC needs to step in and force drastic governance changes within PJM,” said Jamie DeMarco, Maryland Climate Change Commissioner. “You cannot ask a broken system whether it wants change. Change must be forced upon it.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Activists demand CT officials enforce the Trust Act
description: Dozens gathered in Meriden on Thursday with a list of demands for CT officials, including strengthening the Trust Act and its enforcement.
text:
More than 100 people gathered across the street from the Meriden courthouse Thursday evening with a list of demands for state officials, including strengthening the Trust Act and its enforcement and $50 million in legal support for those affected by immigration enforcement.
The rally came as a response to an arrest at the courthouse on Sept. 23, which raised questions about the legality of ICE’s actions under the state’s Trust Act and other laws. The federal agents were masked and at the courthouse with an administrative, not judicial, warrant — potentially in violation of the law. 
Activists and local politicians who spoke at the rally urged the state to enforce and strengthen the Trust Act, create uniform protocol for how state and local officers should interact with ICE, and investigate any possible collusion between ICE and state court marshals and police. Some also questioned the legality of actions taken by court marshals during last week’s arrest.
The rally was organized by a coalition of activists and attended by groups from across the state, including Middlesex Immigrant Rights Alliance, Danbury Unites for Immigrants, Middlesex Indivisible, Hartford Deportation Defense and CT 50501.

Organizer Miguel Castro, with MIRA, speaks during a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“All of us are familiar with the Trust Act and the highlights of what it stands for,” Miguel Castro, an organizer of the event and the second vice chair of the Connecticut Hispanic Democratic Caucus and member of MIRA, said. “They write the law, and now one thing is to implement it.”
Attendees chanted “shame” as speakers recalled the events of last week’s courthouse arrest, including the pepper-spraying of an activist and the masks worn into the courthouse by ICE agents. Many held up signs. Some read “melt ICE” and “due process for all.”

Attendees scream “ICE Out” during a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Meriden council member Yvette Cortez spoke at the rally, urging attendees to fight with love for their community. She said that after the ICE activity last week, the state responded with a shared upset felt by some in the community.
“I’m really grateful that the governor and his office immediately took up phone calls, shared in our outrage, and also agreed to do an investigation,” Cortez said. “Some of the videos indicate that the marshals acted in violation of the Trust Act. I don’t want to make any assumptions, not having been there, not having seen everything, but I do have an expectation that a thorough investigation is completed. I hope that the results of that investigation will be shared with the residents of Meriden, and I hope that anybody who violated it will be held accountable to the fullest extent.”
Cortez said the state police were looking into possible violations of the law, including actions taken by court marshals that may have allowed ICE agents to conduct the arrest in the courthouse without the proper documentation. 
The ACLU of Connecticut told the Connecticut Mirror in a statement that, after administrative review by the organization, there is still an “open question” if last week’s courthouse arrest violated state law.

An attendee holds a hand painted umbrella during a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Because the man arrested by ICE was never in state custody, the organization is unsure if the conduct of court marshals falls under the Trust Act — many of the provisions under the law only apply to people in state custody. The ACLU of Connecticut did obtain a copy of the administrative warrant — not judicial — used in last week’s arrest. 
If the man had been in state custody — like a Connecticut prison — the Trust Act would not allow them to turn the man over to ICE with just an administrative warrant for his arrest.
“The administrative warrant ACLU-CT obtained in connection with last Wednesday’s Meriden courthouse arrest raises more questions than it answers,” a statement from David McGuire, Executive Director for the ACLU-CT, read. “Rather than providing clarity, it leaves Connecticut’s immigrant community more vulnerable and uncertain of how protected they are in Connecticut.”
In the statement, McGuire also stressed the need to enforce state law. 
“Last week’s events show that protections on paper only matter if they hold up in practice and are truly enforceable,” McGuire said in the statement. “Together, the Meriden courthouse attack and these incoming protections create an urgent need for state agencies and legislators to review our existing protections and enforcement options, and ACLU-CT will continue working with partners and legislators to make sure all Connecticut residents are truly protected and feel safe where they live.”
Castro and Cortez said the state was complying with their requests to initiate an investigation. During the rally, speakers thanked Gov. Ned Lamont and Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz for “standing up against ICE.”
“We haven’t had any pushback from our state officials, including the governor and the lieutenant governor, who have been instrumental and critical, especially when initiating the investigation and supporting our efforts to protect members of our community,” Castro said.
A request for comment from ICE after the Meriden arrest went unanswered.
The rally follows a press conference Thursday morning, when advocates and elected officials discussed new protections and cuts to services going into effect Oct. 1 that affect the state’s immigrant community.
The new state law that designates “protected areas” like hospitals, schools and places of worship went into effect Thursday, and refugees, asylum seekers and victims of human trafficking now are no longer eligible for Medicaid in Connecticut.
Sen. Matthew Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chair of the Human Services Committee, said that state lawmakers stepped up last legislative session.
“We are laser-focused on keeping our communities safe, and there is nothing that helps make our communities safe when you have federal agents poking around our schools, our churches and mosques and synagogues, our healthcare facilities and our courthouses,” he said.

Brothers Patrick Leonard, left, 15, and Andrew Leonard, 17, of Berlin, hold signs while attending a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse with their mother Michelle Leonard on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

But Lesser also also addressed the enforcement of the Trust Act and of the new laws.
“I think we are going to ask the tough questions of our judicial branch to see what they can and can’t do, and if we need to tweak the law going forward, we can do so,” Lesser said.
Rep. Hubert Delaney, D-Stamford, said that government officials and advocates “have a responsibility to make clear that due process, dignity and the rule of law are still the standard here in Connecticut.”
But even as the new law goes into effect, some immigrant families are being impacted by the loss of health coverage. Lesser said this will affect some 3,200 Connecticut residents, including:
“600 folks who are lawful refugees in this country, 400 folks who have asylum. We have 500 victims of Vladimir Putin’s aggression in Ukraine who are losing their health care today, and it should be no surprise that the man who used the resources of the federal government to try to protect Jeffrey Epstein and his friends has decided to take health care away from survivors of human trafficking. There are dozens of people in Connecticut who are survivors, documented survivors of human trafficking, who are going to lose their healthcare benefits in Connecticut today because of the actions of this administration.”
On Thursday morning, Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., called it “fiscally stupid,” because it will keep people from getting preventative care.
“What an abomination, that we are cutting off healthcare for people that are legal residents of our community,” he said at a press conference in the Legislative Office Building in Hartford. “It betrays the very nature of what it means to be American.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Republican Joe Mitchell, Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James spar in 2nd District debate
description: Iowa Rep. Lindsay James, a Dubuque Democrat, and Republican Joe Mitchell traded barbs about one another’s backgrounds and positions in a Thursday debate. The two candidates faced off in a debate hosted by Iowa’s News Now as they seek the 2nd Congressional District seat currently held by U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for […]
text:
Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James will face off against Republican former state Rep. Joe Mitchell in the 2026 Iowa 2nd Congressional District race. (Photos courtesy of the James and Mitchell campaigns)Iowa Rep. Lindsay James, a Dubuque Democrat, and Republican Joe Mitchell traded barbs about one another’s backgrounds and positions in a Thursday debate.
The two candidates faced off in a debate hosted by Iowa’s News Now as they seek the 2nd Congressional District seat currently held by U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for U.S. Senate this year. There are two other candidates on the ballot in the 2nd District race — independent candidate Dave Bushaw and Libertarian Rick Stewart — who did not meet the news network’s criteria to qualify for the debate stage.
James and Mitchell answered questions from moderators about a number of issues, including their plans, if elected, to address Iowa’s rising cancer rates, reduce healthcare costs and handle immigration enforcement.
Mitchell said he supports the manner in which the GOP-controlled Congress has approached immigration enforcement in the past year and supported “record funding” for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), criticizing former President Joe Biden’s administration by saying, “he could have closed the border. He did not.”
There has been significant pushback against some immigration enforcement actions taken by ICE in American cities — including incidents that led to two U.S. citizens being killed by ICE agents in Minnesota. When asked by moderators whether federal immigration enforcement efforts needed reform, Mitchell said, “ultimately, I’m going to run to make sure we have a secure border, that we have Border Patrol fully funded, and we get criminals out of our country.”
Mitchell claimed James was against the U.S.-Mexico border wall. The Republican candidate also claimed James supported allowing undocumented immigrants to have access to public assistance programs like Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (SNAP), referencing her vote against a measure requiring non-U.S. citizens verify their immigration status and Iowa residency to receive benefits.
James said Mitchell was being “dishonest and misleading,” and said she was “a mom who believes in keeping our borders secure and our communities safe.”
“That is why I support policies that will secure our border, and I think that both Democrats and Republicans have gotten this wrong,” James said. “I would argue, as well, that I feel like the past administration, the Biden administration, didn’t have strong enough policies when it came to securing the border. I am someone who has departed from my political party on several different occasions, because I have courage of conviction, because I have a moral compass, because I believe in doing right by my neighbors. I want safe communities for my kids. I also believe that we need comprehensive immigration reforms.”
When asked about her vote on legislation requiring immigration status verification, James answered, “Iowans are my priority, and they will always be my priority.”
Both candidates said they did not support federal tax incentives for data centers, but James claimed Mitchell was a person who “received $100,000 doing consulting work for a PR firm for data centers.”
“He is someone who is benefiting financially from that work, and is someone who I question is really going to stand up and fight for everyday, hardworking families to make sure that our communities are safe,” she said.
The comment was made in reference to reporting by The Lever which highlighted Mitchell’s previous work for KAOH Media, a public relations firm. The company’s website currently references its work to support data-center developers. Mitchell said KAOH Media did not begin working with data centers until after he left the firm, saying it was “another lie” from James’ campaign.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Former Republican Idaho attorneys general endorse Democrat in attempt to unseat Raúl Labrador
description: Two former Republican attorneys general in Idaho — along with dozens of former lawyers at the office — on Thursday endorsed the Democratic challenger in the race for the state’s top attorney. Lori Hickman, who’s trying to unseat Republican Attorney General Raúl Labrador, said she wishes the race was nonpartisan. The race, she said, comes […]
text:
Lori Hickman, (right) Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general, stands next to former Republican state attorneys general who are endorsing her: Jim Jones (center) and Lawrence Wasden. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)Two former Republican attorneys general in Idaho — along with dozens of former lawyers at the office — on Thursday endorsed the Democratic challenger in the race for the state’s top attorney.
Lori Hickman, who’s trying to unseat Republican Attorney General Raúl Labrador, said she wishes the race was nonpartisan. The race, she said, comes down to “who’s the best attorney to be the chief legal officer for the state of Idaho.”
“I’m trying to restore the tradition of sound legal advice, regardless of who the clients are or their political affiliations,” Hickman said at a news conference announcing the endorsements. “So I’m running as a Democrat because my opponent’s a Republican.”
Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman stands in front of more than a dozen deputy attorneys general, and two former Republican AGs, who endorsed her in the 2026 election. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
Hickman stood outside the old Ada County Courthouse across the street from the Idaho State Capitol, beside a pool of attorneys who she said collectively have hundreds of years of experience.
Hickman is an Idaho attorney with two decades of experience, including at global tech company Micron, and has served as board chair of Mormon Women for Ethical Government. 
Labrador is a former Idaho congressman and an immigration attorney. He became the state’s attorney general in 2023, after defeating the state’s longest-serving attorney general, Lawrence Wasden, in the Republican primary election.
Wasden was among the pack endorsing Hickman. At the press conference, he and former Idaho Republican Attorney General Jim Jones, who also served as a state Supreme Court justice, cheered by her side. 
In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. Idaho’s last Democratic attorney general was Larry Echohawk in 1995. 
In a statement, the Labrador campaign seemed unsurprised by the endorsements. “Lawrence Wasden, Jim Jones, and disgruntled former employees. Who would have thought?” the attorney general’s re-election campaign said.
The list of endorsers, provided by Hickman’s campaign, included at least eight attorneys whose service in the office ended shortly before or after Labrador was sworn into office in January 2023, according to the Idaho Capital Sun’s review of Transparent Idaho, a state employment dataset. 
“They’ve been in the office. They know how it should run, and they know it is not running in that way at the present time,” Jones said.

 Former AG reads resignation letter from former Idaho deputy attorney general 

A handful of the former attorneys who left under Labrador’s leadership were legally representing the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, an agency that Labrador soon investigated for alleged grant mishandling. Jones read excerpts from the resignation letter of one of those attorneys, Madison Miles, who endorsed Hickman.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
In the letter, which was addressed to Labrador, Miles wrote that she could “no longer be associated with your blatant attempt to provide subpar and even unethical representation to the Department of Health and Welfare.” 
Daphne Huang, a former deputy attorney general who gave the state health agency legal advice about the grants and who Labrador’s office fired, endorsed Hickman. Huang’s whistleblower lawsuit against the Attorney General’s Office, dismissed by a state district court judge, is on appeal to the Idaho Supreme Court. 
Jones also cited a lawsuit that came after a legal opinion Labrador issued to a state legislator. The 2023 opinion said that medical professionals who refer or prescribe abortion pills to pregnant patients across state lines are subject to criminal penalties under Idaho’s strict abortion ban. But years later, Labrador and two county prosecutors reached a legal agreement with a regional Planned Parenthood organization to not prosecute some Idaho doctors for out-of-state abortion referrals. 
In an interview, Wasden said his endorsement of Hickman is his first endorsement in the race since he was defeated. He said he was issuing the endorsement now out of importance to “recognize the rule of law.”
“The rule of law really is the issue that separates us from any other country in the world. That is, that the law applies to everyone, and it’s not based upon someone’s personal political view,” Wasden, who had served as Idaho’s attorney general for 20 years, said. “The Constitution, the statutes apply to everyone.”
Wasden said he hopes his endorsement encourages voters to look at the race and “make an honest assessment of what the attorney general is supposed to do.”

title: Appeals court grants new hearing in lawsuit over petitioning time for South Dakota ballot questions
description: A South Dakota group suffered a setback Thursday in its effort to protect adequate time for petitioning questions onto statewide ballots, as a federal appeals court vacated an earlier ruling in the group’s favor and set a new hearing for next year. In August, a three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled […]
text:
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which includes South Dakota, is based at the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse in St. Louis, pictured here in June 2026. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota group suffered a setback Thursday in its effort to protect adequate time for petitioning questions onto statewide ballots, as a federal appeals court vacated an earlier ruling in the group’s favor and set a new hearing for next year.
In August, a three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that state lawmakers violated the First Amendment last year when they moved up the deadline for submitting petition signatures by three months.
South Dakota’s Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley responded to that ruling by seeking a new hearing with all 11 members of the appeals court. The court granted that request Thursday and set a new hearing for January in St. Louis.
Federal appeals court protects longer petitioning time for South Dakota ballot questions

Petitioners need 17,508 signatures from registered voters to put a proposed law on the ballot in South Dakota, and 35,017 signatures for a proposed state constitutional amendment. South Dakota lawmakers approved legislation last year that moved the deadline for filing signed petitions in a general election year from the first Tuesday in May to the first Tuesday in February.
A group that’s been involved in numerous ballot questions, Dakotans for Health, challenged the law in federal court. A district court judge ruled the law violates the First Amendment, writing that moving the deadline three months earlier “arguably goes beyond merely inconvenient and enters the realm of severe.” The state appealed that ruling.
During arguments heard by the three-judge appeals panel in June, the state argued a shorter deadline gives more time for potential litigation over ballot questions to play out.
Judge Raymond Gruender wrote in an August opinion that the state didn’t provide “sufficient factual or legal support” for its argument that pre-election litigation on petitions would bolster the confidence of voters in the initiative and referendum process. Judge Jane Kelly joined Gruender in the decision.
In a dissenting opinion, Judge James Loken wrote “the Constitution does not authorize this federal court micromanagement of state elections.” The state law furthers South Dakota’s “interest in election integrity by extending the time for pre-election petition litigation,” Loken added.

title: New Mexico attorneys request judge fine Facebook up to $40B for violating state law
description: Attorneys representing the State of New Mexico requested a district court judge on Thursday fine Facebook between $35 to $40 billion after a Santa Fe jury last week found that the social media giant willfully violated state law regarding unfair and deceptive trade practices.
text:
New Mexico First Judicial District Judge Francis Mathew listens to attorney Matthew Nicholson, representing Meta Platforms Inc., during an Oct. 1, 2026, hearing to determine the penalties against Meta, which was found by a jury to have violated a state consumer protection law during a trial last month. (Eddie Moore/Albuqerque Journal)Attorneys representing the State of New Mexico requested a district court judge on Thursday fine Facebook between $35 to $40 billion after a Santa Fe jury last week found that the social media giant willfully violated state law regarding unfair and deceptive trade practices. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
First Judicial District Judge Francis Mathew heard from attorneys representing both parties in advance of ruling on the penalties for Facebook. In its decision, the jury found that Facebook committed close to 44 million violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act through its statements regarding  user data, misinformation and hate speech on the platform, among other issues.
In a news conference last week following the verdict, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said the total cost of violations could reach as much as $219 billion. On Thursday, Randi McGinn, the attorney representing the state, requested Mathew fine Facebook between $35 billion to $40 billion, and said the state is requesting that amount in order to hold Facebook accountable while also respecting its due process rights in case of appeal.
“Not only is that a fair amount,” McGinn said, “it would serve the purpose of deterrence — not just for Meta — but for any big company that would like to lie to the people of New Mexico.” 
Matt Nicholson, attorney representing Meta, told the judge that the state’s price tag is unprecedented and violates the company’s Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
The state, Nicholson said, is “trying to take advantage” of the jury’s ruling and “run up the score on penalties. 
Nicholson said that the state’s request is double the amount that was paid by British Petroleum following the Deep Horizon oil spill, and that while harm was clearly proven in that case, New Mexico did not prove that Facebook caused any harm to New Mexicans in this case to warrant the requested penalty.
He noted that the Supreme Court has “long held that the due process clause prohibits states from imposing statutory penalties that are wholly disproportionate to the offense.”
Mathew told both parties he will render a decision on penalties within two to three weeks.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Opioid settlement spending shows need for more oversight, NJ advocates warn
description: Harm reduction advocates are calling for more oversight after new reports showed some questionable spending of opioid settlement funds.
text:
Some municipalities in New Jersey spent opioid settlement funds on boxes like this to provide free naloxone, an overdose-reversing drug, to passers-by. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)State, county, and municipal officials got more than $60 million in national opioid settlement funds over the past year that was meant to be spent to repair harms caused by the deadly overdose crisis.
Instead, it funded concerts, inflatable bounce houses, DJs, dirt bike demonstrations, police canines, ice cream, movie nights, bicycles and gym gear for cops, graduation parties, college-prep programs, vehicle wraps, attorney fees, pet sitting, fishing, summer camps, meals, and more, according to spending reports released Thursday.
Now, harm reduction advocates are calling on policymakers to tighten oversight of how public officials spend the money, which is part of $1.1 billion the state and local governments will receive through 2038 from drug manufacturers, distributors, and pharmacies to resolve lawsuits.
“We all tend to refer to this as blood money,” said Amanda Devecka-Rinear, executive director of the New Jersey Organizing Project. “We’ve all lost someone to an overdose, and many of those people were lost because they were prescribed a drug that Big Pharma knew was addictive and did anyway. This money is an attempt to rectify that, and so using this funding for something other than expenditures that address the overdose crisis is an absolute disrespect and dishonor to the people we’ve lost and will lose.”
The demands for accountability are nothing new. Former state Comptroller Kevin Walsh urged lawmakers last year to better scrutinize spending after he found Irvington blew more than a half-million dollars on two drug-awareness concerts. Former Attorney General Matt Platkin and other critics seconded that sentiment after legislators diverted $45 million in settlement funds to hospitals struggling with federal Medicaid cuts.
“Nobody’s holding anybody accountable,” said Elizabeth Burke-Beaty, founder and CEO of Ocean County-based Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center.
Advocates hope the details hiding in thousands of pages of spending reports released Thursday will drive change.
The reports show that the state, its 21 counties, and 500-plus municipalities spent the money in all sorts of ways in the last fiscal year, which ended June 30.
Millions went to things that advocates agreed were worthy, met approved uses, and fit the five priorities harm reduction experts support: addiction treatment; prevention; housing; recovery supports like peer coaching; and other supports like job training, transportation, and family reunification programs.
But plenty of the spending raised eyebrows.
Paramus spent $4,200 on a free opioid awareness concert. Garfield paid $2,600 for bounce houses, a DJ, and microphone rentals for a three-hour “Let’s Knock Out Opioid Use Together” event. Willingboro shelled out $12,400 for a “Summer In Motion” series featuring free food, games, and recreational activities targeting youth. Metuchen forked out $3,000 for a “BMX drug awareness program” featuring dirt bikes. Lodi spent $1,900 on a “Say No to Drugs Ice Cream Event.”
Multiple towns used settlement funds for school graduation parties, summer camps, after-school programs, movie nights, and more — events intended to keep kids too busy to dabble in drugs.
“Municipalities are sort of the worst offenders of using the funds very liberally to meet their needs,” Burke-Beaty said. “Expenditures are done under the guise of ‘prevention.’”
Many towns explained expenditures as strategies to reduce barriers to treatment, but advocates said some officials stretched the idea of what constituted a barrier. Somerset County spent $5,000 on Paw of Hope, which provides temporary pet care for people entering recovery.
Harm reduction advocates staged a die-in at the Trenton Statehouse on Monday, June 30, 2025, after legislators — fearing federal Medicaid cuts would hurt hospitals — decided to divert $45 million in national opioid settlement funds to four of the state’s largest hospitals. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)
Advocates also suspected some municipalities are increasingly using opioid settlement funds to plug budget holes as the economy worsens, noting that some expenditures were things public officials normally would pay for out of their general funds such as transportation and food pantries.
Gloucester County spent more than $71,000 on buses for elementary school students to get to after-school programs, with another $179,000 allocated under a two-year agreement with Holcomb Transportation. The primary focus of the spending, officials noted, was to “prevent misuse of opioids.”
Scores of police departments got settlement funds for officers’ salaries, training and conferences, and physical and mental wellness, as well as drug-detection devices and other tools.
Hospitals also were a common recipient. Edison earmarked $1 million for the JFK University Medical Center to fund a three-year contract for treatment and related services.
Advocates eyed such spending as potentially problematic, saying police historically have caused some of the harms experienced by those who struggle with addiction and that community-based harm reduction specialists can be more effective than hospitals.
Cole Zaccaro, manager of harm reduction services at Asbury Park-based Prevention Resource Network, doesn’t automatically see something wrong with “creative” uses of settlement funds. Many of the spending reports, though, are scant enough that they leave more questions than answers, Zaccaro said.
“It’s hard to say from a distance what’s the best use of funding,” they said.
The key is ensuring people with lived experience are involved with the decision-making, and that should be tracked and publicly reported too, they said.
“Ultimately what’s most important is that the purpose of these funds is to address the harms caused by the opioid crisis. So if the benefits are not being directly felt by the people who have experienced those harms, then we’ve missed the mark,” Zaccaro said.
Some states have tightened oversight by barring certain uses of settlement funds, such as police salaries, although New Jersey has no specific prohibitions in place.
Several state legislators recently introduced a bill intended to expand transparency and oversight of state, county, and local spending of settlement funds. The details of the legislation aren’t online yet, because they’re still being tweaked, according to Burke-Beaty, who said she worked with lawmakers on the bill. Bill sponsors Assemblymen Cody Miller (D-Gloucester) and Avi Schnall (D-Ocean) did not respond to requests for comment.
With no action yet from lawmakers, Burke-Beaty’s group launched its own website last month where people can see recommended strategies for spending, check how their towns are using the money, and more.
While settlement fund recipients are required to file reports even if they didn’t spend any money, multiple municipalities did not — including Irvington, Paterson, South Brunswick, and more.
Devecka-Rinear hopes the missing reports and more questionable spending revealed in Thursday’s reports will incite the public to push for accountability.
“Right now, it feels like everyday people are, in fact, the current and best leverage we have to make sure that this funding is spent well,” she said. “We all need to get in the game, but we also need some actual official oversight and leverage to make sure that this money isn’t being misspent.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Confusion and angst follow Montana’s early rollout of Medicaid work rules
description: MISSOULA, Mont. — Bethany Zulick went back to school in January to become a high school English teacher. Years ago, she taught English as a second language overseas and loved it. “It’s so exciting to me to watch someone learn a new word or have that spark of understanding,” she said. Zulick knew she could […]
text:
Rep. Mary Caferro, a Democrat in the Montana House, spoke at a July rally at the Montana Capitol in Helena, criticizing the state’s expedited rollout of Medicaid work requirements. She’s among several Democrats who pushed for the state to delay implementing the rules until the Jan. 1 federal deadline. (Aaron Bolton/MTPR)MISSOULA, Mont. — Bethany Zulick went back to school in January to become a high school English teacher.
Years ago, she taught English as a second language overseas and loved it.
“It’s so exciting to me to watch someone learn a new word or have that spark of understanding,” she said.
Zulick knew she could earn enough money as a substitute teacher to make going back to school financially viable — except for the cost of health insurance. She didn’t want to risk being unable to see her doctor for her allergies, or for preventative care.
The health insurance offered through Montana State University was too expensive, Zulick said, almost as much as her tuition. But then she found a solution that allowed her to make the leap— Medicaid. She wouldn’t have to pay any monthly premiums.
It worked well for a few months, as Zulick taught by day and took online classes at night.
But in June, the state sent a letter that she said left her “completely confused.” She knew Montana was rolling out a system for work requirements over the summer, but she thought she wouldn’t have to prove she met the requirements until next year, when her Medicaid enrollment came up for renewal.
Yet the letter from the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services outlining the new requirements gave conflicting information on when Zulick would have to prove she was meeting them. First it said at her next renewal, which would be sometime next spring. Lower down it told her she would have to submit paperwork to prove compliance much earlier — “within 30 days” of the date on the letter, June 26. She wondered: Was it a boilerplate mass-mailing letter she could ignore, or was her insurance on the line?
Most states must implement the new work requirements by Jan. 1, but three states — Montana, Nebraska, and Arkansas — have already gotten started. Medicaid advocates worry that the expedited timeline in those states will lead to thousands of people losing coverage because they’re confused about the new rules, even if they are eligible for the program — and that Montana may offer a troubling preview of what will happen nationwide next year.
State health department officials maintain they are well prepared and told state lawmakers they plan to process roughly 5,000 enrollees monthly.
  Growing confusion, dwindling help 

Rep. SJ Howell of the Montana House has gotten dozens of calls from confused constituents, specifically about letters like the one Zulick received.
“The notices coming from the department are very, very confusing, and it’s very hard to find help figuring out what’s going on,” said the Democratic legislator, who asked health department leaders about those letters at a hearing in early September. Letters being sent to enrollees have been updated to be clearer, state health officials told lawmakers at the hearing.
In Montana, nearly 71,000 people are subject to the new rules. Medicaid costs are split between the federal and state governments, and states are responsible for administering the program, which provides health insurance for people with low incomes or disabilities.
Under the new work requirements, enrollees must document that they’re working, volunteering, or studying 80 hours per month — or they must show that they qualify for one of a range of exemptions, such as being “medically frail” or being the primary caretaker for a family member.
Montana began with a soft launch of the work requirements in July and gave enrollees until Oct. 1 to comply.
Critics contend that isn’t enough time, because the state hasn’t finished setting up new computer systems or hiring the staff it said it would need. Of the 59 positions, only about 20 were filled, state health department officials told state lawmakers during the Sept. 9 hearing, adding that numbers had fluctuated amid staff turnover.
State health officials have said they’ll eventually be able to automatically verify that students are enrolled in public universities. However, that computer system isn’t expected to be up and running until next year, leaving students like Zulick to track down and submit the correct paperwork to prove their college enrollment.
However, there are fewer outside resources to help residents with these bureaucratic tasks.
For example, Cover Montana, a nonprofit that helps Montanans fill out such paperwork, lost federal funding last year, going from a staff of 18 to two part-time employees working a phone line.
The state does operate a helpline, but federal data shows that Montanans stay on hold much longer than the national average and that many callers hang up before they connect with a state employee.
“We were worried about chaos that could be generated by the state rushing,” said Aaron Wernham, CEO of the Montana Healthcare Foundation, a nonprofit aimed at improving health in the state. “Given how little information the state has provided about what they are doing, I’m much more worried about chaos.”
Wernham pointed to a similar upheaval in 2023, when states undertook a massive process to redetermine the eligibility of all Medicaid enrollees, after regular eligibility checks were paused during the pandemic.
Many Montanans who were financially eligible lost Medicaid coverage for technical reasons, such as incorrectly filling out paperwork — roughly 87,000, according to state data from two years ago.
Even vulnerable Montanans who didn’t need to file paperwork, because their coverage should have been automatically renewed, were dropped from the Medicaid rolls, including people who were homeless.
  Long-sought requirements in state 

The Montana Legislature passed a measure in 2019 expressing its desire to add work requirements to Medicaid, but the state didn’t have permission from the federal government to move forward until now.
Having work requirements creates accountability for people who rely on the social safety net, said Montana Senate President Matt Regier, a Republican.
“In an economy like this, if you’re an able-bodied adult that’s able to work, you really do need to step up,” he said.
Asked about confusion among enrollees about the rules, Regier responded that the Oct. 1 deadline offered more than enough time to work out the kinks in the new system.
In the end, Zulick learned she didn’t need to worry about that deadline, because she got married in July and no longer qualified for Medicaid, although she didn’t know that would be the case when she got the June letter.
But others remain scared about losing coverage, including Heather Reel, who attended a rally at the state capitol in July to push back against Montana’s early rollout.
Reel relies on Medicaid for its mental health coverage. Without it, she said, she would struggle to care for her teenage son, who has autism and is nonverbal. Between her shifts at a fast food restaurant and caring for her son, she’s scared she’ll be too busy to figure out how to report her work hours.
  Montana’s rollout a potential preview 

The handful of states that are implementing the Medicaid work requirements early are building the plane as they’re taking off, said Akeiisa Coleman, who provides Medicaid analysis for The Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit focused on making healthcare more equitable.
“Montana is going to be an example for what we might see nationally as things roll out,” she said.
Although most other states are sticking to the Jan. 1 deadline to build and test their Medicaid systems, they still might not have all the components in place, she said.
If states can’t automatically renew or deny coverage based on the new rules, state workers will have to do so manually, on a case-by-case basis. That could create backlogs and more disruption, leading more people to lose coverage, Coleman said.
Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson for the state’s health department, said in a statement that Montana’s Medicaid office is ready for the change on Oct. 1.
“We are committed to ensuring eligible Montanans maintain coverage while meeting requirements, and we will continue to monitor implementation closely,” Ebelt said.
Democratic state lawmakers have repeatedly asked state health officials to extend the Oct. 1 deadline for enrollees to comply with the new rules, but they’ve said they have no plans to do so.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA’s nation-high minimum wage rising to nearly $18 an hour in 2027
description: Washington’s minimum wage workers will get a 3.5% pay bump in 2027. The state’s minimum wage will climb to $17.73 an hour starting Jan. 1, the state Department of Labor and Industries announced this week. That’s a 60-cent increase from the current hourly rate of $17.13, which is the highest of any state in the […]
text:
(Getty Images)Washington’s minimum wage workers will get a 3.5% pay bump in 2027.
The state’s minimum wage will climb to $17.73 an hour starting Jan. 1, the state Department of Labor and Industries announced this week.
That’s a 60-cent increase from the current hourly rate of $17.13, which is the highest of any state in the nation and more than double the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour.
State law requires the Department of Labor and Industries to adjust the minimum wage annually for inflation. It does so by using the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Agency staff compared the index figures from August of last year with August of this year.
Cities and counties can set minimum wages above the state threshold. Seattle’s rate, for example, will be $22.14 an hour next year. SeaTac, Tukwila, Renton, Bellingham, Everett, Burien and unincorporated King County also will have minimum wage rates higher than the state’s.
In Washington, the wage law applies to workers age 16 and older. Employers can pay 85% of the minimum rate to 14- and 15-year-old employees. Next year, those younger workers will get a 51-cent increase to $15.07 an hour.
Drivers for transportation network companies like Lyft and Uber will get a pay bump beginning Jan. 1, too. Minimum pay for drivers was part of a 2022 state law.
For trips within Seattle, drivers will earn 72 cents per passenger platform minute and $1.69 per passenger platform mile, or $6.34 per trip, whichever is greater, according to the state.
For trips outside of Seattle, drivers will earn 41 cents per passenger platform minute and $1.43 per passenger platform mile, or $3.68 per trip, whichever is greater.
Also in January, more salaried employees could become eligible for overtime pay. Washington law sets minimum salary thresholds below which workers must be paid time-and-a-half for overtime hours.  
Next year, to be exempt from overtime, a worker in a company with 51 or more employees must be paid at least two-and-a-half times the state minimum wage in a 40-hour work week. That’s $1,773 a week or $92,196 a year. Currently, the threshold is $1,541 a week or at least $80,168.
Firms with up to 50 workers must pay at least two-and-a-quarter times the minimum wage to any workers they want to be exempt from overtime requirements. That works out to at least $1,595 a week or $82,976 a year.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware SBI moving to SMART-E fingerprint kiosks Oct. 5
description: New system captures fingerprints, facial images and ID information while connecting customers with remote agents for assistance DOVER, Del. — Delawareans who need fingerprints for employment, licensing, background checks and other purposes will see a different process beginning Monday, Oct. 5, as the State Bureau of Identification moves to new SMART-E kiosks[...]
text:
New system captures fingerprints, facial images and ID information while connecting customers with remote agents for assistance
DOVER, Del. — Delawareans who need fingerprints for employment, licensing, background checks and other purposes will see a different process beginning Monday, Oct. 5, as the State Bureau of Identification moves to new SMART-E kiosks at its Dover and Georgetown offices.
The Delaware State Police said SBI will transition fingerprinting services to IDEMIA’s SMART-E Kiosk, replacing the traditional process in which an employee directly operates the fingerprint equipment.
SMART-E stands for Supervised Multi-Acquisition Remote Technology for Enrollment. The system does more than simply take fingerprints: It captures fingerprints, a facial image and identification documents and connects customers with trained remote agents who can supervise the process and provide assistance.
The “multi-acquisition” part of the name reflects the kiosk’s ability to collect several forms of identity information during a single enrollment.
Customers operate the kiosk themselves while a trained agent remotely monitors the process and can communicate through integrated audio and video technology.
What changes for customers
The kiosk guides customers through each step of enrollment, including capturing a full set of 10 fingerprints and a facial image, scanning government-issued identification and processing payment electronically.
IDEMIA says the system has demonstrated a fingerprint rejection rate below 2%, potentially reducing the need to repeat fingerprint submissions because of poor image quality.
Although the system is more automated, customers will not be left entirely on their own. A remote agent can communicate directly with the customer and provide guidance when necessary.
Potential savings in time and money
The new system also changes the economics of running a fingerprinting operation.
Under the traditional model, a trained employee typically works directly with one customer at a fingerprint station. SMART-E uses what IDEMIA describes as a “1-to-many” model, allowing a remote agent to oversee multiple kiosk enrollments rather than requiring a dedicated employee at every station.
IDEMIA says that model can lower labor costs, reduce facility and overhead expenses and make it easier to expand operating hours because remote agents do not have to be physically located at the fingerprinting site.
For customers, the potential time savings come from automating several steps at the same station — identification scanning, fingerprint and facial-image capture and electronic payment — while also checking fingerprint quality during the enrollment process.
The manufacturer describes the system as a way to provide faster and more efficient enrollment and to increase customer throughput. However, Delaware State Police has not released estimates showing how many minutes the new kiosks will save customers or how much money SBI expects to save after implementation.
That distinction matters: The technology is designed to reduce staffing and operating costs and potentially shorten waits, but the actual savings in Delaware will depend on customer volume, staffing and how the kiosks perform once they are in use.
Appointment still required
Customers should register and schedule their fingerprinting appointment through IdentoGO before going to an SBI office.
They also need to obtain the correct service code and any required paperwork from the employer, government agency, licensing organization or other entity requesting the background check.
Customers must bring an accepted form of government-issued identification and should have an electronic payment method available to complete the transaction at the kiosk.
The change is part of SBI’s continuing effort, in partnership with IDEMIA and IdentoGO, to modernize Delaware’s fingerprinting and background-check services.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Construction of new innovation hub starts at former prison site in Draper
description: The former site of the Utah State Prison in Draper is now a blank canvas as state leaders prepare the ground to build a massive development that’s been named The Point.  Thursday, the construction of its “Convergence Point,” a centerpiece for the project, was celebrated. After receiving $50 million from the Utah Legislature in 2022 […]
text:
Rendering of the Nucleus Institute's planned Convergence Point. (Courtesy of Gensler and FFKR)The former site of the Utah State Prison in Draper is now a blank canvas as state leaders prepare the ground to build a massive development that’s been named The Point. 
Thursday, the construction of its “Convergence Point,” a centerpiece for the project, was celebrated.
After receiving $50 million from the Utah Legislature in 2022 to fund its construction, the hall is envisioned to foster innovation among students of Utah public colleges, researchers, entrepreneurs and industry leaders. The center will offer classrooms, coworking spaces, offices for universities and even dorms for students coming from across the state.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said during the center’s groundbreaking ceremony that it’s “where a statewide idea really begins to take a physical shape.”
Utah officials betting on this institute to become a hub where research and technology materialize

“It will give people a place to meet, to see research firsthand, to work on real problems, and of course, to find the partners who can bring an idea to market,” Cox said. “We want students and researchers, businesses, investors and government all in one space together, sitting at the same table and actually getting to work.”
The center is expected to open in summer 2029.
The groundbreaking also followed the reorganization of what the Legislature called the “Utah Innovation Lab” into the “Nucleus Institute,” which is led by Jefferson Moss, commissioner of Utah’s Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity and former Utah House majority leader. 
“Our goal and ambition here is to make Utah the fastest place in the country, hopefully the fastest place in the world, to be able to move ideas from discovery to impact, to be able to bring those different groups together to solve big problems,” Moss said.
Jefferson Moss and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox speak during a groundbreaking ceremony for the Nucleus Institute’s Convergence Point on Oct. 1, 2026. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)
Those big problems could include housing affordability, water and air issues and furthering emerging technologies, Angela Smith, Chief Operating Officer of the Nucleus Institute said.
“I’m not advocating for one career path over another, but I know that some of our best and brightest students are sitting on the sidelines because they have limiting beliefs and they are forced to choose a career when they haven’t been exposed to a variety of opportunities,” Smith said after talking about her time in Silicon Valley, which inspired her career change from teaching.
When the new center opens, the Utah System of Higher Education will help coordinate the Nucleus Institute’s work to help make the connections necessary.
Rendering of the Nucleus Institute’s planned Convergence Point. (Courtesy of Gensler and FFKR)
The vision for the site also includes “research demonstrations, startup showcases, meetings with investors, workforce programs and public events,” according to a news release. Research is expected to remain within university campuses, but the center “will give businesses and the public a place to see that work firsthand, meet the people behind it and explore ways to put it to use.”
Geoffrey Landward, Commissioner of Higher Education, said he was also excited about the potential of an innovation hub like this one.
“We’re going to take all these stakeholders, gather their ideas, their research, their imagination, their resources, bring them in close quarters, accelerate them, and let them collide,” Landward said. “And just like in physics, we can’t fully predict what comes out of those collisions. And that’s the point.”

title: Douglas County Board responds to state auditor criticism, sheriff says criminal probe still on
description: OMAHA — The Douglas County Board on Thursday announced that it sees no allegations of criminal wrongdoing in a state auditor’s probe of a county program that serves the poor, despite the sheriff’s call for a law enforcement investigation. Sheriff Aaron Hanson said in response that his investigation will go on. He said he didn’t […]
text:
The Omaha-Douglas County Civic Center is the headquarters of city and county government. (Courtesy of Douglas County GIS)OMAHA — The Douglas County Board on Thursday announced that it sees no allegations of criminal wrongdoing in a state auditor’s probe of a county program that serves the poor, despite the sheriff’s call for a law enforcement investigation.
Sheriff Aaron Hanson said in response that his investigation will go on.
He said he didn’t think the County Board’s statement fully addressed all concerns raised in the Sept. 22 report by State Auditor Mike Foley. Hanson contends his department has an obligation “to ensure that taxpayer dollars are not spent or distributed contrary to law.”
The County Board spoke in the wake of Hanson’s pledge last week that he’ll open an investigation into the county’s general assistance program for low-income residents. Sparking Hanson’s push was the Foley report, which flagged alleged and potential improper distribution and use of Dollar General gift cards intended for poor county residents. The review also highlighted high administrative costs, though the County Board has questioned the auditor’s calculations.
Roger Garcia, Douglas County Commissioner (Courtesy of Douglas County)
The County Board in its Thursday statement did not say whether it had communicated with Hanson on the matter. The sheriff is an elected official, as are the seven County Board members. 
Led by Chairman Roger Garcia, the County Board said that based on information available from the state auditor review, it didn’t see any allegations of a crime.
Touching upon gift card problems, the board said the county is moving to stop its use of Dollar General gift cards, and is searching instead for a vendor that does not sell tobacco or alcohol, items that are off limits under county guidelines. 
When the arrangement with Dollar General started, the vendor reportedly did not sell such prohibited items, and county officials said they thought the cards provided an “accessible, cost-effective way” to deliver aid to the target group, low-income county residents who aren’t eligible for other public assistance.
Foley said of participants’ gift card use: “Montego Menthol Silver and Gold cigarettes, Mike’s Harder Lemonade and Natty Daddy beer were popular choices.”
The County Board’s statement said “only 100” of the nearly 26,000 Dollar General cards distributed from 2023 through 2026 were reviewed by Foley’s team “due to specific red flags.” 
Of that sample, the auditor said about 70% of usage was questionable, including about 10% alcohol and tobacco products and items such as food and toys that don’t meet the program’s parameters of clothing, hygiene or cleaning items. 
Hanson said the County Board appears to admit that some gift cards were “impermissibly spent,” and he doesn’t think that should be overlooked.
Douglas County Sheriff Aaron Hanson. Aug. 5, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Foley also criticized the county’s cost to run the program. He said the top three salaries among 18 people ranged from $166,614 to $105,000, and he contended that for every $100 of financial aid to the poor in a three-year period reviewed, the county spent roughly $74 on administrative expenses.
On that issue, the County Board said its ratio of administrative costs has improved from 78 cents per $1 of direct aid in fiscal year 2023 to 50 cents in fiscal year 2026. It said the county tracks costs per fiscal year, which does not align directly with the calendar-year periods used by the state auditor team, “making direct comparison difficult.” The board said it is seeking clarification from Foley on calculations. 
More generally, the County Board said it views the Foley report as an opportunity to improve the general assistance program procedures to protect funds designated for county residents most in need. State law requires counties to have a department that aids the poor, and Douglas County provides help in the form of rent vouchers, cremation services and household items.
The board said it maintains “strong support” for the general assistance program, staff and services.
“Inevitably some will seek to abuse a public benefits program, whether at the federal, state or local level, but we have seen across decades that the vast majority simply need a helping hand while they gain stability and work toward self-sustainability,” the board statement said.
The County Board plans to affirm its statement as a board resolution during its weekly meeting next Tuesday.
