name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Double-digit health insurance increases will hit individual and small group plans in 2027, again
description: Hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans are facing significantly more expensive health insurance next year. The average increase for individual and small group insurance plans is 17% for 2027, the state’s Department of Commerce announced Thursday, raising costs for the 203,000 and 184,000 Minnesotans covered by individual and small group plans respectively. Ind[...]
text:
(Getty Images.)Hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans are facing significantly more expensive health insurance next year.
The average increase for individual and small group insurance plans is 17% for 2027, the state’s Department of Commerce announced Thursday, raising costs for the 203,000 and 184,000 Minnesotans covered by individual and small group plans respectively.
Individuals and their families who are not covered by their employer or by public programs — like Medicare, Medicaid (called Medical Assistance in Minnesota) and MinnesotaCare — buy individual plans from health insurers through MNsure, the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Many people using MNcare can get discounts on their insurance premiums — what people pay upfront to be insured — if they make below a certain income.
Minnesota health insurance rates ballooning in 2026

The rate hikes come at the same time as significant shifts in the individual marketplace from federal policy: Republicans blocked Democratic efforts to extend “enhanced” premium discounts — delivered through tax credits — into 2026, resulting in the amount of discounts and the number of people who can receive those discounts to drop this year. (People can also buy individual health plans outside of MNsure, though they would be unable to get tax credits to offset premium costs.)
Health insurers have raised rates by double digit increases for two years in a row. Last year, individual rates went up 22%, while rates for small groups — which refers to businesses with fewer than 50 people — went up an average of 14%. Increases in the year before that were less extreme.
In a press release, Julia Dreier, the Department of Commerce’s temporary commissioner, attributed the eyewatering cost spikes to “broad changes across our health care system,” including the high prices of medical visits and drugs, people using more healthcare, and “the growing role of profit-driven entities in the delivery and financing of care.”


Only some health insurance companies are approved to sell coverage to individuals and small groups. The Department of Commerce releases the average rate increases for each health insurer, which range from 10% to 21% for 2027. HealthPartners, in the individual market, and UnitedHealthcare, in the small group market, both posted average increases exceeding 21%.
The same day the rate increases were announced, health economists from the University of Minnesota and the University of Southern California spoke at a state Senate human services committee hearing about how hospital consolidation drives up healthcare prices, which in turn drives up insurance prices. Mergers are being proposed at what Erin Conti of the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office called a “breakneck pace” in 2026, with a new merger announced just this week between Essentia and HealthPartners, two Minnesota-based health systems.
Glenn Melnick, a professor at USC, referred to increasingly expensive insurance premiums as a “hidden tax” in employment-based health insurance, where health insurance premiums are either taken out of paychecks or paid by employers, both resulting in lower pay for workers.
Melnick also noted that as insurance rates balloon, the same rate increases refer to larger and larger dollar amounts over time, making it more difficult to curb costs. In other words, since health insurance premiums are so expensive, even 10% growth now means families need to shell out — or sacrifice in wage growth — an additional couple thousands of dollars for higher insurance premiums every year.
Melnick and other health economists point to high hospital prices as a major driver of healthcare prices and, by extension, insurance prices. “If we don’t control hospital spending, we’re not going to effectively control overall healthcare spending,” Melnick said.
The increases come in the heat of midterm elections, and candidates were quick to blame the opposition for the ballooning costs, often in broad terms.
Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth, who is running for governor against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, released a statement: “There is one person in this race responsible for the rising cost of health insurance: Amy Klobuchar. Twenty years ago U.S. Senate candidate Amy Klobuchar promised us lower health insurance costs, but they have skyrocketed over the two decades she’s been in Washington DC.”
Klobuchar, Minnesota’s senior senator, also released a statement. She blamed healthcare cuts from President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act for the rate hikes: “Minnesotans cannot afford a governor whose only plan for their health care is to double down on the Trump policies that are making healthcare more expensive and out of reach in our state and across the country.”
Klobuchar also reiterated her promise, if elected governor, to enact state-level tax credits if federal enhanced premium tax credits aren’t restored.
The Minnesota Council of Health Plans, the trade group for health insurers here, released a statement attributing cost increases to high prices and usage of medical services and prescription drugs.
The trade group also pointed to administrative changes by the Department of Commerce requiring insurers to cover 24/7 in-home nursing care, though neither the trade group nor the Department of Commerce clarified where exactly those changes stood by the time of publication.
Insurers had covered 24/7 in-home nursing care for 15 years, following a 2010 state law requiring them to cover medically necessary nursing care. For 2026 plans, though, some insurance companies placed caps on how much in-home care a person could receive. Bipartisan legislators tried to remove those caps in the 2026 legislative session, but failed to pass a bill. Sen. Liz Boldon, DFL-Rochester, an author of that bill, said that she’s still waiting for plans to be released to see if the Department of Commerce has indeed required insurers to cover 24/7 in-home nursing care.
“For them to say that they are increasing rates because of this care is nonsense to me, because they have been covering it for the last 16 years,” Boldon said in a phone call. “It is not a new thing.”
An analysis from the Peterson Center on Healthcare and KFF found that across the country, ACA marketplace insurers proposed a median increase of 15%, largely driven by higher prices of medical care.
Open enrollment for individuals shopping for health insurance begins Nov. 1.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Democrats’ ad links Ty Masterson to Sam Brownback; Kansas GOP nominee claims it’s a ‘lie’
description: Tax-policy legacy of former Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback is drawn into fray of gubernatorial race between Cindy Holscher and Ty Masterson.
text:
Sen. Ty Masterson, the Kansas Republican Party's nominee for governor, claims a new attack ad from the Democratic Governor's Association misrepresents video clips from 2017 and 2023 to smear his affiliation with former Gov. Sam Brownback and Brownback's disastrous 2012 overhaul of state income tax policy. In this June 1, 2026, image, Masterson chats with reporters as his wife, Marlo, looks on. (Photo by Baya Burgess/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Democratic Governors Association’s latest ad for Kansas gubernatorial candidate Cindy Holscher alleges Republican nominee Ty Masterson claimed a key role in shaping income tax cuts that cast the state into a budget abyss rather than promote economic growth.
Holscher, the Democratic nominee, has sought throughout the campaign to link Masterson with former Gov. Sam Brownback, especially his tax reform catastrophe. The DGA’s ad stresses that theme. Masterson, after reviewing the DGA’s commercial, declared it a “lie.”
The new DGA digital ad pointed to video of a 2017 Kansas Republican Assembly meeting in which Masterson referenced authorship of tax legislation signed by Brownback in 2012 to lower individual income tax rates and shield more than 300,000 business owners from state tax liability. Brownback’s objective was to kill off the state’s income tax and spark a supply-side economic renaissance.
During the Republican Assembly gathering, the DGA ad shows Masterson saying: “The Brownback plan, which by the way, I wrote.”
The DGA commercial included Masterson’s remark in 2023 on High Plains television that Brownback wasn’t the author of the 2012 tax legislation, but “just got blamed for it.”
Johanna Warshaw, deputy communications director of the DGA, said political connections between Masterson and Brownback should be clear to voters ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
“The Masterson agenda is the Brownback agenda,” she said. “No matter how hard Ty tries to distance himself from his role in the failed Brownback experiment, the truth is he wrote the disastrous plan — and he was caught admitting it on tape. Kansans across the aisle do not want to go back to the disastrous Brownback days of four-day school weeks and businesses fleeing the state.”
 
Masterson: It’s a ‘lie’
In response, Masterson said the DGA misrepresented his role in developing the 2012 income tax package. He said the DGA created a deceptive narrative by weaving together snippets from Republican Assembly and High Plains appearances that occurred six years apart. A key piece of video from the Republican Assembly was drawn from Masterson’s comments just over one hour into the forum.
Masterson said he specifically referred during the Republican Assembly to his idea from 2007 or 2008 to use a portion of state revenue increases to buy down the state’s income tax rates. At the Statehouse, such a mechanism has been called a ratchet.
Here is a longer version of Masterson’s qyote: “The original ratchet had nothing to do with the Brownback plan, which by the way I wrote back in 2008, maybe, or seven, I don’t know. All it did was, as long as you had growth in your revenues, a certain portion would ratchet your income tax down.”
Masterson, the Kansas Senate president who has represented Andover in the Legislature for 20 years, said the DGA’s ad perpetrated a “lie” and “they got caught.”
“They have video of me talking about my plan and saying it had nothing to do with the Brownback plan,” Masterson said. “So, they chopped up my own sentence and stitched together a fake video to change the meaning. When you have to doctor a video to make your opponent say something he never said, you’ve admitted you can’t win on the truth. Cindy Holscher’s allies are lying to Kansans, and they should be ashamed and embarrassed.”
 
Tax reform history
In terms of the 2012 tax cut, Brownback referred to the policy overhaul as an “experiment,” but he promised Kansans the changes would deliver an “Pulp Fiction”-style adrenaline shot to revive the state’s sluggish economy. It failed to inspire extraordinary growth in Kansas. From 2013 to 2016, Kansas’ gross domestic product expanded 4.8%. That was less than half the national average of 11.9% for the period.
The law did slash state revenue by nearly $1 billion. Without adoption of equivalent spending cuts, the result was multiple years of state budget shortfalls. The Legislature became desperate to balance the budget and ended up retaining what was to have been a temporary hike in the statewide sales tax. State lawmakers rapidly expanded the state’s borrowing, cannibalized the Kansas Department of Transportation’s budget and interfered with appropriations to K-12 public schools and social service programs.
Masterson served as chairman of the Senate Ways and Means Committee during this period and was partially responsible for advancing gambits aimed at preserving the Brownback tax agenda.
In 2017, a bipartisan coalition of legislators including Holscher but not Masterson voted to spike much of the Brownback tax program. The bill raised individual income tax rates and abolished the business tax loophole. Brownback vetoed the bill, but was overridden. Masterson characterized the repeal bill as “a piece of garbage.”
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Cindy Holscher says her Republican opponent, Ty Masterson, is linked to controversial tax policy signed by Gov. Sam Brownback in 2012. Holscher voted with a bipartisan coalition in 2017 to repeal Brownback’s tax agenda, while Masterson opposed the bill. Here, Holscher waves at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson on Sept. 12. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)
 
Holscher’s view
During the 2026 campaign, Holscher has sought to connect Masterson’s politics to the legacy of Brownback, who at one time was the most unpopular governor in the nation.
During the Kansas State Fair debate with Masterson, Holscher declared her GOP rival the equivalent of “Brownback 2.0.”
“Under Brownback, Kansas public schools cut Fridays and ended the school year early,” said Holscher, a state senator from Overland Park. “Kids lost learning time. Teachers permanently left the profession. It took our state years to recover. Ty Masterson championed that experiment. Now he wants to repeat it. Ty Masterson equals Brownback remastered.”
Global Strategy Group, which regularly works with Democratic candidates and the DGA, says Brownback has remained unpopular. The pollster says 64% of those surveyed viewed Brownback negatively, while 21% viewed the former governor positively.
The Legislature in 2025 adopted a ratchet for lowering individual and corporate income tax rates in Kansas, despite a veto by Gov. Laura Kelly. The trigger for adjusting rates was tied to whether the treasury received revenue above an inflation-adjusted baseline.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey touts Wu endorsement to start October push
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The governor and mayor, both Democrats and each the first woman elected to the chief executive positions in the state and city, are not known to have a close political connection.
text:
BOSTON MAYOR MICHELLE WU formally endorsed Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll for reelection Thursday morning, citing a “partnership to build a Boston and a Massachusetts that work for everyone.”
The governor and mayor, both Democrats and each the first woman elected to the chief executive positions in the state and city, are not known to have a close political connection. They backed opposing candidates in two of last month’s Democratic primaries for state Senate seats and Healey, a former Boston resident who now lives in Arlington, declined to say whether she supported Wu the day before Wu’s mayoral primary against Josh Kraft a year ago.
“I’m grateful for our work together — from a historic summer that delivered economic impact throughout our neighborhoods, to lowering costs, building more housing, keeping residents safe, and expanding opportunity throughout the Commonwealth,” Wu said in a statement provided by the Healey campaign. “I look forward to continuing to work alongside the Healey-Driscoll Administration to keep delivering results, defending our communities, and creating the future we deserve.”
Healey called Wu “such a fantastic partner and a true champion for the people of Boston” and referenced this summer’s era of good feelings around the World Cup and other popular events. “Coming off a great summer for Boston and our whole state, I’m so grateful to have worked side-by-side with her to deliver for our communities,” Healey said of Wu.
In a Tuesday social media video titled “Good luck to the Red Sox tonight!” Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue took a jab at both Healey and Wu. The short starts by showing a clip of Healey and Wu being booed on the field at Fenway Park this April and displays the message, “Looks like fans want someone else up to bat” before Minogue turns towards the camera in what appears to be a Star Trek captain’s chair.
Healey and Wu plan to be available to the press later Thursday. The pair are scheduled to celebrate new retrofits and renovations at Otis Elementary School in East Boston at 11:30 a.m.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Proposal requiring Georgia election workers to ‘shuffle’ ballots at the polls fails to find support
description: A last-minute proposal that would have required poll workers to manually “shuffle” ballots before scanning them in an effort to prevent bad actors from identifying how Georgia residents voted failed to advance Thursday at a special-called meeting of the State Election Board. Election workers and advocates said the proposed rule would be impossible to impleme[...]
text:
State Election Board member Salleigh Grubbs, a top Georgia GOP official who was appointed to the board last year, speaks during a February board meeting held in Barrow County. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderA last-minute proposal that would have required poll workers to manually “shuffle” ballots before scanning them in an effort to prevent bad actors from identifying how Georgia residents voted failed to advance Thursday at a special-called meeting of the State Election Board.
Election workers and advocates said the proposed rule would be impossible to implement before the November midterms and would likely create more problems than it solved.
Georgia’s voter registration deadline is approaching. Here are five things you need to know.

State Election Board member Salleigh Grubbs, a top Georgia GOP official who was appointed to the board last year, argued that emergency rules were needed to uphold Georgia’s constitutionally required ballot secrecy rules. Her proposal would require voters to place their completed ballots into “secure boxes” rather than ballot scanners, which voters use to submit their printed ballot. Under Grubbs’ proposal, ballots would later be scanned by poll workers rather than the voters themselves.
Thursday’s meeting was called to consider Grubbs’ proposal. 
“We cannot continue on the same path with these kinds of vulnerabilities,” Grubbs said. “It must be addressed before the November election so that we can continue on to secure all future elections.”
Janelle King, Georgia Election Board member. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
But other members of the board appeared more skeptical. Janelle King, the board’s vice chair, said she worried that the proposal would likely generate more fear and distrust among voters.
“I also have major concerns about dropping our ballots into a secured box and then having other individuals scan my ballot,” she said. “How do I know that in the shuffling something doesn’t fall out?”
Anne Dover, the Cherokee County elections director, raised concerns that counties could struggle to recruit poll workers if the proposal were approved.
“Elections officials are put in a very difficult position,” she said. “We’ve been accused of fraud. We’ve been accused of being criminals. Our poll workers have been accused of doing things they shouldn’t do, and this atmosphere just gets worse for us as elections officials and poll workers. And I’m afraid we will lose poll workers if something like this is mandated, because they’re going to feel that pressure not to make a mistake.”
The change would also be extraordinarily expensive for counties, Dover said. Cherokee County’s policies mandate that at least three poll workers be assigned to monitor ballots. The cost of hiring enough poll workers to have three people monitoring ballots at every early voting location across the county, she said, would require an extra $80,000 for the midterm elections.
Lawmakers mull cybersecurity concerns as they prepare for overhaul of Georgia’s voting system

Ballot images have been public record in Georgia since 2021, and records dating back to 2024 are available online at the secretary of state’s website. In August, a Princeton University researcher claimed that he was able to use artificial intelligence to tie thousands of voters to specific ballots with relative certainty by putting publicly available data through an AI tool.
In July, Election Director Blake Evans issued guidance to county election workers instructing them to redact ballot record numbers before uploading them to the secretary of state’s website to prevent ballots from being traced back to specific voters. At Thursday’s meeting, VotingWorks executive director Ben Adida, whose company also manufactures election equipment, said the secretary of state’s office had successfully addressed election security concerns.
But some election activists have maintained that Georgia’s system contains critical security issues and are urging the state to take action ahead of the midterm elections. Early voting begins on Oct. 13.
Last week, the Georgia Republican Party and Republican National Committee penned a joint letter to the board raising concerns about Georgia’s voting equipment software in light of the Princeton researcher’s findings and also called on the board to “seek any federal technical assistance required to complete a certified upgrade” of the state’s voting equipment.
Georgia election panel asks Trump administration to help push for election system updates

On Monday, members of the board approved a resolution urging the secretary of state’s office to update the state’s voting machine software and calling on the U.S. Department of Justice and U.S. Department of Homeland Security to step in to ensure that the update takes place.
But Carolyn Roddy, the board’s GOP appointee and sponsor of the resolution, said she shared board members’ concerns about ballot secrecy, but that Grubbs’ proposal went too far.
“I’m not in favor of putting election officials through the ringer on this thing,” she said Thursday. “I think that it will cause incredible conflict that will deter us from other missions.”

text:
Fall foliage in Warren, Vermont on September 29, 2026. Photo by Henry’s Weather Channel

This year, VTDigger is teaming up with Henry’s Weather Channel to help answer the annual question of when and where peak foliage will make its appearance across the state.
Each week, we’ll bring you an updated look at how foliage is unfolding statewide, paired with a weekend forecast, so you can plan your drive, hike or porch-sitting accordingly. Henry brings meteorological experience and on-the-ground reporting with photos and videos from across the region.


Take a look outside — foliage has arrived! It won’t last forever. Here’s how to take full advantage of one of Vermont’s most magical times of year.
Peak has hit the mountains, and it won’t last forever
The leaves are really changing across the state. The current foliage tracker as of Monday shows that moderate color is out across much of Vermont, with high color especially across the southern part of the state and at higher elevations. 

The forecast through Oct. 5 shows big changes coming. Moderate color is expected across the state with high-color areas in the mountains. Foliage along Lake Champlain will be lagging a bit behind. Peak color is expected across the Stratton-Mount Snow area through the weekend and in the Northeast Kingdom. The area of peak foliage will likely expand through the end of next week to include much of Vermont. 

 
Drone video shows the fall colors in Warren, Vermont during the last week of September 2026. Video by Henry’s Weather Channel

Next weekend should be the last full weekend of peak color across the mountains before the leaves start to drop. Enjoy it while it’s here!

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC receives first $45.2M payout from Meta child safety settlement
description: North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Thursday the state has received its first $45.2 million payment from Meta, owner of Facebook and Instagram, as part of a multistate settlement over allegations that the company’s social media platforms harmed children.  The payout is the first installment of a settlement that could bring up to $645 […]
text:
A bipartisan group of  29  attorneys general allege the tech giant Meta deceived the public about the addictive nature and the harms of their product.
(Photo: Getty Images) North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Thursday the state has received its first $45.2 million payment from Meta, owner of Facebook and Instagram, as part of a multistate settlement over allegations that the company’s social media platforms harmed children. 
The payout is the first installment of a settlement that could bring up to $645 million to the state by 2035. The state is guaranteed at least $451 million, with an additional $194 million available if other major social media companies, including YouTube and TikTok, agree to safety measures. 
The state legislature will decide how to spend the money. Jackson has encouraged lawmakers to direct the money toward funding crisis helplines for children and funding after-school and summer programs. 
He also suggested using the money to hire additional school health officials amid shortages of counselors, social workers and nurses in North Carolina’s school systems. 
Meta to pay North Carolina up to $645 million in landmark settlement

“This settlement is about holding Meta accountable and protecting children,” Jackson said. “Not only does it require Meta to make major safety changes to its platforms, but it brings hundreds of millions of dollars to our state.”
Jackson announced the settlement with Meta in August after North Carolina and 32 other states sued the company in 2023. 
The states alleged that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to increase the time children spent on their platforms while downplaying the risks and collecting data from minors without parental consent. 
State officials also cited the company’s internal documents and raised concerns about features such as autoplay, push notifications and infinite scrolling, which they said were designed to increase engagement. 
The settlement requires Meta to strengthen measures keeping children under 13 off Facebook and Instagram and give parents more control over teen accounts. 
Jackson said teens can expect to see several changes to their accounts in the coming months: 

Under the changes, teens will have a new default two-hour daily limit. Once they reach that limit, their accounts will time out, restricting access to their feeds and scrolling. Access to direct messages will still be allowed. 
Meta will also implement an anti-scrolling feature that will pop up every 15 minutes to discourage continuous app usage. 
Feeds will be blocked from midnight to 6 a.m. each night and notifications will be disabled from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. Notifications will also automatically turn off on Facebook and Instagram during school hours on weekdays during the school year. 
Like counts and post reactions will be turned off by default, and beauty filters will be removed on the platforms to limit potential harm to children’s self-esteem and self-image. 

The remaining payments to the state will be made through the next decade, with installments scheduled each Jan. 15 beginning in 2027.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota Supreme Court says father doesn’t have a right to police records about son’s death
description: The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled this week that a father doesn’t have a right to obtain investigation records he wanted about his son’s death. Ryan Pyle, age 37, went missing in August 2020, and his remains were found in November of that year near the Snake Creek Recreation Area in South Dakota, near the […]
text:
The entrance to the South Dakota Supreme Court at the state Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled this week that a father doesn’t have a right to obtain investigation records he wanted about his son’s death.
Ryan Pyle, age 37, went missing in August 2020, and his remains were found in November of that year near the Snake Creek Recreation Area in South Dakota, near the city of Platte. Law enforcement believed he died of hypothermia. His father, Brian Pyle, believed the death may have involved foul play.
Brian Pyle asked a lower court to force the release of reports and records from the investigation into his son’s death. The lower court said no. The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed that decision. 
“The State had no duty to disclose criminal investigative information, nor did Pyle have a clear right to access such information,” wrote the court. 
Pyle’s argument for access included pointing to Marsy’s Law, the South Dakota constitutional amendment passed by voters in 2016 that establishes a formal bill of rights for crime victims. But the court said the record had not proven that a crime occurred, and that Brian “is not a ‘victim,’ as the term is defined under Marsy’s Law, and therefore Marsy’s Law is not applicable.”
Even if Marsy’s Law applied, wrote the court, “none of the nineteen enumerated rights in Marsy’s Law direct or compel the State to disclose investigative reports or records.”  
South Dakota law also specifically exempts law-enforcement investigation records from public disclosure requirements.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Victor Marx isn’t running for Colorado governor. He’s running for state pastor.
description: Victor Marx has made some spectacular headlines. The Republican nominee for Colorado governor can’t say how many people he’s killed. He claims to have participated in extraordinary exploits overseas as part of his ministry but refuses to substantiate what appear to be tall tales. He performs exorcisms — over the phone, even. He faces allegations […]
text:
Victor Marx, the Republican nominee for Colorado governor, speaks at the 2026 summer conference of the Colorado Water Congress in Steamboat Springs on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Victor Marx has made some spectacular headlines.
The Republican nominee for Colorado governor can’t say how many people he’s killed. He claims to have participated in extraordinary exploits overseas as part of his ministry but refuses to substantiate what appear to be tall tales. He performs exorcisms — over the phone, even. He faces allegations of campaign finance violations. A Daily Beast report this week highlighted Marx’s own accounts of committing physical violence against his wife and young son.
It’s easy for voters to get the impression Marx is little more than “a liar and a fraud,” as put by Kyle Cark of 9News during a candidate debate.
Marx’s wild claims deserve every bit of the scrutiny they’ve received. But that attention has obscured an essential quality of his campaign, the one that could be the most disastrous were he to become the chief executive of Colorado: his extreme faith. A Christian pastor, Marx makes no attempt to hide his vision for political leadership, which to him is indistinguishable from religious leadership. Based on his behavior and rhetoric, he appears to be running for lead Christian pastor of Colorado, not governor.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A striking moment during that Clark-moderated debate came at the end, when the three GOP primary candidates were invited to give closing remarks. Marx closed his eyes and prayed. Many politicians pray, nothing wrong with that. But Marx’s decision, in that setting, to fill that crucial time with a public Christian prayer, instead of trying to persuade voters that his plan for the state’s highest political office was superior, signaled to viewers that God was his platform.
It also foreshadowed more explicit expressions of Christianity’s improper place in his campaign. During a Fox31 interview in August, anchor Matt Mauro asked Marx what he’d do to make Colorado more affordable.
“I’m going to consecrate the state back to God,” Marx said. “We need to lead to help our state with integrity and a moral code, and that’s how we’re going to get it back on track.”
An investigation by 9News of Marx’s activities in the last 15 years “indicates that his work casting off demons is at the center of his $7.5 million per year ministry, All Things Possible, and can fairly be described as his life’s work,” Clark wrote. He added, “The ministry leader says casting off evil spirits is his greatest achievement.”
Earlier this month, the campaign called on supporters to participate in a 21-day fast, based on Biblical principles.
“This is not just an election, but this is a spiritual battle against the forces of wickedness,” Eileen Marx, Victor’s wife, said in a video announcement about the fast. In another video about the fast, Eileen said, “We believe God’s going to heal Colorado.”
It’s hardly unusual for politicians to proclaim their faith, but it is unusual for them to stake their entire campaign on their faith.
The implications for Colorado are profound. Marx’s Christianity is not only fundamental to his life and campaign, but it bears odd and extreme qualities that could make a wreck of state policy. Take abortion. Coloradans again and again have supported abortion rights. In 2024, they voted to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution. But Marx, based on his faith, would try to reverse the amendment, as he alluded to in the Fox31 interview. He has a long history of extreme rhetoric on abortion.
Last month, Marx earned the endorsement of Andrew Wommack, a national religious figure. Since Marx made a big deal about the endorsement, saying he was “incredibly honored” to receive it and lauding Wommack for “encouraging Christians not simply to believe their faith privately, but to live it boldly,” it’s reasonable to assume Marx is sympathetic to Wommack’s advocacy for the Seven Mountains Mandate, which says Christians should rule over all aspects of society.
Colorado faces pressing problems. The state budget is buckling under multiple increasing pressures, especially those related to healthcare costs. Housing remains unaffordable. Environmental crises abound.
Scripture might offer fortitude. It doesn’t offer solutions. Those will come from research, facts and earthly debates. But Marx is all piety and no policy.

name: National
title: Community groups lose HIV-prevention money as feds redirect dollars to states
description: Nearly 100 community-based organizations have lost their federal HIV-prevention grants this week as the Trump administration redirects dollars to state and local health departments. The funding change represents a departure from the decades-old national HIV prevention strategy favored by most public health organizations. President Donald Trump launched the E[...]
text:
Participants take part in an HIV/AIDS awareness event held by Big Bend Cares in Tallahassee, Florida. Nearly 100 community-based organizations in 31 states have lost HIV-related funding after federal officials decided not to renew their grants and instead directed money to state and local health agencies. (Photo by Bob O’Lary/Courtesy of Big Bend Cares)Nearly 100 community-based organizations have lost their federal HIV-prevention grants this week as the Trump administration redirects dollars to state and local health departments.
The funding change represents a departure from the decades-old national HIV prevention strategy favored by most public health organizations.
President Donald Trump launched the Ending the HIV/AIDS Epidemic Initiative during his first term in office. Since 2021, the program has disbursed a total of nearly $240 million to 96 community-based organizations in 31 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
Those groups have used the money to pay for testing and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a medication that people at high risk for HIV can take for protection during sex or injection drug use. Preventing new HIV infections and preserving access to treatment for those who have HIV helps prevent further transmission of the virus.
By prioritizing areas with the highest number of HIV diagnoses, the initiative sought to reduce HIV incidence by 75% in five years and by 90% by 2030. It continued under the Biden administration.
But now the Trump administration has shifted course.
Instead of granting money directly to community-based organizations, the administration is offering one-time grants to state and local health departments. It is encouraging the jurisdictions with the most HIV diagnoses to funnel at least 25% of the money to community groups, but there is no requirement that they do so. Health departments in areas with fewer diagnoses are being encouraged to send 10% of their money to community groups.
The state and local health agencies are required to spend whatever dollars they don’t pass on to community groups on HIV surveillance and PrEP access.
When the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced the availability of the original grants in 2020, it noted that since the late 1980s, it had partnered with community-based organizations to fight the spread of HIV because of “their accessibility, history and credibility in the community,” especially among Black and Hispanic people, gay and bisexual men and people who inject drugs.
“CDC has done this for a very long time, specifically because they know that community-based organizations are important players in the community,” said Lindsey Dawson, associate director for HIV policy at KFF, a nonprofit health research group.
“They’re a voice in the community that people trust, and these programs really are able to reach people who are at greatest vulnerability to HIV in a way that the state or federal or local government (would) not be able to do.”
When asked for an explanation of the change, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services referred Stateline to the Office of Management and Budget. Neither OMB nor the White House press office responded to multiple requests for comment.
The National Alliance of State and Territorial AIDS Directors told Stateline that under the new grant program, the federal government will disburse approximately $90 million to state health departments through May 2027. Though that amount is nearly twice as much as the roughly $48 million per year that was handed out under the old grant program, community-based organizations are going to see less money, public health experts say.
In August, KFF estimated that overall, community-based organizations would need about 35% of the new money to match what they were getting before. The National Alliance of State and Territorial AIDS Directors estimates that percentage to be closer to 50%.
In Texas, health officials said the state plans to send about 23%, or about $1.2 million, of its $5.24 million grant to community-based organizations.
Jeffrey Campbell, chief executive officer of Allies in Hope — formerly called AIDS Foundation Houston — told Stateline that he expects his federal funding to be cut by $441,000, which could force him to lay off at least three staff members.
Under the old grant structure, half of all funding had been channeled to organizations in the South, which accounts for more than half of the nation’s HIV diagnoses.
But already, one organization in that region has announced it will have to shut down as a result of the funding change: PowerHouse Charlotte in North Carolina announced in August that it will close. For 16 years, that  organization has provided  free HIV and STD screenings, prevention services and community resources geared toward gay Black men.
In at least two states, Minnesota and Oregon, state health agencies wouldn’t be able to match the amount of money their community-based organizations were getting under the old system even if they gave 100% of their state grants to those groups, according to KFF.
“These community-based organizations are on the ground doing the work with the populations that need it,” said Carl Schmid, executive director at the HIV+Hepatitis Policy Institute, a public health nonprofit that tracks policies related to HIV prevention.
“Some states may have relationships with some of the existing grantees and may be fine, but others, they may not. And so there’s definitely going to be a lapse of funding.”
Emily Schreiber, senior director of policy at the National Alliance of State and Territorial AIDS Directors, said that under the new rules, states don’t have much time to establish new contracts with community-based organizations.
“(States) are trying to turn around things as fast as possible. But simply there (was) not enough time to get that funding through the contracting process and all of that by September 30th, which was really unfortunate,” she said.
“It’s not easy for a health department to create a whole new contracting process overnight. Even in the best-case scenario, this is not a perfect solution.”
Many health departments take between 45 and 90 days to scale new contracts and grants, said Toni Young, executive director and founder of Community Education Group, a nonprofit offering HIV community engagement, testing and outreach across rural West Virginia and the broader Appalachian region.
“We don’t have an infrastructure in many rural communities to address HIV,” she said.
Another challenge for community-based organizations is that because they won’t be getting money directly from the federal government, they will no longer be eligible for discounted drugs under the federal 340B program.
“When you took away this grant, you also took away their 340B status, which is the reason some have had to potentially close or at least stop this entire side of operations,” said Maximillian Boykin, manager of the Save HIV Funding Campaign.
“It leaves a lot of these places very fragile.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Black, LGBTQ leaders call for GOP lawmaker’s resignation after ‘homophobic tirade’
description: The statement said Bernstine must be held accountable for his words and actions, which the caucus leaders said make him unfit to serve in the state legislature.
text:
Rep. Aaron Bernstine, R-Beaver (Courtesy of Bernstine campaign Facebook)Leaders of the Pennsylvania House Black and LGBTQ Equality caucuses called on Republican Rep. Aaron Bernstine to resign after a report he “went on a homophobic tirade” at a Harrisburg bar Tuesday night.
The western Pennsylvania lawmaker allegedly remarked on Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta’s sexual orientation using a slur, and falsely suggested that Kenyatta’s recent weight loss was because he has AIDS, PennLive.com reported. Kenyatta, who is openly gay and has intentionally lost a significant amount of weight over several years, was not at the bar and declined to comment.
On Thursday, a Philadelphia woman told the Capital-Star she received what she considers an “incredibly transphobic” reply to an email seeking Bernstine’s support for a piece of legislation seeking paid family leave for Pennsylvania workers.
“I don’t read emails from anybody who puts their pronouns in their email signature,” the 2023 email from Bernstine to Rachele Fortier said.
Fortier, who has worked on campaigns and issue advocacy in Harrisburg for more than a decade, said she was reminded of the email when she read about Bernstine’s comments about Kenyatta.
“It’s very widely known that making fun of pronouns or having a problem with being asked your pronouns is problematic,” Fortier said, adding that she is a member of the LGBTQ+ community.
Messages left at Bernstine’s offices in Ellwood City, Butler and at the state Capitol were not returned.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Pennsylvania Legislative Black Caucus and the LGBTQ Equality Caucus issued a joint statement Thursday. The groups are chaired by Rep. Napoleon Nelson (D-Montgomery) and Rep. Jessica Benham (D-Allegheny), respectively.
“We are deeply disturbed by reports of hateful, degrading, and untrue attacks directed at our friend and caucus member Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta. Such conduct is unacceptable and has no place in our legislature. Every member deserves to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their identity or background,” the statement said.
The statement said Bernstine must be held accountable for his words and actions, which the caucus leaders said make him unfit to serve in the state legislature.
“We are calling on all House members, but especially Republican leaders, to denounce his behavior, to join us in demanding his resignation, and for Republican leaders to identify the steps they will take to guard against this kind of pathetic behavior within their caucus,” the statement continued.
A spokesperson for House Minority Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) said the allegation against Bernstine is troubling and does not comport with the values and professionalism constituents expect from their state lawmakers, regardless of party or position.
“When they fall short of that standard, it is upon them to take personal and individual responsibility for their actions quickly and appropriately,” spokesman Jason Gottesman said.
Bernstine has served in the House since 2016 and is seeking reelection to the 8th Legislative District, which covers parts of Butler and Lawrence counties.
According to PennLive.com, Bernstine made the remarks at McGrath’s Pub in downtown Harrisburg, blocks from the Capitol, where a Democratic fundraiser was being held following a voting session Tuesday in the legislature.
State Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta (D-Philadelphia) decried the “Big, Beautiful Bill” during a press conference outside Pennsylvania Capitol in 2025. (Photo by Vincent DiFonzo/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The article attributes an account of Bernstine’s remarks to Michael Ford, the secretary/treasurer of the Pennsylvania Building and Construction Trades Council. Ford and Bernstine argued as the lawmaker insulted Kenyatta and Robert Bair, the president of the Building and Construction Trades Council, who was sitting nearby, Ford told PennLive. Bair did not respond to a message seeking comment. 
Ford told the outlet he and Bernstine exchanged words, but there was no physical altercation.
PennLive noted Bernstine has faced criticism in the past for social media posts in which he threatened to run over protesters with his car and a video in which he gave his then 5-year-old son a cigar and encouraged him to make derogatory comments about women.
Kenyatta has been the subject of a verbal attack by a colleague in the past. 
During a debate on a bill that would ban devices that allow semi-automatic handguns to fire rapidly, Kenyatta delivered fiery rhetoric critical of gun rights advocates and their view of the Second Amendment as a bulwark against tyranny.
“Save me your self righteous speeches about standing up [to] tyranny when you do nothing to stand up [to] tyranny, consistently,” Kenyatta said.
A shouting match broke out between several lawmakers on opposite sides of the House.
The incident was not included in a livestream of the House floor and the only indication was Speaker Joanna McClinton calling for the House sergeant at arms to clear the aisle and for lawmakers to take their seats. She later delivered a stern admonition, saying she was disappointed by what occurred earlier. 
“I cannot hear what insults and slurs are said across the aisle to each other, but let me remind each of you, if you make threats, that could be a crime. That’s free legal advice,” McClinton said, adding that the sergeant at arms and Capitol police would conduct investigations.

name: VTDigger
title: Jack Sawyer, accused of foiled school shooting plot 8 years ago, is back in court on unrelated charges
description:
The new charges include allegedly stealing more than $20,000 in items from Sterling College, where he was once a student.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Jack Sawyer, accused of foiled school shooting plot 8 years ago, is back in court on unrelated charges.
text:
The Vermont Superior Court building and the Orleans County Court House in Newport in March 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A Vermont man who spurred gun reform legislation eight years ago, after he was accused of plotting to shoot up a high school, was back in court — this time after allegedly breaking into the now-closed Sterling College.
Jack Sawyer, 27, of Craftsbury, pleaded not guilty Tuesday during his arraignment in Orleans Superior criminal court in Newport to counts of grand larceny, unlawful trespass and unlawful mischief.
Orleans County Deputy State’s Attorney Samuel Swope had asked the judge to impose $1,500 bail for Sawyer.
“I think it does bear pointing out,” Swope said, “that upon information and belief this is the same Jack Sawyer who was a defendant in the infamous Fair Haven alleged school shooting case from years ago.”
In February 2018, Sawyer, then 18, was arrested and charged in adult court in Rutland with three counts of attempted murder for allegedly plotting to shoot up the high school in Fair Haven.

Jack Sawyer appeared by video for an October 2026 hearing from the Northern State Correctional Facility in Newport. Screenshot by Alan J. Keays/VTDigger

Those charges were later dropped after the Vermont Supreme Court ruled that mere planning did not rise to the level of an attempt under state law.
Sawyer still faced misdemeanor charges of criminal threatening and carrying a dangerous weapon with the avowed purpose to commit serious injury or death. 
His case was then handled in a judicial process specific to people under age 21, in which details are confidential and proceedings take place in Rutland Family Court. 
Gov. Phil Scott had cited the Sawyer case and the details in a police affidavit as having prompted him to shift his stance on the need for added gun restrictions. The governor later signed into law new restrictions in April 2018.
Mackenzie Dix, an attorney representing Sawyer in his latest case Tuesday, argued against the need for cash bail. 
“The state’s primary arguments are based on previous conduct,” Dix told Judge Justin Jiron.
Dix said her client was not a risk to flee and had long ties to Vermont. 

READ MORE

The judge said the records provided to him did not show any prior convictions for Sawyer, and he didn’t have many details presented to him Tuesday related to the earlier case. 
“I’m not sure they justify the imposition of bail in any event,” the judge added. “The purpose of bail is to ensure the defendant returns to court, and so there we look to things like the various risks of flight factors.” 
Jiron ultimately agreed not to set cash bail for Sawyer, but did impose an 8 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew. 
The latest charges against Sawyer stem from a break-in at Sterling College in Craftsbury earlier this month.
Vermont State Police reported on Sept. 14 they received a report of a burglary from the school with $20,621 in items stolen, including two arc welders from the blacksmith workshop and multiple backpacks and sleeping bags. 
Police said they later arrested Sawyer and executed several warrants at properties connected to him, leading to the recovery of several of the items reported stolen from the college, which had closed this spring.

text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Crown Heights Christian Church on June 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)Oklahoma Voice released its Nov. 3 general election voter guide Thursday to help voters learn more about the candidates and issues.
The guide is free and not behind a paywall.
In addition to highlighting each of the over three dozen candidates vying for Oklahoma’s statewide and federal offices, the guide also contains information about the Oklahomans competing in contested state House and Senate races. In all, 13 state Senate seats are up for grabs as are 55 House seats. 
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voting Guide

The guide also contains information about the two controversial legislatively-proposed state questions — 845 and 847 — that ask voters to amend the state’s Constitution.
State Question 847 seeks to change how much property taxes could increase each year. State Question 845 would change how the state’s judicial nominating process works.
In general elections, every registered voter, regardless of partisan affiliation, can vote.
With most statewide posts being held by leaders who cannot run again due to term limits, Oklahomans will decide their next governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, corporation commissioner, superintendent of public instruction, treasurer and commissioners of labor and insurance.
They will also decide who will fill the state’s open U.S. Senate seat. Markwayne Mullin resigned earlier this year to serve on President Donald Trump’s Cabinet and lead the Department of Homeland Security. All five of Oklahoma’s U.S. House seats are also on the ballot.
The most high-profile contest features Republican Mike Mazzei facing off against Democrat Cyndi Munson for governor. Three independent candidates are also vying for the post. Gov. Kevin Stitt cannot run again due to term limits.
The deadline to register to vote is Oct. 9. Absentee ballots must be requested no later than 15 days before the election. 
Early voting runs from Oct. 28-31. 
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on election day.

title: Economic development chief leaves. Unemployment, workforce down: Mississippi Marketplace
description: Unemployment was down in the Gulfport-Biloxi, Hattiesburg and Jackson Metro areas month over month and year over year at 3%, 2.9% and 3% respectively, accompanied by decreases in the civilian labor force in all three areas.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Development Authority Director Bill Cork is stepping down after nearly three years leading the state’s economic development agency. 
Gov. Tate Reeves called Cork’s sudden departure a “retirement.”
During Cork’s tenure, Mississippi has seen over $65 billion in investments, mostly from data centers, and the creation of 23,000 jobs. Over Reeves’ two terms as governor, the state has seen a total of $85 billion in investment.
Katherine Lin Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Paul Jerrod “P.J.” Waldrop, the current deputy director and chief operating officer of MDA, will lead the agency. He is the fourth person Reeves has appointed to the job. Reeves has struggled over two terms to keep a permanent, Senate-confirmed director in the position. Cork was his longest serving director by a matter of months.
Unemployment, labor force participation decline
In August, Mississippi’s unemployment rate continued to decline from 3.6% in July to 3.4%. It was one of eight states that saw significant decreases in the unemployment rate, with the rest remaining relatively unchanged. 
But Mississippi’s labor force participation also dropped.
The total number of non-farm employees was up slightly month over month and year over year. However, the size of the overall civilian labor force and labor force participation rate decreased. The seasonally adjusted labor-force participation rate dropped to 54.7% down from 55.7% a year before, the lowest rate since April 2024. Mississippi’s labor force participation rate is second-lowest in the country, behind West Virginia.
Unemployment was down in the Gulfport-Biloxi, Hattiesburg and Jackson Metro areas month over month and year over year at 3%, 2.9% and 3% respectively, accompanied by decreases in the civilian labor force in all three areas.
Companies get low marks on clean energy
A Sierra Club report gave Entergy Mississippi and Mississippi Power an “F” and a “C” respectively for their transition to clean energy sources. Both grades referenced increasing demand partly driven by the state’s economic growth, led by data centers, and customer demand.
Both Entergy and Mississippi Power’s parent companies are seeing exceptional growth thanks to data centers. Southern Power Company, of which Mississippi Power is a subsidiary, saw 49% higher usage year to date according to its recent earnings presentation. 
At the recent meeting of the Southern States Energy Board, Gov. Reeves said that the state is taking an all-of-the-above approach and not relying on any single source of energy.
Other news

A developer is looking to put a $6-billion data center campus on 800 acres in Jefferson Davis County. Eagle Rock Partners held a public meeting this week to talk to residents and answer community questions. The company said construction is set to begin in 2027. 
The Joint Legislative Budget Committee is meeting on Thursday and Friday. Senators and Representatives will hear from 11 agencies on their proposed spending as work begins on a budget for the 2028 fiscal year. The final budget will be determined during the upcoming legislative session. So far, the Office of Workforce Development requested a $7-million budget, up by $3 million to meet the “urgent” need for trained workers, and the Health Department requested level funding for the upcoming fiscal year.
The median sale price of a home in Mississippi is one of the lowest in the nation, around $260,000, compared to over $380,000 nationally. However, the state has not been immune to increasing housing prices. Housing prices in the Golden Triangle are up by nearly $70,000 based on data from the Commercial Dispatch. 
The Ole Miss and LSU game brought in nearly $109 million for Oxford alone. A typical home game brings in $30 million to $70 million. 
The state will use $8.5 million in federal money to increase its short-term workforce training and support its implementation of Workforce Pell Grants at community colleges. The federal financial aid program was expanded last year to cover program costs for eligible short-term workforce education. It’s part of Mississippi’s larger push to encourage Mississippians to pursue jobs that are currently in high demand.
Natchez officials are evaluating a potential data center at the old International Paper mill. It’s been a few months since the last official data center announcement.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Lacking federal approval, New Hampshire forced to hold off on new Medicaid premiums
description: New Hampshire is delaying implementation of its premium system for Medicaid as it awaits federal approval to move forward. “The situation is status quo,” Jake Leon, spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in an email to the Bulletin. “Medicaid premiums have not been implemented. Still waiting on federal guidance on the […]
text:
The premiums were expected to go into effect July 1, but DHHS has not offered a new timeline for when it will start charging the premiums. (Getty Images)New Hampshire is delaying implementation of its premium system for Medicaid as it awaits federal approval to move forward.
“The situation is status quo,” Jake Leon, spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in an email to the Bulletin. “Medicaid premiums have not been implemented. Still waiting on federal guidance on the impact of HR1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act).”
The premiums were expected to go into effect July 1, but DHHS has not offered a new timeline for when it will start charging the premiums.
In order to implement the charges, the state needs approval from the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services because the program is run jointly by states and the federal government.
However, as the Bulletin first reported in January, DHHS officials have been concerned the premium system may conflict with a new federal law. Roughly a week after Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed New Hampshire’s premium system into law in June 2025, President Donald Trump signed H.R. 1 — commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
The federal legislation institutes a cost-sharing program for some Medicaid enrollees in all 50 states. That cost sharing will require enrollees to pay a maximum of $35 per service for most services.
Olivia May, New Hampshire’s director of Medicaid enterprise management, told the Bulletin at the time, “I think there’s open questions about whether you can have both” state premiums and federal cost sharing. Leon said Thursday that DHHS is still waiting on the federal government to answer that question. Some have argued that the premiums won’t be illegal until October 2028 when the federal cost sharing goes into effect. 
Democrats, who have opposed the premiums since their inception, used the potential legal conflict as fresh justification for halting the plan.
“Last spring, the budget enacted premiums for Medicaid before we knew what Congress was going to do,” Nashua state Sen. Cindy Rosenwald said at a legislative hearing earlier this year. “The sensible thing for us to do now is to change course and not waste money on a system we can only use for 18 months.”
The plan, if and when it is implemented, will require some enrollees to pay premiums in order to receive health coverage. The premiums are based on a family’s size and income:

A household of one person earning $15,950 a year — 100% of the poverty level, per 2026’s federal standards — is set to pay $60 a month to keep their coverage under the new system.
A family of two people earning $21,640 is set to pay $80 a month
A family of three earning $27,320 a year is set to pay $90 a month.
A family of four earning $33,000 a year is set to pay $100 a month.
A family of five earning $38,680 a year is set to pay $100 a month.
A family of two earning $55,182 a year — 255% of the poverty level — is set to pay $190 a month.
A family of three earning $69,666 is set to pay $230 a month.
A family of four earning $84,150 is set to pay $270 a month.
A family of five earning $98,634 is set to pay $270 a month.

The plan to charge premiums emerged in early 2025. Ayotte first pitched it in her budget proposal as a means to balance the budget in a tough fiscal environment. GOP lawmakers approved the premiums with some tweaks, and Ayotte signed it into law in June 2025.
Democrats lambasted the plan as “an income tax on the poor.” Ayotte, on the other hand, has defended it by pointing out that many states — 22 as of 2026, according to KFF — don’t offer Medicaid at all to children whose households earn more than 255% of the federal poverty line and characterized this as a necessary step to protect generous eligibility standards.
The premiums are just one of several major changes coming to Medicaid in New Hampshire. At the same time, state lawmakers voted to increase prescription drug copays from $1 to $2 or $3. On the federal level, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, made major changes to Medicaid nationwide. In addition to the aforementioned federal cost-sharing, the federal law creates work requirements for the program beginning next year.

title: New Mexico Election 2026: US House of Representatives, District 3

text:
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) faces state Rep. Martin Zamora (R-Clovis), in the Nov. 3, 2026, general election for New Mexico’s 3rd Congressional District. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Incumbent U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández first won the seat to represent New Mexico’s 3rd Congressional District in 2020, replacing fellow Democrat Ben Ray Luján when he joined the U.S. Senate. 
The 3rd Congressional District covers most of northern New Mexico, and runs the eastern edge of the state to Lea and Chaves counties, as well as a portion of Otero County. Leger Fernández has fended off Republican challengers twice since then and is currently serving her third term.
Leger Fernández faces state Rep. Martin Zamora (R-Clovis) in the Nov. 3 election. Zamora has campaigned on protecting private property against federal regulations, promoting energy sector jobs, cracking down on crime and finishing Trump’s border wall to address immigration. Zamora did not respond to repeated requests from Source NM for an interview.
The position carries a salary of $174,000.
Leger Fernández’s responses have been edited for clarity and concision.
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández is seeking re-election to New Mexico’s 3rd Congressional District. (Courtesy photo)
 
 U.S. Rep Teresa Leger Fernández
A Las Vegas, New Mexico-native, Leger Fernández graduated from both Yale and Stanford Law School, and previously worked as a public public interest lawyer on cases involving voting rights, tribal sovereignty, environment and acequia protection, according to her congressional biography. She also worked as a White House fellow in the Clinton and Obama administrations, focusing on housing issues.
During her tenure in Congress, Leger Fernández has been a vocal critic of the Trump administration’s cuts to food assistance and Medicaid programs, as well as its refusal to release un-redacted files relating to sex offender and trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. In February, she introduced federal legislation that would eliminate statues of limitation in civil cases for victims of sexual abuse and trafficking. 
She has also focused on federal relief for constituents affected by the Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire and subsequent contamination of water, and in August urged a federal watchdog agency to investigate toxic materials in fire retardants in response to dozens of private wells in Mora County showing unsafe levels of toxic materials, including arsenic and uranium. 
What is the most important issue facing this district?
Costs. In my rural district, it is hard to fill up your car, your truck — especially if you need diesel for your tractor or farm equipment. Other items like groceries, energy and healthcare are all also more expensive because of Trump and Republican policies on the Iran War, tariffs and the One Big Beautiful Bill that gave billionaires a tax break. 
What legislation would you prioritize sponsoring in the next term?
I’ve already teed up several bills that will address the high costs of housing, including my Home of Your Own Act, which would get more people into affordable homes. My water rights settlement bills would bring billions of dollars to New Mexico for water projects and certainty to tribal waterways.
We also have healthcare legislation to increase providers in rural areas. We need to take back Congress so we can stop the Iran War, Trump’s tariffs and corruption.
How would you describe the impact of the Trump administration on New Mexico and what would your approach be to working with the Trump administration if re-elected?
Trump does not understand New Mexico values, which center around land, water, air and strong communities. We are proud to be a multicultural, working class state. I think he’s making us poor, hungrier and less safe. 
His policies benefit the billionaire class at the expense of working families. There have been 10,000 New Mexico children who lost federal benefits due to Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, his VA staffing cuts have negatively affected the New Mexico VA healthcare system and even our nuclear safety programs are at risk.
Most of my legislation wins for the state have been bipartisan. For example, I worked with Republicans to get $100 million for water projects across the district.
What policies would you support, if elected, as it relates to border security?
Border security and immigration reform are not mutually exclusive. We can have a strong border that keeps out drugs and criminals, and at the same time have immigration reform that creates a pathway to citizenship.
I also intend to hold ICE accountable. I have a bill to ensure that citizens can sue ICE if they’ve been detained or deported. What ICE is doing is unconstitutional and unlawful. 
You were critical of federal drug enforcement agencies following a report that they allowed hundreds of thousands of pills to be trafficked into New Mexico. How would you hold these agencies accountable if re-elected?
I have been especially critical of the DEA for allowing fentanyl to flow into our community. We cannot let them use New Mexico as a guinea pig or sacrificial lamb to get bigger convictions. We need to bring them before Congress and ask tough questions, and if we find that they’ve engaged in policies that they knew would lead to death — we need to change that policy and allow family members of those who died as a result to bring their own civil lawsuit.
You have constituents in CD3 who have still not been made whole following the Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire, and now are grappling with the prospect of polluted well water. How do you plan to continue addressing this issue if reelected?
Within the first three months of the fire, Sen. Luján and I secured $5.45 billion for victim compensation. The reality is FEMA has taken too long to get the money out, especially after Trump took office. I recently had the Government Accounting Office do well testing in the affected area and I pushed the USDA to pay a million dollars for it.
We know that $3.9 billion out of the total $5.45 billion has gone out the door. That’s money back in the hands of families, ranchers, businesses and communities that were harmed by the federal government starting that fire. But it’s not over and I’m going to continue to fight to force them to get the rest of the money out.
You’ve advocated for the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell, and advocated for greater transparency of the Epstein files. How would you pursue that in a new term?
The American people are supportive of releasing the Epstein files because we are sick and tired of the rich and powerful getting away with this kind of criminal activity. 
When I get back to Congress in November, I will secure the last two signatures to force a vote on a bill we’re calling Epstein Two. This discharge petition will allow a vote to force the release of the millions of files that the federal government has withheld. It will allow New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez to sue the U.S. Department of Justice so that he can bring criminal claims against those who abused, sexually assaulted and trafficked young women and girls in New Mexico.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey asks Trump administration to speed up review of planned gas expansion in latest sign of shifting energy politics
description: As Healey hunts for ways to bring down soaring costs and campaigns for reelection in a race defined by the affordability crisis gripping the state, the governor sees an opportunity to appeal to the Trump administration to bring more gas into the state.
text:
HERE’S SOMETHING you probably didn’t have on your bingo card: The Democratic governor of Massachusetts asking President Trump’s administration to move faster in approving a gas expansion project. 
That’s exactly what Gov. Maura Healey did on Thursday, imploring Energy Secretary Chris Wright in a letter to move with a “sense of urgency” in issuing required permits for the project to quickly move forward.  
Healey, citing her “all of the above” approach to energy issues, previously expressed support for the proposal, a relatively small expansion of 73,500 dekatherms per day of an existing gas pipeline owned by Canadian energy company Enbridge. State regulators approved contracts earlier this year for Eversource to purchase the additional gas from the expansion project, known as the Reliable Affordable Resilient Enhancement, or RARE. 
But now, as Healey hunts for ways to bring down soaring gas and electric costs and campaigns for reelection in a race defined by the affordability crisis gripping the state, the governor sees an opportunity to appeal to the fossil fuel-friendly Trump administration to bring more natural gas into the state to both power and heat homes and businesses.  
What’s more, Healey said that she and Wright have “on several occasions” discussed their “mutual desire” to bring more gas into New England.  
“I ask that you work across the Administration to ensure that the federal reviews and permits needed for RARE move without delay; that agencies establish clear schedules and coordinate their work wherever legally permissible; and that sufficient staff and resources are dedicated to completing the required reviews in time to preserve the project’s planned 2028 in-service date,” Healey wrote to Wright.  
The overture from Healey is noteworthy, too, because of how critical she has been of the Trump administration for raising energy costs by canceling new offshore wind projects and launching hostilities in the Middle East that have sent oil prices surging.  
In this case, Healey is backing the RARE project citing expectations that it would deliver real savings to customers, though the expansion isn’t planned to be ready until 2028. The Department of Public Utilities found that RARE would save about 600,000 Eversource customers roughly $40 million per year over the course of a decade by displacing reliance on more expensive, foreign liquefied natural gas delivered through the Everett Marine Terminal. 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission began its review this past February. 
“While we anticipate significant cost and reliability benefits for our natural gas customers from this precedent agreement, by no means will it solve our region’s energy affordability challenge alone,” William Hinkle, an Eversource spokesperson, said in a statement. “As we continue working to advance the Commonwealth’s decarbonization and electrification goals, it’s our responsibility to evaluate any and all solutions that will improve reliability and affordability for our customers, including additional natural gas supply.” 
High energy costs have emerged as the top household concern in Massachusetts, with electricity prices reaching double the national average, though Bay State voters by and large hold Trump — not Healey — as primarily responsible for that dynamic, according to a recent CommonWealth Beacon poll.   
Natural gas remains the backbone of New England’s electric grid, accounting for roughly half of all electric generation in the region, as power demand is projected to rise.  
Healey’s championing of RARE, though, is likely to ignite the ire of environmental advocates concerned that locking in more natural gas runs counter to the state’s commitment to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Just two years ago, dozens of green groups demanded that Northeast governors oppose a different major pipeline expansion proposal that ultimately fizzled.   
Environmental nonprofit Acadia Center found that despite a sharp increase in the use of natural gas for power and heating in New England since the start of the century, energy prices have only gone up, too. Gas capacity in the region rose by about a third between 2010 and 2024, but prices nevertheless increased, according to the analysis.  
Caitlin Peale Sloan, vice president for climate and energy at Conservation Law Foundation, said in a statement that “this letter unwittingly adopts the false narrative that expansion of gas infrastructure will lower heating costs.” And Amy Boyd Rabin, vice president of policy and regulatory affairs at Environmental League of Massachusetts, said that “more natural gas supply is not the answer to Massachusetts’s rising energy costs.” 
Healey’s letter didn’t stop at advocating for RARE. She cracked open the door to a much larger and potentially more controversial pipeline expansion that Enbridge is actively considering known as Project Beacon.  
That proposal, about four times larger than RARE, would increase gas supply by as much as 10 percent on the Algonquin pipeline system and potentially start operations in 2030. Enbridge executives said on an earnings call over the summer that interest from energy producers and suppliers in purchasing the additional gas “exceeded our initial expectations.” 
Getting RARE quickly approved, Healey said, could be the start of a new paradigm — and a sign that “all of the above” really could mean much more additional gas. 
“There may be,” she wrote to Wright, “more opportunities ahead.”
